title: About Language Packs
text:
Languages and Language Packs

About Language Packs

'Same Language Rendering' and 'Other Language
Translation'

The application language of Family Historian is currently
English only. By this we mean that the menus, screen labels,
dialog boxes (window forms), and messages are all in English (American
or UK English). However, the program is designed to be used to
record genealogical data in most languages of the world. We call
the language in which data is recorded, the project
language. You don't need a language pack to record your data in
English or in any other language. You only need them if you want
reports, diagrams and other output to appear in any language other than
English. We call the language of a report or diagram (or book, or
any other form of output), the output language.

If the project language is not English - if, say, it's French - then
with most reports, those parts of the report that simply output recorded
data, will also be in French. But unless you use a language pack,
the report title, the headings, the labels, and other details, will all
be in English. For that matter, any dates, and ages, will all also
be in English. To get the report to appear consistently in French,
you will need to select a French language pack for that report.
The same is true in diagrams. So that is one use for language
packs: to ensure that the output language matches the project language,
where the latter is not English. Where you use a language pack to
ensure that the output language matches the project language, we call
this same language rendering.

There is another use for language packs though, and that is to produce
output in a different language to the project language. For
example, if you have recorded your data in English and want to send a
report or chart to a Norwegian relative, in Norwegian, you can use a
language pack to do this. We call this other language
translation. For that matter, if your project language is
French, and you want to produce a report or chart in Norwegian, you can
do that too. And that too is other language translation.

Not all reports and diagrams are 100% language pack ready. With
those that are, however (which is all of the main ones), with same
language rendering, it should normally be possible to produce
output that it is 100% in the required language - although sometimes you
may have to do a little work to get there. With other
language translation, typically some parts of reports will not be
translated, and you should expect this. In general, for example, notes
are not translated. Also if you manually override sentences
in narrative reports, these manual overrides are not normally
translated. Where parts of a report or diagram are not translated,
these parts will normally be marked distinctively (e.g. by giving them a
yellow highlight colour) so that the recipient can see at a glance,
which parts of the report have been left untranslated. You have the
option of excluding untranslated notes, or perhaps including it but
leaving it with a distinctive background colour, so that the recipient
can easily see which bits are in a different language.

To learn about using Family Historian to record data in a language
other than English, see How
to Work in Different Languages.

To learn about producing reports and books in a language other than
English, see How
to Produce Reports and Books in Different Languages.

title: Add and Edit Shapes
text:
Map Window

Add and Edit Shapes

This page discusses map shapes. How to add, modify, move, copy,
format, lock, unlock, group, order and delete them.

A shape is a kind of annotation that can be added to a map. They are
comparable to shapes that can be added to diagrams (see Diagram
Elements), although there are some important differences.
There are 4 types of map shapes. These are:

Text Boxes (with optional callout lines)

Polylines

Polygons

Circles

Map shapes always appear in front of the map layer, but always appear
behind markers (see Map Elements).

Overlays

A complete collection of shapes can be saved for later use, or to be
shared with others. A saved collection of shapes is called an overlay.
Family Historian includes a number of standard overlays, but users can
create their own custom overlays. To add an existing overlay to a
map that you already have open, right-click anywhere on the map layer and
choose Add Map Overlay from the menu that appears.

Undo/Redo, Deletion, Groups and Ordering

Shapes can be added, edited, formatted and deleted. The Map Window
supports full multilevel undo/redo for all changes to shapes (see the Undo
and Redo commands at the top of the Edit menu). To delete any shape,
select it (see below), and press the Delete key. Shapes can be
formed into grouped objects that all move as one. To select multiple
shapes, press-and-hold the Ctrl key while clicking on
each shape in turn to select it, without de-selecting the other shapes you
had already selected. Red selection handles will appear around each
selected shape (except for circles, which have red dashes around their
circumferences when they are selected). To form a number of selected
shapes into a group, right-click on any one of them and choose the 'Group'
option from the 'Group' submenu on the dropdown menu that appears. A
group shape behaves very much like any other shape. You could see it
as a 5th shape type. Group shapes can be grouped with other shapes
(including other shape groups), and this can be iterated to any
level. Right-click on any group shape, and choose 'Ungroup' from the
'Group' submenu, to remove the grouping of the shapes within it.

Shapes can be ordered with respect to one another. Right-click on
any shape (or on any one of a selection of multiple shapes), and choose an
appropriate option from the Order submenu.

Text Boxes (text anchors and callouts)

Figure 1. Text Boxes. In the second box, the yellow text
anchor has been dragged up and to the right.

To add a text box to a map, click on the Text button on the Map
Window Toolbar, and then click-and-drag on the map to draw an
initial rectangle. When you release the button, you will be prompted
to enter the text for the text box in the Map
Shape Format Dialog: Text Tab. Click OK to close when you have
entered the text and made any other required changes. Click on a
text box to select it. When selected, 8 little red selection
'handles' will be displayed - one on each corner, and one in the middle,
of the sides of the text box. Click-and-drag anywhere on a text box
to move it. Click-and-drag on the little red selection handles to
resize the box.

When you first create a text box, you should see a little yellow circle in
the top-left corner (see first box in Figure 1 above). This is the text
anchor. If you zoom in and out on a map, unlike other shapes,
a text box may or may not zoom in and out with everything else on the map
(for an explanation of why this is, see the discussion of the Reference
Zoom field in the Map
Shape Format Dialog: Text Tab). However, regardless of what
else happens, the text anchor will always remain at the same point on the
map - that is, at the same latitude and longitude. It anchors the
text box to that specific location. You can click-and-drag on a text
anchor to move it to a different position, without moving the rest of the
text box. You can move the text anchor to a position within the text
box, or to a position outside the text box. If the text anchor is
moved outside the text box, it displays by, default, as a callout
line, connecting the text box to that location. If you want
the text anchor can be outside the text box but with no line connecting
it. To achieve this, untick Enable Callout Line in the Map
Shape Format Dialog: Callout Tab.

If you move the text anchor independently (by clicking-and-dragging on
it), Family Historian will thereafter assume that the position of the text
anchor is now 'fixed'. When the text anchor is 'fixed', if you move
the text box, the text anchor will not also move. You can still move
the text anchor by clicking-and-dragging on it. If you want the text
box and text anchor to move together, right-click on the text box, choose
the 'Format' command, and untick the 'Fix Text Anchor' checkbox in the the
Map Shape Format Dialog:
Callout Tab
Polylines

Figure 2. Polylines. Press the Alt key while clicking
on a line to add (or remove) a red node.

An ordinary line connects 2 points. A polyline connects 2 or more
points. Each point is called a 'node'. To add a polyline to a
map, click on the Polyline button on the Map
Window Toolbar, and then click-and-drag on the map to draw a simple
initial line connecting 2 points. To add a node to a polyline,
press-and-hold the Alt key when clicking on the
line. There is no limit to the number of nodes that a polyline can
have. Click anywhere on a polyline line to select it. Each
node will display a red selection 'handle' (little solid red
circle). Click-and-drag anywhere on a line to move it.
Click-and-drag on a red selection handle to just move that one node.
To delete a node, press-and-hold the Alt key when
clicking on the red selection handle for the node that you want to
delete. A polyline cannot connect fewer than two points. If
you try to delete a node from a polyline that has only two nodes, you will
be prompted to delete the polyline.

Polygons

Figure 3. Polygons. Press the Alt key while
clicking on a polygon to add (or remove) a red node.

A polygon is effectively an arbitrary shape, enclosing an area. A
polygon can connect as many points as you like. Polygons typically
have a transparent 'fill', so they highlight a defined area (a country,
state, county or region say), without hiding all the information about it,
displayed in the map layer. To add a polygon to a map, click on the
Polygon button
on the the Map Window Toolbar, and
then click-and-drag on the map to draw an initial rectangle. To add
a node to a polygon, press-and-hold the Alt key when
clicking either on the edge of the polygon, or anywhere within it.
There is no limit to the number of nodes that a polygon can have.
Click anywhere on a polygon line to select it. Each node will
display a red selection handle. Click-and-drag anywhere on a polygon
to move it. Click-and-drag on a red selection handle to just move
that one node. To delete a node, press-and-hold the Alt key
when clicking on the red selection handle for the node. If you try
to delete a node from a polygon that has only three, you will be
prompted to delete the polygon.

Circles

Figure 4. Circles. Click-and-drag on the circle perimeter to
resize it.

To add a circle to a map, click on the Circle button on the Map toolbar, and then
click-and-drag on the map to draw the radius of the required circle.
The point you initially click on will be the centre of the circle.
Click-and-drag anywhere on a circle to move it. Click-and-drag
anywhere on the circumference of the circle to resize it.

Formatting Shapes (Single and Multiple)

There are numerous options for shapes that can be selected or modified in
the Map Shape Format dialog.
To open this dialog, right-click on any shape and click Format from
the menu that appears.

The Map Shape Format dialog will have different fields, and different
tabs, depending on what type of shape is being formatted.

A very useful feature of the Map Shape Format dialog is that it can be
used to modify values for multiple shapes at the same time, and even to
modify values for the shapes making up a group shape. Any changes
you make to values in the Map Shape Format dialog will apply to all the
shapes in the selection (and that includes all shapes in any selected
groups). This can be very convenient if, say, you have an overlay
that is made up of dozens of polygons. Just right-click on it and
make changes and the changes will be applied to the entire selection. And
if you don't like the changes, click Undo on the Edit menu, to reverse
them. You can do this even if the selection include shapes of
different types. Of course some fields in the Map Shape Format
dialog may not be applicable to all shape types. If you make any
changes to a field like that, these changes will only be applied to those
shapes, within the selection, that they are relevant to. Text, for
example, is only relevant to text boxes. Fill colour, again, is not
applicable to polylines (although it is relevant to all other shape
types). If a selection includes several polylines and several
polygons (say), and you choose to format all of them, you will be able to
change the fill colour. But the change will only be applied to the
polygons. It will have no effect on the polylines.

If you open the Map Shape Format dialog when you have multiple shapes
selected, it will initially show all the values that they all have - if
they all have the same values. If some of them have different
values, the Map Shape Format dialog will not display any value for that
field. If, for example, you had several shapes selected, each with a
different line colour, the line colour field would be blank, indicating
that multiple line colours were being used. You could change other
aspects of the selected shapes, and as long as you do not set the line
colour, this aspect of each shape would be left unchanged when you press OK or Apply.
If, however, you do set a line colour, that change will apply to the
entire selection.

Copying and Pasting Shapes

Shapes can be copied-and-pasted either with one Map Window, or between
different Map Windows. This includes multiple selections of shapes,
and shape groups, etc. When you paste a shape, it will be pasted at
the exact location that it was copied from. This can be a little
confusing, if you paste one shape on top of a copy of itself.

Locking Shapes

Conceptually, shapes are extensions of the map, providing additional
information, and highlighting areas of interest. Once you have
finished creating them, you don't want to accidentally move them.
If that did happen, you could use the Undo command on the Edit menu to
undo the move, of course. But better still, you can lock shapes at
any time, to prevent them from being accidentally moved, resized,
deleted or otherwise changed. To achieve this, just tick the Locked
field, on the Map Shape
Format Dialog: Shape Tab, for the shape or shapes in
question. Once a shape is locked it will be treated as if it is
part of the map layer (see Map Elements).
If you click-and-drag on it, it won't move the shape. It will
behave as if you had clicked-and-dragged on the map layer - which is to
say that it will move the map. You cannot even select a locked
shape. Or at least, you can't so long as the Access button on the Map
Window toolbar is not pressed.
There has to be some way of allowing locked shapes to be selected - and
perhaps unlocked. This is what the Access button on the
Map Window toolbar is for. This button is a toggle. When it
is pressed in, locked shapes behave exactly as if they were unlocked,
and can be selected, edited, formatted, unlocked, and even deleted.

Saved overlays frequently include locked shapes. You can even
copy-and-paste locked shapes.

Tip: If you ever find that you do not seem to be able to
select a shape, the chances are that it is locked. Click the Access
button
on the Map Window toolbar, and try selecting the shape again.

Tip: If you ever find that you do not seem to be able to
lock a shape, the chances are that it in fact it is locked,
but it doesn't behave as if it is, because the Access button on the Map
Window toolbar is pressed. Click the Access button on
the Map Window toolbar to switch that option off. You should now
find that the shape behaves like a locked shape and it doesn't get
selected when you click on it.

If you need to select all unlocked shapes, use the command
"Select All Unlocked Shapes" on the Mapping
Menu. Another useful command on the same menu is
"Select All Unlocked Text Shapes".

title: Add Media to Project Dialog
text:
More Dialog Boxes...

Add Media to Project Dialog

Add Media to Project Dialog

This dialog box is displayed when you add media to a project, either
from a menu (such as by clicking Pictures on the Add menu)
or if you use drag-and-drop to add pictures, or other media, to a
project. It is also displayed if you add media to a project by
using copy-and-paste. The various methods of adding media to a
project are discussed below.

Adding Media Using Drag-and-Drop

Probably the quickest and easiest way of adding media to a project is
to use drag-and-drop. If you are viewing one or more files in File
Explorer (called 'Windows Explorer' in some versions of Windows), or on
the Desktop, or possibly elsewhere, click-and-drag on the files, and
'drop' them (release the mouse) in one of the various 'drop zones'
within Family Historian. Different drop zones perform different
functions. If you just with to add a media file to a project, you
can drop the media file anywhere in the main body of the
application. But you will often want to do more than that.
You might, for example, want to add a media file to a project, and link
it to a particular Individual record. In that case, you should
drop it on the Media tab of the
Property Box, when viewing details of that Individual. See the
list of drop zones for Media, and their various functions,
below.

You can drag-and-drop multiple files in one go. To do this, just
select all the files you wish to drop, and then click-and-drag on any
one of them to drop them into Family Historian.

As well as dropping files, you can also click-and-drag on actual images
viewed in the Web Search Window or
in an external web browser. However, be aware that some web
browsers may not let you do this unless you enable this feature in one
of their options. Also, whether or not an image can be simply
dragged-and-dropped will depend in part on whether this is permitted by
the website itself. Bear in mind also, that images may be
copyright. Just because you can drag-and-drop (or otherwise copy)
an image, does not mean that you are in fact permitted to do so.

Irrespective of where you are dragging images from, the possible drop
zones in Family Historian are these:

Media tab of Property Box for an Individual record
Add the media to the Project and link it to the Individual.

Media tab of Property Box for a Family record
Add the media to the Project and link it to the Family record

Media tab of Property Box for a Source record
Add the media to the Project and link it to the Source record

Media tab of Property Box for a Place record
Add the media to the Project and link it to the Place record

Floating Media Window showing all media linked to a fact or to a
source citation.*
Add the media to the Project and link it to the fact or source
citation.

Anywhere else within the application
Just add the media to the Project

* The floating Media Viewer can be
opened to show fact media, by selecting a fact and clicking the Show
Media button on the Facts
tab toolbar.

When you move your mouse over a drop zone, within Family Historian, the
cursor will change to show white box with a '+' sign. This
indicates that the media can be dropped here. With all drop zones
listed above, except the last, a thick blue box will also display around
the drop-zone, as you move your mouse over it. No thick blue box
will appear with the default drop zone (the 'anywhere else within the
application' drop zone).

To learn more about drag-and-drop within Family Historian, see Drag-and-Drop.

Tip: To cancel a drag-and-drop, simply press the Escape
key, or release the mouse when not over a drop zone. Or you can
simply cancel within the 'Add Media to Project Dialog'.

Fields

Copy File(s) to

When you add media to a project, a media record is created to
represent each media item that you add to the project.
Ordinarily, you will also copy the actual media files into the
project folder and you are recommended to do that, unless you
have a good reason not to. However, you don't have to do
that if you don't want to. If you prefer to leave the
media files where they are on your hard disk, select the option
'<don't copy - link only>'. For most purposes, you
will not be able to tell the difference. You can treat
'linked' media exactly as you do 'copied' media. So why do
we recommend that you should copy media files into the project
folder? The reason is that it is much easier to copy a
project (if you want to give a copy to a relative say, or to a
specialist genealogy printer), or to make a backup, if all files
relating to the project, are stored as part of the
project. Also, if you keep files elsewhere on your hard
disk, the links to these files could get 'broken' if you
accidentally or deliberately, renamed or moved some of the
folders they belong to.

Tip: If you do have any problems with 'broken
links', the External
File Links tool (accessible from the Tools menu) is
designed to help manage links to media - both links to media
kept within the project folder, and media held outside it.

If you opt to copy the media files into the project folder,
you can, if you wish, leave it up to Family Historian to decide
where to put them. In that case, you should select the
option '<Default Location within the Project
Folder>'. Some users prefer to have their own system
for arranging media files within the project folder. If
you have already created folders that you have previously copied
media into, those folders will be listed as options to copy the
media to. If you want to create a new folder, or select an
unlisted one, click on the Location
button.

Note: the option '<don't copy - link only>' will not be
available if you are adding media images that you have copied to
the clipboard, and are pasting into the application.

Save File as
If you are copying a single file into your project folder, you
can if you wish change its name here. This is a good idea,
especially if the current file name is meaningless (for example,
some websites generate file names consisting of random letters and
numbers, for file downloads). You will be warned if there is
already a file with the name you have chosen in the specified
target location.

If you copy more than one file at a time, you will not be given an
option to rename the copied files. Instead the existing
files name will be used, unless they clash with file names already
in use in the target folder, in which case the file names will be
modified very slightly, to ensure their uniqueness.

title: Add Note Dialog
text:
Property Box: Notes Tab

Add Note Dialog

Create Local Note
Use this option to add a note to the current record.

Create Family Note
This option is only available for Individual records. Use this
option to add a note for a married individual, where the note is
as much applicable to their spouse as to them. You must specify
which Spouse Family the note is to apply to.

Add Link to Note Record

Use this option if you want to either create a new note, or
link to an existing note, that is to be shared between more than
one record. For example, you might wish to keep a note about a
famous house that at different times was owned and occupied by
various individuals in your file. You can create the note once,
and then link it to all the individuals who had an interest in
the house, or who were mentioned in the note.

If you take this option, and click on OK, a dialog will appear
showing you a list of existing note records to select from. If
you want to create a new note, ignore the list and click on the
New button instead. You will then return to the Note tab in the
Property Box. A note record will be created, but with no text.
You can type in the required in the Notes tab of the Property
Box. You do not have to switch to viewing the Note record as
such.

This last point is worth emphasizing: whenever you view links
to note records (new or old) you will always be able to see and
modify the actual text of the note record. Bear in mind, if you
do this, that you are modifying a shared note record, and your
changes can therefore be seen whenever you look at the notes
list for any other records linked to this same note record.

title: Add People with Roles Dialog
text:
Property Box: Facts Tab

Add People with Roles Dialog

Add People with Roles Dialog

Any fact type (event or attribute) can have witnesses
associated with it - that is people who participated in the event, in a
non-principal role. With most events, you will add the basic
details of the fact type first (including date and place, if known), and
only later, if at all, will you add associated people in the Witnesses
Window (godparents for a baptism, say). The Add People
with Roles Dialog is displayed when you add a fact type to a
person's record, where the people who will be listed in the Witnesses
Window are really central to the fact itself - and consequently it makes
sense that they should be added immediately when you create the
fact. For example, if you are trying to add details of a person's
Friend List or Friendship Group, it is likely that
you will want to add the friends immediately, at the time you create the
fact. You don't have to. You can close this dialog and add
the people later in the Witnesses Window.
And, of course, you can always update the list there too, at any time.

The Add People with Roles Dialog is used not just with the Friend
List and Friendship Group built-in fact types, but
also with the Enslavement built-in fact type, and it can
optionally be used with any custom fact types you create yourself.
In the case of enslavement, the reason for using this prompt is that it
is possible that a number of people may have been enslaved together (an
entire family say), in which case you can add them all to the same Enslavement
fact. Additionally, you can also add the person or persons who
enslaved them if you want to.

If you create a new custom fact type where it makes sense to prompt for
people with particular roles to be added to the fact when the fact
itself is added to a person's record, you can achieve this by ticking
the option 'Prompt to Add on Create' in the Edit
Role - Advanced Features Dialog.

If you add a Friendship Group fact for a person, you will
find that they themselves are automatically added to the list of friends
in the friendship group. This is because it is assumed
that the principal for the fact is one of the friends in the friendship
group. Equally if you add an Enslavement fact for a
person, you will find that they are automatically added to the list of
people who were enslaved together. Again, it is assumed that the
principal is one of the enslaved persons group. By contrast, if you add
a Friend List fact for a person, they themselves will not be
automatically added to the list of their friends, as it makes little
sense that they should be.

If you create a custom fact type, and you want the principal to be
automatically granted a particular role, you can achieve this by ticking
the option 'Default Role for Principal' in the Edit
Role - Advanced Features Dialog.

To learn more, see How
to Record Non-Family Relationships.

title: Add Query Category
text:
Query Window: General Tab

Add Query Category

The Add Query Category dialog is accessed from the General
tab of the Query Window, when you click on any of the Category
fields and choose <Add New...>. It allows you to
add a new category for the current query. The category or categories
that a query belongs to determines where it will appear in the menu that
is displayed when you click on the Query button on the main
application toolbar. The same categories can also be used for filtering
in the Manage
Queries Dialog.

It is possible to organise your queries into subcategories of arbitrary
complexity. Use a vertical bar to separate subcategories .
Suppose, for example you have a query called "Male Deaths" and you add
the following category for it: "Analysis | Males | Deaths".
When you click on the Query button ,
the dropdown menu that appears will now have a submenu called
'Analysis', which in turn will have a submenu called 'Males', which in
turn will have a submenu called 'Deaths', which will contain your "Male
Deaths" query.

New categories are automatically added to the dropdown menu that
appears when you click on any category field. A category name
automatically disappears when there are no longer any queries belonging
to that category .

It is possible to modify the categories associated with standard
queries. Be aware if you do this, however that standard queries
may revert to their default categories when you apply an upgrade in the
future. You can, at that point, re-apply your changes if you wish
to do so.

Category names may not begin with a period or fullstop ('.') and may
not contain any of the characters: \/:*?\"<>

title: Address Records
text:
Record Types

Address Records

Address records are identified by this icon: .
Whenever you enter details of the address at which an event occurred
(such as where someone was born), Family Historian will automatically
create an Address record to represent this address, if it doesn't
already exist.

Address records are normally associated with Place records. Every
Place record can have one or more Address records associated with
it. For example, the place for an event might be
recorded as "London, England". The address of the same
event might be recorded as "Lewisham Hospital".

Despite the name, an 'address' does not have to be
literally a postal address. You can use the address field (and
Address records) to store details of where an event occurred, which go
beyond the place specification. For example, the address field
might contain a street address and house number, a cemetery name, a plot
number and cemetery name, a hospital name, and so on.

The Address record is used to store any pictures you may wish to record
about the address, as well as notes, and the latitude and longitude of
the address, if known.

Tabs for Address records in the Property Box:

Main
(for Addresses)

Notes

Media

All

Using Place Records and Address Records Together

Users sometimes ask how much detail should be put in place fields, and
how much in address fields. There are different possible
approaches to this. You can, if you wish, specify full address
details in the address field. This may mean, however, that you
have considerable duplication (and even possible conflict) between the
information provided in the place field and the address
field. Another strategy would be to only provide precise
location-specifying details in the Address field. As mentioned
above, despite the name, an 'address' field does not have to be
literally a postal address. You can use the address field (and
Address records) to just store details of where an event occurred, which
add to, and complete, the place specification. For example, the
address field might contain a street address and house number, a
cemetery name, a plot number and cemetery name, a hospital name, and so
on.

Bear in mind is that Family Historian has the ability to output a
single value showing either the address (if only the address is
recorded), the place (if only the place is recorded), or (if both are
recorded) a fusion of the two, with duplicated parts removed. You
can do this in a fact query, for example, by adding a column, "Address
and Place", selected from the "Common Functions" area in the Columns
tab of the Query Window (advanced users may note that this column
uses the built-in function AddressAndPlace,
which can be used in reports, charts and elsewhere, as needed). If
you wish to take advantage of this feature, you should bear in mind that
place details will be appended to address details (albeit with
duplicated parts removed). There are issues about post codes in
relation to this function (see next).

Post Codes

"Post code" and "postal code" mean the same thing in Family
Historian. The two terms are used interchangeably.

You can if you wish record a post code as part of an address field but
this is not recommended, especially if you plan to use the AddressAndPlace
built-in function, mentioned above, as, if you do so, the post code is
likely to appear in the wrong place. For this reason, you may wish
to store the post code separately in the Address record, using the
Postal Code field. You can enter this field in the Main tab of the
Property Box, when editing an Address record.

title: Advanced Diagram Features
text:
Diagram Options
Dialog: Dimensions Tab

Advanced Diagram Features

This dialog provides advanced settings. Only change
the settings if you have been advised to do so by customer support.

Fields

Diagram DPI (logical)
This setting should normally be 'Standard'. In rare
circumstances it may show other values. Do not change this
setting unless you have been instructed to do so by customer
support.

Update layout to latest standard
If this check box is disabled and greyed, so that you cannot
tick it, it means that the current diagram is already using the
latest layout standard (think of a layout standard as a set of
rules concerning how diagram dimensions should be applied, when
building diagrams). Any new diagrams you create will always
use the latest layout standard, so you should normally expect this
field to be greyed. If you open a saved chart, however, that
was created using an earlier layout standard (anything prior to
version 7.0.18 of Family Historian), that layout standard will
continue to be used unless and until you upgrade it. So in
that case, the option of upgrading it will be available.
Ticking this option will upgrade the chart to the latest layout
standard. This is normally recommended, but bear in mind
that ticking this option may cause box sizes, and box positions,
to change. Bear in mind that if you want this change to the
layout standard to be always used, whenever you re-open a given
saved chart, you will need to also click "Save Diagram" on the
Diagram menu.
