title: Check for Updates to Language Pack Dialog
breadcrumb: Check for Updates to Language Pack Dialog
text:
Language Packs Dialog

Check for Updates to Language Pack Dialog

The Check for Updates to Language Pack dialog is used to
manage the addition of updates and new features, to a language pack
selected in the Language Packs dialog.

Important - please read Before Applying Any Updates

If you never personally make any changes to your language pack (for
example, by adding translations to the translation tables), you are not
recommended to use the Check for Updates to Language Pack dialog
to update your current language pack. Instead, if a newer version
of your language pack is available in the Plugin Store, you are
recommended to first backup your existing language pack (see
instructions on backing up below), and then delete it and import the
latest version from the Plugin Store (on the Language Packs dialog,
click the Import button, choose "From
Family Historian Plugin Store" and then select the language pack to
import). Doing it that way will import the newest version of the
language pack in its entirety. There is no need to delete the
current version of your language pack though. Importing a new
language pack will not affect your existing language packs at all.
Imported language packs never replace existing installations of language
packs, even if you already have a language pack for that language.
Each new import is given a 'Variant' value, if necessary, to distinguish
it from other installed language packs you may have for the same
language (i.e. that use the same 3-letter language code). The
newly imported language pack becomes an alternative language pack, in
the list of language packs available for you to use.

It is perfectly normal however, and often necessary, for users to make
changes of their own to their current language pack - such as, to add
translations to the translation tables. If you want to update your
current language pack without losing these updates, the Check for
Updates to Language Pack dialog may be the tool you need.
You use it to apply specific changes to your current language pack

The Check for Updates to Language Pack dialog will only
report (or apply) the following specific kinds of updates...

If there is a language pack in the Plugin Store for the same
language, with a plugin that has a later version number than the
plugin in your language pack, you will be offered the option of
upgrading your language pack to use that plugin, instead of your
existing plugin (which it will replace). Tick the box if you
want to do this. Updating the plugin will only update the plugin
file. If other changes have been made to the language pack,
these changes will not be applied to the language pack you are
updating. If you have made changes of your own to the plugin
file, these will be lost if you take this option.

If your language pack does not include a spellcheck, and there is
language pack plugin in the Plugin Store for the same language, which
has a spellcheck, you will be offered the option to add the spellcheck
feature.

If you have ticked one or more options (if they are applicable), you
can then click the Apply Selected Updates
button to apply them. Before doing so, however, you are strongly
recommended to take a backup of your existing language pack (see below).

Always Backup before Applying Updates

There is no undo feature when you apply changes of any kind to a
language pack (or delete one). You are strongly recommended to
take a full backup of your current language pack before applying any
upgrades to it. To backup a language pack, click the Export
button on the main Language Packs dialog. This will save the
language pack as a file. Keep the file somewhere safe. This
is your backup.

title: Citation Assessment Dialog
text:
More Dialog Boxes...

Citation Assessment Dialog

Citation Assessment Dialog

This dialog box is displayed when you click on "<more
options...>" in the Assessment field of a source citation.
Citations can be assessed under up to four categories:

Warning

Evidence

Information

Source

All four categories are optional. Under each category, you have a
choice of two options, but there is no need to choose either of them,
and typically you won't. For example, if you are not concerned
about a source citation, you should not tick either of the options in
the Warning category. The options in each category are mutually
exclusive. If you tick one, the other will become unticked.
For example, you can choose Questionable or Unreliable for
'Warning', but not both. If you don't want either, make sure that
both are unticked (if an option is ticked, click on it to untick it).

Warning

Questionable
Questionable reliability of evidence - which might apply to
interviews, census, oral genealogies. You might wish to use
this option if there is a potential for bias, as in, for example,
an autobiography.

Unreliable
Unreliable evidence or estimated data.

Evidence

Direct
Direct evidence is evidence that seems to answer the research
question all by itself.

Indirect
Indirect evidence is evidence that cannot on its own answer the
research question, but which must be combined with other evidence
to arrive at a conclusion.

Information

Primary
A source constitutes primary information if it is
provided by someone who had firsthand knowledge of the matter in
question - such as a witness to an event or a participant.

Secondary
A source constitutes secondary information if it is
provided by someone who had secondhand knowledge of the matter in
question (if say they heard about it from others), or had any
other kind of more distant connection to the matter in question.

Source

Original
A source is original if it is in its original form.

Derivative
A source is derivative if it is a copy, or a summary, or some
other kind of version which derives from the original, but which
is not itself the original.

title: Customize Citation
text:
Citation Window

Customize Citation

Customize Citation Dialog

To open the Customize Citation Dialog, click on the "Customize" link
at the bottom of the side panel, in the Citation
Window.

The Customize Citation Dialog allows footnotes, short footnotes and
bibliography entries to be customized - either at the citation level or
(except for free form sources) at the source level.
Free form sources cannot be customized at the source level because there
is no need or point in doing that, as the source text is already free
form.

A footnote (sometimes also called an 'end note'), is the
citation text that appears in reports, that explains the source of some
information in the report (referenced via a numbered superscript).
With reports, you can optionally specify that a shortened version of
this footnote should be used on the second and all subsequent occasions
that a given source is referred to. The details of footnotes are
specified in footnote fields. The details of the shortened version
(the "short footnote") are specified in short footnote fields.
With both reports and books, you can also optionally have a bibliography
section, giving a list of sources referred to. Bibliography
fields are used to specify these bibliography entries. If multiple
sources and citations have the same bibliography text, this duplication
will be discarded, and only one entry for all of them will be included
in the bibliography section. See "Understanding Bibliography Entries"
below for more on this.

Fields that have not been customized are displayed with a brown background in the Customize Dialog.
In the image shown above, none of the fields have yet been customized,
which is why they all have a brown background. All fields are
editable. To customize a field, simply edit it in the normal
way. The moment you modify an uncustomized field, the background
colour of the field will switch from brown to white and the label above
the field will be appended with "(customized)". This way you can
always see at a glance, which fields have been customized and which have
not.

All sources, can be customized at the citation level. With generic
and templated sources (but not free form sources),
you can also customize the formats used to generate the
citations, at the citation level or at the Source record level.
'Formats' are templates containing special codes called source template
codes, that effectively specify how footnotes, short footnotes and
bibliography entries, are to be generated from fields stored in Source
records and as part of citations. To learn more, see What are
Formats? below.

To reset any customized field to its uncustomized state, click on the Reset button and choose the appropriate option
from the dropdown menu that appears.

When you view footnotes, short footnotes and bibliography entries in
the side panel of the Citation Window, the label indicates if it has
been customized, and if so, at what level.

Understanding Bibliography Entries

We saw earlier that if multiple sources and citations have the same
bibliography text, this duplication will be discarded, and only one
entry for all of them will be included in the bibliography
section. This means that any number of Source records can all
share a single bibliography entry. Conversely, a single Source
record can generate multiple bibliography entries if you have multiple
citations associated with that Source record, and each has a distinct
bibliography entry.

Customized Bibliography Entries Can Be Blank

Removing all text for a footnote or short footnote is not
permitted. Customized footnotes and short footnotes cannot be
blank. Customized bibliography entries, however, can be blank - either
at the Source level, or at the citation level. Blank bibliography
entries do not appear in the Bibliography section.

Suppose you have a report which includes a particular citation, and you
customize the bibliography entry of that citation to make it
blank. If you do this, it does not necessarily mean that you will
now see one fewer entries in the Bibliography section of your
report. Suppose, for example, that your citation's bibliography
entry had been "Southern Star Newspaper". In the Bibliography
section of your report you see "Southern Star Newspaper". You edit
the citation to customize the bibliography entry to make it blank.
When you refresh the report, to your surprise, there is still an entry
which reads "Southern Star Newspaper". Why is this? The
answer is that there must be one or more other citations in the report
which also have "Southern Star Newspaper" as their bibliography
entry. One way to get rid of all of them would be to customize
each of these citations individually to make their bibliography entries
blank. Another approach would be to customize the bibliography
entry at the Source Format level, to make it blank. When
you do this, you are customizing the bibliography entry at the Source
record level, which means that this is the new default for all citations
for that source.

If you make changes like this, always remember, if you have the Report
Window open, that you will need to refresh the report by clicking the Refresh Report button before you will see the
effect of your changes.

What are Formats?

For all sources other than freeform sources, footnotes, short footnotes
and bibliography entries are generated from the original source and
citation data. The manner in which they are generated is
determined by expressions called 'formats' - specifically by 'Footnote
Formats', 'Short Footnote Formats' and 'Bibliography Formats'.

Note: the natural word to use for these expressions would
be 'template', but the word 'format' is used instead to avoid potential
confusion with Source Templates.

Different types of source record will normally have different formats.
For templated Source records, the Footnote Formats, Short Footnote
Formats and Bibliography Formats are all specified in fields in the
Source Template record linked to the Source record (by definition, a
templated Source record is one that is linked to a Source
Template). These fields are called "Footnote Format", "Short
Footnote Format" and "Bibliography Format". This is an example of
what a Footnote Format might look like:

{Type}: {Name}, {Date}, {Repository}, {Page_Etc}.

The names in curly refer to fields in the Source record or possibly in
the citation.

For generic sources, the Footnote Formats, Short Footnote Formats and
Bibliography Formats are all specified in the 'Sources' tab of
Preferences (accessible from the 'Tools' menu).

Freeform sources, by definition, do not have any kind of formats.
You just enter the footnotes, short footnotes and bibliography entries
as freeform text.

What is the Difference Between Customizing a Citation and a Citation
Format?

The difference between customizing a 'Citation' and a 'Citation Format'
effectively amounts to this: do you want to use format expressions
(expression which refer to fields) in your customized version or would
you prefer to enter it WYSIWYG ("What you see is what you get")?
If want to use format expressions, you should take the 'Citation Format'
option. If you use a Citation Format it allows you to mix ordinary text
with codes (like "{Date}", say) which reference field values. The
advantage of this is that if the field value changes, you won't have to
remember to change the date in your customized version of the
citation. That part of the citation will update automatically to
reflect the change.

Note: If you want to customize a format at the Source
record level, you have to select "Source Format". There is no
WYSIWYG option in this case.

title: Citation Window with a Prepared Citation
breadcrumb: Citation Window with a Prepared Citation
text:
Citation Window

Citation Window with a Prepared Citation

Figure 1 - Citation Window with a Prepared Citation (visual clues marked
in red)

When the Citation Window is used to display a prepared citation, there
are a few visual clues (all highlighted in red in Figure 1 above), to
show that it is being used for a prepared citation, and not
for an actual citation. The use of the label 'Prepared
Citation' in four different parts of the window is obviously one
signficant clue. Another is the colour of the small shield icon on
the first tab (red instead of green). And finally, there is the
presence of the three buttons at the bottom of the window.

It is important to appreciate that when the Citation Window is used to
view a prepared citation, it is also showing details of the Source
record that the prepared citation links to. The top half of the
window shows the Source record details. The bottom half of the
window shows the 'Prepared Citation Details'. Any changes you make
to prepared citation details will not affect any data records until you
do something with the prepared citation. But if you make any
changes to the Source record, those changes are immediate.
Of course if you make a change and then regret it, you can click on Undo
on the Edit menu to undo it. This applies both to changes to the
Source record and to changes to the prepared citation.

To learn more about prepared citations, including their close
relationship to the Automatic
Source Citation Pane, see Prepared
Citation.

To learn more about the three buttons, and how to use them, see Source-Driven
Data Entry and also Browse/Install
Data Entry Assistants.

title: Citation Window
text:
Citation Window

Citation Window with optional side panel on the right side

The Citation Window is used to display source citation
details (as in the example above). It is also used to set up or
view a prepared citation. In
that case it, will have three buttons at the bottom and there will be
other differences. To learn more about this latter use of the
Citation Window (and associated visual clues), see Citation
Window with a Prepared Citation. The page below describes
the use of the Citation Window to display source citation details.

The appearance of the Citation Window (and in particular,
the fields on display) will vary significantly depending on the source
and citation. For an overview of the different types of sources
and citations, see Sources and
Source Templates.

The Citation Window is a floating
window that can display all details of a given source
citation. A source citation can be viewed as consisting of two
parts:

The Source record details

The citation-specific details

The difference is most easily explained with reference to a concrete
example. Suppose your source is a book. A typical approach
would be to create a Source record to
represent the book, and to link all the facts that you gleaned from it,
back to this Source record. These links will be used by Family
Historian when you later create reports, to generate appropriate source
citation footnotes. For this reason, we often refer to the links
that connect a fact with a Source record as citation links, or
even just as citations.

Let us suppose that you discovered 5 interesting facts within the book
that you want to record within your project - they could be about one
person, or about different people. It doesn't matter. You will
want each of those 5 facts to be linked back to the same Source record,
because that's where they all came from. So there will be 5 links,
from 5 facts, to a single Source record. Some of the source citation
information that you will want to record, are going to be the same for all
5 links: such as the name of the book, the author, publishing details, and
so on. These are all bits of information that most naturally should
be kept in the Source record. However, there may also be bits of
information which are not necessarily the same for all 5 links - most
obviously in this case, the page number. You might have learned
about the first fact on page 11, about the second on page 82, ... and so
on. The page number is an important piece of information, but the
best place to keep it is not on the Source record (where there's no easy
way of associating it within any particular fact), but on the link itself
- because the link is attached to the specific fact that it relates
to. We say that details, like the page number in our example, are citation-specific.

On the main tab of the Citation Window, Source record details are stored
in the top-half of the window, and citation-specific details are stored in
the bottom half. It is important to be clear about the
difference. Changes made to the Source record will affect all
citations to that Source record. Changes to citation-specific
details affect that one citation alone.

How to Access the Citation Window

The Citation Window is used to enter and edit details of new and
existing source citations. Source citations are listed, and can
also be created, in the Citation
List Pane of the Property Box.
See the Citation List Pane
for details of how to create (add) citations, and how to edit and view
existing citations. You can also add source citations directly
into notes, using the Note Window.
Again, the Citation Window is used to enter and edit the source
citation. Within a note, each source citation is represented
within the body of the text by a little superscript number. Each
such number is a link. If you click on it, the source citation
details will be displayed in the Citation Window, where, again, they can
be viewed and edited.

Drag-and-Drop

The Citation Window supports drag-and-drop, which can be a
quick and easy way of adding text and pictures. See Drag-and-Drop
to learn more.

Customizing the Citation Window

To customize the Citation Window, click Customize
Citation Window in the cog button menu. Customizations
are shared (to an extent) with the Property
Box, when it displays Source
record details. See the "Special-handling for Source Records"
section in Customize Property Box
for more details.

title: Configure Columns Dialog
text:
Records Window

Configure Columns Dialog

The Configure Columns Dialog allows you to choose the columns you wish
to see displayed in the Records Window or in a particular Named List.
The same columns are also used in the record selector dialogs, and other
contexts - such as the Media Records List in the Media Window.

The first column only in each case is fixed and not configurable.

Click-and-drag on any column in the list on the left-hand side to add
it to column list on the right-hand side. Alternatively, select a
column on the left-hand side and press the >
button to add it to the column list. You can also click-and-drag on
columns on the right-hand side to reposition them. Or you can use
the 'Move Up' and Move Down' arrow buttons below the list on the
right-hand side to re-order columns.

Select a column on the right-hand side and click Edit
if you wish to change its label or sort order, or other details.

If the column you want is not already in the list, select
'<Other...>' (last item in the list) and click >
to add a custom expression.

You can save column settings as a query, or load the columns used in an
existing query. If the column settings use complex expressions which
require a parameter to be supplied, the column will be blank.

Note On Configuring Named List Columns

As well as being able to configure the columns in Records Window tabs,
as previously mentioned, you can also configure the columns for any
Named List. Named Lists can contain records of any
type. When configuring Named List columns, you can add columns which are
applicable to records of any type. If you add a column which is
only relevant to one particular type of record, that column will be
blank in rows that represent records of other types. For example,
you could add a column for 'Sex'. Only Individual records have a
'Sex' field. So this column will always be blank for all records
of types other than Individual.

title: Configure Language and Accent Characters Dialog
text:
Fact Types Dialog

Configure Language and Accent Characters Dialog

If you use the default option for accent-handling (see the General
tab of Preferences) when you press-and-hold a letter key (any key
in the range a-z), in any text field in the Property
Box or in the Auto
Source Citation Pane, Family Historian will display a little popup
window called the Popup Accent Window (see below) with
a choice of alternative versions of the letter in question which you can
select by clicking with the mouse, by using the arrow keys and pressing
Enter, or by pressing the appropriate number key.

The Popup Accent Window

Typically, the choices in the Popup Accent Window will include accented
versions of the same letter. You can also press-and-hold the upper-case
version of each letter, and some other keys - such as the double-quote
character, the single-quote character, the pound and dollar signs (if
available on your keyboard), the hyphen, the full-stop, the comma, and
even the space bar. The key that you press-and-hold is called the Hold
Key, and the alternative characters displayed in the popup window
are called the Accent List .

The purpose of the Configure Language and Accent Characters
dialog (shown below) is to allow you to see which accent lists are
associated with which hold keys, and to configure them to suit your
purposes.

The Configure Language & Accent
Character Dialog

There are two ways to open the Configure Language & Accent
Characters dialog. You can either click on the little
settings button
on the right side of the Popup Accent Window. Or you can click on
the Menu button
on the Property Box toolbar, and choose Configure Language
& Accent Characters from the drop down menu that appears.

You can use the Edit button to modify the
accent list associated with any Hold Key. Untick 'Hide Unused
Keys' to view any currently unused hold keys. You can of course
configure these too. You can also add accent lists for a number of
languages. Click on the Add Accent Set
button, and choose the language you wish to add. You will be asked
if you wish to replace the existing values, or merge in the values for
the language you have selected. You do not have to restrict
yourself to one language only.

You can temporarily disable the Popup Accent Window by
pressing-and-holding the Insert key before
pressing-and-holding a letter key - if you are using the default option
for accent-handling, specified in the General
tab of Preferences (that is, the value of To Enter Accents
when Typing is 'Press-and-hold letter key'). When this option is
chosen, if the Insert key is pressed, default Windows
behaviour will occur and the letter key will auto-repeat. You can also
disable accent selection altogether in Preferences. Finally, there
is another option: 'Press Insert and letter key'. If this option
is chosen, the Popup Accent Window will only open if the Insert key is
held down when you press a letter key.

How to Display Accents From Multiple Languages in the Popup Accent
Window

Suppose, for example, you wish to always have accent characters
available to you for Norwegian, Swedish and Danish. Start by
clicking the Clear All button to remove the
current settings. Then add the 3 languages in turn, using the Add Accent Set button, choosing the 'merge'
option when prompted. Finally, you may decide to also the Add Accent Set button one last time, and choose
'Symbols' (again, merging). This will make some additional symbols
available as well.

Create Your Own Custom Accent Sets

To create your own custom accent set, just create the set you want
using the usual techniques. Then click Save
Accent Set and give the accent set a unique name.
Thereafter it will be listed when you click on the Add
Accent Set button.

Rename or Delete Accent Sets

To delete an accent set, you create an empty accent set, and save it
using the name of the accent set you wish to delete. To do this,
click the Clear All button to clear the
current accent set. Then click Save
Accent Set and give the name of the accent set you wish to
delete.

You cannot directly rename an accent set, but you can achieve the same
thing by loading an accent set (click Add Accent
Set and use the 'replace' option). Then save it with the
new desired name, using Save Accent Set.
Finally delete the old version.

Import and Export Accent Sets

Accent Sets can be imported and exported using the 'Import/Export'
command on the application File menu.

Buttons and Check Boxes

Edit
Change the values in the Popup Accent List. Click the
'Open Character Map' button to open the character map. You
can copy and paste characters from there.

Add Accent Set

Displays a dropdown list of accent sets. You can
optionally merge the chosen set with the current values, or
replace them.

Save Accent Set

Use this option to save the current values as a named set.
If there are no current values, you can use this option to delete
an existing accent set.

Clear All

Clears all current values. Will automatically untick the
'Hide Unused Keys' option, if ticked.

Open Character Map

Opens the Windows Accessory application "Character Map".
You can copy characters and symbols from the Character Map into
the Popup Accent List for any key (press 'Edit' to allow access
to the list). You can also copy characters and symbols
from the Character Map directly into any field in the Property
Box if you wish to.

title: Confirm Media Link Repairs Dialog
breadcrumb: Work with External File Links Dialog
text:
Work with External Files
Dialog...

Confirm Media Link Repairs Dialog

The Confirm Media Link Repairs Dialog is normally displayed when you
have clicked Auto Repair Links... in the Work with External Files Dialog
to try to fix 'broken links' to media files, in your project. It
can also be displayed when you create a new project, by importing data
from elsewhere, if the project contains 'broken links' to media
files. In that case, you will asked if you want to search for the
missing media files, and, if any are found, the Confirm Media Link
Repairs Dialog will be displayed then too.

The dialog displays a list of media files that were found in the search
location you specified. The list has 3 columns:

Media File - the short name of the media file being searched for
(with file suffix included, indicating file type)

Where Found - the location where the media file was found

Previous Recorded Location - the location that Family Historian had
previously looked for the file, and failed to find it (the broken
link)

At this point no changes have yet been made to any links. You
should review the list of media files found. If any of the media
files are not the right ones, you should remove the checkmark against
them which you can do by clicking on the tick box to remove the tick, or
by selecting one or more rows and clicking Uncheck
Selection. If most of them are wrong, and only a few are
right, you may prefer to start by clicking Uncheck
All and then selectively ticking the small number that are
correct. If none of them are correct, click Cancel.

When you have finished reviewing and have adjusted the checkmarks to
your satisfaction, assuming some at least are correct, click the Repair Links button. When you do this,
Family Historian will adjust all links to the media files that
have a checkmark against them, to use the new location (but see caveat
in the discussion of 'Repair Links' in the table below). Any media
files which do not have a checkmark against them will be skipped and
ignored.

Buttons

Check All

All rows (media files) will be ticked (checked).

Check Selection
All selected rows will be ticked (checked).

Uncheck All
All rows (media files) will be unticked (unchecked).

Uncheck Selection

All selected rows will be unticked (unchecked).

Repair Links

You should only click this button when you are satisfied that
you have checked all the files found, and have ticked (checked)
all the ones that are correct, and have unticked (unchecked) all
the ones that are not correct. When you click this button,
all links to all the checked media files will be repaired to use
the new location, and the dialog will close.

Note: To be accurate, if you are viewing this
dialog in the context of the Work with External File Links
Dialog, the link updates will be recorded but will not actually
be applied until you click OK in
the Work with External File Links Dialog. If instead you
click Cancel within that dialog,
the link updates will be discarded. This does not apply if
you are viewing the Confirm Media Link Repairs Dialog in the
context of creating a new project. In the latter case, the
repairs will be applied immediately when you click Repair
Links here.

View
Open an external viewer to view the selected media file.
You can achieve the same thing by double-clicking on a media file
in the list.

title: Copy Project Dialog
text:
Project Window

Copy Project Dialog

Fields

Name of Copy

This will be the same as the project being copied by default.
You must either change this name to make it unique, or change
the location.

Location for Copy
This will be the same as the location for the project being
copied by default.

Items to Copy

A project folder contains, at a minimum, a (main) project
file; and a project data subfolder which stores all the project
data (e.g. the GEDCOM file and any media which have been copied
into the project). In addition to these, it may contain
other files and folders*. For example, it may contain a 'public'
subfolder, which is designed to hold items which are associated
with the project, but not managed by Family Historian. You
can choose to copy the entire project folder, including whatever
files and folders are in it. Or you can choose to just copy the
'core' project data - that is, the (main) project file and the
project data subfolder.

* If you wish to store any of your own files or
folders within a Family Historian project folder, you are
strongly recommended to put them in the 'Public'
subfolder. That is what it is there for. The
top-level of the project folder should contain no more than 3
items:the project file, the project data subfolder, and the
'Public' subfolder.

title: Create a Simple Text Scheme
text:
Diagram Options Dialog:
Text Tab

Create a Simple Text Scheme

This section gives an example of how to create a simple text scheme
that shows a person’s names, birth, marriage and death details.

1. Create New Scheme

To create a simple text scheme, open the Diagram Options dialog and select the Text Tab. Click on the New
button. The Edit
Text Scheme dialog appears.

The first thing is to give the new scheme a name. In the Edit Text
Scheme dialog, type “My First Text Scheme” into the Scheme Name field
(without the quotes) now.

If you pressed OK now, you would have created an empty text scheme. Any
diagram that used it would have blank empty boxes. So now let us add
some content to the boxes.

2. Add Name

Find Name in the list of Available Items on the left-hand side. Select
it and click the button
to add it to the list of Items Used on the right. When you do this, the
Add Item to Text
Scheme dialog appears. Leave Text Alignment as Centred and press
OK. The Items Used list now contains one item: Name.

3. Add Other Names (‘Also Known As’)

Now the text scheme has some content. Any diagram that uses it will
show one item of text in each box - the person’s name centred within the
box. Or to be more accurate, it will show the first recorded name for
each person. But there is no limit to the number of names you can record
for any given person. To show all other names too, find Name (a.k.a.) in
the list of Available Items. Select it and click the
button to add it to the list of Items Used on the right. Leave the label
as ‘a.k.a.’ (also known as) and the text alignment as Left. Click OK.
The Items Used list now has another item: Name (a.k.a.). Although we
have only added one item for alternative names, this item will create as
many lines as are needed to show all of a person’s alternative names,
however many there are.

Now a text box might show something like this, for a person with 3
recorded names:

Jon Anderssen

a.k.a. John Anderson

a.k.a. John Andersson

4. Add Birth

Now find Birth in the list of Available Items and add it in the same
way (tip: a fast way to add it is just to double-click on it). This time
the Add Item to Text Scheme dialog that appears has more choices. Note
that you can specify the number of Instances to add. It is unlikely that
you will have more than one birth event recorded for any given person,
but if you do, you might as well be able to see them. So leave Instance
at All.

Leave Date, Place and Notes ticked as the Information to include. Let
us assume that you want the words ‘<no birth details>’ to appear
if you have no birth details. Tick ‘No Data’ Text and add ‘<no birth
details>’ in the field next to it (if you’d left this blank, you
would have got a blank line if there were no birth details). Press OK.

This time two lines were added to the Items Used list:

Birth

Birth Notes

When you add an item from the Available
Items list, you may find that several items get added to the
Items Used list. In this case, we get an additional item to show birth
notes. This line will be indented by default, so that it is easy to see
that it is a note about the birth, and not about anything else.

You also opted to see the birth date and place. These details will be
included in the first of the two items.

5. Add Marriage

Now double-click on Marriage in
the Available Items list to add
that. Accept the defaults and press OK in the Add
Item to Text Scheme dialog. You will be asked if you wish to
add special lines for the benefit of the ‘One Box Per Marriage’ display
option. Click on the More >>
button to learn more about this option, and then click on the Yes
button. The option to add these special lines only appears when you add
a Marriage item to a text scheme.

This time 4 new items have been added to the Items Used list. The last
2 are the special lines just mentioned. The Items Used list should now
look like this:

Name

Name (a.k.a.)

Birth

Birth Notes

Marriage

Marriage Notes

Spouse Name (wife) if 'One Box Per Marriage'

Spouse Name (husband) if 'One Box Per Marriage'

You may not be able to see the full text for these items. If not,
resize the Edit Text Scheme dialog to make it bigger (click-and-drag on
any edge or corner). And resize the first column of the Items Used list
by clicking-and-dragging on the line separating the Item and Box Types
column headings.

Family Historian automatically works out where the best place to put
marriage information is, given the prevailing Spouse Display Options.
So, for example, if you are looking at a Descendant diagram, do not
expect marriage details to appear in all boxes necessarily. If you are
displaying spouses in their own box, for example, Family Historian will
automatically arrange for marriage information to be displayed in the
spouse boxes only. You can override the way Family Historian manages
this if you wish (see the discussion of Box Types and Conditions in the
Edit Text
Scheme Item Dialog section).

6. Add Death

Now double-click on Death in the Available Items list. Leave all the
defaults and press OK to add it. This will add 3 more lines:

Death

Death Cause

Death Notes

7. Create Text Scheme and View Results So Far

Now press OK. When you do this, the new text scheme you have specified
is created and added to the list of text schemes. You should be able to
see it in the list of text schemes in the Text tab of the Diagram
Options dialog, and it should be selected at this point. Keeping it
selected, press the Apply button. The Diagram Window is now using your
new text scheme. Confirm that the results are what you would expect.
Notice that within the Text tab, My First
Text Scheme is showing in the Current Text Scheme box.

8. Modify Scheme and Change Font and Styles

At present, all the lines in the text boxes are in the same colour and
font. We will now make changes to improve the look. Assuming that you
are still in the Text tab of the Diagram Options dialog, and My
First Text Scheme is still selected, click on the Edit button.
This opens the Edit Text Scheme dialog again. This time instead of
creating a new text scheme you are modifying an existing one.

If we wished we could add more data items at this point (or any other
kind of item); but instead we will modify the font and style of the
scheme.

Let us assume that we want the first item - name - in each box to be in
a large font and we want its colour to be determined by the sex of the
person (e.g. blue for males and red for females).

As Name is the first item, we can set its font details by changing the
initial font. So click on the Select button to the right of the Initial
Font field, near the top of the Edit Text Scheme dialog. Choose Arial as
the font, choose Bold as the Font Style, and set the size to 12. Notice
that the Allow Colour Override box is ticked. Leave this ticked, leave
the font colour as black, and press OK.

The Initial Font will apply throughout the text scheme until a font
change item is encountered. We want to use these font details for the
first item only – that is, Name. So we need to add a font change
immediately after the Name item. Double-click now on <Font change
(style, text colour etc)> in the Available Items list. When you do
this, the Font dialog will appear again. This time select Arial, Regular
8 at the font type, style and size. Make sure that Allow
Colour Override is unticked this time (it should be unticked by
default). Choose Green as the colour, and press OK. The font change
items is added to the end of the items in the Items Used list. Make sure
that it is selected and click on the Move Up arrow button until it is positioned second in the list, just after
the Name field, and before the Name (a.k.a.) field.

As the Allow Colour Override box was unchecked for this font, all lines
in the text box except the Name field will always be green. The colour
of the Name field however will be black unless it is overridden. You can
override that colour (in the Boxes tab of the Diagram Options dialog), and
specify that you want the colour of these lines to be determined by some
condition (e.g. in the example mentioned, the sex of the Individual
concerned). See the Boxes tab for how to do that.

9. Add Vertical Gap

To make the Name stand out a little from the other details, we will now
add a little extra spacing between it and the other fields. Double-click
on <Vertical Gap> in the Available Items list. This time no dialog
appears. An item labeled <gap> is simply added to the Items Used
list. Select this item (if not already selected) and use the Move Up
arrow button to move it up to second place - just below the Name item
and just after the font change item. By default, the gap is very small
(0.06”), but you can change this if you want to (select it and click
Edit).

10. Picture Marker

A final consideration is pictures. You can specify in the Pictures tab
of the Diagram Options dialog whether or not you want pictures to
display; and if so, whether you want them to the side of the text or
within the text. When you choose the Within the Text option, Family
Historian has to decide where the pictures should go. If there were no
Picture Marker in the current text scheme, Family Historian would
actually place the picture below all the available text. But you may
prefer it to go elsewhere. In this example, we will place the picture
marker just below the Name field.

Double-click on the <Picture Marker> item in the Available Items
list to add it to the Items Used list, and then use the Move Up arrow to
move the <Picture Marker> to just below the Name field.

The Picture Marker has no effect if pictures are not displayed, or if
they are displayed to the side of the text.

11. Save Changes and View Results

If you have followed all these steps, the Items Used list should now
look like this:

Name

<picture marker>

<font = Arial, 8 pt; text colour is Green>

<gap>

Name (a.k.a.)

Birth

Birth Notes

Marriage

Marriage Notes

Spouse Name (wife) if ‘One Box Per Marriage’

Spouse Name (husband) if ‘One Box Per Marriage’

Death

Death Cause

Death Notes

Now press OK. When you do this, the changes you have made to the new
text scheme are applied. If the scheme you were editing was the one
currently being used in the Diagram Window you should be able to see the
changes you made instantly reflected in the Diagram Window. Check these
changes now and confirm that the results are what you would expect. At
this point, the colour of the Name may or may not depend on the sex, and
even if it does, it probably will not be blue for males and red for
females. The colour of the Name field will depend on what conditions (if
any) you have associated with the Text Colour feature in the Boxes tab.
However, the Name field should in any case be in bold, and should be
larger than the other text in the box, all of which should be green.

Tip: The best way to learn how to create text schemes is
to experiment. And the best way to do that is to pick a diagram that
contains a good set of people, zoomed in enough so that you can read the
text. As soon as you have created your text scheme, even before you have
added much detail to it, save it and use the Apply button in the Text
tab of the Diagram Options dialog to make it the current scheme. Then
move the Diagram Options dialog to one side, and edit the scheme. As you
make changes you can press the Apply button within the Edit Text Scheme
dialog itself to instantly see the results of your changes reflected in
the Diagram Window. Using this approach you can incrementally add
features to your text scheme and see at once what the effect is.
However, be aware that unless you specify otherwise in the text scheme,
you do not usually see anything for an item where there is no data. For
example, if you add baptism details (and don’t specify any ‘No Data’
Text), do not be surprised if there is no difference in the Diagram
Window if none of the people in the diagram have any recorded baptism
events.

title: Create Fact Definition Dialog
text:
Fact Types Dialog

Create Fact Definition Dialog

Create Fact Definition Dialog

This dialog is accessed by clicking the New
button in the Fact Types Dialog.

Fields

Fact Name
Must be unique within its fact set
for facts of its type.

Fact Type
Event or attribute.

Record Type
Individual or Family.
Family facts are typically facts in which both spouses in a couple
are equal participants - e.g. marriage, divorce, engagement, etc.
Individual facts are facts in which one person only is who the
fact is primarily ‘about’ - e.g. birth, death, baptism.

Fact Set

When you create a new kind of fact you must give it a fact set
name. This can be the name of an existing fact set, except that
you cannot use the built-in fact set names, ‘Standard’ and
'Extended Set'. It can also be a new, previously-unused
fact set name. When you create a new fact using a new fact set
name, you are effectively creating that new fact set at the same
time.

Click on the down arrow to select from a list of existing fact
sets.

If you are creating a new custom fact and don’t know what to
call the fact set, you could just call it ‘Custom’. You can
always change it at a later date. If you think other people
might be interested in sharing the new fact definitions you are
creating, you should try to group your new fact definitions
sensibly by giving them meaningful fact set names (e.g.
‘Military’, ‘Medical’, ‘Christian’, ‘Islamic’ etc). Later you
can export these new fact sets for others to import - see Importing and Exporting Fact Sets.

Current project only
Tick this box if the new fact definition is for the current
project only (i.e. you are adding it to a project level fact
set). To learn more about project level fact sets, see Work
with Fact Sets.

title: Create Family Record
text:
Fact Types Dialog

Create Family Record

When you add a Family fact (event or
attribute) for an Individual, you
have to specify which family record the fact relates to. This is because
the fact will be stored in the family record. You can either specify an
existing family record (by specifying the spouse), or you can create a
new Family record. If you do so, this dialog is displayed.

At this point you can, if you wish, specify the spouse in the new
Family record. This can be an existing person that you select, or
a new person whose name you provide. You do not have to specify
the spouse however. You can click Create
to create a new Family record even if you do not know who the other
spouse is or was.

Family facts are normally displayed with a red circle
icon in the Facts tab of
the Property Box, in contrast to Individual facts which are normally
displayed with a blue circle.

title: Creating and Deleting Fact Sets
text:
Fact Types Dialog

Creating and Deleting Fact Sets

There are two ways to create a fact set. One way is to clone an
existing fact set, which you can do in the Fact Sets Dialog. You can also create a fact set
by creating a new fact definition, and giving it the name of your new
fact set. Thereafter, you can add more fact definitions to that fact set
by simply creating more new fact definitions and giving them all the
same new fact set name. You can even move existing fact definitions to
the new fact set from other fact sets, by changing their fact set name
to be that of the new fact set. The only exception to this is that you
cannot move fact definitions into, or out of, the built-in fact sets,
Standard and Extended Set.

There is no limit to the number of fact sets that you can have
installed at any one time, or to the number of fact definitions within
any given fact set.

There are two ways to delete a fact set. Custom fact sets can be
deleted in the Fact Sets
Dialog.The alternative is to simply delete all the fact
definitions that belong to that set, or move them to other fact sets.
You cannot delete built-in fact sets. You can hide fact definitions in
built-in fact sets, and you can modify them if you wish to, but you
cannot delete them.

See Work with Fact
Sets for more information about fact sets, and how to create,
delete or modify fact definitions. See also and Importing and Exporting Fact Sets.

title: Customizing Fan Chart Content
text:
Fan Chart Dialog

Customizing Fan Chart Content

This topic is for advanced and technically-minded
users

The text content of fan charts can be customized by clicking on the
'Custom' option in the Contents field of the Fan
Chart Dialog. When this option is selected a
window is opened displaying the 'Custom Fan Chart Contents' dialog where
custom text content can be specified. The Edit
button, to the right of the Contents field (normally disabled) becomes
enabled when 'Custom' is selected, allowing the custom text contents to
be edited.

Custom content for fan charts is specified using Family Historian expressions
- that is, data
references and/or functions.
Internally, even standard options are generated using expressions.
A good starting-point is to look at the expressions used to generate
standard content.

Expressions Used for Standard Content Options

The standard options for fan charts (discussed in more detail in the Fan Chart Dialog page) are the
following:

Name Only

Dates

Ahnentafel Numbers

Ahnentafel & Dates

Blank

Family Historian uses the following expressions to generate content for
these standard content options...

Name Only:

%INDI.NAME%

Dates:

%INDI.NAME%

=ExistsText(%INDI%, "(" . LifeDates2(%INDI%,STD) . ")")

Ahnentafel:

=ExistsText(%INDI%,
Text(AhnentafelNumber(%CUR_BASE%,%INDI%,1)) . ". " . %INDI.NAME%)

Ahnentafel & Dates:

=ExistsText(%INDI%,
Text(AhnentafelNumber(%CUR_BASE%,%INDI%,1)) . ". " . %INDI.NAME%)

=ExistsText(%INDI%, "(" . LifeDates2(%INDI%,STD) . ")")

Modifying the 'Name Only' Expression

The expression used for standard content options are just examples of what
can be done. But they can also form the starting point for
customizations. For example, if you want to see a person's record,
immediately following their name, you could use the expression used for
the "Name Only" option, and add a function to return a person's record id
(the RecordId function) - like this:

%INDI.NAME% =RecordId()

The first part ("%INDI.NAME%") will be substituted with each person's
name. Then there is a space. Then the function "=RecordId"
will be replaced with the person's record id. So, for example, in
the Family Historian Sample project, a fan chart which included Susan
Dowling (whose record id is 3), would display this for her:

Susan Isabel Dowling 3

The normal convention in Family Historian is to put the person's record id
within square brackets. If that's what you want, you might think
that you just need to change the expression to put square brackets around
"=RecordId()" - i.e. like this:

%INDI.NAME% [=RecordId()]

... and actually that works fine for Susan Isabel Dowling. The text
in her segment of the fan chart now looks like this:

Susan Isabel Dowling [3]

The problem with it, however, is that segments which should be blank (i.e.
for unknown ancestors) now have 2 square brackets in them - which is
probably not what you want. What is needed is a way of telling
Family Historian: if the person exists, use the above expression to
display content for them. But if the person's doesn't exist, don't
put out anything for them. The ExistsText
function can be used to achieve that. This function takes 2
parameters. The first is a data reference. The second is
text. If the data reference matches anything, the text is
output. Otherwise, nothing is output.

We can pass a data reference as a parameter to a function that expects
text. And we can pass a call to a function as a textual parameter,
if the function returns text. However, in our example, we want to
pass an expression ("%INDI.NAME% [=RecordId()]") that is actually
made up of 4 parts. These are, in order, a data reference, constant
text, a function call, and more constant text. "Constant text" just
means any text that is not a data reference or a function. Constant
text is text that is output unchanged.

The 4 parts are:

%INDI.NAME%

" ["

RecordId()

"]"

When passing constant text to a function you must always put it inside
double quotes. However, data references and function calls must not
be put within double quotes.

You may have noticed that there is no equals sign, '=', in front of
"RecordId()"? Ordinarily, the start of a function call has to be
signalled by an equals sign. However, if call to a function is
nested within (i.e. forming part of a parameter to) another function call,
it must not have an equals sign in front of it.

If you want to pass more than item of text to a function that is expecting
a single text value as a parameter, you must use the Family Historian
concatenation operator to join them together. Family Historian uses
the character that Americans call a period and Britons call a full-stop,
as concatenation operator. Do not assume that whenever you see a
period/full-stop within an expression, it is the concatenation
operator. It is used for different things in different
contexts. And if used within constant text, it will just be what it
usually is - a period/full-stop. But here, it functions as a
concatenation operator (see Operators
for more on Family Historian operators). So, using the concatenation
operator, the text that we will need to pass as the the second parameter
to the ExistsText function will be this:

%INDI.NAME% . " [" . =RecordId() . "]"

Can you spot the 3 occurrences of the concatenation operator? A
space has been added before and after each of them to make it easier to
read. Family Historian will ignore these (although it won't ignore a
space within constant text, of course).

So that's going to be the second parameter. What of the first
parameter? For that an expression is needed which references each
person. %INDI% is the appropriate data reference for that.
Putting it all together gives this expression:

=ExistsText(%INDI%, %INDI.NAME% . " [" .
RecordId() . "]")

Try it. You should find segments for unknown ancestors are
blank. But segments where the ancestors are known, now have the
ancestor's name, followed by a space and then their record within square
brackets.

Notes ON The 'Dates' STANDARD

This option uses the following expressions:

%INDI.NAME%

=ExistsText(%INDI%, "(" . LifeDates2(%INDI%,STD) . ")")

The second expression uses the ExistsText
function again, as well as the LifeDates2
function. The latter takes 2 parameters. The second of these is
"STD". This appears in the expression without double quotes around
it. This is because it is not constant text. See the LifeDates2
function page for an explanation of the meaning of this parameter value.

%INDI.NAME% is a data reference that designates a person's name.
%INDI% is a data reference that designates an Individual record.
Note the use of the concatenation operator again.

Notes on The 'Ahnentafel' standard option

This option uses the following expression:

=ExistsText(%INDI%,
Text(AhnentafelNumber(%CUR_BASE%,%INDI%,1)) . ". " . %INDI.NAME%)

This expression uses the ExistsText
function again, as well as the Text
function, and the AhnentafelNumber
function. The concatenation operator is used here too (twice -
what may look like the second of three occurrences is actually a
period/full-stop appearing as part of constant text). The Text
function is used to convert the numeric value, returned by the
AhnentafelNumber function, to text.

In addition to %INDI% and %INDI.NAME%, the expression uses another data
reference: %CUR_BASE%. This last is an example of a special kind
of data reference called a "Contextual Data Reference".
Contextual data references are data references which only have meaning
in their specific context of use. If you took a fan chart to
pieces by right-clicking on it, and choose 'Ungroup' from the Grouping
submenu, you could then right-click on any of the text pie shapes and
click 'Format' to view its properties. On the 'Data' tab, you
should see the value for 'Base Person'. This might reference a
particular Individual or (depending on how the fan chart was built), it
might be "Diagram Root". Most diagrams have a diagram root which
you can view and change if you wish to, by right-clicking on the
background of the diagram and selecting 'Diagram Root'.

For more information about the %CUR_BASE% data reference, see the
section "Contextual Data References" in Understanding
Data References.

Next Steps

Hopefully the above examples should give you some ideas of how to
approach creating custom text. To learn more, see the various
sections on functions (starting with Understanding
Functions), and also Understanding
Data References. For more advice and tips, consider posting
questions at the Family Historian User Group website, at https://www.fhug.org.uk.

Troubleshooting

What happens if you make a mistake when constructing an expression?
It is very easily done. If you were to accidentally miss out a
comma, or a closing bracket, or use the wrong number of quotes, there is
every chance that your expression will not work. If you generate a
fan chart with your custom text, the fan chart will appear but the text
will be wrong. You may see some text, but it will almost certainly
not be the text that you were expecting. A good strategy, in that
case, is to try to identify where the problem is occurring, by copying
your expression into a text editor, like Notepad; and then testing the
various parts separately, to see if they work or not. With each
test, you have to generate a new fan chart, using the custom expression
that you are testing.

For example, the following expression contains 2 deliberate
errors:

=ExistsText(%INDI%,
Text(AhnentafellNumber(%CUR_BASE%,%INDI%,1)) . ". " . %INDI.NAM%)
<<
Caution - Contains errors

If you try it, you will find that it doesn't work. Instead, the
expression is output unchanged in every segment of the fan chart. So
how do you work out what the problem is?

One good place to start is to count the round brackets. The number
of opening round brackets should normally match the number of closing
round brackets. The only exception is if the round brackets occur
within constant text, in which case the numbers do not have to match; so
watch out for that.

What about double quotes? Is every opening quote matched with a
closing quote, and vice versa?

If that all looks OK (which it is in the example above), try testing
sections separately. The parameter to the Text function is
this: "AhnentafellNumber(%CUR_BASE%,%INDI%,1)" (without the quotes).

Try it on its own to see if it returns each person's ahnentafel
numbers. You will need to add an equal sign on the front of the
function if you are going to use it on its own (see earlier discussion of
functions and equals signs). So enter this as a custom expression:

=AhnentafellNumber(%CUR_BASE%,%INDI%,1)
<<
Caution - contains error

If you create a fan chart with this custom text, you will find that it
doesn't work. You get the whole expression output unchanged
again. So there is already a mistake here. In fact the mistake in
this case is that the function name has been misspelled. There is
only one 'l' in AhnentafelNumber. Now try the same thing again, with
spelling corrected:

=AhnentafelNumber(%CUR_BASE%,%INDI%,1)

If you try it, you should find that you get a fan chart with just numbers
(and some segments may be blank). This is actually correct.
You specified that you wanted to see Ahnentafel Numbers. You didn't
specify anything else. And ahnentafel numbers is what you got.
So progress has been made. That expression now works.

What about the rest of the expression? If you swap our corrected
expression back into the original, does it now work? The answer is -
it doesn't. There is another mistake:

=ExistsText(%INDI%,
Text(AhnentafelNumber(%CUR_BASE%,%INDI%,1)) . ". " . %INDI.NAM%)

<< Caution - still contains an error

Try swapping out "AhnentafelNumber(%CUR_BASE%,%INDI%,1)" from the
expression, with a single word of constant (e.g. "Hello"). This
simplifies the expression and makes it easier to test. We now have
this:

=ExistsText(%INDI%, Text("Hello") . ". " .
%INDI.NAM%)
<< Caution - contains error

Does that work? No. It doesn't. What about this:

=ExistsText(%INDI%, Text("Hello"))

Actually the Text function is not needed in this context. You could
just as well have written that as this:

=ExistsText(%INDI%, "Hello")

But you're putting these together for testing purposes, so use whichever
is most useful for that. These 2 expressions do the same
thing. They both put out the word 'Hello' in every box where there
is a record. If that's what you see (and if you copy it correctly
you will) - it works! So the problem isn't there. It must be
somewhere in the remaining part of the expression. It could be that
you have too few brackets or concatenation operators or quotes or
percentage signs round data references ... or too few. In this case
it is none of those things. The problem is that %INDI.NAM% is not a
valid data reference. There is a missing 'E' on the end. It
should be %INDI.NAME%. The Custom Fan Chart Contents window has a
button: Insert Data Reference.
This opens the Data Reference Assistant dialog, to help you insert data
references. Using the Data Reference Assistant dialog should reduce
the risk of misspelled data references.

Once you have identified all the errors, put it all together again
(carefully! you don't want to introduce any errors at this point).
You should now have this:

=ExistsText(%INDI%,
Text(AhnentafelNumber(%CUR_BASE%,%INDI%,1)) . ". " . %INDI.NAME%)

If you create a fan chart with this custom text, you should now find that
it works, and shows each person's name, preceded by their ahnentafel
number.

This example illustrates that if you take a methodical approach, you
should be able to track down what the problem is, when a custom expression
does not work.

title: Data Entry Helper Dialogs
text:
Property Box

Data Entry Helper Dialogs

Many types of fields have data entry helper dialogs associated with
them. These are dialogs which provide help in selecting values, or
in constructing complex values. In most cases you can open the
helper dialog by double-clicking on the field itself. Some fields,
have a little button with 3 dots on it, which you can click to open the
helper dialog. In most cases, this button only appears when you
click on the field itself, or tab to it, or if you move the mouse over
the field. In the case of note fields, there is a bar instead of a
button (with 3 dots halfway up it) - and in this case, the bar is
always visible to the right end of the note field. Name fields
have a link to the right of them ("more...") which you can click on to
open their helper dialog.

The table below lists field types and their associated helper
dialogs. Notice that whereas some helper dialogs are only ever
used with their associated fields, and can only be accessed from fields
of that type, some helper dialogs, such as the Note
Window, are not like that, and may be accessed in other ways.

Field Type
Helper Dialog

Name
Names
& Titles Dialog

Date
Date Entry Assistant
Dialog

Age
Age Entry Assistant
Dialog

Place
Work with Data Dialog (places
version)

Address

Addresses can be edited in the Memo Window, or selected using
the Work with Data Dialog
(addresses version)

Note

Note Window

Latitude/Longitude

Latitude & Longitude
Dialog

title: Date Entry Assistant Dialog
text:
Data Entry Helper Dialogs

Date Entry Assistant Dialog

Date Entry Assistant Dialog

The Date Entry Assistant Dialog is available for use with all date
fields, to make it easy to enter complex date information. You can
access it by double-clicking on any date field, or by clicking on the
little button ... to the right of the date
field.

The dialog has 5 tabs for entering 5 different kinds of date
specifiers:

Date

Period

Date
Phrase

Range

Quarter
Date

With fact dates (dates of events or attributes, displayed in
the Facts tab of the Property
Box), you can optionally also enter a separate
sort date.

title: Date Entry Assistant Dialog: Date Phrase Tab
breadcrumb: Date Entry Assistant Dialog: Date Phrase Tab
text:
Date Entry Assistant Dialog

Date Entry Assistant Dialog: Date Phrase Tab

Use a date phrase when you don�t know the exact date, but have some
information which gives helpful information about it. For example, if
all you know about a person�s death is that �it occurred less than 2
months after his wife died�, you can record that note as a date phrase.

If you wish to do so, you can optionally also provide a date, as your
interpretation of the date phrase.

See Simple Date
Fields for help on the date fields.

With fact dates (dates of events or attributes, displayed in
the Facts tab of the Property
Box), you can optionally also enter a separate
sort date.

title: Date Entry Assistant Dialog: Date Tab
breadcrumb: Date Entry Assistant Dialog: Date Tab
text:
Date Entry Assistant Dialog

Date Entry Assistant Dialog: Date Tab

The Date tab is used for entering simple dates.

Fields

Qualifier

Approximate
means the date is not exact.
Calculated
means the date has been calculated mathematically - for
example, from an event date and age.
Estimated
means that the date has been estimated based on an
algorithm, using some other event date.

With fact dates (dates of events or attributes, displayed in
the Facts tab of the Property
Box), you can optionally also enter a separate
sort date.

See Simple Date
Fields for help on the actual date fields. See How to Enter Dates for tips on entering
dates.

title: Date Entry Assistant Dialog: Period Tab
breadcrumb: Date Entry Assistant Dialog: Period Tab
text:
Date Entry Assistant Dialog

Date Entry Assistant Dialog: Period Tab

Use the Period tab to specify a period of time (for example, "John
Smith was resident in Tunbridge Wells from 3rd June 1971 to July 1985").

Use From on its own if you don’t know when the period ended.
Use To on its own if you don’t know when the period began. Use
both if you know both.

See Simple Date
Fields for help on the actual date fields.

Do not confuse specifying a period with specifying a range (see the Range
tab).

With fact dates (dates of events or attributes, displayed in
the Facts tab of the Property
Box), you can optionally also enter a separate
sort date.

title: Date Entry Assistant Dialog: Quarter Date Tab
breadcrumb: Date Entry Assistant Dialog: Quarter Date Tab
text:
Date Entry Assistant Dialog

Date Entry Assistant Dialog: Quarter Date Tab

A quarter date is a date like �Q1 1978�. It means the first 3 months
of 1978. �Q2 1978� is the next 3 months (April to June 1978) and so on.
A quarter date is really a special kind of range (see the Range tab). Use a quarter date when you don�t
know exactly when a date occurred, but you do know the quarter in which
it occurred.

With fact dates (dates of events or attributes, displayed in
the Facts tab of the Property
Box), you can optionally also enter a separate
sort date.

title: Date Entry Assistant Dialog: Range Tab
breadcrumb: Date Entry Assistant Dialog: Range Tab
text:
Date Entry Assistant Dialog

Date Entry Assistant Dialog: Range Tab

A range allows you to specify a date, albeit imprecisely (for example,
"John Smith died some time between 1941 and 1943"). Do not confuse this
with specifying a period (see the Period tab).

If you know the year, but not the month or day (or the year and month
but not the day), you do not have to use a range. It is easier and
better to use the Date
tab, and omit the missing details.

See Simple Date
Fields for help on the date fields.

With fact dates (dates of events or attributes, displayed in
the Facts tab of the Property
Box), you can optionally also enter a separate
sort date.

title: Date Entry Assistant Dialog: Separate Sort Date
text:
Date Entry Assistant Dialog

Date Entry Assistant Dialog: Separate Sort Date

When you specify a date, Family Historian will use this date for
sorting purposes, unless you indicate that you do not want it to do
this, by specifying a separate sort date. Why might you
want to do that? Most of the time, you won't. Suppose, for
example, that you have specified that a child was born, died and buried
in 1987. If the only date you provided for each of these 3 events
was 1987, you might think that you would need a sort date to specify
which order these events should appear in - but you don't. This is
because ordinary fact types ('Birth', 'Death' and 'Burial' in these
cases) have something called a Normal Time Frame associated
with them. You can also associate a Normal Time Frame with custom
fact types that you create. The possible types of Normal Time
Frame are:

Pre-Birth

Birth

Shortly After Birth

Life

Marriage

Post-Marriage

Death

Post-Death

The Normal Time Frames for Birth, Death and Burial are 'Birth', 'Death'
and 'Post-Death'. Unless the dates stored indicate otherwise,
Family Historian will order death events after birth events, and
post-death events after death events. Other events are ordered as
you would expect. The practical consequence is that in many cases,
there is no need to specify a sort date - even if the ordering is not
determined by the date alone - because Family Historian will do the
right thing anyway, based on the Normal Time Frame of the events in
question. To learn more about Normal Time Frames, see Work
With Fact Sets.

Even if the correct ordering of events is not determined by the Normal
Time Frame, there may still be no need to use a sort date. Suppose
for example, you know that a person, Michael, had two children, John and
Paula. Suppose you don't know when they were born but you know
that John is the older of the two. In that case, you still don't
have to use a sort date. You can simply show Michael's record in
the Focus Window, and use the Move Up
and Move Down buttons on the main toolbar, to set the ordering of the
children, so that John comes first. You can do the same thing with
spouses, to specify their ordering. You can also change the
ordering of events in the Facts tab of the Property Box, using the Move
buttons on the toolbar below the fact list, if the events are attached
to the same record, and the ordering of those events cannot be
determined by their Normal Time Frame, or by their date.

What this shows is that most of the time, there is no need to use a
sort date. However, occasionally, the required ordering of facts
and events cannot be determined in any other way. And in those
cases, you can get the desired result by using a sort date. When
you specify a sort date, you must specify a year, at a minimum.
You can also enter a month and year - and leave the day field
blank. Or you can specify a day, month and year (and even a BC
date if you wish). When you specify a sort date, you are not
saying that the event occurred on that date. You are merely
indicating that you wish that event to be treated as if it occurred on
the sort date, for ordering purposes. Sort dates are always
entered as dates in the Gregorian calendar.

Sometimes you may want to enter a sort date on its own - that is,
without entering any other kind of date. To do this, select the Date
tab. Leave the year field blank, tick Separate Sort
Date and enter the sort date you require.

If you want to clear all dates, including the sort date, untick Separate
Sort Date. Select the Date tab. Leave the
year field blank and press OK. You will be asked to
confirm that you wish to clear all date information.

Sort dates are not displayed on the Main
tab of the Property Box, unless you open the Date
Entry Assistant Dialog to view them. They are displayed more
prominently however on the Facts tab
of the Property Box. Any date which has an associated sort date
has a "(s)" suffix, in the first column of the Fact List on that tab.
Also, the sort date is displayed as a link, immediately after Date
field, in the bottom half of the tab. Clicking on this link opens
the Date Entry Assistant Dialog.

See Simple Date
Fields for help on the actual date fields. See How to Enter Dates for tips on entering dates.

General Topics

Date Formats

Some of the settings in the General tab of Preferences
affect how dates are displayed. The most important of these
are:

Preferred Standard Date Format

Preferred Short Date Format

Use 'circa' for approximate dates

To learn more about these options, see Preferences Dialog: General
tab.

You can also make more specific choices about how you want dates to be
formatted in particular contexts, such as reports. The choices you
make about dates in Preferences, will affect how the more
specific choices about dates, are interpreted. We will use
examples to illustrate how this works.

There are 15 different qualifiers that apply to all dates, although
only 6 of these are normally used in reports. These are:

The most abbreviated format is Abbrev(4).

Of these, the last 3 have a special role in that they are designed to

title: Delete Project Dialog
text:
Project Window

Delete Project Dialog

When you delete a project, the entire project
folder is deleted - including all files and all subfolders. Do not
assume that Family Historian will only delete files that it has added to
the project folder itself. When you delete a project all files
in the project folder and its subfolders, will be deleted.

The Delete Project Dialog lists all the files that will be deleted.
You are strongly recommended to check all of these files carefully. If
you are at all in doubt, you should not proceed with the delete.

If you wish to go ahead with the deletion, tick the check box at the
bottom of the dialog box where it says "Please confirm deletion". When
you do this, the Delete All button is
enabled, and you can then click it to delete the project folder. If your
project is stored on a local hard drive with a recycle bin capability,
the entire project folder is deleted by being moved to the recycle bin.
That way if you later change your mind about the deletion, you can
restore the folder from the recycle bin, as long as you have not
previously 'emptied' it.

If your project is located on a hard drive which does not have a
recycle bin capability, it will not be possible to 'undo' the deletion.

title: Designing Source Templates
text:
Sources and Source Templates

Designing Source Templates

You can create your own source templates if you wish to. To do
this, create a source template definition in the Source
Template Definitions Dialog, and thereafter you can add it to any
project as-needed. When designing a source template, this page
looks at some of the issues you may wish to consider.

What Kind of Source?

The first decision to make, when designing a source template, is to
decide what kind of source your template is for. Are you designing
a template for a Spanish birth certificate? Or for birth
certificates from any country at any time? Or are you designing a
template for certificates of any kind? Different genealogists will
take different approaches on this and there is no definitive right
answer (you can see discussions and debates on these and related topics
in the Family
Historian User Group website). Depending on your answer, you
will wish to add different fields to your source template. For
example, if your source is a cemetery, you might wish to add these
fields:

Cemetery Name

Cemetery Location

As the information gleaned from a cemetery is likely to come from
gravestones, you might also add two further fields:

Gravestone Name

Gravestone Location

If we assume that you want one Source record for each cemetery, you
probably would want to make these last 2 fields citation-specific
fields (i.e. you tick the Citation box when you create the
field). What this means is that the information about the
gravestone will not be stored in the Source record, but will be attached
specifically to each citation.

Don't Assume You Need Fields to Record Transcript Information

It might seem that if your source is a form, you should have one field
in your source template definition for each field on the form.
This would be true if you were planning to use these fields to record
transcript information - and you can use source template fields for this
purpose if you want to. But source template fields are not
ideally-suited for that purpose, and in general we recommend that you
don't take this approach. Instead, we recommend that all
transcript information should be recorded separately in Source records'
Text from Source fields, or (if the transcript is not
applicable to the Source record as a whole, but is citation-specific) in
citation-specific Text from Source fields. All Source
records and all citations - whether the source is generic or templated -
have Text from Source fields. These are designed
specifically for storing transcripts. They are long note fields
which can be edited and viewed in the Notes Window. The best and
easiest way of recording transcripts is to make use of the Note Window's
autotext feature, which allows you to design and re-use simple
forms. A form in this case will typically consist of a table with
2 columns, with text labels in the first column, and a blank second
column. Family Historian comes with some pre-designed autotext
forms for transcripts. You are recommended to copy these and adapt
them to your own purposes. You can very quickly and easily create
and save autotext for any document or form, and thereafter use that
autotext for all transcripts of documents or forms of that type.

If you decide that you will use autotext for recording transcript
information within Text from Source fields (if you're
planning to record transcripts at all), it simplifies the process of
designing source templates considerably and also reduces considerably
the number of fields you are likely to need to add to your source
template definitions. When choosing the fields for your source
templates, you now only need to ask yourself - what fields do I need to
include to ensure that source citations can be recorded accurately,
giving enough information to allow anyone to find the original
information referred to?

title: Diagram Box Icons Dialog
text:
More Dialog Boxes...

Diagram Box Icons Dialog

Diagram Box Icons Dialog

The Diagram Box Icons dialog is used to select and/or manage diagram
box icons. It can be accessed from the Diagram
Options Dialog: Boxes Tab (the Diagram Options dialog is accessed
from the Diagram menu, which is displayed when the Diagram Window is
active). Alternatively, it can also be accessed by clicking either
Import Diagram Box Icons or Export
Diagram Box Icons, both of which are accessible from the Import/Export
submenu of the application's File menu.

Websites for hotels, or bed-and-breakfast accommodation, sometimes use
little icons to show what features are included with the room. For
example, a little WiFi icon might be displayed to show that the room
comes with free WiFi. You can use similar icons with boxes in Family
Historian diagrams. For example, you might have a ‘Work-in- Progress’
record flag that you set for records that you are currently working on.
You could perhaps put a ‘Men at Work’ icon below boxes where this record
flag is set. Or you could use a ship icon to mark people whose
occupation is 'sailor'.

A number of standard icons are provided with Family Historian.
But you can also install your own custom icons if you wish. The
recommended format for custom icons is SVG. Free SVG icons are
readily available on the Internet (search for "Free SVG Icons").
You can also create your own custom SVG icons, or modify existing SVG
icons, using standard graphics software, such as the free graphics tool,
Inkscape.

Any custom icons you import will be assigned the category 'Custom'.

Fields

Import
Import one or more icon files. If possible, imported files
should be in SVG format. However, as well as SVG, the
