using %INDI.~FATH[1]>% in the Relation Expression field to map
to his father, why not simply leave the Relation Expression blank,
and choose Arthur Smith's father in the Base Person
field? Actually you could do that, and for many
purposes that might well be the sensible thing to do. But
for some complex objects like fan charts, the Relation Expression
can be very useful. See 'Using Relation Expressions When
Creating Complex Objects' below.

Please note that if you have a multiple selection (that is, have
selected multiple shapes to format), and different text boxes or
pie-shapes-with-text have different values for Relation
Expression, the field will be greyed and simply display the value
'(multiple)'.

Insert Data Reference

Click this button to open the Data Reference Assistant Dialog,
which allows you to select the type of data item you wish to refer
to, and automatically generates Data References for you, for
insertion into the Relation Expression field. This button
will be greyed if the Relation Expression field is greyed.

Using Relation Expressions When Creating Complex Objects

The easiest way to understand the role of the Relation
Expression field, is to look at an example of how it is used -
the fan chart. If you create a fan chart, or insert one into an
existing diagram, you will find if you right-click on it and choose Format that, amongst other things, you can
change the text in the Text tab, and you can change the Base
Person in the Data tab. But you can't change the Relation
Expression field in the Data tab - it is greyed with value
'(multiple)'. Why is that?

When you choose the Format option for a fan chart, it will no doubt
seem to you that are 'formatting' one object - the fan chart
itself. And of course in a sense you are. But a fan chart is
a group object. if you make any changes, what actually happens is
that these changes will be applied to all relevant objects in the
group. A typical fan chart might contain 31
pie-shape-with-texts. All 31 of these have exactly the same
text. They also have exactly the same Base Person.
Because they share the same Base Person, you can change the Base Person
for all of them by simply changing the Base Person for the fan chart as
a whole. There is no need to ungroup the fan chart and change each
pie-shape-with-text separately. And similarly, because they share
the same text, you can easily change that text for the whole fan chart -
again with no need to ungroup it. It is the Relation Expression
that makes this possible. Each pie-shape-with-text has a different
value for its Relation Expression, and it is this fact which allows one
pie shape to be 'about' the father of the centre person, another to be
about the mother of the centre person, another to be about their
father's father, and so on.

If you want to see this for yourself, simply create a fan chart (or
insert one into an existing diagram), right-click on it, and on the
dropdown menu that appears, click Ungroup (on
the Grouping submenu). Each pie shape will be shown selected, with
separate selection markers. Click on the background of the diagram
to unselect them all. Then right-click on one of the pie shapes
and choose Format. Select the
Data tab. Note that the Relation Expression field is ungreyed, and
note its value. Now do the same thing with other pie shapes.
You should see that they all have different Relation Expression values.

If you want to form the fan chart back into a group again, the easiest
way is to zoom right back and click-and-drag on the background of the
Diagram Window to draw a stretchy box round all the pie shapes,
selecting them all. Then right-click on any one of them, and
choose the Group command. If
you then want to delete the fan chart, simply select it and press the Delete key.

Using the above techniques, you can create your own complex objects -
perhaps a new style of fan chart, or some other kind of object
altogether. You can save your object as a custom diagram type or
as a saved chart. Remember that diagram objects, however complex,
can be easily copied and pasted from one chart to another; so saving one
or more useful objects in a saved chart, can be a good way of making
them available to be copied into other charts and diagrams.
However, saved charts are not accessible from different projects,
whereas custom diagram types can be used in all projects.

title: Diagram Shape Format Dialog: Image Tab
breadcrumb: Diagram Shape Format Dialog: Image Tab
text:
Diagram Shape Format Dialog

Diagram Shape Format Dialog: Image Tab

This tab is available when you format Image shapes
(see Diagram Elements). When
you resize a picture, by default the aspect ratio of the original image
is preserved. If you do not want this, untick 'Lock aspect ratio'.

If you want a picture to appear partially transparent (like a
watermark), use the 'Opacity' field with. A value of 50% means that
image is partially transparent. 0% means that the image is not
visible at all. A value of 100% means that the image will be completely
opaque (not even partially transparent).

Remember you can order any diagram item, so you can move a picture
behind all other diagram items if you wish.

title: Diagram Shape Format Dialog: Line and Fill Tab
breadcrumb: Diagram Shape Format Dialog: Line and Fill Tab
text:
Diagram Shape Format Dialog

Diagram Shape Format Dialog: Line and Fill Tab

This tab is available when you format any shape (see Diagram
Elements). When used with rectangles and
pictures, the �line� is the line that acts as a frame for
the rectangle or picture. Choose �No Line� if you don�t want a frame.

title: Diagram Shape Format Dialog: Shape Tab
breadcrumb: Diagram Shape Format Dialog: Shape Tab
text:
Diagram Shape Format Dialog

Diagram Shape Format Dialog: Shape Tab

Any shape in a diagram (see Diagram
Elements) can be rotated - even group items. To rotate an
item, first select it. When you do this, a little green circle
appears on a line above the item, looking like this: . Click and drag on this green circle
to rotate the item. Alternatively, you can also rotate items by
choosing an appropriate value for the Rotation
field - see below.

Fields

Rotation

Specifies the degree of rotation in degrees (0 to 360) for the
item.

Lock aspect ratio
Control the shape of the item. If
this option is ticked, when you resize the item, the ratio of the
item's width and height will be maintained.

Lock position
If you wish to prevent the item from being accidentally moved or
resized, enable this option. You can click on locked items to
select them, but the selection handles will be grey instead of
white for locked items.

Enabling this option does not prevent the item from being grouped
with other items or deleted. A grouped item can be moved and
resized, even if one or more of its constituent items are locked.
If you wish the group to be locked, you need to set this option
for the group item itself.

Locking a shape can also be useful if you want to align other
shapes with it, or resize other shapes to match its width or
height. See, for example, Diagram
Menu Alignment options for more on this.

title: Diagram Shape Format Dialog: Text Tab
breadcrumb: Diagram Shape Format Dialog: Text Tab
text:
Diagram Shape Format Dialog

Diagram Shape Format Dialog: Text Tab

This tab is available when you format Text Box or Text
Pie shapes (see Diagram Elements).
Text is displayed in a rectangle. You can set the font and also the size
and style (bold, italic, underline, etc) of the text by clicking on the
Font button.

Click on << Insert Data Ref to
insert a reference to a data item. If you choose ‘Individual’ the data
will normally be returned from the Individual who is the diagram root -
if the diagram has an Individual as its root. If the diagram has a
couple as its root, the root is in effect a family record. In that case,
use data references under the ‘Family’ heading.

You change the Diagram Root for any diagram by right-clicking on it and
choosing Diagram Root from the dropdown menu that
appears. It is also possible to pick a different person to
retrieve data from - someone who is not necessarily the diagram
root. See Diagram
Shape Format Dialog: Data Tab to learn more.

You can also set alignment and inner margins on this tab.

If the shapes you are formatting include one or more Text Box shapes, a
Word Wrap tick box allows you to specify whether to wrap long
lines of text or not. This option is only applicable to Text Box
shapes. It is not applicable to Text Pie shapes.

If the shapes you are formatting include one or more Text Pie shapes, a
Text Path field allows you to specify whether text should be
displayed in an arc, within each text pie shape, or should radiate out
from, or in towards, the shape's focal point. This option is only
applicable to Text Pie shapes. It is not applicable to Text Box
shapes.

You are normally recommended to ensure that the bottom
margin is not zero when setting the Text Path for a Text Pie shape to
'Radial' (inwards or outwards). This is particularly important if
you have multiple lines of text. You may need to experiment to get
good results. However, be aware that if you format multiple text
pie shapes at the same time (if, for example, you choose to format an
entire fan chart), the likelihood is that the bottom margin value will
initially be blank. This indicates that the selected text pie
shapes have different bottom margins. If you then set the bottom
margin to some particular value, you will be setting that bottom margin
for all the selected text pie shapes. Within a fan chart, each
generation has a different bottom margin. If you set them all to
the same bottom margin, you are likely to find that some or all of the
fan chart text disappears.

title: The Diagram Window
text:
Workspace Windows

The Diagram Window

Diagram Window (marked in red)

The Diagram Window is opened by clicking on the 'Charts' button on the main toolbar, and
choosing a diagram from the dropdown menu that apears. You can also choose
diagrams from the Charts submenu of the View menu.
You will normally be prompted to confirm the Tree Root Type
(individual or couple), and who the tree root (or roots if a couple)
should be. You can also specify the initial number of generations to
display. If you wish, click on the More Options
link to view and change all Diagram
Options.

There are 4 basic types of tree that can be displayed in a diagram. These
are:

the Ancestors tree

the Descendants tree

the Ancestors and Descendants tree

the All Relatives tree

All of these tree types can be displayed in the Diagrams Window.
To learn more about trees (also known as 'smart trees') and the other
elements of Family Historian diagrams, see Diagram
Elements.

Almost every aspect of the Diagram Window can be configured from the
Diagram Options Dialog. To open the Diagram Options Dialog, click on Options on the Diagram menu.

You can save a configuration of the Diagram Window as a new diagram
type, by clicking on Save Diagram As…
on the Diagram menu, and then selecting Custom Diagram Type.

The Diagram Window has its own menu and toolbar, both of which are only
available when the Diagram Window is active. See Diagram menu for an explanation of the function
of the different commands on this menu.

title: DNA Tools
text:
General Topics

DNA Tools

DNA has become an important part of genealogical research, and Family
Historian has a number of tools which can be used to help you work with
DNA data. These include diagrams and queries, and other tools.
None of the diagrams or queries listed here, require that you have done
any DNA testing, or that you have any DNA information about
anyone. Rather, they show you what you should expect to find, in
terms of shared DNA and DNA matches, if the information you have
recorded within Family Historian is correct. Bear in mind that if
you record that one person is the child of another, Family Historian
will assume that the child is a birth child unless you
specify otherwise by indicating that the child is adopted, fostered,
step or de facto (de facto means that the person was
accepted as the natural child of a parent, even if in fact they
weren't). See also How
to Record Birth Parents Correctly for DNA Purposes.

If you have DNA data, and if the information in a diagram or query
conflicts with the DNA data you have, this indicates that further
investigation is needed to work out where, and in what way the error has
occurred. Most likely, some part of your recorded information is
incorrect. For example, a person who is recorded as a birth child of a
parent, may in fact be the birth child of someone else.

If you have some matching DNA information for two people, you may also
be able to use some of the tools provided here, to help you work out how
they are related. For example, if they share X-DNA, you could use
the Overlapping X Chromosome diagram to work out which side of
the family, they must both belong to.

The Family Historian DNA tools are these:

DNA Diagrams

Shared Y Chromosome

Shared Mitochondrial DNA

Overlapping X Chromosome

Shared Autosomal DNA (Blood Relatives)

DNA Flags

See below

DNA Queries

DNA - Shared Y Chromosome

DNA - Shared Mitochondrial DNA

DNA - Overlapping X Chromosome

DNA - Shared Autosomal DNA (Blood
Relatives)

DNA Attributes

See below

DNA Diagram Tools

Diagram Tools are described in more detail below.
In summary, they consist of the following items:

A DNA Flags Preset in the Boxes tab of Diagram Options

A DNA Relatedness Text Scheme

A DNA Relatedness Text Scheme Item

DNA-Related Diagram Icons

Advanced DNA Tools

See Advanced DNA Tools

DNA Diagrams

Shared Y Chromosome

Only males have a Y-chromosome. The Y-chromosome is transmitted
from father to son nearly unchanged. The Shared Y Chromosome
diagram requires the selection of a male person, and shows the people
who should share a Y-chromosome with that selected person if the
information about their relationships recorded within Family Historian
is correct.

The diagram also shows the appropriate DNA Flags
below each person.

Shared Mitochondrial DNA

DNA exists within a cell's nucleus - but that is not the only place
within a cell that DNA can be found. Cells contain specialized
structures called mitochondria, which generate power for the
cell (they are sometimes compared to batteries). Mitochondria also
contain DNA. For human beings, their nuclear DNA
(DNA from the cell nucleus) comes from both of their parents. But
everyone, male or female, gets their mitochondrial DNA from
their mother alone - and mitochondrial DNA is highly conserved during
transmission (not much subject to mutation). This means that
mitochondrial DNA is a useful way of tracing maternal lineage.

The Shared Mitochondrial DNA diagram shows, for a given
selected person, male or female, who they should share mitochondrial DNA
with, if the information about their relationships recorded within
Family Historian is correct.

The diagram also shows the appropriate DNA Flags
below each person.

Overlapping X Chromosome

Males have a single X-chromosome which they receive from their
mother. Females have two X-chromosomes, one of which comes from
their mother, In both cases, these are subject to random
recombination at each generation, which means that although the
X-chromosome comes from the mother, it is unlikely to be an exact match
of either of the mother's X chromosomes, but rather will have parts of
both of the mother's own X-chromosomes.

Daughters inherit one of their X-chromosomes from their father; and as
the father only has one X-chromosome, this will be passed down pretty
much unchanged.

Although X-chromosome inheritance is more complicated than either
mitochondrial DNA inheritance or Y-chromosome inheritance, it can
nevertheless be useful for tracing and narrowing down possible ancestral
lines. The Overlapping X Chromosome diagram shows, for a
given selected person, male or female, who they should share some parts
of their X-chromosome with, if the information about their relationships
recorded within Family Historian is correct.

The diagram also shows the appropriate DNA Flags
below each person.

Shared Autosomal DNA (Blood Relatives)

Each person has 23 pairs of chromosomes. Of these, one pair - the
X and Y chromosomes - together determine a person's sex. The DNA
in the other 22 pairs of chromosomes is called autosomal DNA.
Autosomal DNA is inherited equally from both parents. For any given
blood relatives, it is possible to calculate what percentage of
autosomal DNA, they are likely to share. This figure is not
completely accurate - in fact it becomes less and less accurate the more
generations separate the people concerned. Nevertheless, it too
can be used for genealogical purposes. If you know that two people
share a certain percentage of autosomal DNA, you can compare this with
what you would expect, given what you have recorded about them within
Family Historian. For a given selected person, male or female, the
Shared Autosomal DNA diagram shows all of the people who, if
the information about their relationships recorded within Family
Historian is correct, should share autosomal DNA with them. Each
box in the diagram includes a description of the relationship between
that person and the selected person, and the approximate percentage of
autosomal DNA that they could be expected to share. So, for
example, the box for the brother of the selected person will show the
brother's name, and below that the word 'brother', and, on the next
line, "50% atDNA" - indicating that the brother shares approximately 50%
of his autosomal DNA with the starting person.

Sometimes people have more than one relationship. For example,
two people may be cousins twice over, if both of their parents were
siblings. If a person is related in more than one way, all the
relationships will be listed on separate lines. 'Double cousins'
would show as "cousin and cousin". Where people have more
than one blood relationship, this will affect the percentage of
autosomal DNA that they share. Ordinary first cousins share 12.5%
of their autosomal DNA. Double cousins share 25% of their
autosomal DNA.

The diagram also shows the appropriate DNA Flags
below each person.

DNA Flags

The following flags are used in the DNA diagrams, and in
other diagrams that use the DNA Flags preset:

Person shares a Y chromosome (also known as 'Y-DNA') with the
starting person

Person shares some part of their X
chromosome (also known as 'X-DNA') with the starting person.

Person shares mitochondrial DNA (also known as 'mtDNA') with the
starting person

Person is a half-blood relation of the starting person.
That is to say, they are neither a direct line ancestor or
descendant of the starting person, but they share a common
ancestor. Most relatives who are not direct line ancestors
or descendants of one another, share 2 common ancestors.
Siblings, for example, most commonly share both parents. A
half-blood relation shares one only. If two people are
related in multiple ways, they will only be considered to be
half-blood relations if their closest blood relationship is a
half-blood relationship.

Person is a blood relation of the starting person. Another
way of putting the same thing is that they share some part of
their autosomal DNA (also known as atDNA) with the starting
person. Anyone who has any of the other 4 DNA flags must
also have the blood relation flag. You can however have the
blood relation flag without necessarily having any of the other 4
DNA flags.

DNA Queries

The 4 DNA queries all take a single parameter, which is a starting
person. All of them show relatives (not necessarily all relatives)
of the starting person. And all of them show the following
columns:

Individual - person's name

Record Id - person's record Id

Date of Birth - person's date of birth

Relationship - the closest relationship to the starting person

Half blood - 'Y' if the person and the starting person are not in
the same direct line (e.g. they aren't parent and child, or
grandparent and grandchild), but instead of being descended from two
shared ancestors,they are descended from a single shared
ancestor. For example, they may be half-siblings who share only
one parent, or half-cousins who share only one grandparent.

Share Y-DNA - 'Y' if the person and the starting person share the
same Y chromosome

Share mtDNA - 'Y' if the person and the starting person share the
same mitochondrial DNA

Overlap X-DNA - 'Y' if the person and the starting person share the
same X-DNA, or, more commonly, have some part of their X-DNA in common

Relatedness - A number between 1 and 0, where 1 represents 100% and
0 represents 0%. This figure shows the amount of autosomal DNA
that the person and the starting person, should be expected to share.

DNA - Shared Y Chromosome

See the description for the Shared Y Chromosome
diagram above. This query shows the same information but in the
form of a tabular result set.

DNA - Shared Mitochondrial DNA

See the description for the Shared
Mitochondrial DNA diagram above. This query shows the same
information but in the form of a tabular result set.

Overlapping X Chromosome

See the description for the Overlapping X
Chromosome diagram above. This query shows the same
information but in the form of a tabular result set.

Shared Autosomal DNA (Blood Relatives)

See the description for the Shared Autosomal
DNA diagram above. This query shows the same information but
in the form of a tabular result set.

DNA Attributes

If you have DNA information for a given person that you wish to record
within Family Historian, we recommend that you do this by adding a DNA
attribute for that person, providing summary details of DNA testing done
by that person in the attribute value field, and storing the full
details in a note attached to that attribute. Family Historian
provides an attribute called DNA Markers which is designed to
be used for this purpose. To add this attribute for a given
person, open that person's record in the Property
Box and click the Add Fact button on
the Facts tab. Choose More Fact Types... to open the
Fact Types dialog. Select DNA Markers from the list and
click Add. If you can't see DNA Markers in
the list, it is probably hidden, in which case you need to unhide
it. To do this, click More >>
and then tick the Show Hidden checkbox. You should now see DNA
Markers in the list. To ensure that it remains visible in
the future, select it, click Edit, untick
the Hidden checkbox (bottom right), and press OK.

If a fact type is marked as 'hidden', this does not mean
that facts of that type will not appear in reports. It is just a
convenient way of ensuring that fact types you never use do not appear
in lists (making it easier to find the ones you do use - see Fact
Definition dialog for more on this). However, it may well be
that you do not want the DNA Markers attribute to appear in
most reports. If you wish to exclude it, you can mark it as Private.
By default, attributes marked as 'Private' are excluded from most
reports (unless you override this). Another strategy would be to
include the DNA Attribute in reports but exclude the actual DNA data
stored in the note attached to the attribute. To do that, you can
mark the note contents as private. You do this by adding two
opening square brackets [[ at the start of the note, and two closing
square brackets ]] at the end of the note.

DNA Diagram Tools

Family Historian diagrams can use icons to show particular features -
such as if a person has a Y-chromosome or Mitochondrial DNA in common
with a given starting person. All of the DNA diagrams listed on
this page show these icons, but you can also include the same icons in
other diagrams if you wish. One way to do this is to use the 'DNA
Flags' preset. To select this preset for a given
diagram, open Diagram Options, and click the Presets
button on the Boxes tab. From the dropdown menu that
appears, choose DNA Flags. You can use the set of
conditions and features used in this preset as examples if you wish to
combine some aspects of this preset with other conditions and features.

The DNA Flags preset uses 5 different icons which are taken from a
collection of icons which are designed for use with DNA
information. If you wish to associate one of these icons with a
particular condition (as illustrated by the DNA Flags preset), create
the condition by clicking << Add Condition
in the Boxes tab of Diagram Options. Then on the Box Features
dialog, tick the Icon checkbox and click the Select
button that appears. On the Select Icon dialog, set the Category field
at the top to 'DNA' to view DNA-related icons, available for you to
select.

To learn more, see Diagram
Options Dialog: Boxes Tab.

The Shared Autosomal DNA diagram shows the rough percentage of
autosomal degree that each person shares with the diagram root.
You can show this same information by choosing the DNA Relatedness text
scheme. Text schemes can be created or edited on the Text
tab of Diagram Options. You can also add DNA Relatedness to any
other text scheme. It is one of the available items listed on the
left-hand side when you edit a text scheme. To learn more about
text schemes, see Diagram
Options Dialog: Text Tab.

title: Advanced DNA Tools
text:
DNA Tools

Advanced DNA Tools

This topic is for advanced and technically-minded
users only.

A number of built-in functions provide features which relate to DNA.
Click on the links to learn more.

Functions

DnaBloodRelation

DnaHalfBlood

DnaShareYChrom

DnaShareMtDna

DnaRelatedness

title: Drag-and-Drop
text:
General Topics

Drag-and-Drop

Family Historian provides extensive support for drag-and-drop.
Drag-and-drop is a quick and easy way of moving or copying items (usually
text or pictures) both within Family Historian itself, and also from other
application windows into Family Historian projects. For example,
suppose you want to add a picture into Family Historian. If you are
viewing the picture on your desktop, or within File Explorer (the standard
Windows program for displaying files), you can simply click on the picture
file and, keeping the mouse button pressed, drag it onto Family
Historian's main application window. When you release the mouse
button, a dialog box will appear, prompting you to confirm. And if
you do so, the picture will be added to your current project. This
same method can be used to add not just one picture, but multiple pictures
if you want.

You can't always drag-and-drop either pictures or text into Family
Historian. For this to work, it is not enough that Family Historian
supports it. The program that is displaying the pictures or text has
to support it too. But a little experimentation will quickly show
whether a program supports it or not. Many do. Most
web-browsers will support drag-and-drop of text, and sometimes also of
pictures, for example - though, to make matters more complicated, whether
or not they support this is affected by security settings on your web
browser, and also by the way particular websites are configured.
Nevertheless, if it does work, it can often be the quickest and easiest
way of moving data into Family Historian, so it's worth checking
out. Bear in mind that if you have enabled automatic
source citations, any data added to Family Historian will
automatically be given an appropriate source citation.

Tip: For a wider discussion of methods for extracting data
from websites, see also Web Clipping and
Source-Driven Data Entry.

Drop Targets

As we saw above, the main Family Historian application window is what is
known as a drop target - meaning that you can drop things onto
it (pictures in this case), and useful things will happen when you
do. Pictures can be dragged from other applications which support
this, such as File Explorer. The main application window is not the
only drop target within Family Historian. For example, the Media
tab of the Property Box is another drop target, and so is the Media
Viewer, and so is the Diagram Window.
Dropping pictures onto these specific drop targets can be an
even better option than simply dropping them onto some other application
window. If, for example, you drop pictures onto the Media
Tab of the Property Box for an Individual, the pictures will not
just be added to Family Historian, but they will be added as pictures of
that person. If you open the Media Viewer to display pictures of an
event (a Christening say), and then drop a dozen pictures onto the Media
Viewer, they will all be added as pictures of the christening.

The table below lists some of the drop targets within Family Historian,
and describes what will happen if you drop things onto them.

Family Historian Location
Item that can be dragged-and-dropped
Action

Main application window
Pictures
Pictures will be added to the project (you will be prompted to
confirm). A media record will be created for each picture.

Diagram Window

Pictures
Pictures can either be inserted directly into a diagram or
chart, or they can be added to the project as a Media
record. You will be prompted to choose.

Media Tab of the Property
Box
Pictures
Pictures will be added to the project (you will be prompted to
confirm). A media record will be created for each
picture. Each media record will be linked to the record
(Individual, Family, Source, Place, ... whatever) being shown in
the Property Box.

Media Viewer
Pictures
Pictures will be added to the project (you will be prompted to
confirm). A media record will be created for each
picture. Each media record will be linked to the fact (event
or attribute) that the Media Viewer was showing media for.

Text boxes within the Property Box,
Note Window, Citation
Window, Parents Window, Automatic Source
Citation Pane.

Text

The text will be inserted into the text box. With large
text fields, such as the text displayed in the Note Window, the
dropped text will be simply inserted. With small text
fields however, the behaviour is a little different. In
most cases, If you drop onto the existing text, the existing
text will be replaced. If you drop into the box, but after
the existing text, the new text will be appended to the existing
text.

Tip: If you don't like the results after dropping
the text, click Undo on the Edit menu (if
dropping within the Note Window, it has its own Undo button on
its toolbar).

Links (e.g. Add Mother or Add Father)
in the Parents Window.

Text

A small dialog will appear, with the name details already
filled-in, prompting you to confirm that you want to add the
mother or father. When you confirm, a new Individual record
will created (with the supplied name), as mother or father, of the
person whose parents are being displayed in the Parents Window
(that is, the current record in the Property Box).

Tip: During the process of dragging, when you are moving a
selected item over Family Historian, and before you have released the
mouse button, a thick blue rectangle will appear around any text box,
tab, link, or window, that is a drop target. This is a visual
confirmation that the area is a drop target. This does not apply
to the main application window. No thick blue rectangle will be
displayed in that case.

Tip: If you drag text from some word-processors, the
word-processor may assume that you are trying to move the text, when in
fact you want to copy it. In that case, if you press-and-hold the
Ctrl key while doing the drag-and-drop, this should
ensure that the action is interpreted as a copy and not a move.
The appearance of the cursor during the action should also be a guide.

Drag-and-Drop Within Family Historian

The table above gives examples of how you can add text and pictures to
Family Historian from elsewhere. But you can also use
drag-and-drop extensively within Family Historian itself. For
example, if you select a number of records in the main body of the Records
Window, you can drag-and-drop them into a Named
List, if the Named List pane
is open. In that case, the records will simply be added to the
named list in question. If you drag-and-drop the same records into
the Note Window (remember this is a floating
window) they will be inserted into the text as comma-separated
record links. Some record selectors allow you to choose records
using drag-and-drop. You can also use drag-and-drop within the Query Window to add, move or copy columns
and to move and copy filters. Drag-and-drop is also supported in the Map Window, for geocoding (assigning or
adjusting a latitude and longitude) to a place or address. Look
out for other uses of drag-and-drop within the program. They often
make routine tasks much easier.

The WEb Search Window

If you want to drag-and-drop pictures or text from a web page, this is
probably more likely to work if you display the web page in the Web
Search Window, rather than in an external web browser. See
the Web Search Window for more
details.

title: Duplicate Options Dialog
text:
Diagram Options Dialog:
General Tab

Duplicate Options

Fields

Hide duplicated family branches
If checked, Family Historian will hide all duplicated family
branches when the diagram is built.

Link duplicates in the diagram
Display lines (usually curved ribbons) linking duplicate boxes
or duplicate families.

Use Family links instead of Individual links where possible
Family Historian supports 2 kinds of duplicate links: Individual
links which connect actual boxes together, and Family links which
connect an entire family group. It can happen that an entire
family group is duplicated, and if you use Individual links only
to show the duplicates, you may get a spaghetti effect. To prevent
that, check this option. If checked, Family links will be used in
preference to Individual links wherever possible - that is,
Individual links will only be used to link Individuals where one
or more of their duplicate boxes are not also part of a duplicated
family group. If this option is not checked, Family links are not
displayed.

Hook boxes to Family link lines
By default, Family link lines have coloured ovals (or circles)
at each end, near to the parents of the relevant families. The
parents of the family (either or both) can also be linked to these
family link lines, by additional lines (called hook lines) which
attach them to the ovals.

Treat remarriage boxes as duplicates
Remarriage boxes are a special kind of box that can be displayed
for Individuals who have more than one spouse - it depends on the
Spouse Display Options. You can link an Individual's Remarriage
boxes to their 'primary' box using a choice of different line
types (see Spouse Display Options). However alternatively (or
even, additionally), you can also use duplicate links to connect
them if you wish.

Treat Proxy boxes as duplicates
Proxy boxes are special boxes that are used in 'All Relatives'
diagrams to show where an ancestor fits in the context of their
parents' family. Proxy boxes are always linked anyway, by normal
ancestral lines, to the ancestor for whom they stand 'proxy'. But
you can if you wish opt to also link them with duplicate links.

Display links as ribbons
Links are normally displayed as curved lines, but they can also
be displayed as ribbons if you prefer.

Line Thickness
Thickness of lines. If you are not displaying links as ribbons,
this will be the thickness of the link lines themselves. If you
are displaying links as ribbons, this is the thickness of the
ribbon edge lines.

Family Link Ribbon Width
Only applicable if you are displaying Family links and if you
are displaying links as ribbons. If you set this value to zero,
Family links will always be displayed as single lines instead of
ribbons.

Family Link Curve
Controls how curvaceous Family duplicate link lines are. 100% is
very curvaceous. 0% is a straight line.

Family link colours
This determines how many different sets of colours (line and
fill) Family Historian will use for Family duplicate links. If
this option is set to 1 (the lowest allowed value), Family
Historian will use the same colours for all Family duplicate
links.

Family Link Oval Depth/Width
Whereas Individual Links connect actual boxes together, Family
Links do not connect directly to boxes as such. They connect
instead to an area where there is a family group. The approximate
location of the family group is shown by an oval, on the Family
link line. You can specify the Width and Depth of this oval. If
you want a circle, make the width equal to the depth. If you don't
want an oval at all, set either the depth, or width, or both, to
zero.

Individual Link Ribbon Width
Only applicable if you are displaying links as ribbons. If you
set this value to zero, Individual links will always be displayed
as single lines instead of ribbons.

Individual Link Curve
Controls how curvaceous Individual duplicate link lines are.
100% is very curvaceous. 0% is a straight line.

Individual link colours
This determines how many different sets of colours (line and
fill) Family Historian will use for Individual duplicate links. If
this option is set to 1 (the lowest allowed value), Family
Historian will use the same colours for all Individual duplicate
links.

Hook Ribbon Width
Only applicable if you are displaying hook lines Width of hook
lines (see "Hook boxes to Family link lines" above) and if you are
displaying links as ribbons. If you set this value to zero, hook
lines will always be displayed as single lines instead of ribbons.

Hook Link Curve
See previous. This option controls how curvaceous hook lines
are. 100% is very curvaceous. 0% is a straight line.

The set of colours available for use with Individual and Family links
is displayed. To change the Line or Fill of a given set, click on the
text in the left column, and then click on Edit Line or Edit
Fill as appropriate. Click Set All to choose
between a pre-defined set of Dark, Medium and Light
colours. You can also choose the Default option,
to reset default colours.

title: Edit Book Chart in Diagram Window
breadcrumb: Edit Book Chart in Diagram Window
text:
Book Window

Edit Book Chart in Diagram Window

Edit a Book Chart in the Diagram Window

Any chart which has been added to a book is known as a book chart.
You can edit any book chart, at any time, in the Diagram Window.
To do so, click select a chart or diagram in the Edit
Book Dialog, click the Edit
button and, at the prompt, choose Edit Chart in Diagram Window.
You can make almost any changes you like to a book chart, and that
includes changes to diagram options. These are changes are not
saved automatically. You can save your changes at any time by
right-clicking on the background of the chart and selecting Save
Changes to Book Chart on the menu that appears, or by clicking Save
Changes to Book Chart on the Diagram menu. Alternatively,
if you close the Diagram Window, you will be prompted to save changes at
that point.

When a book chart is displayed in the Diagram Window, the caption of
the window will mention both the name of the chart, and the name of the
book it belongs to. In the example above, the chart is named
"Diagram" and the book is "The Munros in the 20th Century", and both are
mentioned in the caption.

Book charts have their own distinctive icon, which is displayed in the
Navigation Bar when a book chart is being edited in the Diagram
Window. The icon (which appears in the example above) looks like
this:
If there are any unsaved changes, there will be an orange dot in the
top-left corner of the icon area, like this:

You cannot print a book chart in the Diagram Window, and you cannot
change print layout features (such as page size and/or orientation) here
either. Page layout features have to be specified at the book
level in Book Settings or by
clicking File > Print Setup in the Book Window.

Tip: Be aware that the background of a book chart,
displayed in the Diagram Window, will only appear in the book if the Print
background option is ticked, in the Print tab of Diagram
Options, for the book chart in question.

Tip: By default, all pages of a chart will be included in
the book. But you can specify any subset, if you wish to do
so. To select a particular set of pages to appear, see Select
Chart Pages Dialog.

Scrapbooks and Photo Books

The ability to edit book charts in the Diagram Window is useful for all
charts, but it is particularly useful if you are creating a scrapbook or
photobook, and wish to add to it over time. To learn more about
this, see How to Create a Scrapbook
or Photo Book.

title: Edit Book Dialog
text:
Book Window

Edit Book Dialog

Edit Book Dialog

The Edit Book Dialog is a floating
window that is opened by clicking Edit
in the Book List Dialog.
Alternatively, click New in the Book List
Dialog, to create a new book. Once you have provided a name for
the book, the Edit Book Dialog will be opened to allow you to add items
to the book. The Edit Book Dialog can also be accessed by clicking
Edit Book in the panel on the right side of
the Book Window, when viewing a book in
the Book Window.

The Edit Book Dialog is used to manage and edit the content of
books. Books can have a title page, a table-of-contents, an index,
and of course chapters. The contents of the book - the
chapters - will usually consist of reports that you choose to add,
and/or charts and diagrams. These are generated by Family
Historian (configured and tweaked, if necessary, by you, with your
choice of chapter headings etc). If you wish, you can also add free
text (free text is text that you write yourself) as either
chapters, or as additional text inserted into other chapters. You might
also use free text for a preface, acknowledgements, or a copyright
statement.

See How to Add Content
to a Book or Booklet for tips on using the Edit Book Dialog to add
content to a book.

Tip: The Edit Book Dialog is a floating
window which means that you can make any changes you like to other
windows, even while it is open. The Books Dialog, which displays a list
of books in the current project, is another floating window.

Tip: Editing a book is likely to be slower if Auto-Refresh
is ticked; which is why that option is not ticked by default.

Fields

Available Items

List items that can be added to the current books.

Current Book Items

Lists all items that have been added to the current book.

To change the contents of the Title Page, or any chart or
diagram, or any free text item, select the item and click Edit.
The Edit button will be greyed if you select other item types.

Open the Item Settings Dialog
to view or change the settings for the currently selected
item. Every item has settings, so this button will be always
be available when you select an item. The actual settings
vary between items. Reports, for example, will typically
have many settings on many different tabs. All items have an
'item' tab which allows you to specify basic settings that are
common to all items.

Some settings - such as fonts, layout, footers and headers - are
set in the Book Setttings
Dialog (see below).

Clicking the Go To Page button is a quick way of
viewing that item in the Book Window. It will display the
current book in the Book Window, scrolled to view the currently
selected item.

Delete the currently selected items from the book. You can
select multiple items and delete them all in one go if you wish.

Move the currently selected items up one. This button
supports multiple selection.

Tip: A quick way of moving an item from the bottom
of a long list to the top, is simply to select all of the items
that you want to move it past, and click once.

Move the currently selected items down one. This button
supports multiple selection. See also the above tip.

Auto-Refresh Book

If this option is ticked and the current book is open in the
Book Window, it will be refreshed automatically whenever any
change is made to the book in the Edit Book Dialog. It is
normally recommended that this option should be left unticked
because refreshing a book can be slow. Click the 'Refresh
Book' button to manually refresh a book (this button will be
greyed if the book is not currently open in the Book Window).

Note: If auto-refresh is enabled, the book will be refreshed using
the "Standard Build" option (see Book
Build Types).

View Book
Displays the book in the Book Window. If the Book Window
is open but not active, it will be made active.

Refresh Book
Click this button to rebuild the book so that it reflects any
changes you have made in the Edit Book Dialog or elsewhere. If the
book is not already open in the Book Window, it will be displayed
in the Book Window.

Book Settings

Opens the Book Settings
Dialog, which is used to specify Source information, fonts,
heading styles, headers, footers, layout, privacy settings,
language, and more. These settings apply not just to one
item, but to the book as a whole.

title: Add/Edit Bookmark Dialog
text:
Search the Internet Dialog

Add/Edit Bookmark Dialog

The Add/Edit Bookmark Dialog is accessed by clicking New or Edit (when a
bookmark is selected) in the Search
the Internet Dialog. It is used to maintain bookmark details.
Bookmarks are normally just quick links to websites that you add
yourself. However, bookmarks can also be 'search now' bookmarks.

'Search Now' Bookmarks

'Search Now' bookmarks have a search template (that is, a Template
field which is not blank). Creating 'search now' bookmarks is
an advanced feature for power-users.

Some websites allow themselves to be searched directly by programs like
Family Historian using a suitably-constructed URL (web address).
Family Historian can do searches of this kind in the Search
the Internet Dialog. Family Historian users can use this
feature (that is, search directly from within Family Historian, where
supported), by selecting the website to search in the website list on
the Search the Internet Dialog.
They need to supply search details (see the fields below the website
list). The search is initiated by clicking the Search
Now button on that dialog. If the Search
Now button is greyed, direct searching is not supported for the
selected website.

Family Historian will automatically fill in the search
details part of the Search the
Internet Dialog for a given Individual, if you simply click on
that Individual in a workspace window when the Search
the Internet Dialog is open. Using the Search the Internet
dialog in conjunction with a workspace window in this way, is a quick
and easy way of doing fast searches for Individuals.

If you wish to create a bookmark that can be used for this kind of
search (as a 'search now' bookmark), you must supply a template to be
used for searches (see discussion of the Template field
below). Note that if the Template field is blank (the
default case), the bookmark will be an ordinary bookmark that cannot be
used for direct searches of this kind.

Fields

Name
The list name for this bookmark

URL
The website address. A website address might look
something like this:

https://www.a-useful-genealogy-website

Description
A description of the website

Template
This field is normally left blank. It is only not blank if
you wish the bookmark to be used with direct searches of the
website (see above). Specifying a template value is an
advanced feature for power-users (see instructions below).
Bear in mind that you can only use a search template for a website
if the website supports this kind of search. Most websites
will not support this kind of search.

In order to supply a search template, you need to know the format
of terms that the website expects. For example, suppose that
you want to search for John Smith who was born in 1800 and
died in 1860. You might know, or have worked out, that you
can do this, for your bookmarked site, by typing the following
into a web browser:

https://www.a-useful-genealogy-website?firstname=John&lastname=Smith&yearofbirth=1800&yearofdeath=1860

Obviously you don't want to have to type this every time, for each
new person you want to search for. To get Family Historian
to do the work for you, you need to supply a template, that uses
substitution expressions which Family Historian can use to
generate the required search URL. Family Historian supports
the following substitution expressions in this context:

Substitution Expression
Description

<<<givn>>>
Will be replaced by the person's given name

<<<last>>>
Will be replaced by the person's last name

<<<y1>>>
Will be replaced by the person's year of birth if
known. Depending on the website, this may be used
either to specify the person's year of birth, or the year
to start searching from.

<<<y2>>>
Will be replaced by the person's year of death if
known. Depending on the website, this may be used
either to specify the person's year of death, or the end
of the search period.

<<<n+n>>>
Will be replaced by a person's given followed by their
last name, with spaces replaced by the '+' character.

In the example above, the template would be:

https://www.a-useful-genealogy-website?firstname=<<<givn>>>&lastname=<<<last>>>&yearofbirth=<<<y1>>>&yearofdeath=<<<y2>>>

title: Editing Diagram Shapes
text:
Diagram Window

Editing Diagram Shapes

"Shapes" is the name for all diagram elements, other than trees, that
can be added to a Family Historian diagram by a user (see Diagram
Elements for a full list). This page describes the various
techniques for manipulating and modifying them.

Undo/Redo, Deletion

Shapes can be added, edited, formatted and deleted. The Diagram
Window supports full multilevel undo/redo for all changes to
shapes. To undo a change, click the 'Undo' command on the Edit
menu or press Ctrl-Z. To redo a change after undoing it, click the
'Redo' command on the Edit menu, or press Ctrl-Y. To delete any
shape, select it by clicking on it, and press the Delete key.

GroupING and Ordering

Shapes can be formed into grouped objects that all move as one.
To select multiple shapes, press-and-hold the Ctrl key while clicking on
each shape in turn to select it, without de-selecting the other shapes
you had already selected. White selection handles will appear
around each selected shape. To form a number of selected shapes
into a group, right-click on any one of them and choose the 'Group'
option from the 'Grouping' submenu on the dropdown menu that
appears. A 'group' can consist of just one shape, and sometimes it
is useful to do this (e.g. with polygons and polylines - see below).

A group shape behaves very much like any other shape. Group
shapes can be grouped with other shapes (including other group shapes),
and this can be iterated to any level. Right-click on any group
shape, and choose 'Ungroup' from the 'Grouping' submenu, to remove the
grouping of the shapes within it.

Shapes can also be ordered with respect to one another.
Right-click on any shape (or on any one of a selection of multiple
shapes), and choose an appropriate option from the Order submenu.

A tree cannot form part of a group of shapes. But it can be
ordered, front-to-back, with respect to all shapes and all other trees.

LOCK POSITION

Shapes can be locked in position so that they can no longer be resized
or moved. To lock a shape, right-click on it and choose "Lock
position" from the dropdown menu that appears. Locked shapes have
grey selection handles. To unlock a locked shape, right-click on
it again, and untick "Lock Position" on the dropdown menu.

Locking the position of shapes can be a useful guard against
accidentally moving it. It can also be useful when aligning
and resizing shapes with respect to one another - see below.

Alignment

Shapes can be aligned with respect to one another. To align a
number of shapes with one particular shape, first lock that shape.
Then select all the shapes you wish to be aligned, including the locked
one, and right-click on any one of them. Choose an alignment
command form the 'Alignment' submenu. The unlocked shapes will all
align with the locked shape. If none of the selected shapes are
locked when you use an alignment command, the shapes will align with the
leftmost shape if aligning left, the topmost shape if aligning top, the
rightmost shape if aligning right, and the bottommost shape if aligning
bottom. If more that one selected shape is locked, any unlocked shapes
will align with (depending on the alignment type required) the leftmost,
rightmost, topmost or bottommost of the locked shapes.

Trees cannot be aligned with other diagram elements using these
alignment commands.

Size

You can arrange to make shapes have the same width or height as a given
shape. To resize a number of shapes to match one particular shape,
first lock that shape. Then select all the shapes you wish to be
resized, including the locked one, and right-click on any one of
them. Choose a command form the 'Size' submenu: Make the Same
Height or Make the Same Width. The unlocked
shapes will all be resized to match the locked shape in terms of height
or width. If none of the shapes are locked, the shapes will all be
given the height or width of the largest shape. If more than one
shape is locked, any unlocked shapes will be given the height or width
of the largest of the locked shapes.

Trees cannot be resized relative to shapes using these alignment
commands, and some shapes can also not be used with these
commands. Specifically lines, polylines or grouped shapes cannot
be resized using these commands. All other shapes can, however.

Formatting Shapes (Single and Multiple)

There are numerous options for shapes that can be selected or modified in
the Diagram Shape Format dialog.
To open this dialog, right-click on any shape and click Format from
the menu that appears.

The Diagram Shape Format dialog will have different fields, and different
tabs, depending on what type of shapes are being formatted.

A very useful feature of the Diagram Shape Format dialog is that it can be
used to modify values for multiple shapes at the same time, and even to
modify values for the shapes making up a group shape. Any changes
you make to values in the Diagram Shape Format dialog will apply to all
the shapes in the selection (and that includes all shapes in any selected
groups). This allows you to make changes to any number of shapes at
the same time. And if you don't like the changes, click Undo on the
Edit menu, to reverse them. You can do this even if the selection
include shapes of different types. Of course some fields in the
Diagram Shape Format dialog may not be applicable to all shape
types. If you make any changes to a field like that, these changes
will only be applied to those shapes, within the selection, that they are
relevant to. Text, for example, is only relevant to text
boxes. Fill colour, again, is not applicable to polylines (although
it is relevant to all other shape types). If a selection includes
several polylines and several polygons (say), and you choose to format all
of them, you will be able to change the fill colour; but the change will
only be applied to the polygons. It will have no effect on the
polylines.

If you open the Diagram Shape Format dialog when you have multiple shapes
selected, it will initially show all the values that they all have - if
they all have the same values. If some of them have different
values, the Diagram Shape Format dialog will not display any value for
that field. If, for example, you had several shapes selected, each
with a different line colour, the line colour field would be blank,
indicating that multiple line colours were being used. You could
change other aspects of the selected shapes, and as long as you do not set
the line colour, this aspect of each shape would be left unchanged when
you press OK or Apply.
If, however, you do set a line colour, that change will apply to the
entire selection.

Copying and Pasting Shapes

Shapes can be copied-and-pasted either with one Diagram Window, or between
different Diagram Windows. This
includes multiple selections of shapes, and shape groups, etc.

Adding and Editing Images

Images can be added using the Image button on the Shape
toolbar. You can add multiple images at a time. They
can be added either directly from pictures files or form Media
records. You can also use drag-and-drop from
some other application, such as File Explorer, to add pictures directly
into a Diagram Window. And you can use copy-and-paste
to insert a copied image directly into a diagram or chart.

Adding and Editing Polygons

To add a polygon to a diagram, click on the 'Poly' button on the
Shape toolbar, and click on the diagram
to add vertices of the polygon. A new vertex is created for each
click. Double-click to add the last vertex and finish the
polygon. Press-and-hold the Alt key while clicking anywhere on the
edge of a polygon to add a new vertex at that point. Each vertex is
represented by a white selection handle. Click-and-drag on any of
these white selection handles to move it. Press-and-hold the Alt key
while clicking on a vertex selection handle to delete it.

Adding and Editing lines and Polylines

Lines
in diagrams are also known as polylines or multi-segment lines, because
they can have any number of vertices. To add a simple line between
two points, click on the 'Line' button on the Shape
toolbar, and then click-and-drag on the Diagram Window, to add the
line. When you release the mouse button, the line will be
added. To add a polyline (a multi-segment line), click on the
'Multi' button on the Diagram
Shapes toolbar, and click on the diagram to add vertices of the
polyline. A new vertex is created for each click.
Double-click to add the last vertex and finish the polyline.
Press-and-hold the Alt key while clicking anywhere on any line
(including lines that were originally added as a simple line connecting
two points) to add a new vertex at that point. Each vertex is
represented by a white selection handle. Click-and-drag on any of
these white selection handles to move it. Press-and-hold the Alt
key while clicking on a vertex selection handle to delete it.

Tip:It might seem that Family Historian supports two kinds
of 'line' shapes because there are two buttons for lines on the Diagram
Shapes toolbar, one labelled 'Line' and the other labelled
'Multi'. In fact, these really represent two different ways of
adding lines (you can either add a simple line between two points, or
you can add multiple vertices for a multi-segment line). There is
really only one shape type for lines. Lines may have different
number of vertices. But you can add more vertices to any line, and
you can delete vertices from any line. There is only one shape
type for lines.

Resizing and Rotating Shapes

With all shapes except polygons and polylines, you can click-and-drag
on any white corner handle (when it is selected) to resize the
shape. With polygons and polylines, you can either select it and
click-and-drag on each white selection handle on each vertex, or, if you
prefer, you can convert the polygon or polyline into a group object (a
'group' object with only one grouped item if necessary - see
above). Group objects have white corner handles when selected,
like other rectangular shapes, and you can then click-and-drag on any of
these to resize the entire polygon or polygon as if it were a
rectangular object. The same applies to rotation. All shapes
except polygons and polylines can be rotated by clicking-and-dragging on
the little green round rotation handle, that also appears when the shape
is selected. If you convert a polygon or polyline into a group
shape, then they too can be rotated in the same way.

Shift and Ctrl Keys

If you press the Shift key when adding a rectangle, ellipse or pie
shape, you will get a square, circle or segment from a circle,
respectively. If you press it when inserting a line, each line
segment will 'snap' to the horizontal or to the vertical. If you
press the Shift key while moving a vertex for a polyline or polygon, the
vertex will snap to be aligned horizontally or vertically with its two
nearest neighbouring vertices.

If you press the Shift key while resizing a shape, its aspect ratio
(the ratio of width to height) will be maintained as you resize.

If you press the Ctrl key when inserting or resizing most shapes, the
shape will be resized relative to its centre point.

If you press both the Shift and Ctrl keys, the effect of each will be
combined.

title: Edit Role - Advanced Features
text:
Edit Role Dialog

Edit Role - Advanced Features

This dialog is accessed by clicking the Advanced
button in the Edit Role Dialog.

Fields & Buttons

Summary Template

This template is used to provide summary information about the
role that a person has in an event. It is primarily used in
the Facts tab listing of the Property Box, for people who are
listed as a witness to an event - such as the best man at a
wedding. If a person has more than one role in an event,
their first role only will be used. Providing a summary
template is optional and normally not needed. If not
supplied, a default summary will be generated.

Default Role for Principal

This option is normally unticked. Tick this box if the
principal in a fact should automatically be recorded also as a
witness to the same fact, with this role (the role we are now
editing details for). This option is disabled for Family
facts. It is only applicable to Individual facts.

Remember that the principal in a fact is the main person that an
event relates to, and a witness is just a term used to
describe anyone who has a non-principal role in the event.
For example, in a baptism, the person being baptised would be the
principal, and anyone listed as a godparent (say) would be witnesses
with the role godparent. In Family Historian, the
principal person in an event can also be recorded as a witness
to that event, with a particular role. This can be
very useful - most commonly with events that don't really have a
principal in the real world. For example, suppose that you
want to record that several people formed a friendship
group. They were all friends with one another. To do
this, you add the event 'Friendship Group' to any person in the
group (it doesn't matter which), and record them all as witnesses
to this event, with the role of 'Friend'. In that case, the
person who is notionally the 'principal' (the person you added the
event to) should be added as a witness to the event too.
That way, each person in the group will all get a similar
sentence, in narrative reports, saying that they were friends with
the others. So for 'Friendship Group', the option Default
Role for Principal should be ticked.

A slightly different requirement is to add a list of a given
person's friends. This is slightly different from recording
a friendship group, because there is no implication that the
listed friends were also friends of each other, or even knew each
other necessarily. In this case, there is a clear principal:
namely the person that the listed people are all friends of; so
here you would want to add the friends as witnesses with role of
'Friend'; but the principal person is treated a little differently
(it's his or her list after all); so in this case the option Default
Role for Principal should not be ticked.

Terms like 'fact' and 'event', as used in this
context, do not necessarily align perfectly with ordinary
usage. We would probably not think of the fact that a
group of people were friends of one another, as an 'event', even
if one could specify a date period for it. But we need a
term to refer to what we are recording, and this is the
convenient term that is used.

Prompt to Add on Create

This option is also normally unticked. Tick this option if
you want the user to be prompted to specify people with the
current role, when an event of the current type, is added.
For example, if the event you are adding is 'Friendship Group' or
'Friend List' (see previous), you will typically want to record
witnesses to this 'event' with role of friend.
These will be the people in the friendship group or friend
list. You will probably also want to encourage the user to
add the friends when you add the event. So in these cases
the option Prompt to Add on Create should be
ticked. The people added will all be listed as witnesses
with role of friend. You can add people that you
already have records for in the project; or you can add people as
'name only'. Either way, you will have recorded the friend
list or friendship group, and appropriate sentences will be
generated in reports, for all the relevant people.

Note: By ticking this option, you make it easy to
add people with the relevant role, when the user adds a fact of
the relevant kind. All such details can later be modified
at any time in the Witnesses
Window. See also the Add
People With Roles Dialog.

title: Edit Role Dialog
text:
Fact Types Dialog

Edit Role Dialog

Edit Role Dialog

This dialog is accessed by selecting a witness role in the list in the
Witness Roles Dialog, and
clicking the Edit button. All fields
are mandatory.

Fields & Buttons

Role Name
This is a word or phrase that describes the role - e.g.
'bridesmaid' . The name must be unique for the current
fact. No two roles, for a given fact, may share the same
role name. Also, the role name may not be either 'principal'
or 'principals' as these are reserved.

Past Tense
When mentioning that a person was a Witness at a given event or
attribute in the Facts tab
of the Property Box, the word or phrase entered as "Past Tense"
will be placed before a short description of the event or
attribute. So, a suitable value for a bridesmaid, say, might
be "Was bridesmaid at" or even just "Bridesmaid at".

Witness Sentence Template
Must be supplied. The template is used to generate a sentence
for descriptions of witnessed facts, for people who have the
current role, in narrative reports. Click on the <<
Insert Code button to insert a template code into the
template. For a list of sentence template codes and their
meanings, see Sentence
Template Codes.
When you specify, here, a template for a given
witness role for a given fact, it will be used for all
sentences describing witnesses to such facts who had that role -
unless it is overridden. Suppose you are specifying a template
for the role of Bridesmaid for a Marriage event. You can see a
pretty good approximation of the kind of sentence that will be
generated for a given person, by selecting that person in the Witnesses Window,
when viewing the event in question. The relevant sentence
will be displayed in the Sentence field at the bottom of the
Witnesses Window.

The template you have defined may work well for most cases,
but not be quite right in a given case. In that case, you can
override it. Simply click in the Sentence field dialog and make
whatever modifications you want. You can even add or delete
template codes if you wish to. When you override the default
template, the background of the field will become white to show
that it is an override. To revert to the default template for
the given field, simply delete the text in the field completely
and click or tab elsewhere. The field will revert to the default
value.

<< Insert Code
See Sentence
Template Codes. See also the discussion of the Witness
Sentence Template field above

Advanced
Opens the Edit Role -
Advanced Features Dialog.

title: Edit Role - Language Variant Dialog
text:
Fact Types Dialog

Edit Role - Language Variant Dialog

Edit Role Language Variant Dialog

Buttons

<< Insert Code
Insert a sentence template codes into the appropriate sentence
template. See Sentence
Template Codes for more information.

Fields and Buttons

Role Name
Read only. This identifies the role in the default
language. It is never translated.

Translation
This is the translation of the role name

Standard Role Sentence Template
Read only. Sentence template for
the specified role, for this fact type, in the default language
(usually English). This sentence template is defined in the
Edit Role Dialog.

Language Variant Role Sentence Template
Translated role sentence template.

Standard Role Summary Template
Read only. Some reports will use a summary template if
available (if not, they will use the sentence template
instead). This is the default language version. It is
defined (if at all) in the Edit Role - Advanced
Features Dialog (see the discussion of the Advanced button in the Edit
Role Dialog).

Language Variant Role Summary Template
Optional translation of the Role Summary Template.

title: Edit Text Scheme Dialog
text:
Diagram Options Dialog:
Text Tab

Edit Text Scheme Dialog

This dialog is reached from the Text Tab of the Diagram Options
dialog. It is used for editing the contents of an existing text scheme,
or for specifying the contents of a new one. It is also used for
editing language variants of text schemes - see Text
Tab for more details.

See also Create
a Simple Text Scheme which gives an example of how this dialog can
be used to create a simple scheme.

If the text scheme or language variant being edited is the one
currently being used in the Diagram Window (see Current Text Scheme in
the Text Tab), you will see changes reflected immediately in the Diagram
Window when you click OK or
Apply.

Fields

Scheme Name
Name of the current text scheme.

Type
Custom, Standard or Language Variant. This field is not
editable.

Initial Font
The initial font for the text scheme. Press Select
to modify the initial font details. The font information includes
the size and type of the font, and also its style (underlined,
italics, bold, etc), and colour. Additionally you can specify
whether or not the colour can be overridden in the Boxes Tab of
the Diagram Options dialog, where, for example, you may wish to
specify different text colours for males or females. If you do
this, only text lines which have a font that allows colour
override will be affected.
As well as an 'initial font', you will also be able to change
all font information (including text colour, style, colour
override state, etc) as often as you like, within the body of
the text scheme. You do this by inserting a <Font change>
Item at the required place (see Available Items below).

Name Format
Choose from a number of predefined name formats to use
throughout the text scheme.
The list does not include all possible name formats - only
ones that you might wish to use for all names in a text scheme.
see Name Formats
for a complete list of all possible name formats and their
meanings.

You do not have to use the same format throughout a text
scheme if you do not want to. You can use different name formats
within different items if you wish, and choose from the complete
range of name formats. If you are using more than one name
format within a text scheme, the Name Format field will show as
<multiple>.

Date Format
Choose from a number of predefined date formats to use
throughout the text scheme.
The list does not include all possible date formats - only
ones that you might wish to use for all dates in a text scheme.
See Date Formats
for a complete list of all possible date formats and their
meanings.

You do not have to use the same format throughout a text
scheme if you do not want to. You can use different date formats
within different items if you wish, and choose from the complete
range of date formats. If you are using more than one date
format within a text scheme, the Date Format field will show as
<multiple>.

Place Format
Choose from a number of predefined place formats to use
throughout the text scheme.
See Place
Formats for a list of place formats and their meanings.

You do not have to use the same format throughout a text
scheme if you do not want to. You can use different place
formats within different items if you wish. If you are using
more than one place format within a text scheme, the Place
Format field will show as <multiple>.

Available Items
This is the list of available items that you can choose from, to
add to the text scheme. When you add an item from the Available
Items list, you may find that multiple lines are inserted into the
Items Used list (see next).
New lines are always inserted at the end of the Items Used
list, so you may need to use the Move Up/Down arrows ( and ) to move the new items to the desired position
in the Items Used list.

If multiple items have been added, it is usually a good idea
to keep them together and move them all together as one.

Used Items
This is the list of items actually used in the current text
scheme. The items displayed here determine what actually appears
in boxes in the diagram.

Add currently selected item to the list of items used.

Remove currently selected items from the list of items used.

Tip: Used Items list supports multiple selection.
e.g. Press-and-hold the Ctrl key while clicking on an item to
add it to the selection. Or click-and-drag on the background of
the box (or anywhere except the first column) to 'lasso' a
number of items in the first column.

Edit
Edit the item in the Edit Text Scheme Item Dialog.
Tip: The Edit button supports multiple selection
(at least for all standard data items). If you edit multiple
items simultaneously, you can only change features which are
common to all selected items.

Tip: A quick way to open the Edit dialog for an
item is just to double click on it.

Clone Line
Makes an instant copy of the selected item.

Show Templates
If checked, each item's template will be displayed in the list,
instead of the item's name.

Move all selected items up. Works with multiple selection (see
previous tip).

Be careful when moving items which are part of an Item Group.
You will usually wish to move the entire group, or none of it.
To move the entire group, you must select all items in the
group.

Move all selected items down. Works with multiple selection (see
previous tip).
Be careful when moving items which are part of an Item Group.
You will usually wish to move the entire group, or none of it.
To move the entire group, you must select all items in the
group.

Copy all selected items to the clipboard. Works with multiple
selection (see previous tip).

Paste all previously copied items into the current text scheme.

Delete
Deletes the currently selected item or items.

Restore Defaults
Not available for custom text schemes. Sets standard text
schemes back to their initial Installation Defaults.

title: Edit Text Scheme Item Dialog
text:
Edit Text Scheme Dialog

Edit Text Scheme Item Dialog

Item Types

This dialog box will show different fields depending on the type of
item being edited. All possible items of all types can be selected from
the list of Available Items in the Edit Text Scheme Dialog. The Item Type is shown
in the second column of the Available Items list.

The following item types are called standard data items:

Event
An event (e.g. Birth)

Attribute
An attribute (e.g. Occupation)

Data
Some other kind of data item (e.g. a note).

Calculated
An item of data which has to be calculated - e.g. an Ahnentafel
number.

Identifier
e.g. a record identifier, or a custom identifier.

In addition to the standard data items, there are also the following
special items:

Font Change
Insert one of these whenever you want a change in font. You can
use a font change to change any aspect of a font (size, colour,
type, etc) and also whether the text is underlined, in italics, in
bold, etc.

Gap
This item type is used to space out items within a box
vertically. You can specify any size of vertical gap to leave. For
example, you may wish to leave a slightly larger gap than normal
immediately below a person’s name.

Picture Marker
In the Pictures tab of the Diagram Options dialog you can option
to position pictures either to the side of the text or Within the
Text. If you choose to picture them within the text, the Picture
Marker is used to mark where exactly the picture should go. This
item has no effect if you have no picture for a given box, or if
you are not positioning pictures within the text.

Pre- Formatted Data
The ‘<all events and attributes>’ item is an example of a
Pre-Formatted Data item. If you insert this item, a complete set
of a person’s events and attributes, in chronological order, will
be displayed for that item.

Text
A text item is an item which controls exceptional display of
text in a box, where the text is not directly related data in a
record. The only example of this currently is ‘No Record’ text.
Very occasionally, Family Historian may create a box for which
no corresponding record is held. At present, this only happens
if you are displaying a diagram in which spouses appear in their
own box, and a given person is recorded as having children by
more than one spouse, but the other parent for one or more of
the children is not recorded. Unless an extra spouse box was
displayed, the children would have to appear under the wrong
parent. So a spouse box is added for the missing parent, even
though no record is held for him or her.

For this very unusual situation, you can specify which text
you want to appear (e.g. ‘unknown’ or just ‘?’).

Fields and Buttons

Template

Standard data items only. There is no need for ordinary users
to create or edit templates. Family Historian will generate
templates for you as required when you simply add an item to the
list you wish to use in the Edit Text Scheme Dialog. Advanced users,
with very specific requirements, can however write their own
templates, or edit existing templates, if they wish. Use the << Insert button to insert data
references into a template.

Most users will never need, or wish, to get down to this
level; but if you wish to do so, you can. See Understanding Text Templates for an
explanation of how templates work. See Understanding Data References for an
explanation of what data references are and how to use them. And
see Understanding
Functions for a complete list and specification of Family
Historian functions.

Font
Font change items only. Click on the Select button to change any
aspect of the font (including style such as colour, or italics,
underline or bold).

Vertical Gap
Gap items only. Specify the height of the gap to be left, using
your preferred units of measurement.

Description
A brief description of the item.

‘No Data’ Text
Standard data items only. Normally if a given item has no data
associated with it, that item will simply not appear. However, you
may wish to display some text (e.g. “<no birth info>”) if
details are missing.
If you wish to display a blank line for an item if there no
data for it, tick ‘No Data’ Text but leave the associated text
field blank.

Start on New Line
Standard data items only. Normally an item will start on a line
of its own. Tick this box if you would like the item to continue
the previous line.

Group with previous line
If this is ticked, the item forms part of a group of items. See
Item Groups.

Only output if previous item blank
Tick this box if you want this item to only be output if the
previous item is blank. For example, you might want to display
baptism details if, and only if, there are no birth details.

Alignment
Each item can be aligned Left, Right, Centred or Justified
(bearing in mind that a given item may occupy more than one line,
and may even consist of multiple paragraphs).
A common approach is to make the name field centred at the
top, and make other items left-aligned.

Initial Indent
This is the indentation of the first line of this item. Most
items only occupy one line. But if the item happens to be a long
note (say), it could occupy multiple lines, and even multiple
paragraphs. You can specify an initial indent for items that do
not start on a new line and it will be used if space permits.

Paragraph Indent
If an item does (or could) involve multiple paragraphs (e.g. a
long note), this is the indentation to use for the start of each
new paragraph (after the first line of the item).

Wrapped Line Indent
