between the two boxes has been marked.

Try experimenting: add more boxes to your route. Remember that
you can delete a route, or clear it, at any time. Notice that you
can add any boxes at all to a route. But the route will only mark
the lines connecting two boxes if they are directly linked to one
another. In other words, routes can represent 'broken' paths as
well as 'complete' paths.

Tip: If you want to add multiple boxes to a particular
route at the same time, simply select all the boxes and tick the route
that you want to add them to. There are numerous ways of selecting
multiple boxes. If you zoom back, and click the 'Select' button on
the Diagram toolbar, you can click-and-drag on the background of the
dialog to draw a stretchy box round the boxes you wish to select.
Another technique is to press-and-hold the Ctrl
key while clicking on several boxes in turn. This will
select each box without unselecting other boxes. You can also right-click
on a box, and then choose Select Branch
Boxes from the dropdown menu that appears, to select the entire
branch leading off from it. More options are described in How
to Select Multiple Boxes in Diagrams.

Tip: Suppose you want to change the appearance of the
boxes on a route - perhaps to give them a distinctive background colour
say. This is easily done. Select the route in question in
the Family Connection Mapper, and then click on the Select
Route Boxes command (it's on the dropdown menu that appears
when you click on the 'cog' button on the Family Connection Mapper's
toolbar - see below). This will select the boxes on the
route. Now click Format on the
Diagram menu. This opens the Override
Box Features Dialog allowing you to change and override any aspect
of the appearance of the selected boxes.

Fields and Buttons

Connect

Connect two boxes using the currently selected route. In
order for this to work, you must first select the route that you
wish to use. You must also have two boxes selected.
To select two boxes, click on the first box to select it.
Then press-and-hold down the Ctrl key while clicking on the
second box. This will select the second box without
unselecting the first box.

The Connect Two Boxes function will automatically
find a path connecting the two boxes and all boxes on this path
to the chosen route - giving you the choice of replacing the
existing route or adding to it.

You can select any two boxes in the same tree, but you cannot
connect two boxes in different trees. Most diagram options
create a diagram that consists of only one tree. For
example, an All Relatives diagram, however large, will
consist of a single All Relatives tree. Usually
a diagram will only have more than one tree if you 'manually'
added additional trees yourself. The All Relatives +
Indirect Relatives and the Everyone diagrams
are exceptions to this. These usually contain more than
one tree. The Fan Chart and Pedigree diagrams
are also exceptions in that they do not contain any basic family
trees.

New Route

Create a new route. You will be required to specify the
size and colour of the route line, and whether you want this
line to be solid or to match existing line styles (dotted lines
are sometimes used in family trees with 'crossing' lines, to
avoid possible confusion).

Delete the selected route

Move the selected route up - that is, give it priority over
other routes. Routes that are listed first are drawn over
later routes.

Move the selected route down.

Displays a dropdown menu with the following additional
commands:

Clear route: removes all
boxes from the current selected route but does not delete the
route

Select route boxes: selects
all boxes associated with the currently selected route

title: Family Historian User Manual
text:
Family Historian User Manual

Introduction

This document is the Family Historian User Manual. It can be
accessed either from within Family Historian itself, or on the Internet
using a web browser. Both options are available from the Help menu
within the program. When using the program, you can also jump
straight to pages that are relevant to the current context, by pressing
Help buttons wherever you see them, or by
pressing the F1 key on any workspace
window. The in-program version of the user manual has a
contents page, index and search capability. The Internet version
also has contents, index and search; but the search tool is more
powerful and comprehensive.

What is Family Historian?

Family Historian is a powerful genealogy program that lets you organise
all your genealogy research in one or more projects (most people
keep all their data in one project). Where does the data come from? You
can enter it yourself. The data could be information you know yourself,
information you acquire by interviewing your relatives, or information
you acquire through other forms of research. You can also merge in data
that you find on the Internet or acquire by other means from other
genealogists. In this way you build up a collection of records for
Individuals and Families, and store details of events and attributes
relating to them. Importantly, Family Historian makes it easy for you to
also record exactly where all the information came from (your sources).
But you don't just store facts. Family Historian also lets you keep
pictures of people and families (as well as pictures of other things
such as places and events - not to mention scanned images of
certificates and other sources) as well as video, sound recordings, and
other media. Using the genealogy data you have entered or acquired (and
associated pictures, etc) Family Historian will instantly create for you
any of the following:

charts and diagrams

reports

books or booklets

queries - to analyse your data, or to extract portions of it for
use with other software tools

maps - with markers, overlays and annotations

websites

family tree USB sticks, or CD/DVDs

smart folders - for easy browsing and exploring

You can easily share all of these with family members, friends and
other genealogists. If you wish, you can also share your family tree
data files as well. This is because Family Historian uses GEDCOM as the
format in which it stores its data. GEDCOM is the global standard format
for shared genealogical data and all serious genealogy programs support
it (although the extent to which they support it varies considerably).
To learn more, see GEDCOM.

Where Do I Start?

For a quick overview see the Online Tour of Family Historian.
You can access this tour at any time from the Help menu. See also Getting Started.

What's New in Version 8?

Family Historian is constantly being enhanced and improved. See What's New in Family Historian 8 for a list of
new features and enhancements.

Copyright Notice

All parts of this Family Historian User Manual are copyright © Calico
Pie Limited, 2002-2026.

title: Family Records
text:
Record Types

Family Records

Family records are identified by this icon: .
They store information about families, and store links to all the
Individuals who make up the family. You can view and edit Family records
in the Property Box.

It is not necessary to create Family Records directly. Family
Historian will automatically create Family Records for you when they are
needed. You rarely even need to look directly at Family Records in the
Property Box. You can see Family record Notes, for example, in the Notes
tab when viewing the Individual records (in the Property Box) for either
of the spouses/parents of the family. Similarly, you can see Family
record events and attributes in the Facts tab when viewing the
Individual records (in the Property Box) for either of the
spouses/parents of the family.

Tabs for Family records in the Property Box:

Main
(for Families)

Facts

Notes

Media

All

title: FamilySearch Auto-Match Dialog
text:
FamilySearch Window

FamilySearch Auto-Match Dialog

The Auto-Match Dialog allows you to get Family Historian to decide
which as-yet-unmatched Individuals in your project have matches in
FamilySearch Family Tree, and to create these matches. Family
Historian will only match Individuals if it has a high level of
confidence that the matches are correct.

It is important to realise that no actual data is transferred (either
from FamilySearch to Family Historian or vice versa) when a Family
Historian Individual record is matched to a FamilySearch person.
All that happens, when two records are 'matched', is that Family
Historian stores the FamilySearch Id for the matching FamilySearch
record, within the Family Historian record. No change at all is
made to the FamilySearch record.

The Auto-Match Dialog does not make any changes to any Individual
records that are already matched.

If you decide after auto-matching that it was a mistake, just click
'Undo' on the Edit menu to undo the entire auto-match.

Fields

Scope
You can choose to either look to match
all as-yet-unmatched Individuals; or, if you prefer, if you
already have some matched Individuals, you can look for matches
for relatives of a selection of these Individuals. If you
choose the latter option, you will be required to specify the
Individuals in question, and optionally the maximum number of
generations.

Add New Matches to Named List

Tick this option if you wish to keep a record of the new matches
in a named list. You will need to supply the name of the
list (which can be a new one), and whether or not you want the
list to be emptied before the new matches are added to it (clearly
this is only relevant if the list is an existing one).

title: Import from FamilySearch Dialog
text:
FamilySearch Window

Import from FamilySearch Dialog

Import from FamilySearch Dialog

The FamilySearch Import Dialog allows you to import records for
Individuals into your project (either a new one, or an existing one)
directly from either the FamilySearch global tree or from a user
tree. Before you can import from a user tree however, support for
the FamilySearch use tree functionality must have been enabled and you
must already have access to the user tree - either because it is your
tree (you created it) or because you have been granted access to it (see
User Trees for more on
this).

If support for use tree functionality is not already enabled, you can
enable it in Preferences:
FamilySearch tab. When it is enabled, the full list user
trees that you have access to will be shown in the "Tree to Import from"
dropdown list. If support for user tree functionality is not
enabled, or if you do not have access to any user trees, this list will
consist of "Main Tree (global)" only.

If you are importing from the global tree, you cannot import the entire
tree (it contains over 1.5 billion records). In that case, the
only allowed option for "Records to Import" will be "Selected Tree
Branches". However, if you are importing from a user tree
you can, if you wish, import the entire tree (set "Records to Import" to
"Whole Tree" in this case).

Importing Selected Tree Branches into a New/Empty Project

To import selected tree branches into an empty project, you simply
specify the FamilySearch Id of the starting person, decide what kind of
relatives you want to import and the number of generations, and click
the Import button. You can also opt
to import with yourself as the starting person - assuming you have a
record in the relevant tree, identified with your FamilySearch account.

Importing Selected Tree Branches into a Project that is Not Empty

As well as being able to import into an empty project, you can also
import into a project that is not empty - that is, contains one or more
Individual records. If there is no overlap between the Individuals
in the Family Historian project and the FamilySearch tree (i.e. there is
no-one who has a record in both your Family Historian project and in the
FamilySearch tree), you can proceed with the import as if you were
importing into an empty project.

If you do an import thinking that there is no overlap, and later
realise that there was some overlap after all, so that you now have
duplicate records for the same Individuals in some cases, you will be
able to resolve this situation by merging the duplicate records within
your project, by using the 'Merge/Compare Records' command on the Edit
menu.

If you know that there is overlap between the Individuals in
your Family Historian project, and in the FamilySearch tree you wish to
import from, you are recommended to match as many of these Individuals
as possible before starting the import, to reduce as far as possible the
risk of ending up with duplicated records for the same
Individuals. To do that take the option "Auto-match Unmatched
Individuals" on the FamilySearch menu
(see FamilySearch Auto-Match
Dialog).

Where one or more of the Individuals in your project are already
matched to a person in the FamilySearch tree, you can opt to import
relatives for them. In that case, you still use the option
"Selected Tree Branches" for "Records to Import", but instead of
entering the FamilySearch Id of the starting person, you can optionally
click the Select button and pick the
relevant Individual from within your project. In that case, when
you import, the imported tree branches will be added as relatives of the
Family Historian record for the starting person - while checking for,
and avoiding, duplication of records. If the Family Historian
record has close relatives (that is parents, children or spouses) who
are not matched to records in the FamilySearch tree, you will be warned
about this and recommended to cancel the import, and to match each of
these people to an equivalent record (if any) in the FamilySearch tree
before proceeding with the import. If you proceed with the import
without first doing this, there is a risk that duplicate records might
be added (however, again, if that happens you can later merge these
records by using the 'Merge/Compare Records' command on the Edit menu).

When an import has completed, you will be told the number of Individual
records that have been imported and the record id range of the newly
imported records. It is a good idea to make a note of these ids,
so that you can check them later if you wish to.

If you decide after an import that it was a mistake, just click 'Undo'
on the Edit menu to undo the entire import.

Why It Is Not Necessarily An Error If No Records Are Imported

Let us suppose that you specify a starting person that you already have
a Family Historian record for (that is to say, a Family Historian
Individual is matched to your starting person). Let us also
suppose that this person has already got two recorded parents, one
spouse and three children recorded in Family Historian, and that all of
these people are matched to records in the FamilySearch tree. When
Family Historian does the import, it will only explore branch lines
leading off from close relatives of the starting person, if it doesn't
already have a record for the close relative. So if the two
parents, one spouse and three children are all that it finds, it won't
import anything. However, if let us say, it finds a fourth child -
one that you do not already have - it will not only import that child,
but it will also import all additional relatives leading off from that
person, subject to whatever options you specified for the import.

Fields

Select Starting Person

If you specify 'Me (current logged-in user)', the tree will
start with your own record in FamilySearch. Alternatively,
you can choose 'Person with this FamilySearch Id' and enter the
FamilySearch Id of the starting person, by hand. Each
person in FamilySearch Family Tree has his or her own unique id
that might look something like this: A23D-EF8. These can be
found on the FamilySearch website (at
https://www.familysearch.org/). You can also find
FamilySearch ids of matched records within your current project by
clicking 'Select' (see below).

Check

After you have entered a FamilySearch Id, click the 'Check'
button to confirm that the id is valid. If it valid, the
name of the person will be shown below.

Select...

Instead of simply entering the
FamilySearch Id, you can select from a list of matched Individuals
in your project. This is only possible if you already have
one or more matched Individuals in your project. If the
project is empty, this option will not be available.

FamilySearch Starting Person

After you have entered a FamilySearch Id, click the 'Check'
button to show the name of the FamilySearch person with the
specified id.

Relative Types to Import
Options are:

Ancestors

Descendants

Ancestors & Descendants

All Relatives

All Relatives Plus

The default is 'All Relatives'. This imports direct
relatives of the chosen person - that is, ancestors of the chosen
person, up to the specified number of ancestor generations, and
descendants (including descendants of ancestors), down to the
number of specified descendant generations. Spouses of these
relatives are also included.

'All Relatives Plus' option is similar to 'All Relatives' but also
imports indirect relatives of the chosen person.
For example, the parents of the spouse of the nephew of the chosen
person, would count as indirect relatives of the chosen person.

Ancestor Generations
The number of ancestor generations required. Not
applicable and ignored if the Relative Types to Import option
above is 'Descendants'.

Descendant Generations
The number of descendant generations required. Not
applicable and ignored if the Relative Types to Import option
above is 'Ancestors'.

If you specify 2 ancestor generations and 2 descendant generations
when importing 'Ancestors & Descendants' (say), you should
expect to see a maximum of 3 generations, after the import.
This is because the first generation (the generation of the chosen
person), is counted as both the first ancestor generation and the
first descendant generation.

title: FamilySearch Merge Dialog
text:
FamilySearch Window

FamilySearch Merge Dialog

The FamilySearch Merge Dialog (captioned "Review Proposed Merge of Two
FamilySeach Records") is displayed when you have a Family Historian
record that is already matched to a FamilySearch record, and you find a
"possible duplicate" - that is, another FamilySearch record which also
appears to be a record for the same person - and choose the
'Match/Merge' option. What you are doing in this case is merging
the two FamilySearch records. After the merge, your Family
Historian record will remain matched to the resulting FamilySearch
record.

When two FamilySearch records are merged, what actually happens is that
one of the records is deleted, and the other record is kept and
(usually) updated with details from the record that will be
deleted. If the information in the two records is different, you
can choose which items of information in each record should be retained,
and which should be discarded.

The FamilySearch Merge Dialog displays a table with 3 columns.
The first column shows details of the record that will be deleted.
The second column shows details of the record that will be updated and
kept. And the third column shows what the latter record will look
like, after the merge. There are tick boxes against each item of
data in the first two columns. The ticked items of data are the
ones that will be retained. An unticked item of data will be
discarded.

Fields

Merge

Click this button to do the merge.

Swap

In some cases, you can choose which record you wish to keep and
which should be deleted. If permitted, the direction of
merge will be swapped when you click this button. However
FamilySearch will not necessarily allow the direction of merge to
be swapped. You will be informed of this, if so, when you
click the button.

Details

Click this button to view more
information about the selected item of data. To select an
item of data, click on its cell in the table.

title: Reason for Change
text:
FamilySearch Window

Reason for Change

Whenever
you make a change to FamilySearch Family Tree, you are strongly
encouraged to record your reason for making the change. To
make this as easy as possible, Family Historian will remember and
display the last 20 reasons you have used, and if your reason is one
you have used before you can quickly select it from a list. If
the reason is a new one, you should just type it in.

title: FamilySearch User Trees
text:
FamilySearch Window

FamilySearch User Trees

FamilySearch have recently added an exciting new feature which allows
anyone to upload family trees that are completely separate from the
global family tree. These trees are called user trees. They
can be kept hidden from ordinary users of FamilySearch, or you can allow
access to everyone on a read-only basis, or you can allow access only to
individuals that you specify. You can give these individuals
read-only access, if preferred, but you can also optionally allow these
individuals to contribute to the shared tree, and edit and maintain
it. Family Historian allows you to add, edit and maintain records
in user trees in exactly the same way that you can add, edit and
maintain records in the FamilySearch global family tree. To enable
this functionality, tick "Enable FamilySearch User Trees", on the FamilySearch tab of
Preferences. When this is enabled, you will then be able to
choose which family tree to associate with each Family Historian
project, by selecting the required user tree (or the global tree) using
the family tree link at the top-right of the FamilySearch
workspace window. You can match individuals in your project
with the equivalent records in the associated FamilySearch family
tree.

The following functionality is supported with respect to user trees.

You can create a new Family Historian project and import an entire
FamilySearch user tree into it (or if you prefer, you can also import
branches from it).

You can import an entire FamilySearch user tree, or branches from
it, into an existing Family Historian project.

You can match Individual records in your Family Historian project
with the equivalent records in a FamilySearch user tree (as you can
with the global family tree), and compare them.

You can transfer data from matching records in the FamilySearch user
family tree to your Family Historian project or vice versa, and match
linked records.

You can view hints associated with matched records.

Family Historian's implementation of the FamilySearch user tree
functionality is currently 'partial' in that the following features are
not yet implemented:

There is currently no option to automatically sync a Family
Historian project with a FamilySearch User tree. All transfers
of data are 'manual' - i.e. one item of data at a time.

There is currently no option within Family Historian itself to give
other individuals shared access to your FamilySearch User Tree, or to
request access to an existing User Tree; but both of these things can
be done quite easily in a web browser. Family Historian will
open the appropriate FamilySearch web page for you if needed (see tip
below).

Each Family Historian project can only be associated with one
FamilySearch tree (user or global) at any one time. If a project
is linked to a given tree at a particular time, all matches that you see
within the project will be matches to that tree. If you switch to
another tree (which you can do at any time), you may have a completely
different set of matches or none. If you switch back to the first
tree, the matches associated with that tree will still be there.
Match information is not lost when you switch between trees.
Within Family Historian, matches to FamilySearch can be viewed in
the FamilySearch workspace
window, but also as FamilySearch Ids in the Records Window or
Query Window, or in reports or books (if configured to do so), or
signalled using FamilySearch icons in the Focus Window or in diagram
windows. In all cases, the information displayed relates to the
FamilySearch tree (user or global) that your project is associated with
at that particular time. And, as already-mentioned, the
association in question is specified using the tree link, in the
top-right of the FamilySearch
workspace window.

You don't have to match all of your Family Historian projects to the
same FamilySearch tree, and in fact it is unlikely that you would want
to do that. If you have access to a number of FamilySearch user
trees, a good option is to create and maintain a Family Historian
project for each one.

How to Create a FamilySearch User Tree

To create a FamilySearch User Tree, open the project you wish to upload
and switch to the FamilySearch Window.
Click on the FamilySearch menu (called "FamilySearch") that is active in
the main menu bar, when the FamilySearch Window is active. Take
the option "Upload Current Project to New User Tree in FamilySearch",
and follow the instructions. When you have done this, the tree
link menu, which includes all the trees to which you have access, will
include the new tree you have created, and the new tree will be
selected. All Individuals in your current project will be
automatically matched to the Individuals in the new user tree.

How to give other people shared access to your FamilySearch User tree

Giving other users shared access to your FamilySearch user tree is done
on a FamilySearch web page, in a web browser. To find this page,
open the FamilySearch Window.
Confirm that the correct user tree is selected in the tree list
(top-right) and click the "FamilySearch" menu in the main application
menu bar. Click on "Open FamilySearch Web Page", and then choose
"Current User Tree". This will open a web browser displaying the
relevant web page.

How to get access to other peoples' FamilySearch User trees

If you would like access to other users' user trees, you should contact
them and ask them to give you access (they can do this by following the
instructions in the previous section). When you have access, you
will see the tree listed in the dropdown tree list (top-right of the FamilySearch workspace window).

title: FamilySearch Window: Changes Tab
text:
FamilySearch Window

FamilySearch Window: Changes Tab

FamilySearch Window: Changes Tab

The Changes tab shows a list of changes that have been made to the
FamilySearch record.

title: FamilySearch Window: Discussions Tab
text:
FamilySearch Window

FamilySearch Window: Discussions Tab

FamilySearch Window: Discussions Tab

Disclaimer: The contents of the Family Historian sample
project were invented for illustrative purposes only. All data in
the Family Historian sample project is entirely fictitious, as is the
sample discussion above. Any similarity to any real person, living
or dead, is completely coincidental.

The Discussions tab is used for discussions about the FamilySearch
record, with other FamilySearch users. These discussions are
intended to enable collaborative working. Any FamilySearch user
can contribute. Discussions are visible to all FamilySearch users
who can view the FamilySearch record in question (which will be all of
them, unless the record is part of a user
tree).

Discussions are listed on the left-hand side. Details of the
selected discussion are shown on the right-hand side. Click the
links highlighted in blue in the right side panel, to add, edit or
delete comments. You can only edit or delete your own
comments. You can also delete an entire discussion, but only if it
is a discussion you created yourself.

Click the button Create New Discussion
(bottom-left) to start a new discussion.

title: FamilySearch Window: Matches Tab
text:
FamilySearch Window

FamilySearch Window: Matches Tab

FamilySearch Window: Matches Tab,
displaying search results (blurred)

The Matches tab is used primarily for finding a matching between an
as-yet-unmatched Family Historian Individual record, and a FamilySearch
person record in the current
tree. It can also be used for finding more matches for
records that have already been matched, and for searching the current
FamilySearch tree.

All the other tabs of the FamilySearch workspace window are designed to
allow you to perform tasks when you have matched a Family Historian
record to a FamilySearch record. If you haven't yet matched the
current Family Historian record to a FamilySearch record, you will see
messages suggesting that you need to switch to the Matches tab, to find
a match, before you can use the other tabs.

The Matches tab always shows 3 tables, each with their own column
headings. The column headings of the first table are coloured light green,
indicating that it is showing Family Historian records. The column
heading of the 2nd and 3rd tables are coloured light
blue, indicating that they are showing FamilySearch
records.

Tip: These colour codings, light
green for Family Historian and light
blue for FamilySearch, are used in all tabs of the FamilySearch
workspace window, so that you can see at a glance which domain (Family
Historian or FamilySearch) records and data belong to.

The first table, with heading "Family Historian Individual" in the
first column, only ever has one record. This is the table for the
current Family Historian record.

The second table, with heading "FamilySearch Match" in the first
column, also only ever has at most one record. This is the table
for the FamilySearch record in the current FamilySearch tree, that the
Family Historian record is matched to - if there is one. If the
Family Historian record were not yet matched to a FamilySearch record,
the column headings for the second table would be a light grey colour,
and the first row would contain the text "Not matched", also in light
grey, in the first cell. However, in the example above, the Family
Historian record (with Family Historian record id 5) is
matched to a FamilySearch record (one with FamilySearch record id
BM3P-FYB).

In the example above, the FamilySearch record has values which mainly
match the equivalent values in the Family Historian record. Where
values match, the values - such as name, birth date, birth place, and so
on - are highlighted in green.
If there are differences between the two records, which there often will
be, these are highlighted in red
in the FamilySearch record. The use of these colours make
similarities and differences very easy to see. In the example
above, we can see that details match between the Family Historian record
and the FamilySearch record, except for the word 'Lewisham' in the
'Birth Place' field, which is spelled 'Lewissham' in the Family
Historian record.

The third table, with heading "FamilySearch Record" in the first
column, is unlike the other two tables in that it can display multiple
records. The listed records it displays (if any) all come from
FamilySearch, which is why its column headings are blue. There are
4 possible lists that can be displayed in this 3rd table. These
are:

Possible Matches (to the Family Historian record at the top)

Possible Duplicates List (for the Matched FamilySearch record, if
there is one)

Not-a-Match List (for the Matched FamilySearch record, if there is
one)

Search Results (showing the results of the last search, if any)

In the example above, the table is showing the results of a
recent search.

Ian Stephen Munro, and everyone else mentioned in the
Family Historian Sample Project are fictitious. The search results
data in the image above contained data about real people and has
consequently been blurred.

The differences between these lists will be discussed in detail
below. Before looking at these differences, however, note that
immediately above the third table is the name of the current list that
it is displaying ("Search Results" in the example above). Click on
this field to view a list of available lists, and to select the one you
want to view. The "Possible Duplicates List" and the "Not-a-Match
List" are only available when the Family Historian record at the top has
been matched to a FamilySearch record.

To the right of the list name field is a Search
button. Click on this list to open the Search dialog. You
can either start a new search or refine an existing search. When
you do a search, the third table will automatically switch to showing
search results if it was previously showing some other list. You
can switch between lists at any time.

Immediately below the 3rd table, are 4 buttons: Match/Merge,
Unmatch, Compare
and Not a Match - all currently greyed in
the image above. The first button would be replaced with Match
if the Family Historian record had not yet been matched to a
FamilySearch record. These buttons are discussed in the Buttons
section below.

All records displayed in third table, irrespective of which list is
being displayed, will have values highlighted in green
if they match the Family Historian record at the top, and will have
values highlighted in red
if they conflict with the equivalent Family Historian record value.

Possible Matches List

The Possible Matches List, as the name suggests, is a list of
FamilySearch records that look as if they could be a match for the
Family Historian record listed at the top, based on some key details,
such as the person's name, birth date and place (if known), actual or
possible matches between parents and other close relatives; and so
on. This list may contain any number of records, or none. A
person's details do not have to match perfectly to be listed.

If you have not yet matched the current Family Historian record to a
FamilySearch record, the first of the 4 buttons at the bottom will be Match. If you see a FamilySearch record that you
believe is a match for the Family Historian record at the top, click on
it to select it (the checkbox at the start of the row will show a tick
to indicate that the row is selected) and press the Match
button. See the Buttons section below to
learn more.

Possible Duplicates List

FamilySearch maintains a list of possible duplicates for every person
record in every tree. Records get automatically added to this
list, using FamilySearch's own matching algorithm. Because the
possible duplicates list is attached to FamilySearch records, this list
cannot be viewed until you have already matched a Family Historian
record to a FamilySearch record.

Not-Match-List

As well as a duplicate list, FamilySearch also maintains a list called
the 'Not-a-Match' list for every person in every record in every
FamilySearch tree. Sometimes the FamilySearch matching algorithm may
deliver incorrect results. If you spot that one record has
incorrectly been flagged as a possible duplicate for another, you can
correct this by marking the records as 'not-a-match'. When you do
this, the records will be added to each other's not-a-match list, to
indicate that they should not be viewed as duplicates of one another.

Search Results

This is the list of records that match criteria you use when you click
the Search button to do a search.

Buttons

Button

Action

Match

This button will only be displayed when the current Family
Historian record is not yet matched to any FamilySearch
record. To enable this button, select any record in the 3rd
table (any list) so that the record shows a tick in the first
column. Matching a FamilySearch record to a Family Historian
record is not a very signficant act. It involves no changes
at all to the FamilySearch tree. All that happens, is that
the FamilySearch record id is stored in a special field within the
Family Historian record.

When you match a record in this way, you can unmatch it by simply
clicking 'Undo' on the Edit menu. You can also use the Unmatch button (see below).

Match/Merge

This button (instead of the Match
button) will be displayed when the current Family Historian record
is already matched to any FamilySearch record.

If you have matched your Family Historian record to a FamilySearch
record, what do you do if you find another, seemingly identical
FamilySearch record, which you believe is a duplicate? This
could be a record in the Possible Duplicates List (see above); but
it doesn't have to be. It could be any record that you spot
anywhere. If there are two FamilySearch records which are
duplicates, what can you do about it? You can't match your
Family Historian to both of them. Each Family Historian
record can only be matched to at most one FamilySearch record in
any given FamilySearch tree.

This is a fairly common situation. With people all over the
world adding genealogy data, it is inevitable that multiple
records for the same person, will sometimes be created.
FamilySearch encourage you to help them keep their data in a good
state, by merging duplicates when you find them. This is
what the Match/Merge button
does. It effectively merges the two FamilySearch records
into one, and then matches your Family Historian record to the
resulting merged record. Full details of the proposed merge
will be displayed and you can tweak and override aspects of it,
before proceeding with the merge.

To use this button you must select the record in the 3rd table
that you wish to match with the FamilySearch record shown in the
second table.

Unmatch

If you wish to undo a match between a Family Historian record
and a FamilySearch record, click on the FamilySearch record in the
2nd table, and click Unmatch to
unmatch them

You can unmatch all records in the current project
- either for the current FamilySearch tree or for all
FamilySearch trees. To do this, click on the cog menu in
the top-right of the FamilySearch
Workspace window, and choose "Clear All Matches..." from
the dropdown menu that appears. You will be prompted to
choose between clearing matches in the current tree, or all
trees.

Compare

The 3 tables only display a limited number of fields. If
you have matched a FamilySearch record to your Family Historian
record, you can view the differences between them in full detail
in the Share
Data tab. However, if you haven't already matched
them, or if you want to do a detailed comparison of another
FamilySearch record with the Family Historian record, select the
FamilySearch record and click the Compare
button to open a separate window to compare them. This
window will display the two records side-by-side, in a similar way
to the Share
Data tab.

Not a Match

If you see a FamilySearch record in the 3rd table that you
believe is not a match for the FamilySearch record in the 2nd
table (if any), select the record in the 3rd table and click the Not a Match button. See Not-a-Match
List for more on this.

title: FamilySearch Window: Notes Tab
text:
FamilySearch Window

FamilySearch Window: Notes Tab

FamilySearch Window: Notes Tab

The Notes tab shows notes stored in the Family Historian record, on the
left, and in the FamilySearch record, on the right. Many of the
details of this tab are similar to those in the Share
Data tab (and for that matter, to the Sources
tab and the Ordinances
tab). For example, the Family Historian notes, on the left
are colour-coded with a light
green background and the FamilySearch notes, on the right (only
one in the example above) are colour-coded with a light
blue background. And again, the record names at the top
of the tab, are links you can click on to view the Family Historian
record in the Property Box, or to view
the FamilySearch web page for the FamilySearch source record,
respectively. See the Share
Data tab for more details.

Menu Commands

As with the Share
Data tab, wherever you see the little arrow in a circle looking
like this (or
like this
when move your mouse over the text in bold) there is a menu of commands
available to you. To access the menu, click on the text in bold
or the icon itself (or right-click on the row). The
menus on the Family Historian side will have these menu commands:

Menu Command

Description

Add Note to FamilySearch

Add this note to the FamilySearch search record. Notes in
Family Historian can have word-processing features, such as font
and colour changes, bold, italic, underline, tables, hot links and
much more. None of these features are supported in
FamilySearch. So notes will be converted to plain text
before being added to the FamilySearch record.

Notes in FamilySearch have a title. You will be able to
adjust this before adding the note to FamilySearch.

Locate in Property Box

Locate and display the relevant note for the Family Historian
record in the Property Box.

The menus on the FamilySearch side will have these menu commands:

Menu Command

Description

Add Note to Family Historian
Copy the note to Family Historian. Notes will be attached
as record notes for the current individual. The title will
be inserted as the first line of the note.

Edit Note in FamilySearch

Use this menu command to edit the note, and it's title, within
FamilySearch.

View Details

View full details of the FamilySearch note, including the
details of the FamilySearch contributor who contributed it, in a
popup window.

title: FamilySearch Window: Ordinances Tab
text:
FamilySearch Window

FamilySearch Window: Ordinances Tab

FamilySearch Window: Ordinances Tab

The Ordinances tab is a special tab that is only visible if LDS Support
is enabled (see the General
tab of Preferences). LDS Support is only relevant to members
of the LDS Church (see LDS Church
Features to learn more).

The Ordinances tab shows ordinances stored in the Family
Historian record, on the left, and in the FamilySearch record, on the
right. Many of the details of this tab are similar to those in the
Share Data tab.
For example, the Family Historian ordinances, on the left (blank in the
example above) are colour-coded with a light
green background and the FamilySearch sources, on the right,
are colour-coded with a light
blue background. And again, the record names at the top
of the tab, are links you can click on to view the Family Historian
record in the Property Box, or to view
the FamilySearch web page for the FamilySearch source record,
respectively. See the Share
Data tab for more details.

Menu Commands

As with the Share
Data tab, wherever you see the little arrow in a circle looking
like this (or
like this
when move your mouse over the text in bold) there is a menu of commands
available to you. To access the menu, click on the text in bold
or the icon itself (or right-click on the row). The
menus on the Family Historian side will have these menu commands:

Menu Command

Description

Delete from Family Historian

Deletes details of that particular ordinance from the Family
Historian record.

Locate in Property Box

Locates and displays the relevant ordinance in the Property Box.

The menus on the FamilySearch side will have these menu commands:

Menu Command

Description

Sync to Family Historian

Only completed ordinances (that is, ordinances with status
'Completed') can be copied to Family Historian. This option
will be greyed (disabled) for ordinances that are not completed.

If there are already some details for this ordinance within the
Family Historian record, they will be updated to match the details
in FamilySearch. If there as yet no details, a new ordinance
event will be created within the Family Historian record.

View Details

Opens a popup window to display full details of the relevant
ordinance.

Buttons

Button

Description

Sync Completed to Family Historian

This button syncs all completed ordinance details to the Family
Historian record. In each case, if there are already some
details for an ordinance within the Family Historian record, they
will be updated to match the details in FamilySearch. If
there as yet no details for a given ordinance, a new ordinance
event will be created within the Family Historian record.

Ordinances that are not completed will not be copied to Family
Historian.

Reserve Ordinances...

Click on this button to open a web page within the FamilySearch
web site, where ordinances can be reserved, and other temple work
tasks can be performed.

Although the most common purpose for visiting this web page is to
reserve ordinances, you can also click the Reserve
Ordinances button if you just want to view the web page
for ordinances for the person in question, in the FamilySearch
website.

When you click on this button, you may be required to login to
FamilySearch.

Tip: To minimize the number of times you may be
required to login to FamilySearch, you are recommended to avoid
unnecessarily closing your web browser between visits to the
FamilySearch site.

If you make changes on the FamilySearch website, after doing so
you can click the Refresh button
in the toolbar, in the FamilySearch workspace window within
Family Historian, to refresh the page to reflect your changes.

title: FamilySearch Window: Share Data Tab
text:
FamilySearch Window

FamilySearch Window: Share Data Tab

FamilySearch Window: Share Data Tab

The Share Data tab shows details of the current Family Historian record
on the left-hand side (with a light
green background), with the equivalent details from the
matching FamilySearch record on the right-hand side (with a light
blue background). You can copy details from the
FamilySearch record into Family Historian or from Family Historian into
FamilySearch. You can also add missing records for relatives into
Family Historian from FamilySearch or vice versa. And you can
match (and unmatch) relatives too.

If there is, as yet, no matching FamilySearch record, the right-hand
side will be blank and a message will tell you to use the Matches
tab to find possible matches.

Differences on either side are highlighted in yellow
to make them easy to spot. There is no presumption about which is
right. In the example above, Lewisham is incorrectly spelled as
"Lewissham" in the Family Historian record, and Farmborough is
incorrectly spelled as "Farmburgh" in the FamilySearch record. So
the natural thing would be to correct the Family Historian spelling of
'Lewisham', and to correct the FamilySearch record with respect to the
spelling of 'Farmborough'.

Record Names are Links

At the top of the tab, the records names are displayed with their
record id in square brackets after the names. Between the two
names is an equals sign
indicating that the records are matched with one another. Each
record name is a link. Click on the Family Historian record name
to view the record in the Property Box. Click on the FamilySearch
record name to view the FamilySearch record's page within the
FamilySearch website. An external web browser will be opened to
display the page. You may be required to login.

Menu Commands for 'Vital' and 'Other' Information

Wherever you see a little icon showing a downward pointing arrow in a
circle, , there
is a menu of commands available to you. To access the menu, click
on the cell containing the icon, or right-click anywhere on the same
row. When you move your mouse over the first cell, the icon will
light up, like this: .
The exact menu commands displayed will vary depending on the field type,
and depending on whether the field belongs to the Family Historian
record to the FamilySearch record. When you click on a Family
Historian field in either the 'Vital Information' or the 'Other
Information' sections, the dropdown menu will typically look like this:

When you do the same thing with a FamilySearch field. the dropdown menu
will typically look like this:

If you're copying data to FamilySearch you may be able to choose
between modifying an existing in FamilySearch field (if there is one) or
inserting a new one. And the same is true when copying from
FamilySearch into Family Historian. If you are not offered the
option to insert a new fact within FamilySearch this may be because
FamilySearch only allows one instance of that fact type.

As can be seen, you have the option to delete facts in either Family
Historian or FamilySearch.

If you click "Locate in Property Box", Family Historian will display
the specific item of data in the Property Box. As always, you can
make any changes you like in the Property Box at any time, and the
FamilySearch window will update immediately to reflect the change. So,
if you want to correct the spelling of "Lewissham" for example, you do
not have to change it by copying from FamilySearch. You could just
delete the extra 's' in the Property Box. You should use whichever
method feels easiest in the moment.

The 'View Details...' command on the FamilySearch-side menu, opens a
popup window to show more details of the particular fact, including
details of the FamilySearch contributor who contributed that
fact.

Menu Commands for 'Family Members'

The 'Family Members' section shows close family members.
Individuals on either side who look like possible matches will be
automatically aligned. Individuals who are already matched will
have a little 'equals' icon
between the two records, to indicate that they are matched. This
is a smaller version of the equals icon that appears at the top of the
tab, between the names of the matched records.

When you click on the menu icon
(or anywhere in the first cell) in the "Family Members" section, the
menu displayed will vary depending on whether the record is already
matched or not. On the Family Historian side you will see menu
commands such as these:

Menu Command

Description

Match

Match the record on the Family Historian side with the record on
the FamilySearch side. Is only available for unmatched
records.

Unmatch...

Unmatch two already-matched records. Is only
available for matched records.

Compare...

Open a Compare Window (similar to the Share Data tab) for
comparing two records side-by-side.

You cannot edit field values within the Compare Window but you can
select different records to compare, you can match and unmatch
records, and you can even open nested Compare Windows for
comparing relatives.

Add into FamilySearch as Parent/Spouse/Child
Add the Family Historian record into FamilySearch as a new
parent/spouse/child. Before doing so, you will be shown a
list of possible matches for the Family Historian record within
FamilySearch. The list may be empty if none are found.
It is an opportunity for you to double-check that there isn't
already a record for this person within FamilySearch - or to match
to that record, if there is.

Set as Window Root

Make this person the current "Window Root" for the FamilySearch
workspace window; so that the Share Data tab (and all other
tabs) now show information about them. You can return
to the person who is the current window root, by clicking the 'Go
Back' button (immediately to the left of the tab headings).

Properties...

Open the Property Box to view the Family Historian record.

On the FamilySearch side you will see menu commands such as these:

Menu Command

Description

Match

Match the record on the Family Historian side with the record on
the FamilySearch side. Is only available for
unmatched records.

Unmatch...

Unmatch two already-matched records. Is only
available for matched records.

Compare...

Open a Compare Window (similar to the Share Data tab) for
comparing two records side-by-side.

You cannot edit field values within the Compare Window but you can
select different records to compare, you can match and unmatch
records, and you can even open nested Compare Windows for
comparing relatives.

Add into Family Historian as Parent/Spouse/Child
Add the FamilySearch record into Family Historian as a new
parent/spouse/child.

Set Matched Record as Window Root

Matched records only. Makes the matched Family
Historian person the current "Window Root" for the FamilySearch
workspace window; so that the Share Data tab (and all other
tabs) now show information about them. You can return
to the person who is the current window root, by clicking the 'Go
Back' button (immediately to the left of the tab headings).

View in FamilySearch

Opens the FamilySearch web page for this person, in the
FamilySearch web site, using an external web browser. You
may be required to login.

Citing Your Sources

When you copy data into Family Historian, you can use all the usual
methods for recording the source of your information. For example,
you can add a source citation in the Property Box, or copy-and-paste
one, or you can use Family Historian's automatic
source citation pane in the normal way.

Undo/Redo

Whenever you make changes to Family Historian records, you can use the
Undo/Redo commands on the Edit menu, to undo (or redo) them. This
is true of all change, including insertions and deletions of both fields
and records. You can even undo (and redo) a whole series of
changes - perhaps extending right back to the start of your Family
Historian session. All of this works, regardless of how you make
the change - and this applies to changes made by copying from
FamilySearch too. However, there is no equivalent to this with
changes made to FamilySearch. You cannot simply click an 'Undo'
command to undo them. If you add a fact to FamilySearch and later
decide that it was a mistake, you will need to reverse the change
yourself - for example, by selecting the newly added fact and deleting
it.

Note that matching and unmatching both involve making changes to Family
Historian records (only); so these also be undone or redone on the Edit
menu.

Standardized Place Names

If you add a fact to FamilySearch, it will always keep a record of the
place details as you specify them within Family Historian. But it
will also try to match the place details to its own internal database of
standardized place descriptions. The match does not have to be
perfect. If it can find a match with an adequately high
level of confidence, it will accept that. If you look at the
FamilySearch record for the person, and if you click on the fact to view
and edit full details, it will show both the place details as originally
supplied by you, and, in addition, it will show what it considers to be
the standardized version of the place, if different.

If FamilySearch is unable to find a good match for a place, it will
still record the place details as supplied, but when you look at the
record in FamilySearch it will show the text "Non-standardized Place"
below the provided place name. It may also show a red circle with
an exclamation mark in the "Research Help" area, indicating that the
place details are missing.

For example, in your records you might record a place as "Ballantrae,
Scotland". The standardized version of this in the FamilySearch
database is "Ballantrae, Ayrshire, Scotland, United Kingdom".
FamilySearch will happily accept "Ballantrae, Scotland" and will
automatically match it to its standardized version. If, however,
there was a typing mistake and the place was specified as "Bollantrae,
Scotland", it would not match this with any standardized place.

Again, if you specify "Paris, Texas" FamilySearch will accept that, and
will automatically match it to "Paris, Lamar, Texas, United States".

Does it matter if FamilySearch cannot match the place description to a
standardized place? The answer is - yes and no. It won't
prevent you adding information to FamilySearch. But it does mean
that other researchers may see the information provided as, in this
respect, somewhat incomplete. If you find that FamilySearch
regularly fails to recognise place details as you supply them, there are
various things you can do. You can always edit the record within
FamilySearch and select from a list of standardized place names
there. However this could be laborious if you have many
recorded events with the same place details. Another option would
be to change the way you record place details to match the FamilySearch
standard. But you might not want to do that, for any number of
reasons. Finally there is a third option, which for many people
may be the best. Family Historian allows you to record a
standardized version of any place name. This is the field labelled
"Standardized", which is displayed when you view or edit the Place
record. You do not have to use this field. It is entirely
optional. And there is no reason to make use of it, if your
ordinary place descriptions are recognised by FamilySearch anyway.
But if you do specify a standardized version of the place details,
Family Historian will supply this to FamilySearch, along with the
ordinary version, whenever you copy data from Family Historian into
FamilySearch that references this place. And FamilySearch will use
both versions, when looking for a match to its own standardized version
of the place. Again, just as there is no requirement that your
ordinary place details need be an exact match of FamilySearch's
standardized version, the same is true of the version in the Standardized
field. This doesn't have to be an exact match either.

Of course depending on what you put in the Standardized field,
it might not necessarily help FamilySearch. If it contains typing
errors, say, FamilySearch might still not be able to match your place
details with a standardized version. And if it is a duplicate of
the original, with no more details, it will clearly not have any
benefit. But although there is no guarantee, providing a suitable
standardized version of the place details, should make it more likely
that FamilySearch can find a standardized version to match to, if the
ordinary version on its own is not enough.

title: FamilySearch Window: Sources Tab
text:
FamilySearch Window

FamilySearch Window: Sources Tab

FamilySearch Window: Sources Tab

The Sources tab shows the sources linked to the Family Historian
record, on the left, and to the FamilySearch record, on the right.
Many of the details of this tab are similar to those in the Share
Data tab. For example, the Family Historian sources, on the
left, are colour-coded with a light
green background and the FamilySearch sources, on the right,
are colour-coded with a light
blue background. And again, the record names at the top
of the tab, are links you can click on to view the Family Historian
record in the Property Box, or to view
the FamilySearch web page for the FamilySearch source record,
respectively. See the Share
Data tab for more details.

Citation-Handling

Again, like the Share
Data tab, you can copy details from Family Historian into
FamilySearch, or vice versa. However, the way that FamilySearch
handles citations is different to the way that Family Historian does
it. Both Family Historian and FamilySearch store Source
records. In Family Historian, a 'citation' is effectively a link
between a field within an Individual record (or other type of data
record) and a Source record. For example, if a Source record
provides the details of a person's birth, the Source record can be
linked directly to their birth field. In FamilySearch, the Source
record is not directly linked to the birth field. Instead it is
linked to the person's record and you set tags to indicate which field
or fields within that record, the Source is relevant to. So, for
example, you would set a 'Birth' tag to show that the Source record
provided information about the person's birth. If it also provided
details of a person's death and burial, you would set those tags
too. In Family Historian, you would link the death and burial
facts directly to the Source record.

Menu Commands

As with the Share
Data tab, wherever you see the little arrow in a circle looking
like this (or
like this
when move your mouse over the text in bold) there is a menu of commands
available to you. To access the menu, click on the text in bold
or the icon itself (or right-click on the row). The
menus on the Family Historian side will have these menu commands:

Menu Command

Description

Add Source to FamilySearch

Add this Source record to FamilySearch. You will be able
to confirm details. The tags that are applicable to the new
Source record will be ticked automatically, but you can confirm
that these are correct before continuing (see Citation-handling
above)

View Family Historian Source Record...

Display the relevant Source record in the Property Box.

The menus on the FamilySearch side will have these menu commands:

Menu Command

Description

View Web Page in External Browser

Displays the relevant FamilySearch Sources web page in a web
browser.

View Web Page in Web Search Window
Displays the relevant FamilySearch Sources web page in the Web
Search window. This option may be more convenient for web
clipping.

Add Source to Family Historian

Add this Source record to FamilySearch. You will be able
to confirm details, including which fields the Source record
should be linked to (see Citation-handling
above)

Edit Source in FamilySearch

You can modify details of the FamilySearch source, including
selecting the tags which indicate which data the source relates to
(see Citation-handling above).

View Details

View full details of the FamilySearch source in a popup window.

title: The FamilySearch Window
text:
Workspace Windows

The FamilySearch Window

The FamilySearch Window (marked in red)

FamilySearch is Free

FamilySearch is a nonprofit family history organization, based in Utah,
USA, operated by The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints
(sometimes abbreviated as "the LDS Church"). It maintains a collection
of records, resources and services designed to help people learn more
about their family history. Everyone is welcome to create a free
account, to access FamilySearch resources. FamilySearch hosts a
huge, global, shared family tree, which is open to the world.
Anyone can access the tree and anyone can contribute to it - by
providing more details about people who are already in the tree, by
adding new people to the tree, or by correcting errors. The tree
currently has information about approximately 1.7 billion persons.
It is the world's largest online family tree. The system permits
conflicting assertions of fact, allowing differences of opinion.
Facts can be supported by source citations, and you can also add notes,
and have discussions with other contributors.

Although the system is designed to connect everyone up, it can happen
that a given person acquires more than one record in the global family
tree. To resolve this, the system allows duplicate records to be
merged.

Users are strongly encouraged to record their reasons for making
changes. Before making any changes however, please be sure to read
"Understanding Privacy Issues With FamilySearch" below.

To learn more, see the FamilySearch web page: FamilySearch Family
Tree.

User Trees

FamilySearch have recently added an exciting new feature which allows
anyone to upload family trees separately from the global family
tree. Trees uploaded in this way are called user trees.
They are owned by the person who uploaded them, who can control who can
access and contribute to their tree. This feature is also
supported in Family Historian. You can upload any Family Historian
project as a new user tree, if you wish to. See "Tree Selection
and the 'Current' Tree" below, to learn more. See also FamilySearch User Trees.

Historical Records

As well as tree data in the online family tree, FamilySearch also has a
large number of historical records. Within Family Historian, you
will often see references to "FamilySearch" records. Unless it is
explicitly stated that the records are historical records,
you should always interpret this as short-hand for records in a
FamilySearch tree.

Accessing FamilySearch Trees From Family Historian

As well as being able to access family trees (global or user trees)
from the FamilySearch website at https://www.familysearch.org,
FamilySearch's trees can also be accessed directly from within Family
Historian. Using the FamilySearch Window, a workspace
window, you can easily match individuals in your projects to persons in
a FamilySearch tree. By default, Family Historian will assume that you
want to match your records with the main (global) FamilySearch
tree. However, you can link a Family Historian project to any
other tree that your account has access to, if preferred. When you
match a Family Historian record to a FamilySearch record, you can view
the two records side-by-side, and you can quickly and easily move
information from FamilySearch into Family Historian. If you wish,
you can also move information the other way round too - from Family
Historian to FamilySearch - and become, yourself, a contributor to
FamilySearch trees, without ever needing to leave Family
Historian. All you need is a free FamilySearch account. You
can transfer facts, relatives and relationship information, sources and
source citations, notes, and discussions. You can check for
matches between your records and records in FamilySearch trees; and you
can easily compare possible matches.

When you match a Family Historian Individual with a FamilySearch
person, Family Historian stores the FamilySearch Id for that person, in
their record. An individual is deemed to be matched if they have a
stored FamilySearch Id, and unmatched if they don't. You can view
this id at any time in the 'All' tab of the Property Box. You can
also display it in queries, in record lists, or in diagrams or reports,
as you wish. You can optionally display a FamilySearch icon in the
Focus Window, or in diagrams, so that you can see a glance, which of the
individuals in your project are matched. When an individual is
matched in this way, you can, at any time, quickly view the latest
information held about them in FamilySearch in the FamilySearch
Window. If you wish, Family Historian can also display hints about
FamilySearch matches. To learn more about this, see Internet
Data Matches in the Preferences
Dialog.

Of course, as well as matching people, you can always unmatch them, if
you wish to. You can do this in the FamilySearch Window, or by
simply deleting that persons FamilySearch Id, in the 'All' tab of the
Property Box.

Although you don't need to leave Family Historian, the program provides
links, from each referenced FamilySearch person, so that you can easily
jump to viewing the FamilySearch record in a web browser or in the Web
Search window, if you wish to.

Login tip: If you view a FamilySeach web page in a web
browser, or even in Family Historian's Web Search workspace window, you
may need to login. This is true even if you are already logged in
to FamilySearch within Family Historian. FamilySearch requires a
separate login for web browsers. Family Historian will remember
your FamilySearch login details between sessions. Web browsers may
not. To minimize the number of times you need to login, you are
recommended to avoid closing web browsers unnecessarily, that you use to
access FamilySearch web pages.

Tabs

The FamilySearch Workspace has either 6 or 7 tabs, depending on whether
LDS Church support is enabled or not (see Preferences:
General tab). These are:

Matches Tab

Share Data Tab

Sources Tab

Ordinances Tab
(if LDS Church support is enabled)

Notes Tab

Discussions Tab

Changes Tab

Click on the links above to learn more about each tab.

Auto-Matching And Importing

The FamilySearch Window is designed to help you match persons, and
share data (from FamilySearch to Family Historian or vice versa).
However, there is also an auto-match feature which you can use
to get Family Historian to automatically match Individuals in your
projects to FamilySearch - where matches can be found. To use this
feature, click Auto-match Unmatched Individuals on the FamilySearch
menu. This menu is only available when the FamilySearch
Window is active. It can also be accessed by clicking on the Cog
menu button on the FamilySearch toolbar. To learn more, see FamilySearch
Auto-Match Dialog.

You can also import family trees (or branches of related Individuals),
direct from FamilySearch into Family Historian. To learn more, see
Import from FamilySearch.

the Current Tree (and How to Change it)

By default, each Family Historian project will be compared and matched
against the FamilySearch global family tree. However, you can
switch at any time, to comparing and matching against any tree, global
or 'user', to which you have access. The tree that a project is
currently matched against, is known as the 'current' tree for that
project. The name of the current tree is shown in the top-right
corner of the FamilySearch workspace window (just below your username if
you are logged-in). In the example above, the current tree is
"Family Tree (global)". This field is a link, called the 'tree
link'. If you click on it, a dropdown menu appears, listing all
the trees to which you have access. Click on any listed tree to
switch to make that tree the current tree for the project. The
FamilySearch workspace window, and any other window that displays icons
or information related to FamilySearch, will all update immediately to
reflect the change. See also FamilySearch
User Trees to learn more.

Understanding Privacy Issues With FamilySearch

FamilySearch protects the privacy of living people by restricting who
can see their records. Within its global family tree, you can see the
record of a living person only if you created the record. The system
hides records that you create of living people from everyone else,
including the people themselves and other family members. However,
this only applies to living people. In all other cases, if you add
a record, or an item of data, or make any kind of change to the global
FamilySearch tree, you should be aware that your changes, and the
information you have added, will be visible to anyone, anywhere in the
world, who has a FamilySearch account. This is because in updating
the global tree, you are participating in a joint project. If you
have other family members who are also researching your family, you can
use the FamilySearch global tree as a place for you both to record and
share your research findings - just as long as you appreciate that it is
not just other family members that you are sharing the data with, but
potentially everyone.

If you want to share data with some people, but not everyone, consider
using a FamilySearch user tree, with controlled access.

If you don't want to upload information to FamilySearch, you don't have
to. FamilySearch trees are never updated automatically by Family
Historian. If you want to make updates to a FamilySearch tree,
from within Family Historian, you can only do so in the FamilySearch
window, and only by explicitly choosing to do so - that is, by selecting
a menu command, or similar, to add or update a FamilySearch
record. Even if you plan to never update any FamilySearch tree,
you can however still use FamilySearch effectively in 'read-only' mode,
as a source of information. An important thing to appreciate is
that when you match a Family Historian record with a FamilySearch
record, this is private to you. You aren't updating any
FamilySearch tree at all. Other FamilySearch users will not be
aware that you have matched the records. All that happens (in data
storage terms) when you match the records in this way, is that you store
the FamilySearch Id for the person, in your Family Historian record for
that person. This is not necessarily a permanent thing. You
can delete the FamilySearch Id (unmatch the records) whenever you want
to. However, if you find a FamilySearch record that is a match for
one of your Family Historian records, it is often a good idea to match
them. When you do so, you can then transfer data from the
FamilySearch record into the Family Historian record, or vice versa,
using the Share Data tab of the FamilySearch Window. It also means
that you can receive hints about other, possible duplicate records,
which may also contain useful information. And you can also
receive hints about historical records that FamilySearch has found,
which appear to relate to the same people.

title: Fan Chart Dialog
text:
Diagram Window

Fan Chart Dialog

Fan Chart Dialog

The Fan Chart dialog is displayed when the Fan Chart option is
chosen on the Charts menu, or when a fan chart is inserted
into an existing diagram (which can be done via the Shapes toolbar). It provides
options for the fan chart. It is also possible to change many
aspects of a fan chart after it has been displayed. One
way to do this is to right-click on it and choose 'Format' from the
dropdown menu that appears. You will be able to change the colour
of lines, and their thickness, as well as other aspects of the fan
chart.

A fan chart in a diagram, is implemented as a complex shape
object. More specifically, it is a collection of text pie shapes
that have all been grouped together. So if you wish you can do all
the things with it, that you could do with any shape object. You
can rotate and resize it, for example (and undo/redo any changes).
If you ungroup a fan chart (that is, right-click on it, and choose
'Ungroup' on the Grouping menu) you will be able to access the various
text pie shapes of which it is composed. You could, for example,
change the background colour or other details of individual text pie
shapes, and then, if required, select all the text pie shapes and group
them all back together once again. This could be useful if you
wanted to highlight some particular individuals, for example.

Another thing to be aware of is that you can double-click on any person
in a fan chart, to open the Property Box to view and edit their
details. If the Property Box is already open, just clicking on a
person will cause the Property Box to show their details (if it is
synced to the current selection). Text pie shapes (and text shapes
for that matter) can be selected for this purpose, even if they have
been combined into a larger group shape object, if they are linked to a
record node (see the 'Data' tab of the Format dialog for these shapes).

Fields

Root Person
The person who will be the root of the fan chart.

Chart Type
Options are:

Quarter Circle

Half Circle

Three-Quarter Circle

Full Circle

Root Circle

This tick box is only available when
the Chart Type is Three-Quarter Circle.
In that case, if Root Circle is ticked, the root (only)
will be displayed in a full circle.

Generations
The number of generations to display. The maximum is 12.

Radials From
The text for each ancestor is normally initially displayed in an
arc, centred on the root. However, as the ancestral
generations get higher, the space allocated to each ancestor gets
narrower and at some point,it makes sense to switch the layout of
the text, so that instead of being displayed in an arc, it is
displayed in radial lines emanating outwards from the
centre. The value for Radials From specifies the
generation from which to switch to radial lines. For
example, if the value for Generations is 8, this means
that 8 generations will be displayed in total. If the Radials
From value were 6, that would mean that radial lines would
be used instead of arcs, when laying out the text, for generations
6, 7 and 8.

If the Radials From value is higher than the Generations
value (which is allowed), this means that radial lines will
not be used.

The maximum is 13 (this is so that you can always set the Radials
From figure to a larger number than the number of
generations).

Contents
The options for the contents of each segment in a fan chart are:

Name Only

Dates

Ahnentafel Numbers

Ahnentafel & Dates

Blank

Custom

The first 5 options do the following:

Name Only: each person's name is displayed (only)

Dates: each person's name is displayed, together with their
life dates if known

Ahnentafel Numbers: each person's name is displayed,
preceded by their ahnentafel number, calculated with respect
to the root (so that the root's ahnentafel number is '1').

Ahnentafel & Dates: each person's name is displayed
(preceded by their ahnentafel number), together with their
life dates if known

Blank: the entire fan chart is blank. This could
be useful if you wanted to, say, print out a fan chart as a
template to give family members for them to fill in.

The final option for Contents is 'Custom'. When this
option is selected a window is opened displaying the 'Custom Fan
Chart Contents' dialog where custom text content can be
specified. The Edit button,
to the right of the Contents field (normally disabled) becomes
enabled when 'Custom' is selected, allowing the custom text
contents to be edited. Specifying
custom content for text in a fan chart is an advanced option
for technically-minded users. Ordinary users, who
are not technically-minded, may find constructing custom content
a challenge. Another option, in that case, for users with
complex requirements that are not met by the standard contents
options, would be to post a question on the Family Historian
User Group website (https://www.fhug.org.uk).
There may be users there who can advise on how to achieve the
desired results.

For technical details on customizing fan charts, see Customizing
Fan Chart Content.

Colour
Options are:

White

1 Colour

3 Colours

7 Colours

Colours can be customized by clicking on the Colours
button. The colours listed have the following labels:

Root Person

Father

Mother

Father's Father

Father's Mother

Mother's Father

Mother's Mother

Depending on the option chosen for the Colour field, the labelled
colours are used as follows:

White: all segments are white - i.e. labelled colours are
not used.

1 Colour: all segments are the 'Root Person' colour.
Other labelled colours are not used.

3 Colours: the root person is the 'Root Person'
colour. The father and all of his ancestors are the
'Father' colour. The mother and all of her ancestors are
the 'Mother' colour. Other labelled colours are not
used.

7 Colours: the root person is the 'Root Person'
colour. The father is the 'Father' colour. The
mother is the 'Mother' colour. The father's father and
all of his ancestors are the 'Father's Farther' colour.
The father's mother and all of her ancestors are the 'Father's
Mother' colour. The mother's father and all of his
ancestors are the 'Mother's Father' colour. The mother's
mother and all of her ancestors are the 'Mother's Mother'
colour.

Generation Depth (arcs)
The depth of each segment where the text is displayed in an arc
(see Radials From above).

Generation Depth (radials)
The depth of each segment where the text is displayed in radial
lines (see Radials From above).

Font
The font that will be used in the fan chart.

title: Features of the Merge/Compare Dialog
text:
Merge/Compare Dialog

Features of the Merge/Compare Dialog

The Merge/Compare dialog is used for Basic Record Merging, Branch
Merging and File Merging (the last is used for Project Merging). It is
also used for comparing records, files, and branches.

The dialog has some similarities to the Records
Window. Like the Records Window, it displays record information,
with one tab per record type. However, there is no facility to hide
record types.

In File Merging, the dialog will display a tab for a record
type if and only if that record type occurs in at least one of the two
files. If there are no Source records
in either file, for example, there will be no Source record tab in the
Merge/Compare dialog.

In Basic Record Merging the dialog will display only one tab -
for the record type of the two records being merged (they will always be
the same type).

In Branch Merging, the dialog will display one tab for each
type of record being merged. By definition, if it is a Branch Merge,
this will mean that it will display two record types: one for Individuals
and one for Families.

Each tab of the Merge/Compare dialog has three panes. These are:

the Information pane

the Merge Into pane

the Merge From pane

When doing a File Merge, the “Merge Into” pane will simply be labelled
“Current Records”, and the “Merge From” pane will be labelled “Imported
Records”.

If you scroll any of these panes vertically, or expand any of the
records in the Merge Into or Merge From panes, you
will find that they all move together. You should think of each row as
extending across all three panes.

Each row will display a record (or field, if you 'expand' the record)
