want to have additional headings within your scrapbook or photo book,
there are two ways of adding them. You add them yourself in the
Diagram Window as text boxes, by clicking the Text icon on the
Shape Toolbar. Text boxes can have any font, size and colour, with
any colour background or none. The second way of adding a heading
is to select the scrapbook item in the Edit
Book Dialog (and remember your book can have multiple scrapbook
items if required), and click the "Settings" button (not the
"Book Settings" button) below the item list. Then set the 'Format'
item to 'Chapter' or to some other heading level, as required. You
can specify the content of the heading on the same window. The
advantage of the former option is you have complete flexibility and can
easily arrange headings in whatever way you like. However, if you
want your book to have a table of contents, and if you want your
headings to appear in the table of contents, you will need to use the
latter option. In this case, the headings will display within the
chart area. It is your responsibility to ensure that this is done
in a way that looks good and does not result in headings that overlap
chart text or images. See How
to Manage Chart and Diagram Headings to learn more.

Creating a Scrapbook or Photo Book as a Saved Chart

Instead of creating your scrapbook or photo book within the context of
a book, you can also create it as a saved chart. To do this, click
on the Charts button on the main application toolbar, and choose
"New Blank Chart (Scrapbook)". Add images, captions and other
items, as described above. Then when you have finished,
right-click on the background of the chart and click "Save Changes to
Chart". You will be required to give the chart a name. If
you later want to view this chart, click on the Charts button again, and
choose "Saved Charts...". Then select your chart and click Open.

If you want to make changes to your saved chart, click the Shapes
button to display the Shape
toolbar if not already showing. Make changes in the usual
way. When you have finished, right-click on the background of the
chart and once again click "Save Changes to Chart".

If you have created a scrapbook or photo book as a saved chart, and
later decide you want to add it to a book, you can do that.
However, the page size of a chart within a book is likely to be
different to the page size of a saved chart, even if the printable paper
size is the same. This is because, within a book, a chart has to
fit within the header and footer area. You can modify a chart to
make it compatible with a book, by clicking on "Book Layout
Compatibility" on the Diagram menu. Select the required book and
follow the prompts. Be aware that this is likely to change the
page size of the chart which may mean a significant amount of working in
moving pictures and other items, so that they do not overlap page
boundaries (see tip below).

To learn more, see Book
Layout Compatibility for Charts.

Tip: Making a chart book layout compatible, may result in
changes to the page layout. For this reason, you may want to
consider making a copy of the chart as a backup, before doing it.
Or you could make a copy and try making the copy book layout compatible,
to see what the effect will be. To copy a saved chart, click "Save
Diagram As" and then "Family Historian Chart" on the Diagram menu.
You will need to give the copy a name.

title: How to Add Content
text:
Books

How to Add Content

For instructions on how to create a new book, see How
to Create a Book or Booklet.

Add Title Page, Table of COntents, Index, Bibliography, Etc.

In the Edit Book Dialog, when
viewing your book, you may wish to add a title page, a table
of contents, a bibliography and perhaps an index.
You can add them in any order and at any stage. To add them,
select each item in turn in the list on the left side ("Available
Items") and click the Add Item > button,
to add them to the list on the right ("Current Book Items").

See How to Add a Preface,
Acknowledgements, etc. for tips and advice relating to that.

Add Chapters

When you add reports to a book, each report will, by default, become a
chapter in its own right, automatically referenced in the
table-of-contents and index (and sources will automatically be
referenced in the bibliography). Readers often like narrative
reports, so you might consider adding one of the five narrative reports:
the All Relatives Narrative report, the Individual Narrative report, the
Ancestors by Generation Narrative report, the Descendants by Generation
Narrative report, or the Register report. You can add as many
copies as you like of any report to any book. If the report you
want is not in the list, click Other
Report... to see a complete list of all reports. When you add a
report, you can select more than one person as the person that the
report will be about. Each person you select will be given their
own chapter using that report.

Notice that when you add the reports, Family Historian automatically
keeps the index at the end. You can re-order book items at any
time, however, by using the arrow buttons on the toolbar below the list.

If you wish to write your own chapters ("free text") you can. See
How to Write Your
Own Chapters or Sections to learn more.

Add Pictures, Maps, or Figures

Adding visual elements such as pictures, maps, figures, charts and
diagrams, will make your book more appealing. Most reports
include, or can include, pictures (see the report options for the report
in question). If you wish to include additional pictures, or maps
or figures, with an optional caption, in the Edit
Book Dialog select "Picture, Map or Figure" in the list on the
left-hand side, and click the Add Item >
button, to add to the list on the right ("Current Book
Items").

When you add a picture, map or figure to a book, the picture, map or
figure will normally fit somewhere within a single page of a book, and
will not normally occupy the whole page. See How
to Insert a Picture, Map or Figure to learn more.

Add Full Page, or Multi-Page Diagrams and Charts

You can add any type of diagram to a book, including any custom diagram
types you have created yourself. Select the required diagram from
the list of available items on the left-hand side of the Edit
Book Dialog and click the Add Item >
button, to add the diagram to your book. The page size of any
diagrams you add will be automatically adjusted to match the page size
of your book. You will be prompted select which pages of the
diagram you wish to include (see Select
Chart Pages Dialog). You can also add pedigree charts and
fan charts to a book. And you can add any saved chart to a book
(choose "Saved Chart..." from the list of available items on the
left). See Book
Layout Compatibility for Charts for a discussion of issues that
can arise if the book page layout is different from the page layout of a
saved chart.

We saw previously that when you add a picture, map or figure to a book,
the picture, map or figure will normally fit somewhere within a single
page of a book, and will not normally occupy the whole page. That
is different from charts and diagrams. When you add a diagram or
chart to a book, the diagram or chart will always occupy at least one
entire page - that is, everything between the header and the footer -
and may occupy multiple entire pages. See How
to Manage Chart and Diagram Headings for advice on issues relating
to headings for charts and diagrams.

A chart or diagram that has been added to a book is called a 'book
chart'. You can edit book charts at any time in the Diagram Window
- see Edit Book Chart in
Diagram Window to learn more.

See also How to Create a Scrapbook
or Photo Book.

Adjust Fonts and Page Layout

Fonts and other layout settings for your book can be changed by
clicking on the Book Settings button to
open the Book Settings Dialog.

Books can have any page size you like, portrait or landscape. To
adjust these settings, click the Printer Setup
button when viewing the book in the Book
Window. Page margins are adjusted in the Book
Settings Dialog. See How
to Change a Book's Page Size and Orientation to learn more.

title: Add Records to a Named List
breadcrumb: Add Records to a Named List
text:
Named Lists

How to Add Records to a Named List

To add records to a named list, in the Records
Window, open the Named Lists Pane by clicking on the Named Lists
Pane button
on the the Records
Window toolbar. Then select the list you want to add records to in
the top panel of the Named Lists Pane. Finally, click on each record
that you wish to add to this named list and click on the Add
to Current List
button on the Records Window toolbar (or press F4). You can also
click-and-drag on selected records in the Records Window, and drag them
into the named list on the right-side. See Drag-and-Drop
for more details.

You do not have to be in the Records Window to add records to a named
list. You can add records to a Named List at any time, in any window, by
selecting the records you wish to add and clicking on Add
to Named List on the Edit menu. You can press the New List... button in this dialog, to create a
new named list if needed.

title: Add Relatives by Click-and-Drag in Diagrams
breadcrumb: Add Relatives by Click-and-Drag in Diagrams
text:
Diagrams and Charts

How to Add Relatives by Click-and-Drag in Diagrams

To add relatives in diagrams, click-and-drag on the box that you want
to add a relative to. Drag down to add children, drag sideways to add
spouses, and drag up to add parents. When you do this Family Historian
will try to 'guess' what you are trying to do. If a relative can be
added at the point you have dragged to, a box with a dotted frame will
appear showing roughly where the new relative will go. If you release
the mouse button at this point, a menu will appear giving you the chance
to confirm which relative type you were trying to add.

This simple version needs a few caveats:

The above-description assumes that your diagram is oriented
top-down. If you are using a different orientation, adjust
accordingly.

You cannot add relatives if moving/resizing is enabled - if, that
is, the Enable Moving/Resizing button is pressed (see the Diagram toolbar).

You cannot add a relative to a tree if the tree does not display
that kind of relative. For example, you cannot add a child to an
ancestor in an ancestor tree. For this reason, users often prefer to
use All Relatives trees for adding
relatives by clicking-and-dragging.

Keep an eye on the status bar (the bar at the foot of the
application window) when dragging. If a box can be added in the
position to which you are dragging, the status bar will tell you what
kind of relative Family Historian thinks you are trying to add. If a
box cannot be added in this position, there will be a message in the
status bar telling you why not.

When adding spouses and children, you can indicate, by appropriate
positioning, where the new spouse or child is to go, in the existing
list of spouses or children.

title: Add Sound & Video
text:
Pictures and Other Media

How to Add Sound & Video

You can add as many sound and video (and other media) files as you
like. Adding sounds and videos is just like adding pictures (see How to Add a Picture for an Individual), except
that the issue of linking to faces does not apply. To insert a picture
into the Media Window, click Add
> Other Media instead of Add
> Pictures. To add a sounds or
videos using the Media tab
of the Property Box, click on the Add Media button on the toolbar (the same button
you would use with pictures), and then click on Insert
From File. In the file selection dialog that appears, click on
the Files of type field, and change
the value from Image Files to Sound or Video
files - or, if necessary, to All files.

When linking a sound or video file to a record in the Media Window, be sure to add simple links
and not frame links.

Family Historian will use the default Windows application to display
videos and play sound files. This will probably be the Windows Media
Player by default, if you haven't installed some other application that
you prefer to use instead.

See also Media Records
and the Media Window.

title: Add Spouses, Parents & Children
text:
How to...

How to Add Spouses, Parents & Children

There are numerous ways of doing this. Choose the one that is most
convenient.

Within the Focus Window

Make the person the focus person (person displaying at the
top of the Focus Window) by
double-clicking on their box. Within the "Spouses & Children" tab
you can click on links in boxes near them - such as "Add Child", "Add
Wife/Partner" etc - to add children, spouses or parents. If the person
already has one or more spouses and one or more sets of parents, click
on the "Add More Relatives..." link at the bottom of the window and
follow the menu options.

Within the Property Box

To add a new spouse in the Property Box,
choose an empty spouse tab and click on the "Add Spouse/Partner" link.
To add children for the person by a given spouse, choose the correct
spouse tab and click on the "Add Child" link in the table of children at
the bottom of the window (you may need to resize the Property Box to
able to view this table properly). To add a parent, click on the 'Up'
button in the Property Box toolbar.

Within the Diagram Window

See How
to Add Relatives by Click-and-Drag in Diagrams.

Anywhere

Select the person you want to add a relative to, click on the Add
menu, and then choose Parent, Spouse or Child
as appropriate.

title: How to Append Data into a Project
breadcrumb: Compare, Merge,  Append and Split Projects
How to Append Data into a Project
text:
Compare, Merge,
Append and Split Files

How to Append Data into a Project

The difference between merging and appending is this: suppose your
ordinary project data has 500 records and you receive another file which
has another 500 records. If you simply append the second file
into your project, the records from the second file will be added to the
first file, and you will end up with a file that contains 1,000 records.
You append one file into another when the two files have no 'overlap' -
that is, none of the records are about the same people.

If however you merge the second file into the first file, you
don't just add records from one file to the other. Instead, records that
are about the same people are matched. Then when you merge the
two files, the matching records are merged. This means that although you
might end up with a file that had 1,000 records, this would only happen
if no matching records were found. If all 500 records in each file
matched, you would end up with a file that still contained only 500
records. Or, depending on which records matched, you could end up with
anything in between.

Although Family Historian will automatically check for matches for you
(but you can always check and override its 'recommendations'), this can
be a slow process if you have very large files; so you may prefer to
tell it not to do so, if you know that there are no matches, and you
want to append one file into another. In this case, follow the
instructions in How
to Merge Two Projects except that when you are given the choice
(when the Record Matching Options Dialog appears), choose the option Do
Not Match Any Records. Then when the Merge/Compare Dialog appears, all records will be
shown unmatched and you can click Merge to
append the one file into the other.

title: Books
text:
How to...

Books

This section looks at how to perform various tasks that have to do
with books and booklets:

How to Create a Book or
Booklet

How to Add Content

How to Insert a Picture,
Map or Figure

How to Create a Scrapbook or
Photo Book

How to Add a Pedigree Chart

Book
Layout Compatibility for Charts

How to Add a Preface,
Acknowledgements, etc.

How to
Change a Book's Page Size and Orientation

How to Write
Your Own Chapters and Sections

How to Manage
Chart and Diagram Headings

See also Workspace 6: The Book Window

title: How to Change a Book's Page Size and Orientation
breadcrumb: Change a Book's Page Size and Orientation
text:
Books

How to Change a Book's Page Size and Orientation

Books can have any page size you like and can be orientated either
portrait or landscape. To adjust these settings, click the Printer Setup button when viewing the book in
the Book Window. Page margins are
adjusted in the Page
Layout tab of the Book Settings
Dialog. You can also adjust header details (and header
depth) and footer details (and footer depth) on the same tab.

Changing page size and orientation can affect layout of reports, and
may cause layout issues with charts that have been added to the
book. For this reason, you are usually recommended to decide early
on what page size, orientation and margins, you want for your book; and
then only change them if really necessary. See Book
Layout Compatibility for Charts for more on this.

title: How to Change the Appearance of Lines in Diagrams
breadcrumb: Change the Appearance of Lines in Diagrams
text:
Diagrams and Charts

How to Change the Appearance of Lines in Diagrams

If you want to control the appearance of all lines in a diagram - or
some types of lines, such as lines connecting divorced or separated
couples - you can do this using the Lines
tab of Diagram Options.

If you want to change some specific lines connecting specific boxes, or
entire branches, or if you want to create a 'path' connecting two boxes
across a diagram, you can do all of these things using the Family
Connection Mapper.

title: How to Change the Appearance of Boxes in Diagrams
breadcrumb: Change the Appearance of Boxes in Diagrams
text:
Diagrams and Charts

How to Change the Appearance of Boxes in Diagrams

If you want to control the appearance of all boxes in a diagram, or all
boxes that fit some criteria that you specify, you can do this using the
Boxes
tab of Diagram Options. For example, you could change the
background colour of a box, or the colour and thickness of its frame, or
the shape of the box, or the icons shown beneath it, based on the sex of
the person, or their relationship to the diagram root, or the generation
they belong to; or based on almost any criteria you can think of.

To change which pictures appear, or the position of pictures, see Diagram Options Dialog: Pictures Tab.

If you want to change the appearance of just a few specific boxes, see
How to
Override Box Features for Particular Boxes.

title: Change the Contents of Boxes in Diagrams
breadcrumb: Change the Contents of Boxes in Diagrams
text:
Diagrams and Charts

How to Change the Contents of Boxes in Diagrams

Open a diagram (see How
to Display a Diagram). Open the Diagram Options Dialog. Select the Text
tab. A list of text schemes is displayed. A text
scheme is a stored set of instructions which determine what text is
displayed in boxes, how it is laid out, what fonts, styles and indents
are used, etc.

To try out the different text schemes, select each in turn and press Apply. You should see the diagram behind the
Diagram Options Dialog change when you do this. Bear in mind that the
diagram cannot show data that you haven't entered. So, for example, if
you choose a diagram which is supposed to show a persons occupation (or
occupations), it cannot do so if you have not recorded what the person's
occupation was.

You can edit and modify existing text schemes or create you own new
ones. To create a new one, click on the New
button (see Create
a Simple Text Scheme). To modify an existing one, select it and
click on the Edit Text Scheme button.

To learn more see Diagram
Options Dialog: Text Tab.

To change which pictures appear, or the position of pictures, see Diagram Options Dialog: Pictures Tab.

title: Change the Order of Spouses, Children or Events
breadcrumb: Change the Order of Spouses, Children or Events
text:
More Family &
Relationship Tasks

How to Change the Order of Spouses, Children or Events

Changing the Order of Fields in Records

The order that fields are stored within records (e.g. as
displayed in the All tab of the
Property Box), is important because Family Historian will take note of
this ordering for various purposes. Also, it may be an ordering
that you wish to see when you look at the All tab of the Property
Box. However, it is not the only order that matters. Events
and attributes are typically ordered chronologically - see the next
section below.

If you enter dates for events, birth dates for children and marriage
dates for spouses, Family Historian will automatically keep them all in
date order within their records - at least as long you use the Property
Box to enter all these details. However, it can happen for various
reasons (e.g. if the data was created elsewhere and merged in) that
spouses, children or events are held in the wrong date order.

You can automatically re-sequence all spouses, children and events, in
date order, for a given person, by selecting their record and clicking
Re-order Events by Date on the Edit menu. Despite the
name, this will re-sequence children and spouses too, if they are not in
the correct date order. A quick way to do this is simply to select the
Individual record in question and press F9.

You can also automatically re-sequence all spouses, children and
events, in date order, throughout the whole file. To do this, click on Re-order Out-of-sequence Data on the Tools menu (see Re-order Out-of-Sequence Data Dialog).

It can also happen that events are recorded in the wrong order when
you don't have any date information for them. For example, you might not
know when two people were born but you might nevertheless know which
order they were born in. You can re-sequence spouses, children or events
manually. To re-do this, look for Move Up
and Move Down buttons . These are available (in different sizes) in many
different contexts. They are available on the Main Toolbar, on the Main
tab of the Property Box (two sets: one for re-ordering spouses,
and another set for re-ordering children), on the Property Box Facts
tab toolbar (for re-ordering events and attributes), and in the
top-right corner of the All tab of
the Property Box (for re-ordering any field relative to other fields of
the same, or similar, type). In fact they are available in other
contexts as well. In all contexts they can be used for re-ordering
items. For example, if you are viewing a child in a diagram, you can
re-order a child relative to its siblings, by selecting the child's box
and clicking the Move Up or Move Down buttons on the Main toolbar.
You can re-order spouses in the same way.

Automatic Sequencing by Event Type

In many cases, you do not have to sort events, as Family Historian will
intelligently take care of this for you. For example, if birth,
baptism, death and burial all occurred within a single year (and no
other date details are provided) Family Historian will automatically
sort them in that order.

Changing the Chronological Order of Events in Lists

If Family Historian is sorting events chronologically in a way that is
not what you want, consider using a sort
date, to override this. Sort dates can be entered and edited
on the Date Entry Assistant
Dialog, which you can access by double-clicking on any date field,
or by clicking on the little button ... to
the right of the date field.

title: How to Choose Preferred Look for Standard Diagrams
breadcrumb: Choose Preferred Look for Standard Diagrams
text:
Diagrams and Charts

How to Choose Preferred Look for Standard Diagrams

The "Choose Preferred Look for Standard Diagrams" dialog is accessed by
clicking on the "Charts" toolbar button on the main application
toolbar, and selecting "Choose Preferred Look for Standard Diagrams" in
the dropdown menu that appears.

The six most important standard diagrams are Ancestors, Descendants,
Ancestors & Descendants, All Relatives, All Relatives + Indirect
Relatives, and Everyone. You can give these six diagrams whatever
look you prefer, and you can easily switch the look of any or all of
them, at any time and as often as you wish. To do this, select the
standard diagrams you wish to change - all of them, if you wish, or any
subset - and click the Copy Option Set...
button. You will be prompted to select a diagram from a list of
diagrams. These can be custom diagrams you have created yourself
(or that may have been created for you if you upgraded from a previous
version), or other standard diagrams. Select whichever diagram has
the kind of look you are after. The diagram options from the
selected diagram will be copied to the standard diagrams in the list of
six that you previously selected.

Two of the six standard diagrams, the Everyone diagram
and the All Relatives + Indirect Relatives diagram, are multi-tree
diagrams - that is, they are diagrams which when opened may already
contain multiple trees. Background stripes do not in general look
good with multi-tree diagrams, as the stripes will only align with the
boxes from the primary tree in the diagram. For this reason,
background stripes and other background options are omitted when you
copy an option set into either of the two multi-tree diagrams.

The diagram options that are copied will not change the character of
any of the standard diagrams. The 'Ancestor' diagram will still be
an ancestor diagram, the 'Descendant' diagram will still be a descendant
diagram, and so on. But all the other details that together make
up the overall look of the diagram you have chosen to copy, will be
copied over to the selected standard diagrams.

You should feel free to experiment with different looks as much as you
like. At any time, you can restore any or all of the six standard
diagrams to their installation default look, by selecting them and
clicking the Restore Defaults button.

When you change the look of standard diagrams, this has no effect on
diagrams that have already been created, such as saved charts, charts in
books, or diagrams that are already open in the Diagram Window. It
only affects new diagrams that you create after changing the look.

title: Colour Each Generation Differently
text:
Diagrams and Charts

How to Colour Each Generation Differently

Open a diagram (see How
to Display a Diagram). Open the Diagram Options Dialog. Select the Boxes tab and
click on the Presets button at the bottom.
From the menu that appears choose 'Generations'.

To learn more about options with respect to the display of boxes (or
their absence) in diagrams, see Diagram Options Dialog: Boxes Tab.

title: Compare another Person's Research with Yours
breadcrumb: Compare, Merge,  Append and Split Projects
How to Compare another Person's Research with Yours
text:
Compare, Merge,
Append and Split Files

How to Compare another Person's Research with Yours

If you are downloading family tree data from the Internet, the chances
are that it will arrive in the form of either a GEDCOM
file or possibly a GEDZIP
file. When you receive either kind of file from whatever source,
the first thing to do is to load it into Family Historian. The
recommended way to do this is to create a new project within Family
Historian, and import the file into that project (see
New Project Wizard, accessible from the Project
Window).

When you have created the new project, now open your ordinary project
- the one that you want to compare the new file with. If you plan to
merge the data in, you are recommended to make a backup copy of your
project before proceeding. A file merge is one of the very few changes
to your data that cannot be undone by clicking on Undo on the Edit
menu. You need to backup mainly in case you make a decision which you
subsequently regret. It also means that you have a previous version
which you can later use as a check (as sort of 'audit trial') if you
want to remind yourself what changes have occurred and when. When you do
a merge in Family Historian, you can automatically set source citations
for all the newly merged data. But it never hurts to have more than one
way to work out where data came from.

To merge and/or compare a second project with your main project, open
your main project, click on Merge/Compare File on the File
menu, and select the project to be compared. When the Record Matching
Options dialog appears, make sure that Suggest candidate matches
for merging is chosen.

See also Merge/Compare
Dialog and File
Merging and Comparing.

If you know another genealogist and want to compare their research
with yours, you should normally ask them to send you either a GEDCOM
file or a GEDZIP file. If they use Family Historian, they can use Export
GEDCOM File dialog to create the GEDCOM file or Export
GEDZIP File Dialog to create a GEDZIP file. To access the
export options, click on the File menu, then choose Import/Export
and then Export. If they don't use Family Historian, they
should look for export options within their program. Any genealogy
program should have an option to export data in the form of a
GEDCOM file.

It is also possible that they might instead send you their entire
project. The easiest way for them to do this would be for them to
backup their project to a compress 'zip' file, and then send you
that. To backup the project, click Backup/Restore on the File
menu, and then choose Full Backup (Entire Project
Folder). When you receive the file, you can turn it back
into a project by using clicking on Backup/Restore on the File
menu, and then choosing Restore Backup. Having done that,
you can again use Merge/Compare File (see above) to compare the two
projects, and optionally merge them.

Family Historian can import data directly from some other genealogy
programs when you create a new project. So another possibility, is
that the other genealogist could send you their original data file, and
you could import from that when you create a new project. See Transferring Data into
Family Historian to learn more.

title: Compare, Merge, Append and Split Projects
breadcrumb: Compare, Merge,  Append and Split Projects
text:
How to...

Compare, Merge, Append and Split Projects

This section looks at how to perform various big tasks that have to do
with Family Historian projects as a whole.

title: Copy and Paste Source Citations
text:
Sources & Source
Citations

How to Copy and Paste Source Citations

Open the Property Box to view a
record, and then open the Citation
List Pane. The Citation List Pane displays the source citations
for whatever is displayed in the Sources
For field at the top of the pane - and this changes
automatically whenever you click on any field in any tab of the Property
Box (see How
to Record the Sources for Your Data).

To copy a source citation, select it in the list and click the Copy Citation button
just below the list.

To paste a source citation, first click on the field in the main body
of the Property Box, for the item of data that you want to add the
citation to. This can be in any tab of the Property Box (even the All
tab), and the data can be almost any item of data in any record.
When you do this, the Sources For
field shows the citations for that item of data that you already have
(if any). Click the Paste Citation
button below the list of
citations, to add the new citation. There is no limit to the
number of citations you can have for any one item of data.

When you copy and paste a citation, any additional details (including
assessment, notes, and even media) which are directly attached to the
citation, are also copied and pasted. You can view these
additional details (and add and edit them) in the Citation
Window.

title: How to Create a Book or Booklet
text:
Books

How to Create a Book or Booklet

To create a new book, click Books on
the Publish menu. This opens the
Book List Dialog which displays a list
of all the books in the current project, if there are any. On this
dialog box, books can be created, edited, cloned, viewed or deleted.
Click New to create a new book. Once
you have provided a name for the book, the Edit
Book Dialog will be opened to allow you to add items to the book.
The Edit Book Dialog can also be accessed by clicking Edit
Book in the panel on the right side of the Book
Window, when viewing a book in the Book Window.

See also How to Add
Content, How to Insert
a Picture, Map or Figure, How
to Create a Scrapbook and How
to Add a Pedigree Chart.

Tip: Editing a book can be much slower if the book is
currently being displayed in the Book Window and 'Auto-Refresh Book' is
enabled in the Edit Book Dialog.
If the Book Window is open and performance is slow, either close the
Book Window or untick 'Auto-Refresh Book' in the Edit Book Dialog.
If 'Auto-Refresh Book' is not ticked, and you have opened the Book
Window, you should remember to click the Refresh
Book button after making changes, to see the changes reflected
in the Book Window.

title: Create a Custom Fact (Event or Attribute)
breadcrumb: Create a Custom Fact (Event or Attribute)
text:
Facts (Events and
Attributes)

How to Create a Custom Fact (Event or Attribute)

Family Historian comes with a large number of pre-defined fact types,
such as Birth, Death, Marriage, Divorce, etc (see How to Record Facts About a Person's Life and How to Access the
Extended Set of Fact Types for lists of these), but you
nevertheless may want to create some custom events or attributes of your
own. For example, suppose you wanted to record what people's hobbies
were. 'Hobby' is not a standard attribute, but you can easily add it as
a custom one. To create a new event or attribute click on the New
button in the Fact
Types Dialog and fill in the details in the forms displayed. Once
you have created a new custom event or attribute, that event or
attribute will always afterwards be available for you to use, and add to
any Individual's record, exactly as you can use any standard events and
attributes. So, for example, once you have created a new fact definition
for your 'Hobby' attribute you will be able to add a Hobby fact
(as many times as you like) to any Individual's record to record
information about their hobbies.

See also Work with
Fact Sets.

title: How to Create a Custom Fact Flag
text:
Facts (Events and
Attributes)

How to Create a Custom Fact Flag

As mentioned earlier, any fact (event or attribute) can be flagged as Preferred,
Private, Tentative or Rejected (see How
to Flag a Fact as Preferred, Private, Tentative or Rejected).
This ability to set a flag on a fact can be useful. But what if
you want to set a different flag, one of your own choosing?
Suppose you wanted to create a flag to mark some facts as speculation
or rumour or to-be-deleted or sensitive
or contradicted-by-X or marked-for-some-future-activity?
You can create any kind of custom fact flag you want. Custom fact
flags do not display in the Facts
tab of the Property Box and cannot be set there. To view or
set a fact flag, open the record for the Individual or Family in
question in the Property Box, and switch to the All
tab. Expand the relevant fact by clicking on the little
square box to the left of it. For example, if you view the All
tab for Ian Stephen Munro in the Family Historian Sample Project,
you should see a line that says "Born 5 January 1953 in Lewisham,
London, England". If you expand this, any flags for this fact will
be listed in a subfield labelled "Flags", which can also be
expanded. To set a flag, right-click on the fact name (in our
example, this would be the word 'Birth') and select a flag from the 'Set
Flag' submenu. If the flag you want doesn't exist, choose '<New
Flag>' instead to create it.

When you have created a flag in a project, you can access this flag in
queries, smart folders, customized columns in list, and in any other
suitable context.

Fact flags are different from, and should not be confused with, record
flags.

title: Create a Custom Query
text:
Queries

How to Create a Custom Query

Custom queries can be created by clicking on the Query menu button on the main application toolbar, and then choosing New
Custom Query from the dropdown menu that appears.
Alternatively, within the Query
Window, you can create a new custom query by clicking on the menu
button
at the end of the Query toolbar and then choosing New
Custom Query fromn the menu that appears. Give the new
query a name and select a query type. There are 15 query types.

Another approach, which is often preferable, is to copy an existing
query (custom or standard) and modify the copy. To do this, find
the query you want to copy. Within the Query Window, select the query you wish to
copy in the Query list at the top of the window. Then click on the Query Menu button
at the end of the Query
toolbar, and choose Save As Custom
Query from the dropdown list that appears. Give the saved copy
a name.

Changes made to custom queries are saved as you make them. You can
modify them whenever you want. By default, when you create a new
query it will be created with default columns. These vary with the
query type. You can add more columns if you wish, and you can
delete, modify or re-order any existing columns.

To learn how to make changes to a custom query, see Query Window.

You can run a custom query from within the Query Window by choosing it
at the top of the window and by clicking on the Run Query button in the Query toolbar. You can also run any
custom query from the Query menu button on the main application toolbar. If you have
specified one or more categories for your custom query, it will be
listed under those categories (see Query
Window: General Tab). If you haven't, it will be listed
under "New/Uncategorised Queries". Finally, if you choose the
"Manage Queries" option, you can see a complete list of all queries in
the Manage
Queries Dialog, Tick the "Custom Only" box at the top, to restrict
the list to custom queries only. Custom queries can also be
renamed, copied or deleted on the Manage Queries Dialog. This
dialog can also be accessed from the Query
Window.

title: How to Create a Language Pack
breadcrumb: How to Create a Language Pack
text:
Languages and Language Packs

How to Create a Language Pack

Before creating a language pack, you should first check whether the
language pack you require already exists or not - see How
to Install a Language Pack. If the language pack you want
isn't available (or there is one, but it isn't adequate for your
purposes), you can create your own.

If you decide you want to create a new language pack, you should ask
yourself what you want this language pack to do. Typically, a language
pack for a given target language, will serve some or all of the
following functions:

It will allow reports and diagrams for projects that have content in
the target language, to be rendered in that language (e.g. it
may allow French content to be rendered in French, say - with French
reports titles, and dates in French, etc). This is called same
language rendering.

It may also allow reports and diagrams for projects that have
content in English, to be translated into the target language (e.g.
English content, translated into French say). This is other
language translation.

Finally, it may also allow reports and diagrams for projects created
in yet other languages, to be translated into the target language
(e.g. Polish content, translated into French say). This is also
other language translation.

Think about what you want to achieve and keep this in mind as you
proceed.

To create a new language pack, open the Language Packs window once
again (click on Language Packs on the Tools menu)
and click the New button. Fill in the
details required (in two dialogs: New
Language Pack - Step 1 and New
Language Pack - Step 2), and a new language pack will be
created. Creating it, however, is just the start of the process. A
newly-created language pack does not do very much. The work
involved in building a properly-functioning language pack consists of
the following steps (not necessarily in this order):

Updating the language plugin

Creating language variants of diagram text schemes

Creating language variants of fact definitions

Supplying all necessary translations for language pack translation
tables

Some of the work has already been done for you, however, when you
created the language pack. Family Historian will have created
language variants of text schemes for example. It will also have
created a 'skeleton' version (a first draft version) of the language
plugin. And it will have supplied some of the values that need to
be translated in the language pack translation tables. The following
sections look at each task in more detail.

Bear in mind that all the work done in all of these sections, is saved
in files, which form part of the language pack. If you export the
language pack, all of these files will be included in the export.
Equally, if you delete the language pack, you will delete all of these
same files.

Updating the Language Plugin

This is the most complex of the various tasks, and potentially the most
daunting. Anyone who is already familiar with Family Historian
plugins should not find it a problem. But if you haven't got
previous experience of working with plugins (and especially if you have
no previous experience of computer programming or writing scripts), we
recommend that you consider seeking advice from more experienced
users. Hopefully, even if you have no confidence in your own
ability to change plugins, you may find some other Family Historian user
who is willing to help (e.g. at the Family Historian User Group website
www.fhug.org.uk).
Language plugins are at the heart of the way language packs work.
They are tremendously powerful and can be used to provide any special
processing your language may require. You can view the skeleton
plugin that has been created for you, when you created your new language
pack, by selecting your new language pack in the Language Packs window,
and clicking the Plugin button. The
plugin itself contains comments describing some of the things you need
to do. Search for the text "TODO" to find various tasks you need
to do - starting with two tables at the top of the plugin, containing a
list of month names that need to be translated, and a list of number
adjectives ('First', 'Second', etc). There are numerous
occurrences of "TODO" throughout the plugin, each accompanied by
suggestions of proposed, or possible, changes you may need to make.

Creating language variants of diagram text schemes

The text displayed in boxes within diagram trees, is determined by diagram
text schemes (see Diagram
Options Dialog: Text Tab), and these too can be translated using
language packs. In fact much, if not all, of the work needed here
should already have been done for you when you created the language
pack. However, you can modify or extend the work done at any
time. To view language variants of text schemes, open a diagram
(any one will do), and then open diagram options (e.g. click on Options
on the Diagram menu). Select the Language
tab and pick your new Language Pack. Then, still within
Diagram Options, click on the Text
tab. Notice that the language you chose is shown on the
right-hand side (above the Margins & Tabs
button). The tab shows a list of standard and custom text schemes, that
you can choose from. Each text scheme specifies the content to be
displayed in a diagram. To try one out, select and click the Apply button. Every text scheme that
has a green tick showing in the rightmost column (labelled 'Lang') has a
language variant associated with it. Select any item in the list,
and press Edit Language Variant to edit the
language variant. If you choose an item that doesn't already have
a language variant, you will be prompted to create one, by copying the
'base-level' version.

Bear in mind that although you edit language variants for text schemes
in this dialog, it remains the case that the files associated with
language variants are stored as part of the language pack.

Creating language variants of Fact Definitions

Creating language variants of fact definitions is a very important step
(especially for translating and rendering reports). No work will
have been done for you in this area, during the process of creating the
initial language pack.

To create language variants of fact definitions, click on Fact
Types on the Tools menu. Pick the first fact in
the list and press the Edit button to open
the Fact Definition dialog for
that fact. Within that dialog, press the Go
To Language Variant button. Choose your new language pack
from the dropdown list that appears. Fill in the required fields
in the Fact
Definition Language Variant Dialog (using the base-level values as
a model). You should do this for all fact types. Use the Next and Previous
buttons to quickly and easily 'step' through each fact type in turn,
until you have translated all of them. Press the Help
button for more help on doing this. Be sure to translate not just
the core fact values, but also the associated roles (for 'witnesses') if
any.

Once again, bear in mind that although you edit language variants for
fact definitions in this part of Family Historian, it remains the case
that the files associated with these language variants are stored as
part of the language pack.

Note: At a minimum, we recommend that you translate all standard
and custom fact definitions. Better still, translate the
Extended Set too. The Extended Set of fact definitions are
hidden by default, so you probably need to tick the Show
Hidden tick box, on the right-hand side, to view
them.

Supplying all necessary translations for language pack translation
tables

Translation tables are accessed by the language pack plugin; however,
they can be edited easily and separately. To view these tables,
open the Language Packs dialog
once again (click Language Packs on the Tools
menu), select your language pack and click the Edit
button (or just double-click on your language pack in the list).
The translation tables are displayed in the Language
Pack Translation Tables Dialog. There are 3 tables, and all
of them are accessible from the same window (see options at the top of
the window). The translation tables are:

Attribute Values

Places

Miscellaneous

All 3 tables already contain a list of items of text (in the 'From'
column) that need to be translated (the translations will be listed in
the 'To' column). We recommend that you translate all values in
all 3 tables. Later, you may find that you need to add additional
values to all 3 tables. But initially you can concentrate on
translating the values that are already listed.

To translate an item, select it and cick the Edit
button (or just double-click on it); then type the translation into the
"Translate To" box and press Save to save
it. Click the Help button for advice
on special case handling.

The Miscellaneous table, as the name suggests, lists
miscellaneous items that need to be translated - such as report titles,
and report headings.

The Attributes Values table lists translations of attribute
values. An attribute is a fact type such as Education or
Occupation. The value for an Occupation attribute might, in
English, be 'Engineer' or 'Farmer'. Attribute values only need to
be translated from the project language into the output language, if
these are different. For example, if your project language is
French, an attribute value might be 'Ingénieur' (i.e. engineer).
If you are rendering your output in French, no translation is
required. However, if you are rendering English into French, a
translation is required. If you supply a translation of 'Engineer'
as 'Ingénieur', Family Historian knows to only make use of it, when
doing other language translation, and not when
doing same language rendering.

Finally, the Places table is used to translate place part
names. A complication about place part names is that some are
translated, but not all. And the decision about which place names
are translated, varies from language to language. It is up to you
to decide which place part names to translate. For example, if you
were creating a French language pack and you had a place name like
"Greenwich, London, England", you might decide to translate "London" and
"England" (to "Londres" and "Angleterre"), but not translate
"Greenwich".

As with Attribute Values, Family Historian will by default only use the
Places table for translations, if it is actually using the language pack
for other language translation, as opposed to same
language rendering.

Add a SpellCheck dictionary to your language pack

Spellcheck dictionaries for most languages are freely available on the
Internet. With very little effort you can add one to your language
pack, so that anyone who installs your language pack can have spellcheck
in that language. For instructions on doing this, please see How
to Add a Spellcheck Dictionary to your Language Pack.

Consider Submitting Your Language Pack to the Family Historian Plugin
Store

If you have completed your language pack, please consider submitting it
to the Family Historian Plugin Store, so that others can benefit from
your work - even if there is already one or more language packs in the
Plugin Store, for your target language. Your language pack may be better
than others, or have a different style. Some language packs may
have a specific role and not cover all the functions that yours
provides. In any case, it's good for users to have a choice.
For more on this, please see How
to Share Your Language Pack with Others and How to Submit a Language Pack to the Plugin Store.

title: Create a New Named List
text:
Named Lists

How to Create a New Named List

In the Records Window, open the Named
Lists Pane by clicking on the Named Lists Pane button
on the Records
Window toolbar. Then create a new named list by clicking on New
Named List on the Lists menu. Click-and-drag on
any records in the main part of the Records Window, and drop them into
the middle panel of the Named Lists Pane, to add those records to the
selected named list. Press the Ctrl key while
clicking on records in the main part of the Records Window, if you want
to select multiple records.

Alternatively, you can add records to a new Named List at any time, in
any window, by selecting the records you wish to add and clicking on Add to Named List on the Edit menu.
Then press the New List... button in this
dialog, to create a new named list.

title: Create a New Record Flag
text:
Record Flags

How to Create a New Record Flag

Select the Individual or Individuals (this works with a multiple
selection) who you wish to have the new flag, and click on Edit
> Record Flags. In the Record Flags dialog box, click on the
New button. Give the new flag a name and
press OK. Then tick the flag in the list to
assign the flag to the Individuals you selected.

title: Create a Note About a Marriage
breadcrumb: Create a Note About a Marriage
text:
More Family &
Relationship Tasks

How to Create a Note About a Marriage

If you want to create a note about a marriage event (the actual
occasion of marriage) select the Marriage event (or add one if you
haven't already got one) in the Facts
tab of the Property Box, when
viewing record details for either spouse. Then enter the note in the
Note field below. You may find it convenient to double-click on
the field to open the note in the Note Window
if it's a long note. You can also open the Note Window by clicking on
the little button with 3 dots, to the right of the Note field.

Sometimes, however, you want to enter a note that is not about the
marriage event as such, but is about the whole married life of a couple.
It makes no sense to add this as a note to just one of them, or to
duplicate the note and give them a copy each. Instead you should create
a Family note
which is applicable to both of them (and shared between both of them).
To do this, open the record for either spouse in the Property Box. It
doesn't matter which you use. Then choose the Notes
tab, and click on the Add Note button
on the toolbar. Select Shared Note for a Couple from
the dropdown menu that appears, and confirm which couple you want it to
apply to. A new (empty) note is created and is selected in the list of
notes in the top half of the dialog. By default the note will then
display in the Note Window, where you can
enter the text.

Although it may appear that you have only entered the note for one of
the spouses, in fact you will find if you look at the other spouse in
the Property Box that you can view and edit the same note there too (in
the Notes tab, and also in the Main tab if it's their
first or only shared note).

title: How to Create a Website or Family Tree USB Stick
breadcrumb: Websites and Family Tree USB Sticks
Create a Website or Family Tree USB Stick
text:
Websites & Family Tree
CD/DVDs...

How to Create a Website or Family Tree USB Stick

This page looks at how to create a website, how to create a family tree
on a USB stick, and how to create a family tree CD/DVD.

How to Create a Website

To create a website, you need to perform the following steps:

Click Websites & Family Tree USB Sticks on the
Publish menu, to open the
Websites & Family Tree USB Sticks dialog. This dialog
shows you a list of packages that you have already created
in the current project. Each package represents a website or
Family Tree CD/DVD (or both) that you are working on. If you are
just starting off, there won't be any packages. Click New to create a new package. Give it a
memorable name and click Create.
The package will be created, and the Website
and Family Tree USB Stick Wizard will be opened, to allow you to
specify the contents of the package. Follow the instructions in
the wizard to create the package. Click Help
for more information if needed. Don't worry about getting it
right first time. You will be able to view the results, and go
back and change anything, as often as you like, until you get it
right. When you have specified everything you need, click
Finish on the last page of the wizard, and
it will generate the files for your website or USB stick for
you. You will be asked if you wish to view the
content. If you choose to do so, a web browser will open,
allowing you to view your package contents. What you are viewing
looks exactly like a website. The only difference is that it
hasn't yet been put up on the Internet, or copied to a USB
stick. At this point, everything is still stored locally on your
PC.

The package you created in step 1 is stored within your current
project. Whenever you want to, you can revise it, or view it
again. To access it, open the
Websites & Family Tree USB Sticks dialog. Your package
should be listed there. Select it and click Edit
to revise it, or click Preview to view
the contents again. You can also click Rebuild
to rebuild it at any time without revising it. You might want to
do this if, for example, you wanted to sure that your package reflects
the latest changes you may have made to the data and records in your
project.

You can take as long as you like to get your package exactly the way
you want it, and revise it as often as you like. When you are
satisfied that it is ready, the next step is to export it. Up to
now the package files have been stored within your project folder and
managed for you by Family Historian. The easiest and safest way
to access them, is to copy them to a convenient location on your hard
drive. This is what happens when you click Export.
You will be asked if you wish to create a website, USB stick, or a
Family Tree CD/DVD. You will then be prompted to choose
the required location to export to, and the files will be copied
there. If you are creating a website, the next step is to put
your website on the Internet (see next).

How to Put Your Website on the Internet

To put your website up on the Internet, you need to copy your files to
an appropriate location on a web server.
A web server is a computer that is connected to the Internet, and which
runs the necessary software to make your website work.

If you have access to the Internet, you will presumably already have
an Internet Service Provider (I.S.P.). There is a good chance that your
account with your I.S.P. includes free web
space - that is, space on their web server for a website. If
you are unsure, contact your I.S.P. and ask them. If they do support
this, they will also be able to give you all the instructions you need
for copying your website files to an appropriate location on their web
server.

You will need to know the address (URL) of your web space, and you
will almost certainly also need a user name and password to connect to
it.

If your I.S.P. does not provide web space, you could either change to
another one who does, or you might consider using a free website host.
At time of writing, various companies provide free web space.

Transferring files to a server on the Internet is called uploading.
To upload your files you will need a program called an FTP
client (FTP stands for ‘File Transfer Protocol’). At time of
writing, the program Filezilla is a free FTP client (see http://filezilla.sourceforge.net/). There are
numerous other FTP client applications available for download from the
Internet (mostly not free).

When you have your FTP client working, and have connected to your web
space, you must copy all the website files to the web space using your
FTP client.

Mention of any product or offer from any other
company, here or elsewhere in Family Historian, does not constitute an
endorsement or recommendation of any kind. If you decide to use any
mentioned products, or try any mentioned offers (such as free web
space), you do so entirely at your own risk. We do not take
responsibility of any kind for any problems or issues you may have with
any mentioned products or offers.

How to Create a Family Tree USB Stick

Creating a Family Tree CD or DVD is exactly like creating a
website. Follow steps 1-3 above. The only difference is that
when it comes to step 3, and you click Export
make sure that you choose the option for creating a family tree USB
stick, and copy the files to a USB stick (sometimes also called a 'USB
flash drive', 'memory stick' or 'pen drive'). Why is it so
similar? This is because the contents of your family tree USB
stick will look like a website, and if you give the USB stick to
someone, and they open it, Windows will automatically display the
contents in their web browser. The big advantage of doing this is
that you do not need any web space, and there is no risk of anyone
seeing the content that you would not wish to see it.

How to Create a Family Tree CD/DVD

As well as creating a website or a family tree USB stick, you can also
create a family tree CD or DVD. This is exactly like creating a
website or family tree USB stick. Follow steps 1-3 above.
The only difference is that when it comes to step 3, and you click Export make sure that you choose the option for
creating a family tree CD/DVD.

The reason you have to choose "Family Tree CD/DVD" when exporting in
Step 3, is that Family Historian will add some additional files, to get
the CD or DVD to automatically start, when the CD or DVD is put into a
CD or DVD drive.

Of course, by the time you have completed these steps, you have created
the content for your CD or DVD. The next step is to burn this
content to an actual CD or DVD (see next).

Burning CD/DVDs

When you have created the content for your Family Tree CD/DVD, the
next step is to ‘burn’ it to one or more CDs or DVDs. The actual burning
of a CD or DVD is beyond the scope of this help. You will not use
Family Historian for this. But we can offer some pointers.

To burn a CD or DVD you need a DVD write or DVD rewriter. Any DVD
writer or rewriter should hopefully also burn CDs. It will almost
certainly have come with burning software that will do everything you
need. When you use this software, you may be asked what kind of CD/DVD
you want to create, e.g. data or audio. If asked, you want to create a
data CD or DVD - one that is suitable for distribution to other
computers.

In the unlikely event that you have a DVD writer or rewriter but it
did not come with software for burning a CD or DVD, you should be able
to do it anyway. Every version of Windows since Vista has the
capability built in.

When you use software to burn a CD or DVD, you will have to specify
which files are to be copied to the CD or DVD. These are the files you
exported in Step 3 above. If you have done everything correctly,
the CD/DVD will have the following files only in its ‘root’ folder:

autorun.inf

start.html

load.exe

fh.ico

It will also have a folder called ‘data’ which will contain numerous
other files.

Note Window

How to Create, Edit and Delete Autotext

title: Delete a Record Flag
text:
Record Flags

How to Delete a Record Flag

You cannot delete the Private and Living record flags. These are
built-in and are always included in record flag lists.

If you want to get rid of a record flag you have created, there are
two parts to this. First, you need to clear the flag on all records in
your project. Second, you need to stop the record flag appearing
in lists of record flags. One quick way to clear a particular flag on
all records is to use the Work with Lists
and Flags dialog which permits you to perform various tasks
with flags, including clearing them on all records (click on Named Lists and Record Flags on the
Tools menu to open this dialog). Clearing the flag on all records won't,
of itself, prevent a record flag you created appearing in lists of
record flags though. To stop that, you must again use the Work with
Lists and Record Flags dialog. You need to select the flag in
question and click on the Flag Status
button. When you do this, the Record Flag Status dialog
appears. Untick Always include this record flag in flag lists
in this dialog, and press OK.

If you do both of the above, the next time you open your project, you
should find that the unwanted record flag has gone.

title: How to Delete Records and Change Relationships
text:
How to...

How to Delete Records and Change Relationships

In Family Historian most data entry tasks involve the Property Box. It is here that you add
details of important events in a person's life - dates, places, etc - as
well as notes, and much more. You can also, if you wish, use
the Property Box to add spouses, children and even parents. But
you do not use the Property Box for deleting records or for removing
relationships. Here are some common ways (not the only ways) to delete a
record, change a relationship, or perform other common tasks:

HOW TO

COMMON METHODS

Delete a person's record
Select the person in the Focus
Window by clicking on their box, and press the Delete
key. You will be asked to confirm.

If the person is not currently visible in the Focus Window, there
are numerous ways to find them. One way would be to open the
Records Window
(Individuals tab), find their entry there, and click the Focus
button on the main toolbar, to show them in the Focus
Window.

You can also delete any record in the Records
Window by selecting it and pressing the Delete key. You
will be required to confirm.

If you are viewing the person in a diagram, you can delete them
there too. Click on their box and press the Delete
key. In this case, you will be asked what type of deletion
you require. You should take the option to delete data
record(s) if that's what you wish to do.

Delete the record for a person's son or daughter, spouse or
parent
This is the same thing again, and the method is the same,
assuming that you really do want to delete the record (if you
don't, see the next paragraph). It doesn't make any
difference whether you are viewing a person as a parent, or as
child, or as a spouse or grandparent, or as none of these
things. If you want to delete their record, and if you can
already see it in the Focus Window, click on their box and press
the Delete key (see above). If you can't see their record in
the Focus Window, follow the instructions in the paragraph above
for showing them in the Focus Window.

Remove a relationship without deleting any records

Suppose you have a person called John Smith, and you have added
a son for him, called Peter Smith. You now realise that
Peter Smith was not John Smith's son after all. Suppose
you don't want to delete your record for either Peter Smith or
for John Smith - you just want to remove the relationship that
links them as father and son. In Family Historian, this is
called unlinking. One easy way to do this is to
show John Smith in the Focus Window, pick a tab which shows his
children (e.g. the Spouses and Children tab) so you
can see Peter Smith listed as a son. Then click on Peter
Smith using the right mouse button and choose Unlink Record
from the menu that appears. You can use the same
technique to unlink spouses and parents.

Alternatively, you can also select a person, in any
context, and click Unlink From on the Edit menu,
and follow the instructions.

Create new relationships without creating new records
In our previous example, we changed the relationship between
John Smith and Peter Smith, so that the latter was no longer the
son of the former. Now suppose that we have discovered that
Peter Smith was really the son of Arthur Smith - and we already
have a record for Arthur Smith so we don't want to create a new
one. How do we link Peter Smith as the son of Arthur
Smith? One easy solution is to arrange to show Arthur Smith
as the focus person (box at the top) in the Focus
Window, and then, in the Spouses & Children tab,
click on the Add Child link to add a child for
him. You will be asked if you want to Create a new
Record or Link an Existing Record. Take the
latter option.

If Arthur Smith has a recorded wife, and Peter Smith is her son
too, this technique will work fine. If he has more than one
spouse, make sure you pick the Add Child link for the
right spouse.

If Arthur Smith has one or more recorded wives, but Peter Smith is
not the son of any of them, don't click on any Add Child link.
Instead click on the Add More Relatives for Arthur Smith
link, at the bottom of the Focus Window, and follow the
instructions.

A similar technique can be used to add spouses or parents.
You can also select Arthur Smith and choose appropriate options
from the Add menu.

Change the ordering of Spouses and Children
Suppose now that you have added Peter Smith as the son of Arthur
Smith, but he has been added as the last child, and you know that
he was the first. To correct this, make sure that the Focus
Window is showing Arthur Smith as the focus person.
Then, on the Spouses & Children tab, select Peter
Smith's record where he is listed as the last child of Arthur
Smith, and click the Move Up button on
the main toolbar, as many times as are needed to move him to the
correct position.

To change the order of a person's spouses, if he or she has more
than one, make sure you are showing the person's details in the
Focus Window (again, you want them to be the focus person at the
top), then click on one of the spouses and press the Move Up
or Move Down buttons ( and ) on the main toolbar, to move them to
the correct position.

You can also re-order spouses and children in the Main
tab of the Property Box, when viewing an Individual
record. This tab can have up to two sets of its own, small,
move up/down buttons. One set is used for re-ordering
spouses and is only available when the Individual record shows two
or more spouses. In that case, the move up/down buttons
display on the right-hand side of the Property Box, opposite the
Spouse label. There is another set which is used for
re-ordering children. This set is in the top-right corner of
the child list. The buttons in this set are always visible,
but may be greyed if no child is selected, or if no movement is
possible. With these buttons you have to click on the row
for the child you want to move, to enable the buttons.

title: Diagrams and Charts
text:
How to...

Diagrams and Charts

This section looks at how to perform various tasks that have to do
with diagrams and charts.

title: Display a Diagram
text:
Diagrams and Charts

How to Display a Diagram

To view a diagram, select the person who you want to be the root of
the diagram (almost all workspace windows have some way of
selecting an Individual record - you don't have to be in the Focus
Window). Then click on the Charts
button
and select from the available diagrams.

title: Display a Diagram for a Couple
breadcrumb: Display a Diagram for a Couple
text:
Diagrams and Charts

How to Display a Diagram For a Couple

Any diagram in Family Historian that has a root (which is the vast
majority of them) can be based on either an Individual, or on a couple.
A diagram based on a couple as root is very similar to a diagram based
on a single Individual as root, but there are subtle differences of
emphasis.

The easy way to display a diagram based on a couple is to open the
diagram (see How to Display a
Diagram). With most diagrams, when you open them, you will
be presented with a prompt asking you to confirm the root person for the
diagram. The first field on this dialog is "Tree RootType", the
value of which defaults to 'Individual'. Change this to 'Couple'
and
select the couple you want.

title: DNA
text:
How to...

DNA

Family Historian has tools relating to the use of DNA information
in a genealogy context. This section covers How
to Record Birth Parents Correct for DNA Purposes. For more
information about DNA tools and how to use them, see DNA
Tools.

title: How to Enter Accent Characters
text:
How to...

How to Enter Accent Characters

To enter accent characters into any field, press-and-hold the key that
you want to add an accent to. For example, if you want to add an
accent for a lower-case 'e', press-and-hold the 'e' key. When you
do so, a small popup window will appear looking like figure 1 below,
giving you a choice of accents for that letter.

Figure 1

If you wanted to add an accent for an upper-case 'E', press the shift
key and then press-and-hold 'E'.

If the kind of accent you want is not available, you can configure the
Accent popup window to show it. See Configure
Language and Accent Characters to learn more.

You can temporarily disable the Popup Accent Window by
pressing-and-holding the Insert key before
pressing-and-holding a letter key - if you are using the default option
for accent-handling. In that case, if the Insert key
is pressed, default Windows behaviour will occur and the letter key will
auto-repeat. For more options relating to entering accent
characters, see the discussion of the "To Enter Accents When Typing"
field, in the General tab
of Preferences.

title: Enter a Person's Name
text:
How to...

How to Enter a Person's Name

You specify a person's name in the Name
field in the Main tab
of the Property Box
(see How
to View an Individual's Record in the Property Box). When
you enter a person's name that consists of more than one word, Family
Historian will always assume that the last name is the surname, unless
you explicitly indicate otherwise by using slash characters to mark the
surname. Suppose, for example, that Elizabeth Powell Smith's surname is
'Powell Smith'. If you entered her name simply as "Elizabeth Powell
Smith", Family Historian would assume that 'Smith' was the surname. To
mark her surname correctly you would need to put slashes round 'Powell
Smith' like this: "Elizabeth /Powell Smith/". If the name had been
hyphenated however (as 'Powell-Smith') there would have been no need for
slashes as Family Historian would have treated the hyphenated name
'Powell-Smith' as the last name, and hence the surname.

In some languages, the surname may not necessarily appear at the end of
the name. For example, "Mao Tse-Tung" should be entered as "/Mao/
Tse-Tung" because 'Mao' is the surname. If you only enter only one word
as the name (e.g. 'Jane') Family Historian will, by default, assume that
it is not the surname and will automatically add two slash
characters on the end of the name to reflect this ("Jane //"). If
actually 'Jane' was the surname, and that's the only name you had, you
would need to enter it as "/Jane/" to make this clear. Of course,
the alternative is to use a question mark or something similar, to mark
the unknown name part - for example, "Jane ?" or "? Jane".

Why does Family Historian need to know which part of the name is the
surname? It needs to know this so that it can provide a number of
different services, such as automatic capitalization of surnames,
surname-based sorting, surname-first name ordering, and
search-by-surname.

When viewing names in Name fields, for editing purposes, Family
Historian can, if you wish, always put slashes round the surname, to
make it clear which part of the name is the surname. However, for
aesthetic reasons, Family Historian by default keeps the use of slashes
to a minimum, and only puts slashes round the surname when this is
needed for clarity - that is, if the surname is not the last name, or if
there is only one word in the name. See the Show Surnames
Between Slashes option in Preferences: Property Box
tab for options relating to this.

Other points:

Enter each person's name in the normal order in which it is given
in their culture. So, for example, in the West, the surname normally
appears at the end of the name; consequently, "Arthur Boyd Smith"
should be entered as "Arthur Boyd Smith" (without the quotes) and
not as "Smith, Arthur Boyd".

We recommend that you do not enter the surname in upper case. It
will, by default, be displayed in upper case in diagrams, reports
and elsewhere anyway; but you should enter it (and all other parts
of the name) in mixed case as it would normally be written. For
example, the surname McCracken should be entered as shown.

If you don't know a person's surname, enter the names you do know,
but put two slashes at the end to show that the last name is not the
surname - for example, "John Peter //". If you prefer, you can
instead put a question mark, or perhaps "(unknown)", instead of the
slashes, to mark where the surname should be.

Use maiden names for women. See also How to Record a Woman's Married Name.

If you want to record a nickname, or an alternative name, or
specify which given name a person used, or record their titles, see
How
to Record Alternative Names, Nicknames, Titles, etc . There
is no limit to the number of names that you can record for a person.

title: Enter Dates
text:
How to...

How to Enter Dates

When you enter a date into a date field, Family Historian will try to
determine what date you mean. If it cannot do so, it will warn you that
the date is invalid and ask you to correct the date information. It is
important that Family Historian can determine which date you mean. It
can use this information for a variety of purposes, such as filtering
and sorting on dates, warning of improbable or inconsistent dates,
offering alternative display formatting options, and calculating age
information.

If you are not sure how to specify a particular date, you can always
use the Date
Entry Assistant Dialog to help you enter the date. You can open
this dialog by clicking on the button with 3 little dots at the right
end of the date field, or by double-clicking on the date field itself.
However, when entering simple dates you should not need to use this
dialog box.

As well as warning of unrecognised dates, you will also be
warned if you try to enter an invalid date into a date field -
for example, if you specify the 31st day of a month that only has 30
days. If you really wish to store an invalid date like this you can do
so. When the "Invalid Date" dialog appears, leave the date unchanged and
press OK to close it. You will be
warned again that the date is invalid. Press OK
to confirm that you wish to keep it anyway.

Occasionally, you may wish to enter a date into a date field, as a
simple textual phrase, which Family Historian cannot be expected to
interpret. In that case, simply put the date into quotes (e.g. "3 weeks
after his wife died"). Family Historian will not try to interpret any
date in quotes.

Where dates are entered with the month specified as a digit (e.g.
3/12/1918), the interpretation of this will depend on your preferred
'short date format', as specified in the Windows Control Panel. In the
UK, this would normally be 'dd/mm/yyyy' (i.e. as 3 Dec 1918); but in the
U.S. (except in the U.S. customs) this would normally be 'mm/dd/yyyy'
(i.e. as 12 Mar 1918).

If Family Historian can determine what date you mean, it will display
the date in different formats depending on the context and on options
you choose. See Date
Formats for more details.

How to Enter Simple Dates

Family Historian tries to be as flexible as possible in allowing you
to enter dates in a wide variety of styles. The table below gives just
some examples of how you might enter simple dates.

All of the dates in the left column are acceptable to Family
Historian. The right column shows how it will interpret them. As you
will see, for each possible date there are numerous ways of entering the
same information. Where the interpretation will vary, depending on your
preferred 'short date format', both interpretations are given.

Text Entered into Date Field
Interpretation

1910
1910

Dec 1910
Dec 1910

December 1910
Dec 1910

d 1910
Dec 1910

12/1910
Dec 1910

12.1910
Dec 1910

12\1910

12 1910
Dec 1910

3 Dec 1910

3dec1910

3 Dec 1910

3rd Dec 1910
3 Dec 1910

Dec3 1910
