3 Dec 1910 (if 'dd/mm/yyyy') or 12 Mar 1910 (if 'mm/dd/yyyy')

3 12 1910
3 Dec 1910 (if 'dd/mm/yyyy') or 12 Mar 1910 (if 'mm/dd/yyyy')

How to Enter Complex Date Information

If you want to enter complex date information - such as a date range,
period, quarter, etc - you will usually find it more convenient to use
the Date Entry
Assistant Dialog to help you enter the date (see above, first
paragraph on this page, for instructions on how to open it). If you
frequently enter complex dates, however, you may prefer to use some of
these shortcut techniques:

Enter a '?' character, or the word 'approx' or '(approx)' or 'app'
or '(app)' or 'about' or '(about)', either before or after a simple
date, to show that the date is approximate. For example, "1910?" and
"?1910" will both be interpreted as meaning that the date is
approximately 1910. You can also enter 'circa' or 'c.' or 'c'
before a date to show that it is an approximate date.

Enter a '~' character, or the word 'est' or '(est') or 'estimated'
or '(estimated)', either before or after a simple date, to show that
the date has been estimated.

Enter the word 'cal' or '(cal') or 'calculated or '(calculated)',
either before or after a simple date, to show that the date has been
calculated.

2 dates with a hyphen between them (e.g. "Jan 1910 - May 1914" or
"1921-1923") will be interpreted as a date range (between ... and
...). You can also prefix the 2 dates with 'btw', 'bet' or 'between',
or separate them with 'and' instead of the hyphen (e.g. "btw 1910 and
1920").

2 dates with a hyphen between them, but preceded by the word 'from'
will be interpreted as a period (from ... to ...). You can also prefix
the 2 dates with 'frm', or separate them with 'to' instead of the
hyphen (e.g. "from 1910 to 1920").

A single date preceded by 'from' or 'frm' will be interpreted as a
period ('from ...').

A single date preceded by 'to' will be interpreted as a period ('to
...').

A single date preceded by 'bef' will be interpreted as a date range
('before ...')

A single date preceded by 'aft' will be interpreted as a date range
('after ...')

The letter 'q' followed by 1, 2, 3 or 4, and then a year will be
interpreted as the 1st, 2nd, 3rd or 4th quarter of that year (e.g. "q4
1910")

title: Facts (Events and Attributes)
text:
How to...

Facts (Events & Attributes)

In Family Historian the word 'fact' is used as shorthand for 'event or
attribute'.

This section looks at how to perform various tasks that have to do
with recording facts about a person or family.

title: Find Out How Two People Are Related
breadcrumb: Find Out How Two People Are Related
text:
More Family &
Relationship Tasks

How to Find Out How Two People Are Related

Use the How Related tool,
accessible from the Tools menu.

title: Fix Pictures that Won't Display (Repair 'Broken Links')
breadcrumb: Fix Pictures that Won't Display (Repair 'Broken Links')
text:
Pictures and Other Media

How to Fix Pictures That Won't Display (Repair 'Broken Links')

If a picture used to display correctly and no longer does so, the most
common reason is that the picture is stored externally on your hard
disk, and owing to some change on your computer, the stored 'links' to
this external file (called 'external file links') have stopped working
and become 'broken'. There is no need to delete the picture and
re-insert. You can check all external file links, and easily manage and
fix any broken ones, using the Work
with External File Links Dialog. To open this dialog, click
on External File Links on the
Tools menu.

It is well worth taking the time to understand how this dialog works.
It may appear a little complicated but at first, but it is actually much
simpler than it may seem; and once you have understood how to use it,
you may find that a single minor change in one place can fix any number
of bad links at a stroke and potentially save you a great deal of time
and effort as compared to any other technique you might care to use to
repair bad links (see Work
with External File Links Dialog).

Tip: There are two useful links at the bottom of the Media
Record tab in the Media
Window Display Pane (when viewing a single picture), labelled
'File' and 'Location' respectively. Clicking on the first link
opens the media file (the file on your hard disk containing the media
item) in an external viewer, and is the equivalent of clicking on the Open
Editor/Player button on the toolbar. Clicking on the
second link, the Location link, opens File Explorer to display the media
file in its location on your hard disk. If the media file cannot
be found on the hard disk, the first link will display in red, prefixed
by 'File not found - '. In that case, clicking on the link will
open a File Not Found dialog box, with options for
locating the missing media file - which includes letting Family
Historian search for the file for you.

title: Flag a Child as Adopted, Illegitimate, etc
breadcrumb: Flag a Child as Adopted, Illegimate, etc
text:
More Family &
Relationship Tasks

How to Flag a Child as Adopted, Illegitimate, etc

There are various different ways to do this. The most common ways
are these:

When viewing a person's record in the Focus
Window, right-click on a row for a child, in the Children
area. The dropdown menu that appears has a submenu labelled
'Relationship to Parents'. Choose an appropriate option from
this menu.

When viewing a person's record in the Property
Box, their children are displayed in a table called the Children
Grid, in the bottom half of the Main
tab. The last column in this grid is labelled 'Rel.' which
is an abbreviation for 'Relationship to Parents'. It is blank if
the relationship is 'birth child'. It shows a single letter for any
other relationship type, if the child has the same relationship to
both parents. It shows two letters, one for each parent, if the
child's relationships to its parents are different. For example,
if the child was adopted by his father, but the birth child of his
mother, the 'Rel' field would show "ab". Click on a cell in this
column to view a dropdown menu with different options to choose from.

The two previous methods start from the parent, and show you how to
change the relationship status of their children. If you are
already viewing a person in the Property Box and want to change their
relationship to their parents, without changing the selection in the
Property Box, you can do this too. Click on the Show Parent
Window icon on the Property Box toolbar, to show the person's
parents in the Parents Window.
You can specify the person's relationship to their parents using the
field labelled 'Relationship to Parents'.

It doesn't matter which technique you use. The effect is the same
in every case. You should use whichever technique is most
convenient for you.

title: How to Flag a Fact as Preferred, Private, Tentative or Rejected
breadcrumb: Flag a Fact as Preferred, Private, Tentative or Rejected
text:
Facts (Events and
Attributes)

How to Flag a Fact as Preferred, Private, Tentative or Rejected

You can set flags on facts (events or attributes) listed in the Facts
tab of the Property Box. The following fact flags are available:

Private

Preferred

Tentative

Rejected

To set any of these flags for a fact, select the fact and click on the
cog menu button
on the toolbar below the fact list. On the dropdown menu that
appears, choose an option under Fact Flags. Alternatively, if
you right-click on the any fact in the list (that is, click using the
right mouse button) you will also be able to see the Fact Flags options
on the dropdown menu that appears.

Fact flags can be set in any combination but the Rejected flag
effectively has priority and overrides all others. If the Rejected
flag is set, a fact is rejected, regardless of what other flags may be
set. This means that a fact with the Rejected flag is not also
treated as preferred, even if it has the Preferred flag set. The
meaning and purpose of the flags, subject to the priority of the
Rejected flag, is described in the table below.

Private
Set this flag is you do not wish this fact to appear in
reports. Facts flagged as 'Private' will be excluded from
most reports by default - unless you choose to override this.

Preferred
Set this flag to mark as being the most important fact of its
type, for the given person. For example, a person may have
had numerous occupations, but one may be more important than
others. In that case, you should mark that one as Preferred.

If a person has multiple occupations, you can if you wish mark
more than one of them as Preferred. But there is
little point in doing so. If a person has more than one
occupation marked as Preferred, Family Historian will
treat the first one as the Preferred one for them - and
the same applies to all fact types. The only exception to
this is if a fact which is flagged as Preferred, is also
flagged as Rejected (see below for more on this).

What is the effect of flagging a fact as Preferred?
The main tab of the Property Box for an Individual shows a number
of events and attributes - such as the person's occupation, birth
and death. In each case, it is the default fact
of that type that is displayed. The default fact,
of any given fact type, is the Preferred one if there
is a Preferred fact of that type, and the first one if
there isn't (again, assuming that none of them are also flagged as
Rejected). So, for example, if you have recorded 3
birth events for a given person (which you might do if there were
3 different theories as to when they were born), the birth details
that will display on the main tab of the Property Box, will be the
default birth details.

It is not just the main tab of the Property Box that can show default
or preferred facts. You can optionally
choose to display default or preferred facts in reports or
queries. To learn how to reference default or preferred
facts in reports and queries, see Understanding
Data References - an advanced topic.

Tentative
When you add facts for a person, you
are encouraged to show where you got the information from by
providing source citations for that fact. With each source
citation, you can use the Assessment field to indicate
how reliable you consider that source citation to be.
However, sometimes you may want to go further than simply
assessing a source citation. You may wish to flag a fact to
show that you have reservations as to whether it is correct or
not. For this, you should use the Tentative flag.
It indicates a level of uncertainty.

Setting the Tentative flag is primarily a reminder to
you that the supposed fact may not be solid. It will not
usually affect the way information is presented in diagrams or
reports. However, you can also choose to exclude tentative
facts (and/or rejected facts) when you export to
a GEDCOM or GEDZIP file.

Rejected
Suppose you don't just have reservations about a supposed fact -
you actually think that it is wrong. In that case, you can
flag that fact as Rejected. But then you may ask -
if it's wrong, why record it at all? There are two reasons
for this: first, it may be that it is you who are wrong. If
you have recorded all the details, you are then in a position to
re-appraise your conclusion at any time. Second, even if you
are correct, by recording all the details, it shows that you are
aware of this claim and that you have considered it and rejected
it. If you didn't record the information, it might appear
from your research that you were simply unaware of this theory.

Suppose, for example, you encounter two rival theories as to when
a particular person was born. In that case, we recommend
that you create two birth events for the person, and provide
source citations for each of them, linking the information back to
where you got it from. If you think that any of the sources
are wrong, you can use the Assessment field to mark the
source as unreliable or questionable, if you wish. The two
theories cannot both be correct. So we recommend that you
also flag at least one of the Birth facts as Rejected.
You can remove this flag at any time. By setting the flag,
however, you are telling Family Historian not to include the
information in diagrams, reports and books; and not to rely on it
for other purposes - such as for calculating a person's age.

Evidence versus Conclusions

Family Historian allows you to record evidence and draw conclusions
from them. For example, if you record in a birth fact for X
that their father was Y (you can do this by adding Y as a witness with
role of father in the Witnesses dialog), you can provide full source
citations both for the details of the birth and, separately, for the
fact that Y was X's father. So far you may have recorded the
evidence in an entirely neutral way. You haven't (yet) assumed or
concluded that any of this evidence is actually true or
not. That is fine, as far as it goes, but if you want to view
diagrams in which people's relationships are laid out in a meaningful
way, you have to be willing to go one step further and effectively say
that you are not just neutrally recording the claim that Y was the
father of X - you want Y to be treated as the father of X for diagram
purposes, and for reporting and other purposes. At no point do you
have to make a final decision that this is correct. You can always
easily change your mind at any point, if the weight of evidence
changes. But at some point, you will need to be able to form some
kind of view, however tentative, about which evidence is actually
correct. When you do so, you are moving beyond an entirely neutral
approach. In Family Historian, you do this, in the case of the
parent-child relationship, by linking Y as the father of X. Yes
you may have recorded evidence to justify doing this, but the act of
linking is not itself evidence - it constitutes a conclusion that
you have drawn from the evidence. Setting the Tentative and
Rejected fact flags are also examples of a move from evidence
to conclusions - possibly tentative conclusions, and certainly easily
revisable conclusions, but conclusions nevertheless. They affect
how the information is presented in diagrams, reports and
elsewhere. For this reason, you may wish to also record why you
came to the conclusions you came to, and why you set the flags as you
did - see next.

Documenting Your Conclusions

Just as it is good practice to cite your sources, so too, it is good
practice to document why you arrived at your conclusions - especially in
the case of the Tentative and Rejected flags.
The recommended way to do this is to insert a #Research hash tag into
the note for the fact in question, and explain there why you set the
flags as you did. You can even attach source citations to back up
your conclusions, if you wish to - see Note
Window to learn more.

Fact Flags vs. Record Flags

Fact flags are not the same as record flags. Do not confuse
them. See Record Flags to
learn about the differences.

See also How to Create a
Custom Fact Flag.

title: Handle Unmarried Couples & Children Born Out of Wedlock
breadcrumb: Handle Unmarried Couples & Children Born Out of Wedlock
text:
More Family &
Relationship Tasks

How to Handle Unmarried Couples & Children Born Out of Wedlock

To record that two people were an unmarried couple you should treat
them as if they were married and add one as the spouse of the other (see
How to
Add Spouses, Parents & Children). Then on the Main
tab of the Property
Box, set the Status field for
them to
Unmarried Couple.

To record the parents of a child born out of wedlock, you should again
treat the parents as if they were married, even if they weren't. If the
parents did have a relationship of some kind, even though they never
married, you should set the Status
field for them to
Unmarried Couple. If the
child's parents did not marry, and could not accurately be described as
being a couple in any sense, you should the Status
field to
Never Married which does
not imply that they had any kind of relationship.

title: How to Install a Language Pack
breadcrumb: How to Install a Language Pack
text:
Languages and Language Packs

How to Install a Language Pack

To install a language pack, click on Language Packs on the Tools
menu, to open the Language Packs window. If the language
pack you are looking for isn't listed there, click the Import...
button and choose From Family Historian Plugin Store.
This will show a list of available language packs. You can select
one and click Import to import it.

If instead of installing from the Plugin Store, you have a language
pack file that you wish to install, do the same thing, but when you
click on the Import... button, instead of
choosing From Family Historian Plugin Store, choose From
File, and select the language pack file.

Family Historian will never allow an imported language pack to replace
an existing language pack. If you import a language pack with the
same language id as one already installed on your PC, Family Historian
will modify the id of the new one, to make it unique. For example,
if you have a French language pack installed, with language id "FRA",
and you install another French language pack with the same id, Family
Historian will modify the newly installed language pack's id to "FRA
2". You can delete unwanted language packs at any time, and also
rename them or their ids, as required.

If you have an old language pack and you want to upgrade to the latest
version, simply install the latest version from the Plugin Store.
This will install the new version alongside your old version. If
you no longer want the old version, you can delete it.

If the language pack you want isn't available (or there is one, but it
isn't adequate for your purposes), you can create your own - see How
to Create a Language Pack.

title: Link Individuals to Their Face in a Picture
breadcrumb: Link Individuals to Their Face in a Picture
text:
Pictures and Other Media

How to Link Individuals to Their Face in a Picture

If you have not yet added the picture into your project, follow the
instructions for doing this in How to Add a Picture for an Individual.

Pictures can be added either in the Media
Window, or in the Media tab of
the Property Box. It doesn't matter
which you use. The instructions for linking a person to their face
differ slightly depending on which approach you use.

How to Link a Person to Their Face in the Property Box

To link a person to their face in a picture, from within the Media tab
of the Property Box, you need to use the Edit Media Item dialog box. If you insert a
single picture in the Media tab of the Property Box, this dialog box
will automatically be opened for you when the picture is inserted. If
you insert multiple pictures, it won't be automatically opened.
You will need to select each picture in turn and click on the Edit
button on the Media toolbar to edit it.

To link a person to their face, click on the Link
to Face button and then move the cursor over the picture. You
should notice when you do this, that the cursor now looks like a cross.
You click-and-drag on the picture to draw a stretchy box round the face.
When you release the button, he or she should have a rectangle round
their face with 8 little white boxes on the sides and corners. You can
click-and-drag inside the rectangle to move it, or click-and-drag on any
of the white boxes to re-size the box. Once you are satisfied, you can
press OK to save changes.

If later you wish to reposition the 'frame' round the person's face,
click on the Select Frame button. The 8
little white boxes will appear round the rectangle and once again, you
can click-and-drag inside the rectangle to move it, or click-and-drag on
any of the little white boxes to resize the box.

If you want to delete the frame, click on the Select
Frame button then press the Delete
key.

How to Link a Person to Their Face in the Media Window

This is explained in the Media Window
page.

title: How to Manage Chart and Diagram Headings
text:
Books

How to Manage Chart and Diagram Headings

Book Charts and Page Layout

It is possible to insert an image within a page, without necessarily
occupying the full page (see How
to Insert a Picture, Map or Figure). However when you insert
a chart or diagram, it will always occupy at least one full page - that
is the area between the page header and the footer - and may occupy any
number of pages. This is also the area where book headings,
if any will go. Allowing book headings to overlap the chart area
can be visually striking and effective if handled well. Glossy
magazines do this kind of thing all the time, for good reason. But
care is needed. This page discusses the issues.

The 'Format' Field

By default, when you insert a chart or diagram it will be created with
the "No heading" setting in the 'Format' field. To view the
'Format' field for a book chart (the name used for a chart or
diagram that has been inserted into a diagram) select it in the list of
current book items in the Edit Book
Dialog, and click the 'Settings' button in the list below (not
the 'Book Settings' button which is different). The Format field
is where you specify whether a book item represents the start of a
chapter or a section. In either case, it will have a heading of
some kind. Sections have up to 3 heading levels. You can if
you wish change the Format setting for a book chart. If, for
example, you want a book chart to be listed in the table-of-contents,
you will need to set the 'Format' field to 'Chapter'.
However, any value except 'No heading' will result in a heading being
created for the chart or diagram. As the chart occupies the full
area of the page, the heading will overlay the chart area. This is
not necessarily a problem in itself, but can be an issue if the heading
overlays chart text or images.

Heading Options If Format Field Is Set to "No Heading"

If you want your chart to have a heading, but want to leave the
'Format' setting as 'No heading' (which avoids risk of overlaid text),
you need to add the heading within the book chart itself. See Edit Book Chart in Diagram
Window for more on this.

Heading Options If Format Field Is Set to "Chapter" or to Some Heading
Level

If you set the Format field to "Chapter", or to "Heading Level 1",
"Heading Level 2" or "Heading Level 3", you are effectively asking
Family Historian to insert a heading into the chart page for you.
The heading will be whatever text you specify in the "Heading" field
(above the "Format" field).

If you want a book chart to have a heading of this kind, unless you
happen to be fortunate, you may need to carefully arrange the chart so
that there is a suitable space made available for the inserted heading
so that it does not overlap anything important. One way to do this
is in the Select Chart Pages
Window. With this window you can reposition the chart across
one or more pages, to leave space for the heading. You can
also, if necessary change the scale of the chart. See Select
Chart Pages Window to learn more.

Tip: If the chart has its own background colour, you can
get rid of this, if you want to, by unticking "Print Background" on the
Print tab of 'Options' for the book chart in question. To access
Diagram Options for a book chart, click the Options
button in the Select Chart
Pages Window.

Yet another option is to edit the book chart itself, to move trees or
tree branches items, to leave space for the heading on the first
page. See Edit Book
Chart in Diagram Window for more on this.

title: Mark a Couple as Separated or Divorced
breadcrumb: Mark a Couple as Separated or Divorced
text:
More Family &

How to Mark a Couple as Separated or Divorced

To mark that a couple were separated or divorced, open the Property
Box for either of them (see How to View an Individual's Record in the Property
Box), and set the Status
field for their marriage to Separated
or
Divorced. If they
divorced, you can also add a divorce event for their marriage if you
wish (see How
to Record Details About a Marriage). Although 'Divorce' is a
standard event, 'Separation' is not. However, you can add it as a custom
family event if you wish (see How to Create a Custom Fact (Event or Attribute)).

If you wish, you can use a distinctive line style to display the
marriage lines between divorced and separated couples, in diagrams and
charts (e.g. they can be crossed-out). This is an option in the Lines
tab of the Diagram
Options dialog.

You can use the Assessment field

least for that particular item of data (see How to Record the Sources for Your Data).

title: How to Merge Two Projects
breadcrumb: Compare, Merge,  Append and Split Projects
text:
Compare, Merge,
Append and Split Files

How to Merge Two Projects

If the data you wish to merge, comes from someone else, please read the
instructions in How to Compare Another Person's Research with Yours.
That describes how to create a new project and import the data into
it.

When you merge two projects, what happens is that you open one of the
projects and merge the other project into it. The second project
is left unchanged. It is the first project only that is changed.

Having opened the first project, click on Merge/Compare
File on the File menu, to open the Merge/Compare Dialog. You will be prompted
to select the file to merge in. You should normally select a
project file, but it is also possible to merge in a GEDCOM file
directly. At this point, you will be able to compare the 2
files. To merge the data, click on the Merge
button within the Merge/Compare
Dialog. Before doing so however, click on the Help
button and carefully read the advice there. Merging one file into
another is not a minor change, and you should make sure you know what
you are doing before you do it. Also, always make sure you take a backup
copy of your own data first.

See also File
Merging and Comparing.

title: Move Boxes and Branches in Diagrams
breadcrumb: Move Boxes and Branches in Diagrams
text:
Diagrams and Charts

How to Move Boxes and Branches in Diagrams

Family Historian supports 5 kinds of drag-move action types in
diagrams:

Box Move

Bar Move

Fixed-Point Move

Tree Move

Everything (position on page)

To do any of them you must first enable moving/resizing which you do
by clicking on the Enable Moving/Resizing
button on the Diagram
toolbar. As well as enabling moving/resizing, this also
opens the Movement
Control Box.

When moving/resizing is enabled you can perform box moves by
clicking-and-dragging on any box, and you can perform a bar move by
clicking-and-dragging on any child bar (descendant diagram) or parent
bar (ancestor diagrams). If you want to perform fixed-point moves or
tree moves, you must select these action types in the Movement Control
Box.

To learn more about all kinds of action types, see Movement Control Box.

title: Named Lists
text:
How to...

Named Lists

It is often useful to be able to put together, and keep lists of records.
Here are just some lists you might want to keep:

a bookmark list as a shortcut to frequently accessed records

a list of work-in-progress records

a list of possible duplicate records you wish to check

a list of records where Family Historian re-sequenced the fields,
and you asked it to create a list of updated records for you to
double-check

a list of records you want to delete

a list of records that you wish to edit, grouped together for ease
of access

a list of records you have selected for a report

a list of records you wish to send to someone

a list of pictures (Media records)
waiting to be linked to other records

a list of famous or infamous people

a list of relatives to invite to a reunion

a temporary list to be used in conjunction with queries, to allow
you to effectively create more complex queries

a ToDo list of records that you plan to work on when
you visit a certain record office (with notes about what you plan to
do)

In short, named lists can be used in a variety of different ways, and
for a variety of different purposes. Unlike record
flags which can only be used with Individual
records, you can add records of any type to any Named List.

Tip: Although named lists are useful for many purposes,
bear in mind that there are other tools, such as queries,
smart folders, record
flags and Research Notes,
that might be a better choice, depending on what you want to do.
For example, you can keep lists of records in Research Notes too
(as record links), if you want to.

title: How to Override Box Features for Particular Boxes

How to Override Box Features for Particular Boxes

You can specify general rules about how you want boxes to appear, in

Diagram menu (or right-click on a box and select Format from

You can change the appearance of any number of boxes
simultaneously. You just need to select them all before you click
Format (see How
to Select Multiple Boxes in Diagrams).

To learn more, see Override Box
Features Dialog.

Reports

How to Print a Complete Report About a Person

If you are more concerned to have a complete report, than with layout

title: Print a Report About One or More Individuals
breadcrumb: Print a Report About One or More Individuals
text:
Reports

How to Print a Report About One or More Individuals

Family Historian comes with a number of reports pre-installed,
including Individual and Family
reports, narrative reports, outline reports and record detail reports.
You can also add to this list by making your own custom reports. All of
these reports are available from the Publish
Menu (click the Publish button
on the main toolbar to view this). Browse and try out various reports
until you find one that suits your needs. When you choose a report, in
most cases you will be prompted to first select one or more Individuals
(or other records) that the report will be about. Often you will only
want to select one record, but in some cases you may want to select
several records. Most reports have extensive configuration options
and you can change these in the Report
Options Dialog, either before or after opening the report.

To print a report, click on the Print
button in the panel on the right side of the Report Window, or click on
Print on the File menu.

For more information see Report Window and the Report
Options Dialog.

If you want a report laid out in tabular fashion (row/column) you can
alternatively run a query and print off the results as a report.
See the How to Use
Queries for more details.

title: How to Produce Reports & Books in Different Languages
breadcrumb: How to Produce Reports & Books in Different Languages
text:
Languages and Language Packs

How to Produce Reports & Books in Different Languages

Introduction to Key Concepts

See About Language Packs for a
quick introduction to the varied uses of language packs. This page
discusses how to use Family Historian to produce reports or books in
different languages. Notice that there are some minor differences
(see the table in Guide to Colour Markings below) depending on
whether you are using the language pack for same language rendering
(project language and output language are the same) or for other
language translation (project language and output language are
not the same). See About
Language Packs for more on this distinction.

How to Select a Language Pack for Your Report or Book

To produce a report in a language other than English (or even in
English, if the project language is not English), open the report and,
within the report options, select the Language
tab. Choose an appropriate language pack for the Report
Language field. If there is no language pack listed for the
language you require, see How
to Install a Language Pack, or How
to Create a Language Pack. Selecting a language pack for a
book is similar. Click Book Settings
in the Edit Book Dialog, and then
select the Language
tab.

If your project language is not English and you always want
reports to be in the project language, you can make this the default
output language. See the section "Specifying the Project Language"
in How to Work in
Different Languages.

Not All Reports Are Fully Language Pack Ready

Most Family Historian reports support language translation (that is,
are language pack ready), but not all. All reports
support language packs to some degree, but some may not be fully
language pack ready. The ones that aren't, or may not be, are
custom reports, and some of the reports in the Miscellaneous category.

Translation Tables

In general, owing to the high level of configurability of Family
Historian and for other practical reasons, it is not possible to
guarantee that all parts of a report can always be fully translated by a
language pack, without some action being required by you, the
user. However, if some part of a report is not being translated,
the untranslated parts can optionally be marked distinctively in
different colours, so that it is easy to spot untranslated
portions. In most cases, you can easily fix any problems with
untranslated text by adding entries to translation tables that
form part of your language pack. There are 3 translation
tables in each language pack: one for place names, one for attribute
values (values for attribute facts, like 'Occupation' or 'Religion'),
and a third one, "Miscellaneous", for everything else.

When you have selected an output language in Report Options (Languages
tab), or Book Settings (also Languages tab), there will be an extra
'Translate' button in the panel on the right-hand side. Click on
this button and choose "Translation Tables" from the dropdown menu, to
access translation tables for the current report or book. You can
also click on "Translation Tables" on the "Report" menu, when viewing
the Report Window, or click on "Translation Tables" on the "Book" menu,
when viewing the Book Window. In each case, you must previously
have selected a language pack for your report or book.

The Translation
Tables dialog is a floating window. This means that you can
leave it open while you are viewing your report or book, and make
changes to it as needed. You do not need to close it before you
can see the changes in your report or book. However, be aware that
any changes you make in translation tables will not be reflected in your
report or book until you refresh it.

To learn how to use the Translation Tables, and how to interpret colour
markings, see the next section: Guide to Colour Markings.

Guide to Colour Markings

The different colours of the markings are your guide to what you need
to do to correct the problem, if anything. See the table below for
details:

However, both kinds of text can be translated by adding the

An untranslated place name is not treated as an error, or marked

from the Place translation table.

Add the separate place parts that you

language pack (see Language

example, if the place is "Greenwich, London, England", and your

for them to read.

Queries

title: Record Alternative Names, Nicknames, Titles, etc
breadcrumb: Record Alternative Names, Nicknames, Titles, etc
text:
How to...

How to Record Alternative Names, Nicknames, Titles, etc

If a person had more than one name, we recommend that you pick one as
the name which you intend to use to identify the person, and enter that
in the Name field of the Main
tab of the Property Box as described in How to Enter a Person's Name.

If the person had two or more names, you can enter all alternative
names in the Names/Titles dialog
for the person in question. To access this dialog, open the person's
record in the Property Box, and click on the more... text
link, to the right of the Name field in the Main tab.

The advice in How
to Enter a Person's Name about how to enter names, still applies
when names are entered in the Names/Titles
dialog.

Titles can also be added in the Names/Titles dialog. Click on
the Add button and then choose Title
from the dropdown menu. You can add also add titles in the Facts
tab of the Property Box. It doesn't matter which you choose. If you add
them in the Facts tab, you will be able to see them in the Names/Titles
dialog, and vice versa. You will find though that you can enter more
details about titles in the Facts - even if you didn't originally add
them there.

There is no limit to the number of names or titles that a person can
have.

Nicknames can also be entered in the Names/Titles dialog.

It sometimes happens that a person was not usually known by their
first name. For example, if Jean Clare Smiley was always known as Clare
by everyone who knew her, enter 'Clare' in the Given
Name Used field. If the person was always known by their first
name you should leave the Given Name Used
field blank, as this is the default. If Jean Clare Smiley was always
known as Jean Clare, enter 'Jean Clare' in the Name
Used field.

If the person had a name prefix (such as Dr, Sir, Colonel,
etc), these should be entered in the Name
Prefix field. If the person had a name suffix (e.g.
Jr), these should be entered in the Name
Suffix field.

Do not confuse titles (such as Lord Dittington) with name
prefixes (such as Dr).

If you wish to record an event of the person changing their name, you
would need to create 'Name Change' as a custom event, and use that to
record the name change. See How to Create a Custom Fact (Event or Attribute).

See also How
to Record a Woman's Married Name.

title: Record a Person's Age at the Time of an Event
breadcrumb: Record a Person's Age at the Time of an Event
text:
Facts (Events and
Attributes)

How to Record a Person's Age at the Time of an Event

Events and attributes are recorded in the Facts
tab of the Property Box (see How to View an Individual's Record in the Property
Box). Click on the event in question and enter the person's age at
the time of the event in the Age field. If you just enter a
number, this will be assumed to be the age in years. But you can also
specify months and/or days if you wish. You can also specify more
vaguely whether the person was a child, infant, or younger or older than
a given age. To enter this kind of more complex age information,
double-click on the Age field or click on the little button ...
to the right of the age field, to open the Age Entry Assistant Dialog.

A special use of the Age field is to record stillborn births. To
record a stillborn birth, select Stillborn
in the Age Entry Assistant Dialog for the Birth event.

title: How to Record a Shared Event
text:
Facts (Events and
Attributes)

How to Record a Shared Event

If two people are married, or at least are linked as a couple in a Family record, they effectively share
all of the Family events, such as Marriage, Divorce, etc. That is
one way that two people can share an event. Sometimes, however,
you want to record an event which is shared between numerous
participants, and it may be that none of them are a couple in any
sense. Suppose, for example, that four people all lived together
for four years. It would make sense to create a single Residence
fact which they all share. To do this, you need to create a
Residence fact for one of them (it doesn't matter which one), and then
add all four of them as witnesses (that is, non-principal
participants) to that fact, with role of 'Resident' (see How
to Record Witness Details). Notice that even the person you
originally added the fact to, can be a witness to their own fact.
And if they are, this will override their status as the fact owner (for
purposes like sentence generation in narrative reports, say). What
this means is that they will be treated exactly like all the others, in
all output. Of course you can treat them differently if you want to, and
even give them a different role (if say, they were the tenant).
The point is that you don't have to. In practical terms, this
means that you can have events which are shared equally between all
participants.

In Family Historian, any event which has one or more witnesses, is
called a shared event. See Witnesses
and the Witnesses
Window to learn more.

title: Record a Stillborn Birth
text:
Facts (Events and Attributes)

How to Record a Stillborn Birth

This is covered in the section
How to Record a Person's Age at
the Time of an Event.

title: Record a Woman's Married Name
text:
More Family & Relationship Tasks

How to Record a Woman's Married Name

There is no one standard way of doing this. Here are some options:

You could mention this information in a note about their marriage (see
How to Create a Note About a Marriage)
or add this as a note to their marriage event (see
How to Record Facts About a Person's
Life).

You could create your own custom 'Married Name' attribute (see
How to Create a Custom Fact (Event
or Attribute)) and record the information there. This would have the advantage that you could also associate
the name change with a date, or even with a period of time (see
How to Specify a Date Range,
Period, or Other Complex Date).

Or you could simply add the married name as an alternative name for the person (see
How to Record Alternative Names,
Nicknames, Titles, etc).

title: How to Record Birth Parents Correctly For DNA Purposes
breadcrumb: Record Birth Parents Correctly for DNA Purposes
text:
Record Flags

How to Record Birth Parents Correctly For DNA Purposes

Most of the time, recording a person's birth parents is very
straightforward. When you add a person's mother and father, Family
Historian will assume by default that these are the birth parents.
However, occasionally things can get more complicated.

In Family Historian, as in most genealogy programs, family
relationships are stored in Family
records. Each Family record allows you to record up to two parents
(who can be same sex parents), and as many children as you like.
Within each Family record, each child can have a recorded relationship
to their parents in that Family record. If nothing is recorded
about the child's relationship to their parent, this is treated as
implying that they have the default relationship to both parents -
namely that they are the birth child of both parents. You can if
you wish record that the child was adopted, step, fostered or de
facto (accepted as a birth child, even though they may not have
been really). You can also explicitly record that their
relationship is birth if you really want to - but you are
recommended to only do this if you have some particular reason to do so
(e.g. if you want to emphasize that the child was the birth child,
perhaps because questions had been raised about this). The child
can have the same relationship to both parents, or different
relationships to each parent. A child could be the birth-child of
the mother, for example, and the step-child of the father.

Each child can be listed as a child in more than one Family
record. In fact, they can be a child in as many Family records as
you like. However, this can potentially create
inconsistencies. Suppose a given person X is listed as a child in
two Family records. Let us imagine that X's parents in the first
Family record are given as Allison and Brian. And X's parents in
the second Family record are given as Camilla and David. If in
each Family record, Allison and Camilla are each recorded as X's birth
mother - that would be an inconsistency. They can't both be.
Equally, if both Brian and David were recorded as X's birth father -
that also would be inconsistent.

Theoretically, it might seem that there would be nothing inconsistent
or wrong in recording Allison as X's birth-mother and Brian as X's
step-father in the first Family record, while also recording Camilla as
X's step-mother and David as X's birth-father in the second Family
record. And it's true that as far as that goes, there's nothing
obviously wrong about that. But it is problematic because of the
way Family Historian determines who a person's birth parents are (see
next).

See also How
to Flag a Child as Adopted, Illegitimate, Etc.

The Birth Family Record

When trying to determine for any given person X, who X's birth parents
are, Family Historian will look for X's birth Family record.
X's birth Family record is the first Family record for X in which both
parents are listed (explicitly or implicitly) as birth parents - if
there is one. If no such Family record exists, the birth Family
record is the first Family record for X in which at least one parent is
listed (explicitly or implicitly) as birth parent. If
no such Family record exists, X does not have a birth Family record.

Just to be clear, if X has a birth Family record, that doesn't mean
that Family Historian will treat the parents in this Family record as
X's birth parents. It just means that when trying to determine who
X's parents were, Family Historian will only look at this Family
record. So, for example, if the father in X's birth Family record
is recorded as his step-father, Family Historian will treat X as having
no recorded birth-father.

What this means is that in the situation mentioned earlier, if you want
to have a Family record in which Allison and Brian are recorded
respectively as X's birth-mother & step-father, and if you want to
have another Family record in which Camilla and David are recorded
respectively as X's step-mother and birth-father, then for Family
Historian to be able to correctly determine who X's birth parents are
(which it needs to do, to calculate DNA information correctly and for
other purposes), you need to have a third Family record in which Allison
and David are recorded as X's birth-mother and birth-father. All
of these Family records can be in any order - most people would probably
record them in order of importance from X's point-of-view - but they
must exist.

Multiple Marriages To the Same Person

Suppose two people, X and Y, got married twice (having presumably
divorced once). Should you record this using one Family record or
two? You could record it using two Family records, but our
recommendation would be that you should use only one, and simply record
both marriage events and the divorce event, within this Family
record. If you really want to record it using two Family records,
you could. However, if you do that, you should be careful to
ensure that exactly the same list of birth children are recorded in each
Family record. If you do not do so, this would be another way of
recording inconsistent information, which could lead to errors in DNA
calculations, etc.

title: Record Details About a Marriage
text:
More Family &
Relationship Tasks

How to Record Details About a Marriage

To record that two people are a couple (married or not) you add one as
the spouse of the other (in the Focus Window
or using any other technique). When you have done this, you can record
further details about their marriage using the Property
Box (see How to View an Individual's Record in the Property
Box). It doesn't matter which spouse you use when you do this.
After you have entered all such details, you will find that all the
marriage details will be equally visible (and can be changed or deleted
equally well) when you are viewing either spouse's record details. This
is because marriage details are actually stored in a separate Family
record, access to which is shared between both spouses. This is all
taken care of for you 'behind the scenes' by Family Historian.

You can enter basic details in the Main
tab of the Property Box. To record more details about the events
and attributes that relate to their marriage (e.g. to record a note
about the marriage event, or to record the event of their becoming
engaged, or divorced, or whatever) you must go to the Facts
tab of the Property Box. To add marriage events and attributes,
click on the Add Fact button on the Fact
List toolbar, and select all the events or attributes you wish to add.
When you choose an event or attribute which applies to a couple, you
will be required to confirm which couple they apply to. Family
events and attributes (the ones that apply to a couple) have a red dot
in the listing. Individual events and attributes have a blue dot.

See also How
to Create a Note About a Marriage.

title: Record Facts About a Person's Life
breadcrumb: Record Facts About a Person's Life
text:
Facts (Events and
Attributes)

How to Record Facts About a Person's Life

Use the Property Box to record facts
about a person.

The most important tab in the Property Box, for the purpose of
recording facts (events or attributes) about a persons life is the Facts
tab. You can enter some basic details in the Main
tab. But to record more than just the basics, you should use the
Facts tab.

Events and attributes can either be Individual
events and attributes, or they can be Family
events and attributes. The former apply primarily, in the first
instance, to one person (e.g. Birth, Death, Occupation). The latter are
equally applicable to two people - the husband and wife in a family
record (e.g. Marriage, Engagement, Divorce).

To add any kind of event or attribute, click on the Add

Fact button on the Facts tab toolbar. If the fact you wish to
add is not listed in the short menu that appears, choose 'More Fact
Types...'. This opens the Fact
Types dialog. You can either select all the events and attributes
you wish to add, one at a time, and press Add
after each one (untick Close Dialog After
Adding to prevent the dialog closing every time you add an
event or attribute); or you can add multiple events and attributes at a
time by pressing-and-holding the Ctrl key while clicking on items to
select them.

The standard events and attributes, which are included when Family
Historian is installed, are:

Adoption

Annulment

Baptism

Bar Mitzvah

Bat Mitzvah

Birth

Blessing

Burial

Census

Census (family)

Child Count

Christening

Christening (adult)

Confirmation

Cremation

Death

Divorce

Divorce Filed

Education

Emigration

Engagement

First Communion

Graduation

Group/Caste Membership

Immigration

Marriage

Marriage Banns

Marriage Contract

Marriage Count

Marriage Licence

Marriage Settlement

National Identity Number

National or Tribal Origin

Naturalisation

Occupation

Ordination

Physical Description

Possessions

Probate

Religion

Residence

Retirement

Title

U.S. Social Security Number

Will

If the fact type you want is not in this list, there is
also an additional set called the Extended Set, which may have
the one you want (see How
to Access the Extended Set of Fact Types).

You can also create as many custom events and attributes
as you want (either for Individuals or Families) - see How to Create a Custom Fact (Event or Attribute).
Once created, these custom events and attributes will be added to events
and attribute lists, so they can be selected, added and used exactly
like standard events and attributes.

If there are some standard events and attributes that you are never
likely to use, you can hide them if you wish, to make the list more
manageable (see Fact
Types Dialog).

You can add more details about each event or attribute in the Facts
tab. For each one, you can specify a date, age, place, address and note.
With some events or attributes there may be other fields too. For
example, with the Death event there is a Cause field in which you can
record the cause of death. To enter or view these extra details, simply
select the relevant event or attribute. The additional details are
displayed below the list, and can be edited there.

To specify complex dates (periods, ranges, date phrases, quarter
dates, imprecise dates, and so on) use the Date Entry Assistant Dialog. To open this dialog,
click on the Date field, or just move the mouse over the field, to
activate the helper dialog button ... -
then click on this button. Alternatively, you can also simply
double-click on the Date field itself. Other fields, apart from
date fields, also have helper dialogs which can be opened in the same
way.

You can add more than one instance of each event or attribute - in
fact you can have as many instances as you like. For example, if a
person had multiple occupations and you wish to record them all, you
should have one Occupation attribute for each occupation (see How to Record Multiple Occupations). Again, if a
person lived in many different places, you could if you wished have one
Residence attribute for each place they lived (see How to Record Where a Person Lived).

Sometimes you may want to record additional details about people who
played in role in an event (or more rarely attribute), without being the
principal or one of the principals (the bridesmaids or best man at a
wedding, say). Such people are called witnesses within
Family Historian. See the Witnesses
Window for details about how to record witness details.

See also How
to Record Details About a Marriage.

title: Record Flags
text:
How to...

Record Flags

Record Flags vs. Fact Flags

Do not confuse record flags with fact
flags. Fact flags are attached to facts (events or
attributes). These can be Individual facts or Family facts.
Record flags are attached to Individual records (only). You can
create your own custom record flags. You can also create custom
fact flags if you wish. It is possible though to have record flags
which have the same name as fact flags - in fact, by default, there is a
built-in record flag called 'Private'. There is also a 'Private'
fact flag. But even when they have the same name, record flags are
always distinct and separate from fact flags.

To learn more about fact flags, see the How
to Flag a Fact as Preferred, Private, Tentative or Rejected and How to Create a Custom Fact
Flag.

About Record Flags

Family Historian comes with only 2 built-in record flags. These are:

Private

Living

The Private flag is used to mark Individuals who you wish
to be excluded from reports, from a website you are creating, or from a
family tree USB stick, CD or DVD you want to make. The Living flag
is used mark Individuals who are currently alive. You can use this for
various purposes. A common requirement is to only show basic details -
no events or dates - for living people, and you can use the Living flag
to do this.

With both Private and Living flags, you need to choose the appropriate
options for your report, book, website, USB stick, CD or DVD, if you
wish Individuals who have these flags to be treated specially.

Although there are only 2 built-in record flags, there is no limit on
the number of record flags that you can create yourself. Having created
a flag, you can then test for its presence in queries and in text schemes. For example, most of the time you
can tell what a person's sex is from their name. But sometimes you
can't. You could, if you wished have a 'Display Gender' flag. You could
set this on all people who have sexually ambiguous names. Then in a
diagram text scheme you could include information about a person's sex,
but make it conditional upon the 'Display Gender' flag being set (see How
to Change the Contents of Boxes in Diagrams).

Here are just a few suggestions of things you might wish to create a
record flag to record:

that a person is another genealogist

that a person is a twin or triplet

that a person is famous or infamous

that a person is known to you personally

that a person has an occupation you are keeping track of

that a person should be highlighted in a special way in diagrams

As well as making any line of text in a diagram conditional upon the
presence of a record flag, you can also make any box feature conditional
upon the presence of a record flag (see Diagram Options Dialog: Boxes Tab). So you could
have a flag for 'Died of a heart attack' if you wished, and put a thick
red surround with a yellow background (or whatever you wanted) on boxes
for people who have this flag. Or you could create one flag for each of
the censuses, and display an icon (another box feature - this is a
little image that appears below a box) for each census. Then in any
diagram, you could see at a glance, which people have been found in
which census.

title: Record Multiple Occupations
text:
Facts (Events and
Attributes)

How to Record Multiple Occupations

Add one Occupation attribute, in the Facts
tab of the Property Box, for each of the person's occupations (see
How
to Record Facts About a Person's Life).

It often happens that a person may have had multiple occupations, but
one of them is much more important that others, and may even form a part
of their identity. In that case, you may wish to mark the relevant
attribute as Preferred. See How
to Flag a Fact as Preferred, Private, Tentative or Rejected to
learn how to do this.

See also How to View an Individual's Record in the Property
Box.

title: How to Record Non-Family Relationships
text:
More Family &
Relationship Tasks

How to Record Non-Family Relationships

There are many ways that people can be associated with one another,
apart from just family relationships. A person might be another person's
old friend, business partner, employer, teacher, pupil, godparent,
lawyer, doctor, neighbour ... and so on. In Family Historian you can
record any kind of relationship - not just family relationships.
There is built-in support for many kinds of relationships, but if the
specific kind of relationship is not already covered, you can define
your own.

The standard mechanism for linking people together in a non-family
relationship, is a fact. A fact is an item of
information which you add to a person's record in the Facts
tab of the Property Box. You should normally think of a fact
as an event (like birth, death, marriage, divorce, and so on)
or an attribute (like religion or occupation). Every
fact has either one or two principals (the person being born or dying,
or the couple getting married or divorced). But other people can
also have non-principal roles, such as bridesmaids at a marriage, or the
god parents at a baptism. These non-principal participants are
called witnesses.

When it comes to deciding how to record non-family relationships, the
question to ask is - is there already a fact which allows this
relationship type to be recorded? And if not, what is the most
appropriate fact to use to record it? A few examples should help
make this clearer...

Godparent

Suppose you want to record that someone is the godparent of
someone else. There is no pre-defined god parent fact,
as such, in Family Historian. You could create one if you wanted
to, but you don't have to because godparent is a pre-defined role that a
person can have with respect to a Baptism fact (event).
So a standard way to record that a person was a godparent, is to record
the baptism event and include details of the godparents as part of the
details that you provide for that fact. This is done in the Witnesses
window, for the fact in question.

Business Partner or Employer

What about business partner or employer? Again, these are not
pre-defined fact types. But there is a standard fact type for Occupation.
When you record a person's occupation, you could also record who their
employer was, or who their business partner was. Although Occupation
is a standard fact type, it does not come with any pre-defined
roles. However, that is not an issue because you can create new
roles for any fact type and attach people to that fact with those
roles. Again, this is done in the Witnesses
window, for the fact in question. So probably the best
solution is to add Business Partner and/or Employer
as additional roles for the Occupation fact.

When you add a new role type, you will be prompted to specify a
sentence template. The sentence template will be used when
generating sentences about people with this role, in narrative
reports. Click the Help button for
guidance on how to do this.

Teacher

What about teacher? Again, this is not a pre-defined fact.
But there is a standard fact type for Education. This is
normally used to record details of a person's time at school, college or
university. This fact type does not include Teacher as a
pre-defined role; but again you can easily create this role, and record
this relationship that way. As always, this is not the only
possible approach, but it is a natural one that will work well to
achieve the desired result.

Pupil

If you want to record that one person was the pupil of another person,
the simplest approach (usually the best) would be to mentally swop them
round and record instead that the second person was the teacher of the
first person. So you add an Education fact to the first
person, and, in the Witnesses Window, record the second person as their
teacher.

Friend

Family Historian provides two pre-defined facts, either of which could
be used to record that two people are friends. The first is Friend
List. This fact can be used to record a list of a person's
friends. It is fine to use this with just one friend if
required. The other is Friendship Group. The
difference between Friend List and Friendship Group is that with the
latter, the implication is that everyone in the group is or was a friend
of everyone else in the group, whereas with Friend List, there is no
implication that the listed people even knew one another necessarily,
let alone that they were also friends. But although there is a
difference, the difference does not apply if you only want to record a
friendship between two people. Either fact could be used in that
case.

This example is of interest for a number of reasons. With all the
other examples that we have looked at so far, the relationship we were
recording was an aspect of a particular fact type (an event); but the
relationship was not central to this event. In the case of Friend
List and Friendship Group, the relationship, or
relationships, are not just an aspect of the fact type, but are central
to it. The fact was created specifically to record relationships
of this kind.

Also, in every other case that we have looked at so far, there has
always been a fact which has a principal. The principal
has been the person whose occupation we were recording, or who was being
baptised, or who had an education. In the case of a Friend
List, there is also a principal - namely the person whose friends
we are recording. But in the case of a Friendship Group,
there isn't an obvious principal at all. If you have, say, 5
people who are friends of one another, which of them do you add the fact
too? The answer is that you have to pick one of them at
random. Conceptually, this is a fact with no principal. But
in practice there has to be one, because every fact is attached to an
Individual or a Family. When you add Friendship Group to an
Individual, that person will automatically be added as a witness to
their own fact, with role of 'Friend'. You will also be prompted
to add everyone else who was part of the friendship group. These
people will also be added to the same fact, also with role of
'Friend'. Thereafter, in any narrative report about anyone in the
group, their friendship with all the other people in the group will be
included in the information about them. So if Amy Jones was
friends with Susan Dowling, Catherine Powell and Liz Smiley, a report
about Amy Jones would say "She was friends with Susan Dowling, Catherine
Powell and Liz Smiley". And, based on this same fact, with no
additional work required, a report about Susan Dowling, for example,
would say "She was friends with Amy Jones, Catherine Powell and Liz
Smiley". In practice, the information is presented in a
completely symmetrical way in all contexts, as if there were no
principal.

Adding a Friend List is similar but also subtly
different. If you want to add a list of a person's friends, you
would add the fact to that person, and you would then be prompted to add
their friends. But they themselves would not be in the list, as
they are not their own friend. If you added Susan Dowling,
Catherine Powell and Liz Smiley to a friend list for Amy Jones, a report
about Amy Jones would say "She was a friend of Susan Dowling, Catherine
Powell and Liz Smiley". Note the use of "a friend of" instead of
"friends with". If you then viewed a report about, for example,
Susan Dowling, it would say "She was a friend of Amy Jones". It
would not mention any of the others in the friend list, because they are
all Amy Jones's friends, and not Susan Dowling's friends.

We might say that Friend List is an example of a one-to-many
relationship that is, a list for one person with, potentially, many
friends. But Friendship Group is a many-to-many
relationship. Everyone in the group is friends with everyone else.

If you look at the definition of both the Friend List and
Friendship Group fact types, you will notice that they are both
classified as 'events'. We don't usually think of either a friend list
or a friendship group as constituting an event. This is just a
terminology issue. We need a term to distinguish different kinds
of fact, and 'event' serves the purpose well. Bear in mind too
that one can associate both friend lists and friendship groups with
dates and places.

Neighbour

Suppose you wanted to record information about neighbours.
That is not a pre-defined fact type, but there is a standard fact type
Residence. There is no pre-defined role of 'Neighbour' for
the Residence fact type, but you could add one. That would be a
perfectly reasonable approach. Another option would be to create a
new custom fact type, just for the neighbour relationship.
If you wanted to record a group of neighbours, viewed as all being
neighbours of one another (a mutual relationship), the natural thing
would be to model the new fact on the Friendship Group fact
type.

If you created a new fact type, when you come to use it to record that
some group of people were neighbours, you will again have to pick one
person at random to be the principal - even though conceptually, there
is really no need for any person to be the principal.

Enslaved and Enslaver

You might want to record that one person was enslaved by another.
But it often happens in practice that an entire family might be enslaved
together. The natural thing would be to create one fact that
records all of them as being enslaved together. As part of this
same fact, you might also want to record the identities of the person or
persons who enslaved them - and there might be more than one
person. Family Historian includes a built-in fact type, Enslavement,
which allows both sets of people to be recorded. This is another
example of a fact type which exists solely to record a non-family
relationship.

In the case of both Friend List and Friendship Group,
friends were all added to the relevant fact with the same role - namely,
'Friend'. With the Enslavement fact, however, there are
two possible roles: 'Enslaved Person' and 'Enslaver'. What this
example shows is that even with fact types which exist solely to record
a relationship, it is not necessary that everyone should have the same
role. It is worth bearing this example in mind if you need to
construct a custom fact like it.

For a given Enslavement fact, there may be numerous enslaved persons,
and possibly more than one enslaver. Again, there is no obvious
principal. The fact type is designed from the point-of-view of the
enslaved person in the first instance, so you should randomly pick one
of the enslaved persons to be the 'principal' whose record the fact is
attached to.

LiveD Together

How do you record that various people all lived together at some place
or time? There is a standard fact for this. In fact it has
already been mentioned: Residence. When you add this
fact type, you can optionally add as many people as you like as
witnesses with role of 'Resident' - optionally also including the
principal. That way, in reports, they will all be listed as living
together. This same fact, Residence, can also be used on its own,
with just one principal and no witnesses, to record the fact that this
person lived in a particular place at a particular time.

In Conclusion

Hopefully the above examples should help give you some ideas about the
different kinds of approach you can take to recording any kind of
relationship. To learn more, see Witnesses
and the Witnesses Window.

title: Record Same Sex Relationships
text:
More Family &
Relationship Tasks

How to Record Same Sex Relationships

Same sex spouses and partners can be added in the same way that
other-sex spouses and partners are added. When you add a spouse or
partner as a new record, Family Historian will usually assume by default
that the spouse or partner of a man is female, and that the spouse or
partner of a woman is male. If this assumption is wrong, simply change
the person's sex to the correct one.

If you link an existing person as a spouse, the selection dialog may
by default filter out males if you are looking for a spouse or partner
for a man, or filter our females if looking for a spouse or partner for
a woman. If you are looking to add a same-sex partner, change the filter
to show all Individuals. Then you will be able to select the person you
wish to link to.

title: How to Cite Sources for Relationships
text:
More Family &
Relationship Tasks

How to Cite Sources for Relationships

Most family relationships can be expressed as combinations of two basic
relationships: the parent-child relationship and the spouse
relationship. To provide source information for a spouse
relationship, you record a marriage event for them and attach source
information to that. Providing source information for a
parent-child relationship, is also straightforward. Suppose you
want to record your sources for the fact that X is son of Y (or that Y
is the parent of X - it makes no difference). To do this, create a
birth event for X, if you don't already have one. Then switch to
the Facts tab of the Property
Box (if not already there), select the birth event, open the
Witnesses Window (click on the Witnesses button
on the Fact List toolbar) and add Y as a witness to this
event, with role of father, mother or parent. Make sure that the Citation List Pane is open
in the Property Box. When you
select Y's role as witness in the Witnesses Window, you should be able
to see that the 'Sources for' field in the Citation List Pane will
update to refer to that witness role. You can then add source
citations for this witness role in the Citation List Pane in the usual
way.

Normally when you add someone as a witness to an event, they will get a
sentence in narrative reports, describing their role in the event.
But you don't want that to happen with a parent because the narrative
report will list their children anyway, and the sentence would
consequently be redundant. For this reason, by default, the
father, mother and parent roles for a birth event are marked to be
excluded from reports (you can mark any sentence to be excluded from
narrative reports by clicking on the little button to the right of the
Sentence field, and choosing Exclude Sentence on the
dropdown menu that appears).

If the relationship you wish to record a source for, is not a family
relationship, but some other kind (such as best man, bridesmaid, etc),
you will normally record these relationships by making them witnesses to
the relevant events, with the relevant roles. Again, when you
select the relevant witness role in the Witnesses Window, you can add
source citations for them in the Citation List pane of the Property Box.

To learn more about witnesses, see Property
Box Facts Tab or the Witnesses
Window.

See also Sources and Source
Templates.

title: Record that a Person is a Step-Parent
breadcrumb: Record that a Person is a Step-Parent
text:
More Family & Relationship Tasks

How to Record that a Person is a Step-Parent

A parent in a family might be a step-parent to some of the children, but not to all. For this reason, a parent
is flagged as being a step-parent effectively by flagging each child as a step child (or not) with respect to
either parent. See
How to Flag a Child as Adopted,
Illegitimate, etc for details on how to do this.

title: Record the Sources for Your Data
breadcrumb: Record the Sources for Your Data
text:
Sources & Source
Citations

How to Record the Sources for Your Data

To view already-recorded sources for any item of information, open the
relevant record in the Property Box (see How to View an Individual's Record in the Property
Box) and open the Citation
List Pane (see How
to View the Property Box's Citation List Pane).

Whenever you click on any item of data in any tab of the Property Box,
the Citation List Pane will be updated automatically to show the sources
(if any) for the item of item data in question. For example, if you
click on the Name field in the Main
tab of the Property Box, when viewing an Individual record, the Sources
For field at the top of the Citation List Pane will display 'Name', and the Citation List below it
will show all citations for the Name (or be empty if there are none). To
add a new source citation for the Name field (or whichever item of data
it is), click on the Add Citation button on
the Citation List Pane toolbar (see Citation
List Pane for more details). The new source citation will
be added to the list of citations in the Citation List Pane. Remember,
this list only show the citations for whatever is displayed in the Sources For field at the top of the
Citation List Pane (Name, in our example).

The actual details of the source citation are entered and viewed in the
Citation Window.

See also Source Records,
How to
Copy and Paste Source Citations, How to Use Automatic Source Citations and the Citation List Pane.

title: Record Where a Person Lived
text:
Facts (Events and
Attributes)

How to Record Where a Person Lived

Add one Residence fact, in the Facts
tab of the Property Box, for each of the person's residences (see
How
to Record Facts About a Person's Life). See also How to View an Individual's Record in the Property
Box.

If you want to share a Residence fact between all of the people who
lived together at the time, you can do this too. See How
to Record a Shared Event for details.

title: How to Record Additional Roles such as Bridesmaids at a Marriage
breadcrumb: Record Additional Roles, such as Bridesmaids at a Marriage
text:
Facts (Events and
Attributes)

How to Record Additional Roles such as Bridesmaids at a Marriage

When you record a marriage event, you will obviously want to record the
details of the couple getting married, and the date and place of the
marriage. But might also want to record details of other people
who participated in the marriage - such as the best man, bridesmaids,
minister, and so on. This issue applies to may events. You
might want to record that a person made a will, using a Will
event. If so, you might also want to record who the beneficiaries
of the will were, and perhaps also who the executors were. Again,
if you record that a person was baptised, you might also want to record
who the god parents were. You can do all of this and more in
Family Historian. In fact you can record details about additional
people who had a role in any event. In Family Historian
terms, anyone who had a role in an event, without being a principal (or
one of the principals), is called a witness. See Witnesses
to learn more about witnesses, and see the Witnesses Window for details about how
to record witnesses and their roles.

title: Remove Records From a Named List
breadcrumb: Remove Records From a Named List
text:
Named Lists

How to Remove Records From a Named List

To remove records from a named list, you need to be using the Records
Window. Open the Named Lists Pane by clicking on the
Named Lists Pane button
on the Records
Window toolbar. Now select the list you want to remove records
from in the top panel of the Named Lists Pane. Then, in the middle
panel of the Named Lists Pane, select each record that you want to
remove and press the Delete key. You
can use the usual techniques to select multiple items if you wish to
delete several records at a time. For example, you can click on the
first record in a range, and then press-and-hold the Shift
key while clicking on the last record in the range, to select all the
records in-between.

title: Reports
text:
How to...

Reports

This section looks at how to perform various tasks that have to do
with reports.

title: How to Select Multiple Boxes in Diagrams
text:
Diagrams and Charts

How to Select Multiple Boxes in Diagrams

It is often useful to be able to select more than one box at a time in
diagrams. Here are some alternative techniques that you can use to
do that:

Press-and-hold the Ctrl key while
clicking on several boxes in turn. This will select each box
without unselecting other boxes.

Click on the Drag Select button on the Diagram
toolbar. Then click-and-drag on the background of the dialog to
draw a stretchy box round the boxes. When you release the button
they will all be selected. If you want to select a group of
boxes that are difficult to select because they are too near other
boxes, consider using a 'Box & Branch' action with the Movement
Control Box to pull the different branches apart temporarily.

Right click on a box, and then choose Select
Branch Boxes from the dropdown menu that appears, to select
the entire branch leading off from it.

Open the Family Connection
Mapper, select a route, click on the Menu
button (the last button on the toolbar under the list of routes), and
choose Select Route Boxes from the
dropdown menu that appears to select all boxes on a specified route
(see the Help for Family
Connection Mapper for an explanation of what a 'route'
is).

Press Ctrl-A to select all boxes
in a diagram. You can also do this by clicking Select
All Boxes on the Selection &
Marks submenu of the Diagram menu.

Click Invert Selection on the
same submenu to invert the current selection. Boxes that had
previously been selected will be unselected, and boxes that had
previously been selected will be unselected.

You can 'mark' boxes by selecting them and pressing Ctrl+M
(or use the Mark/Unmarked Boxes
menu command) By default, marked boxes have a yellow
background. When you have marked numerous boxes, you can then
use the Select Marked Boxes command
to select them all. Later you can use Clear
All Marks to remove the marks.

You can use a query to select boxes. Effectively this is
two-stage operation. First use the query to mark the boxes you
want to select using Set/Clear Marks Using
Query. Then use the Select
Marked Boxes command to select them all. Again, the
relevant commands are on the Selection
& Marks submenu of the Diagram menu. By using a
query, you can select all and only boxes for Individuals that have (or
don't have) a particular record flag, or are in a particular named
list or not in a particular list, or satisfy any other condition you
can think of.

title: Set or Clear Record Flags
text:
Record Flags

How to Set or Clear Record Flags

To set a Record Flag, select the Individual
or Individuals (this works with a multiple selection) who you wish to
have the flag in question, and click on Record Flags on the Edit
menu. Then tick the record flag in question and press OK.
If the record flag you want does not already exist, click on the New button to create it.

To clear a flag for one or more Individuals, do the same thing but
untick the box for the flag in question.

Record Flags can only be set on Individual
records.

See also Named Lists.

title: How to Share Your Language Pack with Others
breadcrumb: How to Share your Language Pack with Others
text:
Languages and Language Packs

How to Share Your Language Pack with Others

The best way to share a language pack with others is to add it to the
Family Historian Plugin Store. That way, any Family Historian user
will be easily able to see it and install it. All they will have
to do is open the Language Packs
Dialog, click on the Import button,
and choose 'From Family Historian Plugin Store' on the menu
that appears They will then see a list of language packs,
including yours, and they can select it and click to import it.
