Thereafter it will be available on their system as one of the available
language packs.

If you have written a language pack, or even if you have adapted and
significantly improved somebody else's language pack, please consider
submitting it to the Family Historian plugin store. You can do so
anonymously if you wish, or you can use your real name - it's up to
you. Obviously if yours will be the first language pack for a
given language, it will be greatly valued. But even if there are
already other language packs for your language, please consider
submitting yours anyway. Different language packs may have
different styles or benefits. It's good for users to have a
choice. A user of a given language will be able to download and
install multiple language packs for the same language if they want to,
and easily compare them. So there's no problem about having more
than one language pack for the same language. It's also not a
problem if you have created your language pack by adapting someone
else's language pack - even if you previously downloaded that language
pack from the plugin store. More on this below.

You will be able to make as many changes and improvements as you want
to your language pack after you have submitted it to the Plugin Store,
so don't assume that it has to be perfect before you submit it!

For instructions on how to submit your language pack to the Plugin
Store, please see How
to Submit a Language Pack to the Plugin Store.

title: Show or Hide Pictures in Diagrams
breadcrumb: Show or Hide Pictures in Diagrams
text:
Diagrams and Charts

How to Show or Hide Pictures in Diagrams

To add pictures for individuals see How to Add a Picture for an Individual. Family
Historian can automatically display these pictures in boxes in diagrams.
To do this, open a diagram (see How
to Display a Diagram), and then open the Diagram Options Dialog (click on Options
on the Diagram menu). On the
Pictures tab, set Preference (top-left corner) to '1' to
view pictures in boxes, or set it to 0 to hide them. Press OK.

You can also 'manually' insert pictures into diagrams. To do
this when viewing a diagram in the Diagram
Window, click on the Diagram
menu, and then choose Insert into Diagram, and finally Picture.
Pictures inserted in this way are not affected by the
options you set in Diagram Options. You can position them where you
want, or resize them, and you can move them in front of, or behind,
other diagram elements. You can even 'fade' them if you wish (that is,
make them partially transparent). Right-click on any picture inserted in
this way and a dropdown menu will appear with menu commands relating to
it.

title: Show Text Only (No Boxes) in Diagrams
breadcrumb: Show Text Only (No Boxes) in Diagrams
text:
Diagrams and Charts

How to Show Text Only (No Boxes) in Diagrams

Open a diagram (see How
to Display a Diagram). Open the Diagram Options Dialog. Select the Boxes tab and
click on the Presets button at the bottom.
From the menu that appears choose 'No Box'.

To learn more about options with respect to the display of boxes (or
their absence) in diagrams, see Diagram Options Dialog: Boxes Tab.

title: Sources & Source Citations
text:
How to...

Sources and Source Citations

This section looks at how to perform various tasks that have to do
with recording the sources of your information (where your data came
from). A source citation (also
just known as a citation) is
the link that binds an item of information to the Source record that stores information about the
source.

Facts about a person are usually entered using the Property Box. Sources and source citations are
often created, and accessed, in the Property Box's Citation List Pane (see How to View the Property Box's Citation List Pane).

title: Specify a Date Range, Period, or Other Complex Date
breadcrumb: Specify a Date Range, Period, or Other Complex Date
text:
Facts (Events and
Attributes)

How to Specify a Date Range, Period or Other Complex Date

Most dates apply to events or attributes. These are recorded in the Facts tab of the Property Box (see
How
to View an Individual's Record in the Property Box). Click on the
event or attribute in question and the fields in the bottom half of the
Facts tab will show more details about that event or attribute. The Date
field is used to record date information about it. The date in question
can be a simple date, or it can be a complex date. It can be an
imprecise date or an estimated date. It can be a period (from
some date, or to some date, or from one date to
another). It can be a date range (before, after or between).
It can be a Quarter Date. It can even be a phrase such
as "2 weeks after his wife died", which can also be given an interpretation,
if you wish.

To enter complex dates - not just for events and attributes, but for
any date - double-click on the Date field, wherever you see it, or click
on the button ... next to it, to open the Date Entry
Assistant Dialog.

title: Make Someone the File Root
text:
How to...

How to Make Someone the File Root

Normally one person in every project is the designated file root.
You can change a file root at any time. You can also clear the file root
(have no file root) if you wish. However, it is usually desirable to
have a file root. The Focus Window
always shows how the focus person (person displaying at the
top of the Focus Window) is related to the file root, for example. The Records
Window normally shows how everyone is related to the file root, in
its Relationship to Root column, in the Individual
records tab.

To make someone the file root, if you are in the Focus
Window, right-click on their box and click on Make File Root
from the dropdown menu that appears.

If you are in any other window, select the Individual's record and
then, on the Edit menu, click on File Root, and
then Set as File Root.

title: How to Split Off Part of a Project
breadcrumb: Compare, Merge,  Append and Split Projects
How to Split Off Part of a Project
text:
Compare, Merge,
Append and Split Files

How to Split Off Part of a Project

To split off part of a project, you need to make a copy of it.
Then you use the Split
Tree Helper tool (see Split Tree Helper on the File
menu) to delete unwanted parts of each copy. To take a simple
case: imagine you have one project with 100 records in it, including 40
Smiths and 60 Armstrongs. Suppose you want to separate the Smiths
from the Armstrongs. First - make a backup copy of your
project, in case anything goes wrong. Then create a copy of your
project. In one copy, use the Split Tree Helper tool to delete all
the Smiths. In the other copy, use the Split Tree Helper tool to
delete all the Armstrongs.

Always be very careful when using a tool like Split Tree Helper to make
big changes to your project. The most important rule is: always
make sure that you take a full backup before you start, in case anything
goes wrong. Also, when you use the tool, think carefully about
what you're doing, and make sure that you do not get confused about
which project you are working on. Split Tree Helper is a very
powerful and useful tool, but it can do damage if not used correctly.

To create a copy of a Family Historian project, select the file you
want to copy in the Project Window,
and click on the More Tasks button, and
then choose Copy Project.

See also Split
Tree Helper: Delete Unwanted Data.

Note: If you are working on a standalone GEDCOM file, and
you want to split that, the technique is similar. You first copy
the GEDCOM file and then delete unwanted data from each file using the
Split Tree Helper tool. To copy the GEDCOM file, click on Gedcom
File Tasks on the File menu, and choose Save a
Gedcom File Copy.

title: Book Layout Compatibility for Charts
text:
Books

Book Layout Compatibility for Charts

Whereas reports will, in the main, automatically change their layout if
you change any settings which affect the available space (such as page
size, orientation, and margins), charts do not. The only exception
to that is a pedigree chart which has been inserted by adding the
"Pedigree Chart" item in the list of 'Available Items' in the Edit
Book Dialog. A pedigree chart, inserted in that way, will
automatically reformat itself to fit appropriately, using the available
space when you rebuild the book. But other charts do not do
this. For this reason, you are usually advised to decide early on,
what page size, orientation and margins you want for your book, and
avoid changing them later, unless really necessary. If you do
change them, you may have work to do, to ensure that charts look good,
and are laid out appropriately, in the resized pages.

Although, in the main, reports automatically adjust to a
changed layout, if you change the available space for a book, to make it
narrower than previously, you may sometimes want to adjust column
indents in the Page Layout tab of book settings, if some columns have
insufficient space.

With all books and all charts, you can specify a printer, page size,
page orientation (landscape or portrait) and margins. With books
you can also specify a header and footer. For a multi-page chart
to look good when inserted into a book, it is desirable that the page
layout of the chart should match the page layout of the book. That
way, the page breaks that you see in the Diagram Window will match the
page breaks that you see in the book. When a chart's layout
matches that of a given book, it is said to be book layout
compatible. What this actually means is the following:

the chart's printer is the same as the book printer

the chart's page size (e.g. Letter, A4, etc) is the same as the
book's page size

the chart's page orientation (landscape or portrait) is the same as
the book's page orientation

the chart's left and right margins match those of the book

the chart's top margin is the same size as the book's top margin and
header depth combined

the chart's bottom margin is the same size as the book's bottom
margin and footer depth combined

If any of these don't match, there is a risk that the page boundaries
of the chart may change when a saved chart is added to a book, in a way
that does not look good.

It may make sense that the various dimensions must match
for the chart and book to be compatible. But you may be wondering
- why must the printer itself also match? In fact, it isn't always
essential. But a simple change in printer, without anything else
changing, can affect how diagrams are laid out. The reason is that
family tree dimensions are affected by tree box dimensions.
And tree box dimensions are affected by text size, which is determined
by font sizes. There can be tiny differences in the way different
printers may render particular sizes of fonts. These tiny
differences can accumulate and become significant within the context of
a large diagram.

Book charts (that is charts that have been added to a book) are always
automatically book layout compatible. But ordinary diagrams and
saved charts may not be. To check whether or not a diagram or
chart is book layout compatible, click 'Book Layout Compatibility' on
the Diagram menu, and select the book in question. If the chart or
diagram is not book layout compatible with the specified book, you will
optionally be able to make it compatible.

Pedigree charts are a special case. This is because a pedigree
chart normally consists of multiple 'sub-charts' each of which is
designed to fit on a different printed page. This means that the
required page layout details must be known before the pedigree chart is
generated. For this reason, there is a special option for
specifying book layout compatibility when you generate a pedigree chart,
using the "Pedigree Chart (as Chart)" option, on the Diagram menu.
Alternatively, you can also add a new pedigree chart directly to any
book, from the list of available items in the Edit
Book Dialog. For more on this, see How
to Add a Pedigree Chart.

title: Correct Relationship Mistakes
text:
More Family &
Relationship Tasks

How to Correct Relationship Mistakes

If you have recorded an incorrect relationship between two people, you
can correct this by unlinking the two
records. If, for example, a person is incorrectly displayed as a spouse
or child in the Focus Window,
right-click on their box and click on Unlink Record from the
dropdown menu that appears.

If you are not in the Focus Window, select the record you wish to
unlink and click on Unlink From on the Edit menu,
and then choose the appropriate option.

title: Use Automatic Source Citations
text:
Sources & Source
Citations

How to Use Automatic Source Citations

When you have a source information of whatever kind (be it a
certificate, a book, a census return, an interview with someone, or
whatever) there may be quite a lot of data that you want to enter that
comes from that source. Manually citing the same source each time you
add an item of data (each name, each event, etc) could be slow and
tedious. There are better options. One option is to create a prepared
citation in the Citation Window, and
then copy that citation and paste it into all the other data items (see
How to
Copy and Paste Source Citations). Another solution however is to
use automatic source citations. See Automatic
Source Citation Pane for more details.

See also Source-Driven Data
Entry and Prepared Citation,
as well as Sources and Source
Templates and Source
Records,

title: How to Use DNA Tools
text:
Record Flags

How to Use DNA Tools

See DNA Tools.

title: How to Use Drag-and-Drop to Add Pictures
text:
Pictures and Other Media

How to Use Drag-and-Drop to Add Pictures

See the discussion of drag-and-drop in Add
Media to Project Dialog.

title: Use Queries
text:
Queries

How to Use Queries

Queries are stored sets of instructions which can be used in a number
of ways for different purposes. For example, suppose you want to look at
girls names used in different families at different times; or look at at
ages of death in certain countries in particular centuries; or find out
how many of your ancestors died of a stroke: a query is usually what you
need. Sometimes the information may be provided by smart
folders. But in many cases, these may be created using
queries too. You can use queries to generate reports, to analyse
data, to select pictures to view, to mark boxes on diagrams, to split
files ... and for many other purposes. If you use spreadsheets,you might
want to use a query to extract data to copy into a spreadsheet, so that
you can use your spreadsheet application to analyse the data and draw
graphs.

To find out about queries, and how to use them, see Query Window.

title: View All Pictures
text:
Pictures and Other Media

How to View All Picture

Click on the Media button on the main toolbar. When you
do this a dropdown menu will appear. click on View
All Media. All Media records in the current project will be
displayed in the Media Window.

title: View All Pictures for an Individual
breadcrumb: View All Pictures of an Individual
text:
Pictures and Other Media

How to View All Pictures for an Individual

Select the person's record (in whichever window happen to be in) and
click on the Media button on the main toolbar. When you do this a dropdown menu
will appear. Click on View Pictures (etc)
of .... This will open the Media Window with all pictures and
other media of the selected Individual(s). See the
Media Window for more details.

You can also view all pictures for a given Individual in the Media tab
of the Property Box.

title: View Pictures of a Select Group of People
breadcrumb: View Pictures of a Select Group of People
text:
Pictures and Other Media

How to View All Pictures of a Select Group of People

Use multiple selection to select all the individuals in one go and then
click on the Media button on the main
toolbar. When you do this a dropdown menu will appear. Click on View Pictures (etc) of Selected Individuals.
This will open the Media Window with all
pictures (and other media, if any) of the selected Individuals.

title: View an Individual's Record in the Property Box
breadcrumb: View an Individual's Record in the Property Box
text:
How to...

How to View an Individual's Record in the Property Box

Almost whatever you are doing, you can easily see a person's record in
the Property Box. If
you are viewing the Focus Window you
normally just need to select their box by clicking on it. Unless you
have a small screen, the Property Box will usually be docked on the
right side, and will automatically show the record for the person you
clicked on. If you are viewing another workspace window (e.g. the Diagram
Window, Records Window or Query
Window) double-clicking on the person's box, row or cell will
normally open the Property Box with their record details. In the Media
Window, you can even double-click on their face in a picture if
the face has been linked to their record.

Alternatively, you can select the record and click on the Property Box
button on the main
application toolbar.

title: View Named Lists
text:
Named Lists

How to View Named Lists

Named Lists can be viewed in the Named Lists Pane in the Records Window. To display the Named
Lists Pane, when viewing the Records Window, click on the Named Lists
Pane button
on the Records
Window toolbar.

The Named Lists Pane has 3 panels. The topmost panel shows all named
lists in the current project. The middle panel shows all records in the
selected named list (that is, selected in the list in the top panel).
The bottom panel is used to show, or edit, notes attached to list items
- that is, to the item selected in the middle panel.

title: How to View the Property Box's Citation List Pane
breadcrumb: View the Property Box's Citation List Pane
text:
Sources & Source
Citations

How to View the Property Box's Citation List Pane

See How
to View an Individual's Record in the Property Box for
instructions on opening the Property Box. To open the Citation List
Pane, click on the Show Sources button
in the Property Box toolbar. The Citation List Pane is a yellow pane
which normally appears either at the bottom, or on the right side, of
the Property Box, depending on whether the Property Box is docked or
floating. Click on the Show Sources button again to hide it at any
time. To learn more, see the Citation
List Pane.

title: How to Work in Different Languages
breadcrumb: How to Work in Different Languages
text:
Languages and Language Packs

How to Work in Different Languages

See About Language Packs for a
quick introduction to the varied uses of Language Packs. This
section discusses how to use Family Historian to record data in any
language other than English.

Specifying the Project Language

If the language used in a project (the project language) is
not English, it is important that you specify this in the Header record
for the project. To open the Header record, click on the Header
Record menu command, which is on the Special Records
sub-menu of the View menu. Pick the language from the
dropdown list in the Language field. This field
can be left blank if the project is English, as that is the assumed
default if no language is specified. You only have to specify the
project language once. And of course if you have multiple projects in
different languages, they don't all have to be the same language.
Each project can be in whatever language you like.

Data entry is not affected in any way by the specified project
language. It only matters when it comes to producing output, such
as reports and diagrams. Suppose, for example, that your project
data is all in French and you opt to produce a report in French.
If Family Historian doesn't realise that the data is already in French,
it will try to translate terms that do not need to be translated.
It may even mark words as untranslated when in fact they are already
correct. For example, suppose that a person's Occupation is
recorded as "Ingénieur" (French for 'engineer'), if Family Historian did
not realise that the project data was already in French, it would not
only look up this word in its translation tables (which is unnecessary),
but it might even incorrectly mark this word as untranslated.
Specifying the correct language for the project will prevent this
happening.

Data Entry Issues

Field Values and Notes

With all fields that require you to type in a value as text, enter the
value in the project language. For example, a field may be
labelled in English as "Occupation", but if you are working in French,
you should nevertheless enter the value in your project language (e.g.
"Ingénieur" if the project language is French, and the person was an
engineer). Equally, all notes should also be written in the
project language. Data entry in most languages should not present
any special problems. Family Historian uses Unicode, which allows
characters from most languages to be recorded correctly.
Press-and-hold any key to enter accent characters. If the accent
you need is not there, you can configure the window to show the accents
you need. See How to
Enter Accent Characters and Configure
Language and Accent Characters to learn more.

Names, Places and Addresses

Enter all names, places and addresses in the project language - if
there is even a question of translation, which with most names at least,
there isn't. If you are recording data in, say, French, and you
would normally use a French word for some parts of place names, you
should also do so when entering place name information (or address
information) into your project. So, for example, if you would
normally refer to Greenwich, London, England as "Greenwich, Londres,
Angleterre" (i.e. by translating 'London' and 'England', but not
'Greenwich'), then that is how you should enter that place
reference - i.e. as "Greenwich, Londres, Angleterre". Individual
names, however, should never be translated, whatever language you are
working in. So "Peter Grimes" would be entered as "Peter Grimes"
and never as (say) "Pierre Grimes".

Dates, Sex, Age, Etc

Even if your project language is not English, when you look at the
project in Family Historian, the dates will normally be shown in the
Property Box in English. Within the program, dates, sex, and other
specialist fields like that (with computer-controlled options and
values), are currently always displayed in English. They are
stored internally in a special format that Family Historian
understands. This internal format will always be the same
regardless of the language that a user might be working with.
Fields such as dates, that are stored in a special format, do not
therefore count as being 'in' any particular language - even if they are
currently displayed in English. In the future Family Historian may
provide options to allow such fields to be displayed within the program
in other languages. For this to happen there would be no need to
change the way these fields are stored internally at all.

Dates can be entered using any of the techniques outlined in How
to Enter Dates. It is important to appreciate that this does
not include using non-English month names (assuming you're
using the Gregorian calendar which almost everyone will). You
cannot currently use your own language month names for data entry.
The important thing is that Family Historian should recognise the date
information you specify. As long as it does so (and it will warn
you if it doesn't), it should be able to subsequently output the date
information in your required language correctly, as long as you have a
suitable language pack. As already stated, dates will be displayed
in English within the program. If you see a date displayed in a
non-English language like this: "3 février 1987" (i.e. with double
quotes around the date), something has gone wrong. The double
quotes around the date mean that Family Historian has interpreted the
date as a date phrase, and it has no idea what date this
refers to. A date phrase is used when you don't know the date, but
want to record whatever clues you have about it (e.g. "two weeks after
his wife died"). If you have a genuine need to use a date phrase
such as that, you should record it in the language of your content (the
project language). But that is the exception. In every other
respect, entering dates in a non-English project is exactly as if you
were entering the same dates in an English project.

When you enter sex or age information, you will be required to choose
from options that are given in English, and the value chosen will be
displayed in English. Again, do not assume that this means that
all output will also be in English. As long as Family Historian
has the information recorded correctly, it should be able to output it
correctly in any language. And the same applies to any fields
where the possible values are constrained to a fixed list, by Family
Historian.

Working in Multiple Languages Within a Project

Family Historian currently assumes that the content of any given
project is all in the same language; but there is nothing to stop you
from using a mixture of languages within a single project, if you wish
to do so - and sometimes (particularly with notes and transcripts),
there may be good reason to do that. This might mean that such
text might be marked as 'untranslated' in a report, when in fact it did
not need to be marked in that way (because the text was already in the
output language). If this ever happens, you can switch off marking
in any case, if you need to.

Specifying the Default Output Language

If you plan on working in a language other than English, you will
probably want to specify the default output language to be your project
language. To do this, open Preferences (last command on the Tools
menu). Choose the International tab. You
can choose the default language pack to use (for reports, diagrams etc)
on this tab. If there is no language pack for the language you
require, see How to Install a
Language Pack, or How to
Create a Language Pack.

See also How
to Produce Reports in Different Languages.

title: Work with Multiple Diagrams Simultaneously
text:
Diagrams and Charts

How to Work with Multiple Diagrams Simultaneously

Usually, if you already have a Diagram
Window open when you try to open a diagram, Family Historian will
open a new diagram window, for the new diagram. You can switch
between the various diagram windows (and icons) by clicking on the
appropriate icon on the Navigation bar (the bar down the left side of
the main application window).

title: How to Write Your Own Chapters or Sections
breadcrumb: Write Your Own Chapters or Sections.
text:
Books

How to Write Your Own Chapters or Sections

Typically, most if not all of the contents of a book, will be generated
by Family Historian using reports, charts and diagrams. But there
is nothing to stop you adding your own text if you wish to. To do
this, open your book in the Edit Book
Dialog, select Free Text in the
list of available items on the left side, and click the Add
Item > button to add it. Enter your text in the dialog
box that appears, and click OK.
At this point, the Item Settings
Dialog will appear. Change the Heading to something
suitable. Even if you don't want your text to have a heading in
the book itself, it will still be useful for you to have a memorable
heading for the text you are adding, so that when you see it in the list
of items in the book, you will remember what it is.

Do you want the text you have entered to be a chapter in its own
right? If so, set Format to
'Chapter'. Otherwise, pick an appropriate heading level or 'No
Heading' if you don't want your text to have a heading of its own.
Choose whether you want it to start on a new page, on the next odd Page,
or continue on the same page.

You can change the text or settings at any time by selecting the item
in the list on the right side of the Edit Book Dialog, and clicking Edit or Settings.

title: How to Modify a Source Template
breadcrumb: How to Modify a Source Template
text:
Sources and Source Templates

How to Modify a Source Template

If you haven't already done, please be sure to read Source
Template Definitions and Source Template Records, for an explanation
of the difference between a source template definition and a
Source Template record. Although frequently confused, these
are not the same and it is important to understand what they both are and
how they are used.

To explain how to modify a source template, we will work through an
imaginary example.

Worked Example: How to Modify the "Testamentary Record" Source
Template

Let us suppose that in your project you have added the source templates
from the Essentials collection (that is, you have one Source Template
record for each source template definition in the Essentials collection),
and you are now using creating Source records based on these Source
Template records. Let us say that some of your Source records use
the "Testamentary Record" source template (that is, are linked to the
"Testamentary Record" Source Template record). When you enter
details of these sources, there is a field labelled 'Reference'. Let
us suppose that you find this a useful field and make use of it. By
default, you notice that the 'Reference' field is not mentioned in
footnotes or short footnotes, in source citations in reports, that relate
to these Source records. Let us suppose that you consider that this
is important information and you want this information to be included in
footnotes and short footnotes. How do you achieve this? This
page discusses two ways of doing it. The first involves only
changing the Source Template record. The second involves changing
both the source template definition, and also the Source Template
record. The first approach is fine if you are only interested in one
particular project. The second approach is preferable if you are
likely to want to make the same change to multiple projects and even
possibly to use the your modified source template in future projects.

Method 1: Modify the Source Template record only

Locate the "Testamentary Record" Source Template record, in the Records Window. To do this, open
the Records Window and choose the
'Source Templates' tab if there is one. If there is no 'Source
Templates' tab, right-click on the background of the Records Window
and choose "Records Window Options" from the menu that appears.
Then within the 'Record Type Display Options' area of the window that
appears, set "Source Templates" to 'Always show'.

Right-click on the 'Testamentary Record' record in the list, and
choose 'Properties' from the dropdown menu that appears. The
Source Template record for "Testamentary record" is displayed in the
Property Box.

In the Main tab of the Property Box, you should see fields labelled
"Footnote Format" and "Short Footnote Format". These specify how
source citations in reports will be displayed in footnotes and short
footnotes respectively. They contain field codes for
substituting in actual values from source records. The Footnote
Format field looks like this: "Testamentary records, {Country},
{Date}, {Principal}, {Type}, {Repository}." The field code for
the 'Reference' field that you want to insert, is "{Reference}".
So modify the Footnote Format field to look like this
(say): "Testamentary records, {Country}, {Date},
{Principal}, {Type}, {Reference}, {Repository}." The exact
ordering is up to you. This is just an example.

The Short Footnote Format field looks like this: "Testamentary
records, {Country}, {Date}, {Principal}, {Type}." Change it to
(say) "Testamentary records, {Country}, {Date}, {Principal}, {Type},
{Reference}."

That's all you need to do. You do not need to make any further
changes to any other records. Now when you display a report which
references any "Testamentary Record" Source record, including Source
records that were created before you made this change, you will see that
the 'Reference' field (if not empty) is now included in footnotes and
short footnotes.

How are you supposed to know what field code to use for a field?
If the field name consists solely of alphabetic characters, you just
need to put curly brackets round the field name, and that will be the
field code. If the field name contains a space, substitute the
space with an underscore. So, for example, the field code for a
field labelled "Page Etc" would be {Page_Etc}.

To learn more about source template formats and field codes, see Source
Template Formats.

Method 2: Modify the Source Template Definition and the source
template record

Click "Source Template Definitions" on the Tools menu to open the Source Template
Definitions Dialog. The "Testamentary Record" template
definition is a standard one and, as such, cannot be modified.
So you need to copy it and modify the copy. To copy it, select
the "Testamentary record" template, select it and click the Clone
button. Give the copy an appropriate name - e.g.
"Testamentary Record (mod)". You can leave the collection
name as 'Custom'.

Select your new source template definition and click the View/Edit
button to open the Source
Template Definition Editor. You should see fields labelled
"Footnote Format" and "Short Footnote Format". These specify how
source citations in reports will be displayed in footnotes and short
footnotes respectively. They contain field codes for
substituting in actual values from source records. The Footnote
Format field looks like this: "Testamentary records, {Country},
{Date}, {Principal}, {Type}, {Repository}." The field code for
the 'Reference' field that you want to insert, is "{Reference}".
So modify the Footnote Format field to look like this
(say): "Testamentary records, {Country}, {Date},
{Principal}, {Type}, {Reference}, {Repository}." The exact
ordering is up to you. This is just an example. Notice
that although you can type the field code into the field if you want
to, you can also insert it by clicking the <<
Add button next to the field and choosing 'Reference' from
the field code submenu. It will automatically insert the correct
field code, which is handy if you are not sure what the field code
should be.

The Short Footnote Format field looks like this: "Testamentary
records, {Country}, {Date}, {Principal}, {Type}." Change it to
(say) "Testamentary records, {Country}, {Date}, {Principal}, {Type},
{Reference}." Again, you can use the <<
Add button to insert the field code if you want to.

Click the Save button to save your
changes, and then Close.

So far, we have just now changed our source template definition.
Now we want to copy the change to the appropriate Source Template record
in the current project. To do that, still within the Source Template
Definitions Dialog, make sure that our new source template
definition is selected and click on the Compare/Sync
with Source Template Record... button. This will open
the Source
Template Definition Compare Dialog. The "Source Template Definition"
field at the top should already have pre-selected the new source
template definition you just created. Click on the field below
it to select the correct Source Template record
("Testamentary Record" in this case). You should see a cross in
the "Match" column where you have made changes - i.e. indicating
that the fields are no longer identical. There is no need
to sync the Source Template name (you can if you want to), but more
importantly, you should see a cross in the rows for "Footnote Format"
and "Short Footnote Format". Select the "Footnote Format" row
first and click the View/Sync
button. Confirm that the values are what you expect, and then
click on the Perform Tasks button and
choose "Update record (right-side version) to match left-side version"
from the dropdown menu that appears. Then do the same for the
"Short Footnote Format".

Now close the various windows, and that's all you need to do. You
do not need to make any further changes to any other records. Now
when you display a report which references any "Testamentary Record"
Source record, including Source records that were created before you
made this change, you will see that the 'Reference' field (if not empty)
is now included in footnotes and short footnotes.

To learn more about source template formats and field codes, see Source
Template Formats.

title: Importing and Exporting Fact Sets
text:
Fact Sets

Importing and Exporting Fact Sets

Anyone can create a new fact set whenever they like (see Creating and Deleting Fact Sets). For example, if
you are a Muslim and you wish to record events and attributes which are
specifically relevant to Islam, you could define an appropriate set of
events and attributes and give them all the same fact set name:
‘Islamic’ (say). When you do this you would define useful narrative
templates for each fact in the set and specify other details for them.
Wouldn’t it be nice if other Muslims could make use of the same fact set
and share the results of your work? Well they can. All you have to do is
click on Import/Export on the File menu, and then choose Export >
Fact Set. You then select the appropriate fact set in the list and click
on the Export button. Your fact set is
exported as a file. You can send it to other Family Historian users you
wish to share it with; or you could upload it to a website for others to
download.

When others want to make use of your fact set, all they have to do is
get a copy of this file, by downloading it or by any other means, and
then click on Import/Export on the File menu, and choose Import >
Fact Set. They select the fact set file they wish to import and click on
the Import button. And that’s it. From now
on they can use the new fact set exactly as if they had defined it
themselves.

When you import a fact set, it is by default given a ranking of 1 -
i.e. it has precedence over all other fact sets you already have on your
computer. Fact set rankings only have any significance at all if you one
or more fact sets contain facts with the same name. See Work with Fact Sets for more on this issue. If
the fact names in your new fact set are all unique, you do not have to
worry about fact set rankings.

title: Including Maps in Diagrams and Books etc.
breadcrumb: Including Maps in Diagrams and Books etc.
text:
Map Window

Including Maps in Diagrams and Books etc.

If you wish to include a map in a diagram, book, report or website, you
must first save it - that is, the map view you want - either as a Media
record, or, at least, as a JPEG image. To do that, choose "Save Map
As..." on the Mapping menu, and pick, either
Media record or JPEG File.

To add an image to a diagram or chart, click on the Image button on the Diagram
Shape toolbar. You will be prompted to add the image from
either a file, or from a Media record. Just select the map you previously
saved. All images can be ordered front-to-back within a diagram, so
you can add a map behind family trees if required. You can also make
it partially transparent.

Another option would be to add a map as the diagram background (see the
'Background' option in Diagram
Options Dialog: General Tab).

To add a map as an image to a book, click on "Picture, Map or Figure" in
the list on the left-hand side of the Edit
Book Dialog, and click Add Item > to
add it to a book. This is a good option if you want to add the
map as an image that fits within a single page, or part of a page.
If you want to include a map as part of a multi-page photo book or
scrapbook, you could alternatively select "New Blank Chart (Scrapbook)" in
the Edit
Book Dialog, and click Add Item > to
add that to the book. You can edit this chart at any time in the
Diagram Window, and add the map (along with any other images you may want)
using the Image button
on the Diagram
Shape toolbar. Charts which are part of books are called book
charts. You will be prompted to save changes back to the book, when
you close the Diagram Window.

Of course you could use a similar approach to add a map to any ordinary
saved chart. It doesn't have to be part of a book.

If you want to incorporate a map into a website, you can add it as picture
in the Website Wizard - Step 4.

If you want to include a map in a report, you may want to add it as a
Media record, and associate the Media record with one or more events - or
Individuals, Families, etc. - that are connected to the map. If you
do so, this image can be included in reports in the normal way that any
image can be incorporated into a report (see options on the Pictures tab
of Report Options for the report in question).

title: Individual Records
text:
Record Types

Individual Records

Individual records are identified by this icon: .
They store information about individuals. You can view and edit
Individual records in the Property
Box.

The default tabs for Individual records in the Property Box are:

Main
(for Individuals)

Facts

Notes

Media

All

You can add more tabs using the Customize
Property Box dialog.

title: Search the Internet Dialog
text:
More Dialog Boxes...

Search the Internet Dialog

The Search the Internet Dialog is a floating
window that is used to find, and in some cases search, well-known
genealogy-related websites ("standard sites"). You can also add your own
bookmarked websites to this list. The dialog is accessed by clicking 'Search
the Internet' on the Internet menu, or
on the dropdown menu that appears when you click on the Web button ,
on the main application toolbar. You can also access it by
clicking the 'Search the Internet' button
on the Web Search Toolbar,
displayed at the top of the Web Search
Window.

If a site can be searched directly from this dialog, it is called a
'search now' site. With search now sites, you specify
search details at the bottom of the window and click the Search
Now button to initiate a search.

You can filter on standard sites, search now sites or
bookmarks. The list of standard sites changes over time, as new
sites emerge and old sites disappear. You can keep the list of
standard sites up-to-date by periodically clicking on the
Search Tool Updates button. Updating the list of standard
sites does not affect any bookmarks you may have added to the list.

To make the list more manageable and to make useful websites easier to
find, you can hide any standard sites that you are unlikely to want to
use, if you want to. You will be able to 'unhide' them again later
if you want to.

Tip: As previously mentioned, this dialog is a floating
window. That means that you do not have to close it before doing
tasks elsewhere in the program. If you select an Individual record
in any workspace
window, the 'Search Details' fields will automatically update to
reflect the selection. This means that you can easily use the
Search the Internet Dialog in conjunction with other windows, to
do quick Internet searches for people.

Tip: If you find useful information (text or pictures) in
websites, you may be able to use copy-and-paste or drag-and-drop
to bring the data into your Family Historian project. If there is
a significant amount of information to bring in, you may also wish to
consider using automatic
source citations.

Fields, lists and check boxes

Show
Filter on standard sites only, 'search now' sites only,
bookmarks only, or all.

Use External Browser
If ticked, any websites will be displayed in your preferred
external web browser. Otherwise, websites will be displayed
in the Web Search window.

Website
Website list. The 'Type' column will show 'Bookmark' for
bookmarks.

Search Details
These fields are available for use with 'search now' sites
only. Specify the search details before clicking the Search Now button to initiate a search.

Search Now
See previous. This button will be greyed if the currently
selected site is not a 'search now' site. Search results
will be displayed by the website itself - either in an external
web browser, or in the Web Search window, depending on whether
'Use External Browser' is ticked or not (see above).

Go to Site
Click this button to view the selected site. The site will
be displayed in an external web browser, or in the Web Search
window, depending on whether 'Use External Browser' is ticked or
not (see above).

More >>

<< Less
Display or hide additional buttons or check boxes down the right
side.

New
Opens the Add/Edit Bookmark
Dialog to create a new bookmark. You can also create
bookmarks on the Web Search Window
by clicking the 'Bookmark' button (a star) on the Web
Search Toolbar.

Edit
Opens the Add/Edit Bookmark
Dialog to edit a bookmark. This button will be greyed
unless a bookmark is selected.

Delete
Allows deletion of one or more bookmarks. If the selection
includes one or more standard sites you will be warned that they
these will be hidden, and not deleted.

Show
Click this button to unhide selected bookmarks or standard sites
that you previously had hidden. You will need to previously
have ticked "Show Hidden" to be able to select hidden bookmarks or
standard sites.

Hide
Click this button to hide selected bookmarks or standard sites.

Check for Search Tool Updates
Updates the list of standard sites from the latest list of such
sites, maintained by Calico Pie. An internet connection will
be required. This has no effect on bookmarks.

Show Hidden
When ticked, previously hidden bookmarks or standard sites will
be displayed.

title: Introduction to Merging - the Three Types
breadcrumb: Introduction to Merging - the Three Types
text:
Merge/Compare Dialog

Introduction to Merging - the Three Types

Basic Record Merging

This is the simplest and most common kind of merging. It consists of
merging two records into one. Suppose, for example, you discover that
you have two Individual records for what is, in reality, the same
person. You select both records and merge them. When you do this, Family
Historian will take care of managing any links from or to either record.
If person A was listed as a child in family F
for example, and person B was listed as a spouse in
family G, after the merge there will only be one
record where there had been two, and the resulting person will be listed
as a child in family F and as a spouse in family G.

You can merge records of any type with Basic Record Merging. For
example, it sometimes happens that you find you have two source records
for a single source, and you wish to merge them into one. You can use
Basic Record Merging for this.

For more information about Basic Record Merging, see Basic Record Merging and Branch Merging.

Branch Merging

Imagine that you have a record for one �Abe Smith� and another record
for an �Abraham Smith�, and you discover that these two are in fact the
same person. You could, of course, use Basic Record Merging to merge
their records into one. But suppose, that Abe Smith and Abraham Smith
are not the only two duplicates. You might discover that you also have
duplicate records for their mothers, fathers, siblings, children,
grandparents, cousins, and so on. It is surprisingly easy for these
situations to arise. What should you do about it?

One option would be to take each pair of duplicate records in turn and
merge them. That can be done. It is not necessarily the best or the
easiest way of doing it, but it is one way of solving the problem. You
should remember if you do this, that although most details about
Individuals are stored in Individual records, details about family
relationships (who is whose parent, spouse, child etc) are stored in
Family records. So you would need to locate all of the duplicate
Individual records and merge them. And you would also need to locate all
the duplicate Family records and merge these too.

An easier alternative to merging the records one at a time is to use
the Merge/Compare Dialog to help you locate a cluster of duplicated
records and merge them all (or as many as you wish) in one go. This is
called �Branch Merging�. Branch Merging is essentially the same as Basic
Record Merging except that instead of merging just one pair of
duplicated records, you can merge two entire branches of duplicated
relatives. Branch Merging can only be used to merge Individual and
Family records.

For more information about Branch Merging, see Basic Record Merging and Branch Merging .

File Merging

File Merging is used where you have an entire file (or project) that
you want to merge into your current file (or project). If merging
two projects, it is really the GEDCOM files
that are merged; but you can also merge 'standalone' GEDCOM files. If
you only want to compare another file with the current file the
procedure is the same except that you simply cancel at the end, instead
of pressing the Merge button.

There are two standard scenarios:

the file you are merging in, or comparing, was created
independently of the current project

the file you are merging in, or comparing, was not created
independently of the current project

It often happens that you discover that another person has been doing
research that overlaps with yours and you want to compare their research
with yours, and possibly merge it in. That would be scenario (1).

It might also happen that you give a copy of your work to someone else
to review and make corrections and additions. The file you are
comparing/merging could be your own file, with these corrections and
additions. That would be scenario (2). A variant on scenario (2) would
be where two or more people collaborate to do research together and
periodically merge the results of their work.

In both scenarios, you can compare the entire files and see exactly
how they differ and where. In File Merging you can also treat the file
being merged in as a source and create a record for it. New, updated or
confirmed data can be given source citations which link it to this
source record.

For more information about File Merging, see File Merging and Comparing.

title: Introduction to Source-Driven Data Entry
text:
Source-Driven Data Entry

Introduction to Source-Driven Data Entry

Why Source-Driven Data Entry?

When you learn how to use Family Historian, you are likely to start by
learning how to perform standard tasks like adding a person, adding
relatives of that person, adding facts about these people, adding
pictures of people and events, and hopefully also learning how to add
source citations. And that's fine. But those person-directed
tasks don't map very elegantly onto what genealogists actually spend
most of their time doing - which is all about inputting information that
comes from a source of some kind, that they have somehow
acquired by whatever means (often from the Internet these days, but not
necessarily).

Let's take an example. Suppose you download an image of a census
record that has some interesting stuff in it. Here are some of the
things you might want to do with it:

Create new records for family members (and maybe others too) that
you don't already have records for, and record their relationships

Record facts about those people that you have gleaned from the
census record

Create a Source record to represent the census entry and record all
the details about where the census entry came from (maybe both online,
and originally).

Maybe attach the image of the census record to that Source record.

Maybe record a transcription of the census entry (in a Text
from Source field), so that it can be searched-for, using
search tools, and browsed, and so that you have documented your
interpretation of the (potentially hard-to-read) handwriting in the
census. Maybe you even want to take advantage of Family
Historian's ability to embed links into notes, to add links to the
records for the people mentioned in the transcript. That will
make it easier later to move around your own project data later when
you come back and browse the transcripts, and remove possible
ambiguities of reference (your interpretation of who these people
are).

Link all the facts you added in step 2, to your new source record,
and maybe even link previously existing facts to the new Source record
too (because it confirms them), and add appropriate details to the
links themselves, as needed (we call these links source citations,
because it is these links that will be used by Family Historian to
ensure that sources get cited appropriately in reports and
books).

And that's just one source.

Now of course you may have no wish to do all of that. Maybe you
have no wish to do most of that. But if you've done a
good job of learning how to use Family Historian, you should be in a
position to do all of it, if you want to - but probably not that quickly
and not that easily. Doing it all involves moving around between
different parts of the program. It's easy to miss things. There
are decisions to be made along the way and it's hard to always be
consistent (consistency of approach is a good thing in any kind of
research). So for those who want to do this kind of stuff, what is
needed is...

A New Workflow

This is the new workflow (introduced in version 7), facilitated by new
tools to make it all possible:

You get a new source (acquire a new document say).

You open Family Historian and click the Source button . You choose one of
the first 3 options on the menu (more on these later). If it's
one of the first two, a new Source record is created. Either
way, the Citation Window opens.

You fill in a few details in the Citation
Window. If you're using the "Source from Template" option,
hopefully the fields will closely match the information in the source
in front of you, so there will be little need for decisions to be made
about how to record the data (no more debates about what to put in the
'Author' field when your source is a census, say; which is the kind of
thing you have to think about if you use generic sources).

You now have 3 options (all buttons at the bottom of the Citation
Window at this point):

Ideally you click on the Data Entry
Assistant button and a Data Entry Assistant tool (more on
these later) is launched which does most of tasks 1-6 above for you,
with minimal effort on your part, and producing better and more
professional-looking results than you could realistically have hoped
to achieve doing it all yourself 'by hand'.

If there is no Data Entry Assistant for the particular source you
have, you're going to have to do more of the work yourself.
But it's still not that hard. Because the chances are that
most of the information you're going to want to input from the
source, should all get the same source citation. You can set
up all the details and click the Enable
Automatic button. That enables automatic
source citations. You can now quickly add all the people
and facts, and source citations will be automatically added, saving
a lot of fiddling about. If you need to tweak details of
particular source citations, that's no problem. Don't forget
to disable automatic source citations when you've finished working
on your source. But you're not likely to forget because the
automatic source citation pane will be visible at the top of the
screen, with a big 'Enabled' button, when automatic source citations
are enabled.

The third option can be combined as-needed with the second (or
with the first, for that matter). Suppose your source tells
you some things that you already knew and have already
recorded. You may not have any new facts to add, but you may
still want to add a source citation for the facts you have already
recorded, because the source is additional confirmation that those
facts are correct. So you click Copy
Citation. This copies the source citation to the
source clipboard. Now select each of the facts that it applies
to, in turn, in the Property Box and
click the Paste Citation button
on the Citation List
pane toolbar. That will add the source citation to those
facts. Of course you could use this approach with new facts too, if
you wanted to.

You may still have a few other tasks that have not been done. For
example, you might want to add an image for the source (4. in the list
above). But that's easy too. Just drag-and-drop the image
onto the media tab of the Citation Window.
There's even a Data Entry Assistant that will help with naming of source
media files, to keep them all consistent.

In summary, the new workflow, and the new tools, are designed to do
the following...

Keep data entry to a minimum, and reduce or eliminate duplication of
effort (entering the same information in more than one place).

Automate everything that can be automated so you don't spend time
doing mundane tasks that can be done for you.

Make it as easy as possible to do these things while producing high
quality, consistent and professional-looking results - better results
than realistically you would be likely to achieve if you did it all
'by hand'.

Try to ensure that the tasks you have to complete within the
software relate closely to the 'real-world' documents in front of you,
so that the process of data entry feels as natural and intuitive as
possible.

To learn more, see Source-Driven
Data Entry and Sources
and Source Templates.

title: Item Groups
text:
Diagram Options Dialog:
Text Tab

Item Groups

Do I Need to Know What Item Groups Are?

You do not usually need to understand about Item Groups as Family
Historian will create them for you automatically when you add items from
the Available Items list into the Used Items list in the Edit Text Scheme Dialog. However, some
understanding of what groups are, and how they are used, may be helpful
if you move parts of a text scheme around using the Move Up
and Down arrows. You can
move items within a group, but moving an item out of a group, or
changing the first line of a group, will not usually have desirable
results (and it’s easy to do). Also, if you want to change the font used
within a group, it is helpful to have some understanding of what groups
are, and what they’re for.

What Are Item Groups?

It is easy to recognize a group in the listing of items used in a text
scheme (see Edit
Text Scheme Dialog). All the lines items in the group (except the
first) have a bent arrow pointing back up to the previous line, like
this:

Name

Name (a.k.a.)

Occupation

Occupation, age at

Occupation Notes

Death

Death Cause

Death Notes

In this example, there are 2 groups. The first group consists of the
Occupation line and the 2 lines that follow it. The second group
consists of the Death line and the 2 lines that follow it.

A group is formed when you tick the Group with previous line box in a
Text Scheme Item (in the Edit
Text Scheme Item Dialog). That item then forms a group with the
previous item (and in the listing it has the bent arrow to the left of
its entry). If the previous item also has Group with previous line
ticked, the group includes the item before that too, and so on until you
reach an item where this box has not been ticked. This item - that is,
the first item in the group - sets conditions for the group as a whole.
If the conditions for the first line of a group are not met, the other
items within the group will not be output, even if their conditions are
met.

Repeating Item Groups

The main reason for forming a sequence of items into a group is if you
wish them to repeat for all instances of the data in question.

An item in a text template typically corresponds, to a single type of
data. For example, an item might show a person’s occupation. Sometimes,
as in the example above, you may want several items relating to a single
event or attribute, however. For example, you might have one line for a
person’s occupation, and another line again for the person’s age at the
time of the occupation, and perhaps another line (another item) for any
notes about that occupation. So the part of a box that relates to a
person’s occupation might look like this:

Occ: Farm Labourer in Blackburn 1912-1914

Age 17

Unskilled

But what if a person had multiple occupations? Do you need multiple
items - one for each possible occupation? The answer is that you don’t.
You can specify a single item to repeat, so that it shows all instances
of a given item of data. And you do not need a group to do this. But
what do you do if you have multiple items which all relate the same
thing, such as a person’s occupation and you want them all to repeat?
The answer is that you form them all into a group. That way, the entire
group can repeat. In the example below, the person has 3 occupations:

Occ: Farm Labourer in Blackburn 1912-1914

Age 17

Unskilled

Occ: Shop-assistant in Blackburn 1918-1927

Age 22

Boots Chemist.

Occ: Store Manager in Birmingham 1927-1945

Age 31

Army & Navy Stores

As previously stated, the first line in a group sets conditions for
the group as a whole. A group does not necessarily have to loop - that
is, repeat for all instances of the data item in question. Whether or
not it does loop is determined by the template for the first group item
(see Understanding Text Templates). Although the first line of a group
does not have to be a standard data item, the group will not repeat for
all instances if it doesn’t; so it is usually better to ensure that it
is. It is not recommended that you start a group with a font change, for
example.

Font Changes Within Item Groups

If you wish, you can change the font within a group. A common
requirement is to use one font for the first line of an item group, and
use a different font, or font style, for all the other lines, to make
them stand out. To do this you must add font changes into the group,
like this:

Occupation

<font=Arial, 8 pt,
italic; text colour is Teal>

Occupation, age at

Occupation, Notes

<font=Arial, 8 pt;
text colour is Black>

This could be used to give this kind of effect:

Occ: Farm Labourer in Blackburn 1912-1914

Age 17

Unskilled

Occ: Shop-assistant in Blackburn 1918-1927

Age 22

Boots Chemist.

Occ: Store Manager in Birmingham 1927-1945

Age 31

Army & Navy Stores

You need to use the Move Up/Down arrows to position the font change
items correctly. Also, you need to double-click on each, and tick its Group with previous line box to make it
part of the group.

Note that the group contains 2 font changes: one to switch the font to
teal (a shade of green) and italics; and another to reset it back to
black, with no italics. If you don’t include the second font change item
as part of the group, the change of font will persist from then on, and
the result would look like this:

Occ: Farm Labourer in Blackburn 1912-1914

Age 17

Unskilled

Occ: Shop-assistant in Blackburn 1918-1927

Age 22

Boots Chemist.

Occ: Store Manager in Birmingham 1927-1945

Age 31

Army & Navy Stores

which is presumably not what you want.

When you move a group, using the Move Up/Down arrows in the Used
Items List in the Edit
Text Scheme Dialog, make sure that you move all parts of the group
at the same time. To select them all, click on the first item, then
press-and-hold the Ctrl key while clicking on other items to select them
all. It is very easy, when using the Move Up/Down buttons to break up a
group. But you are unlikely to get sensible results if you do.

title: Item Settings Dialog
text:
Book Window

Item Settings Dialog

The Item Settings Dialog is displayed whenever an item is selected and
the Settings button clicked in the Edit
Book Dialog. It can have various tabs or just one.
The actual tabs vary depending on the item type. But all items
always have at least one tab: the Item
tab.

The dialog is similar to the Report
Options Dialog for reports displayed in the Report Window - and
indeed many of the tabs will be the same as the tabs used in that
dialog, when a report item's settings are viewed. However, even in
that case there are some differences. Whereas with a report in the
Report Window, all settings are accessible in the Report
Options Dialog, this is not the case with the Item Settings
Dialog. In the latter case, any settings which apply to the entire
book (e.g. headers, footers, margins, and so on) will be set in the Book Settings Dialog, and not in
the Item Settings Dialog.

title: Keyboard and Mouse Shortcuts
text:
Keyboard and Mouse Shortcuts

Keyboard Shortcuts

Ctrl+A
Select all. For example, select all text when editing a
note in a separate window, or select all rows in a list.

Ctrl+C
Copy selected item(s).

Ctrl+D
In Records Window, and similar contexts, move keyboard focus to
the Search field at the top of the Window.

Ctrl+Shift+D
Same as Ctrl+D, except that it also sorts the list in
alphabetical order.

Ctrl+F
Open Find Record dialog.

Ctrl+G
Go to record.

Ctrl+H

Finds a particular record (selected from a record list) in the
current diagram. Can be used even if the Diagram Window is not
active, in which case it will find the chosen record in the
last-visited diagram. Uses the currently selected record, if
any, as default selection in the record list.

Ctrl+I

Insert. If used in the Facts tab of the Property Box it
will act like a click on the Add Fact
button. If used in the Note tab it will act like a click
on the Add Note button. If
used in the Media tab, it will act like a click on the Add
Media button. If used in the Citation List Pane
of the Property Box, it will act like a click on the Add
Citation button.

Ctrl+K
Zoom Out (Diagram Window).

Ctrl+L
Zoom In (Diagram Window).

Ctrl+M
Set/clear Mark (Diagram Window).

Ctrl+O
Open file

Ctrl+P
Print

Ctrl+S
Save changes to file.

Ctrl+U
Switches focus alternately between the Source pane of the
Property Box, and the main part of the Property Box. Has no effect
if the Source Pane is not open.

Ctrl+V
Paste

Ctrl+X
Cut selected item (to clipboard)

Num+
Zoom In (+ on numeric keyboard)

Num-
Zoom Out (- on numeric keyboard)

Shift+Del
Cut selected item (to clipboard)

F1
Help (for current context)

F3
Find Next (Diagram Window)

F4
Add record to current named list (Records Window)

Alt+F4
Close application

Ctrl+F4
Close the current workspace window (you cannot close the Focus
Window however)

F5
Process and validate current field contents without exiting
field (Property Box).

F6
Next pane (e.g. in Records
Window). When used in a record list within a record
selection dialog, it will move the focus to the filter fields
above the list, or back (if there are filter fields above the
list).

Shift+F6
Previous pane (e.g. in Records Window)

Ctrl+F6
Switch to next workspace window.

Ctrl+Shift+F6
Switch to previous workspace window.

F7
Move selected item up one (e.g. use this to re-order siblings in
diagram, or to re-order fields in Records Window)

F8
Move selected item down one

F9
Re-order events in the selected record by date

F10
Activate the main menu (for selection using the arrow keys)

Enter
Expand/close the branch for the current box (Diagram Window) or
field (Records Window). When used within a single record
selection dialog, if the focus is on the record list, it will act
like a click on the 'OK' button. That is, if there is a
selection, it will close the dialog as if 'OK' had been
pressed. When used within a multiple record selection dialog
it behaves a little differently. If the focus is on the left
side record list, it will act the selection to the right side
list.

Alt+Enter
Open Property Box for selected record

Del
Delete the selected item

Spacebar

Activates link if a link is selected. In the Focus Window, it
sets the focus to the currently selected person. In the Diagram
Window it temporarily enable ‘grabber mode’ so that you can
click-and-drag on a diagram to scroll around within it. In the
Records Window (and elsewhere) it selects or unselects the
current item.

Ctrl+Spacebar
If pressed when in an editable field in the Property Box, opens
a Helper dialog box, if there is one. For example, pressing
Ctrl+Spacebar in a date field opens the Date Helper dialog. In an
age field, it opens the Age helper dialog. In a place field,
it opens the Place helper dialog. In an Occupation field, it
opens the Occupation helper dialog. And so on.

If you press Ctrl+Spacebar in a note field in the Property Box, it
opens the note in the Note Window.

Arrow Keys
Move between boxes (in the Focus Window or in diagrams) or
fields and branches (Records Window, and ‘All’ tab of Property
Box).

Ctrl+Left Arrow
Go Back

Ctrl+Right Arrow
Go Forward

Tab
Move to next editable field e.g. in dialog boxes or Records
Window (if no records are expanded, there will be no editable
fields to tab to). In the Property Box the tab key will also cause
the entered or modified field contents to be processed and
validated (i.e. you will be warned of erroneous, or possibly
erroneous data).

Shift+Tab
Move to previous editable field.

Ctrl+Tab
Switch to next workspace window (or next tab in a tabbed dialog,
such as the Focus Window or the Property Box).

Ctrl+Shift+Tab
Switch to previous workspace window (or previous tab in a tabbed
dialog, such as the Focus Window or Property Box).

Esc
Cancel current dialog box (usually) or current mode (e.g. in
diagram).

Home
Jumps to the root of the Focus Window (toggles positions) or to
start of row (Query Window result set), or jump to first record
(Records Window).

Alt+Home
Display the Root Person in the Focus Window.

Ctrl+Home
Jump to first row in a Query Window result set.

End
Jump to end of row (Query Window result set) or jump to last
record (Records Window).

Ctrl+End
Jump to last row (Query Window result set).

Shift+Home
Select all cells from the current cell to the start of the row
(Query Window result set).

Shift+End
Select all cells from the current cell to the end of the row
(Query Window result set).

Ctrl+Shift+Home
In the Query Window result set, this can be used to select all
cells from the current cell to the first row (same column).
In a list, such as a record list, this can also be used in lists
to select all rows from the current row to the first row in the
list.

Ctrl+Shift+End
In the Query Window result set, this can be used to select all
cells from the current cell to the last row (same column).
In a list, such as a record list, this can also be used in lists
to select all rows from the current row to the last row in the
list.

Page Up
Scroll up vertically one page. This can be used in the
Diagram Window, Records Window, or Query Window result set.

Page Down
Scroll down vertically one page. This can be used in the
Diagram Window, Records Window, or Query Window result set.

Mouse Shortcuts

Double-Click
If on a record, usually opens the Property Box (for the Record
Window, this is configurable in the Record Window Options Dialog).

Shift+Click
Select all items between the currently selected item, and the
item clicked on. Useful technique to select multiple items
quickly. Typically this works on lists - e.g. as in the Records
Window.

Ctrl+Click
Select/unselect the clicked on item, without unselecting other
items. Useful technique when selecting multiple objects. Works in
the Records Window. Also works on boxes in the Diagram Window.

Click-and-Drag
If you click-and-drag on a box in the Diagram Window, this
usually will allow you to add relatives to the person clicked on.
If you click on the background of a window, you can create a
stretchy box to ‘lasso’ items that fall within the box. This works
in both the Records Window and the Diagram Window.

Right Click
Usually brings up a ‘context’ menu. This is a menu which shows a
list of things that you can do with the thing you clicked on.

Mouse Wheel
When used over the central area of the Records Window or Book
Window, the mouse wheel scrolls the report or book
vertically. With the Diagram Window and Map Window it zooms
in or out. With the Diagram Window, you can alternatively
scroll vertically if you press the Ctrl Key while turning the
mouse wheel. With the Map Window, the mouse wheel is
sensitive to what you're pointing at when you scroll.
Whatever you're pointing at when you scroll will remain under the
mouse pointer after the scroll.

When used in the Report Window or the Book Window, the wheel does
different things depending on where the mouse pointer is
positioned. If the pointer is over the a page of the report or
book, you will scroll up and down within the report or book. If
the mouse is over the two small arrow buttons to the right of the
Page field, it will scroll forwards and backwards through the
report or book, moving always to the start of each page.

Other Shortcut Behaviours

Typing any letter key in a records list will cause selection to move
forward to the first record with name matching that letter. This also
works in many other lists.

title: Language Pack Header Dialog
text:
Language Packs Dialog

Language Pack Header Dialog

The Language Pack Header Dialog is used to view and edit the header
information for a language pack.

Fields

Language
The language of the language pack

Name
The English name of the language. This is usually
determined by the Language selection, but you can optionally
modify it if you want to..

Internal Name
Also called 'Endonym', this is the language name as it would be
in the language itself. For example, the internal name, or
endonym, for French is Français. As with the Name field
above, this is usually determined by the Language selection, but
you can modify it if you want to.

3-Letter Code
This is the 3-letter ISO code for the language. More
specifically it is the 639-2/T code. You do not have to
enter this code - indeed you can't. The code is determined
by your selection in the Language field above.

ISO stands for 'International Organization for Standardization'.

Variant
Every language pack has a unique "Language Id", which is used to
identify it. Typically this will consist simply of the
3-letter code for the language. So, for example, you might
have a language pack for french, with language id "FRA". If
you want to have more than one language pack for french, you
must add a value to the Variant field to allow the variant to be
distinguished. A single letter or number would
suffice. If a variant is supplied, the language id
will consist of the 3-letter code followed by the variant value,
with a space separating the two parts. So, for example, if
the Variant value for a second french language pack was '2', the
language id would be 'FRA 2'.

If you are creating a language pack which is used for translation
from one language into another, where neither language is English,
you are recommended to use the Variant field to indicate
this. For example, if you want to create a language pack for
translating from Polish to Russian, the 3-letter code will be
'RUS' because you are translating into Russian. But you
should set the Variant to "[project=POL]" (or similar) to indicate
that the language pack expects the project language to be Polish.

Author*
Name of the language pack author or authors. This value is
read-only in this context. If you wish to change it, you
need to modify the "@Author:" field in the plugin header. If
this is your language pack, you can put your own name in the
Author field. If you plan to submit the plan to the Family
Historian plugin store, you can use a pseudonym if you wish to be
anonymous.

Version*
Version number. This value is read-only in this context.
If you wish to change it, you need to modify the "@Version:" field
in the plugin header.

Contributors*
Names of language pack contributors. This value is
read-only in this context. If you wish to change it, you
need to modify the "@Contributors:" field in the plugin header.

Description
Describes what the language pack does. If this is your
language pack, it is a good idea to use this field to describe the
purpose of the language pack. For example, if it supports
both same-language rendering (e.g. French-to-French), you can say
this. If it also supports other-language translation (e.g.
English-to-French) you can mention this too.

Licence*
If supplied, is displayed read-only below the 'Description'
field. To add or change the licence text you need to modify the
"@Licence:" field in the plugin header. If you wish to submit a
language pack to the Family Historian plugin store, please be sure
to set the @Licence:" field in the plugin header to look like this
(except that you should set the year to the current year):

@Licence: This language pack is
copyright (c) 2020 author and contributors,

and is licensed under the MIT License which is hereby
incorporated by reference

(see
https://pluginstore.family-historian.co.uk/fh-plugin-licence)

All fields marked with an asterisk are taken the from the language
pack plugin header. For example, the language pack version
number is stored in the plugin header (click the Plugin
button in the Language Packs
Dialog to view the plugin header).

title: Language Packs Dialog
text:
More Dialog Boxes...

Language Packs Dialog

Language Packs Dialog

The Language Packs Dialog displays a list of installed language
packs. The first column shows the name of the language in English,
followed by the language id in brackets. This is a
unique identifier, made of up 3 characters or more. The first 3
characters of a language id are the standard ISO code for the language.
The Internal Name of a language pack is the name of the
language as it would be in that language. This is sometimes also
called an endonym.

To learn more about language packs, see Language
and Language Packs.

Buttons

New
Create a new language pack in two steps. See New
Language Pack - Step 1 and New
Language Pack - Step 2.

Edit
Opens the Language Pack
Translations Dialog to allow translations to be added,
edited and deleted

Clone
Makes an copy of the selected language pack. A variant
value will be set to ensure that the copy has a unique language
id, but this can be changed if required (see Header below).

Plugin
Caution: This is an
advanced feature. Proceed with care! You should
always take a backup of the current contents of the plugin (e.g.
use copy-and-paste from the plugin editor to save the contents
into a text file) before making any changes to a plugin.
Incorrect changes could easily stop the language pack from
working. If in doubt, seek advice (e.g. from the Family
Historian Users group at www.fhug.org.uk)
before proceeding.

Every language pack has a plugin which controls the
translations. Click the Plugin
button to view the plugin in the Plugin Editor, where it can be
edited, tested and debugged. There is extensive help and
advice on writing plugins, including language pack plugins, in the
Family Historian Plugin Help. To access the Family Historian
Plugin Help, open the Plugins Dialog
(click 'Plugins' on the Tools menu), click the More
>> button, and then click the How
to Write Plugins button.

Header
Opens the Language Pack
Header Dialog to allow the language pack header to be viewed
and edited.

Delete
Delete the selected language pack. Caution: this action
cannot be undone.

Import
Import a language pack from the Family Historian plugin store,
or from a language pack file (you will be offered the
choice). Language pack files have a '.fhlang' suffix.

Export

Export a language pack to a language pack file. Language
pack files have a '.fhlang' suffix.

title: Language Pack Translation Tables Dialog
text:
Language Packs Dialog

Language Pack Translation Tables Dialog

The Language Pack Translation Tables Dialog is used to view and edit
translation tables for a given language pack. Translations are
case-sensitive. So, for example, "Book" needs a separate
translation from "book". Translations are displayed initially in a
fixed, unsorted order (i.e. not in alphabetical order). This is so
that related translations, which may not be close alphabetically, can be
grouped together. You can sort them alphabetically by clicking on
a column header. To sort them in reverse order of alphabet,
press-and-hold the Alt key while clicking on a column header. To
revert to unsorted order, click on the 'Unsorted' tick box on the
right-hand side.

Fields and Buttons

Translation Table
There are 3 tables: Attribute Values, Places
and Miscellaneous. The Places table is used for
