Book Window, it will always display exactly as it will appear when
printed. For this reason, if you wish the background of the
diagram to appear, you must tick the option Print
background in the Print tab of Diagram
Options. Unless this option is ticked, the background of the
diagram will not appear. You can choose the kind of background you
want (e.g. a picture, or stripes perhaps) by clicking on the Background
field in the General tab
of Diagram Options. But this option will appear to have no effect
if Print Background is not also
ticked on the Print tab.
You can access Diagram Options by clicking on the Options
button, or by right-clicking on the diagram and selecting Diagram
Options from the dropdown menu that appears.

Fields

Scale

You can either enter a value directly into the Scale field, or
click-and-drag on the slider - whichever is most convenient.
The default value (unscaled) is 100% - which is also the topmost
position on the slider. If, unusually, you want to alter a
diagram to make it bigger rather than smaller, simply type the
value you want directly into the Scale box (e.g. 150).

Mouse Action

Choose 'Select Page' if you want to be able to select a page by
clicking on it. If you choose 'Position on Page', you can
adjust the position of the diagram on the printed page, by
clicking-and-dragging anywhere on the diagram. As you move
the mouse, the diagram will move, relative to the grid of pages.

Avoid Page Boundaries
Tick this option if you want boxes of diagram trees (if the
chart contains diagram trees) to be moved so that they do not
overlap page boundaries. If 'Position on Page' is the chosen
mouse action and you click-and-drag on the diagram to move it, the
diagram will appear to move in a somewhat jerky and disjointed
way, if 'Avoid Page Boundaries' is also ticked. This is
normal, and a consequence of the requirement to avoid boxes
overlapping page boundaries.

Select All Pages

When ticked all pages of the chart will automatically be
included in the book.

Clear All

Unselects all pages. At least one page must be selected
when you press OK.

Options

Opens the Diagram Options
Dialog, which gives access to numerous options for the
diagram.

title: Select Timeline Facts Dialog
text:
Property Box: Facts Tab

Select Timeline Facts Dialog

You can view events and attributes (facts) in the
life of an Individual, in the Facts tab of the Property Box, when
viewing their record. Often, you will get a much better sense of
the most important events in the life of a person, if you see not only
their own events and attributes, but also key events in the lives of
their close relatives. To enable the display of these timeline
facts, as they are called, click on the Show Timeline
Facts button
on the Facts tab toolbar. When timeline facts are displayed, they
are shown with a light grey background, so that they can easily be
visually distinguished from other facts.

The Select
Timeline Facts Dialog allows you to specify which facts you
wish to see when the display of timeline facts is enabled. To open
it, click on the menu button
on the Facts tab toolbar, and select Timeline Facts... from the dropdown
menu.

Column Headings

Birth+
For each relative of the chosen type
(parent, sibling, spouse, child or grandchild), a recorded birth,
baptism or christening event will be displayed. If a person
has more than one of these recorded, only the first will be
displayed. Also, if a person has any recorded adoption
events, these will be displayed.

Marriage
For each relative of the chosen type, all marriage events will
be displayed.

Divorce
For each relative of the chosen type, all
divorce events will be displayed.

Death+
For each relative of the chosen type, a recorded death, burial
or cremation event will be displayed. If a person has more
than one of these recorded, only the first will be displayed.

Fields & Buttons

Parents
Required values for parents (a person may have more than one
set).

Siblings
Required values for all siblings - including half-siblings.

Spouses
Required values for all spouses.

Children
Required values for all children.

Grandchildren
Required values for all grandchildren.

Select All
Tick all boxes.

Cut Off Date
If the Individual's date of death is not known, it will be
estimated.

Show Surnames
Display surnames for relatives.

Clear All
Untick all boxes.

Restore Defaults
Reset options to installation defaults.

title: Sentence Template Codes
text:
Fact Types Dialog Sentence Template Codes Sentence template codes are mainly used to define sentences for narrative reports. There are two kinds of sentences: Principal sentences and Witness sentences. Principal sentences define a fact from the point-of-view of the principal (or from the point of view of one of them if there are two). Witness sentences describe a fact from the point-of-view of a witness. A Witness can be defined more than once, with more than one role, for any given fact - in which case they will get a Witness sentence for each role, in any narrative report about the Witness. A Principal isn't usually defined as a Witness in their own fact, but they can be if required. Even if they are, however, they will nevertheless only get one sentence for the fact, in any narrative report about the Principal - and this will be a Principal sentence. Most sentence template codes can be used in either Principal sentences or Witness sentences - but not all. Where a code can only be used in one context, this will be mentioned in the code description. To learn more about sentences (and witnesses, principals and roles), see the help for the Witnesses Window, which also explains how to override sentences. This can be a good way of testing your sentence templates to make sure that they deliver the results you were expecting. To clear an overridden sentence, click on the button to the right of the Sentence field and click on Reset Sentence from the dropdown menu that appears. Simple sentences can be defined using standard codes. However, if you have more complex requirements, you can also use data references or even functions in sentence templates (see How to Add Data References or Functions to Sentence Templates below). Comparison with Source Templates Sentence templates are similar to source templates (used in reports, to specify the formatting of source citations). Although there are many points of similarity, there are also important differences and you are advised to be careful not to confuse the two, and to treat them as separate and distinct. In general, the expressions you can use to construct source template formats, are more flexible and powerful than the expressions that can be used within sentence templates. For more on source templates, see Source Template Formats. Standard Data Codes Code Sentence Type/ Fact Type* Description {individual} Either/any Will be replaced by the name of the individual or 'he' or 'she', depending on the context. {individual/him/her} Either/any Will be replaced by the name of the individual or 'him' or 'her', depending on the context. {individual's} Either/any Will be replaced by the name of the individual or 'his' or 'her', depending on the context. {his/her} Either/any Will be replaced by 'his' or 'her', depending on the sex of the individual. {principal} Witness/Individual Will be replaced by the name of the fact-owner. For example, if the fact is baptism, it will be replaced by the name of the person being baptised. {principals} Witness/Family Will be replaced by the name of the fact-owners. For example, if the fact is marriage, it will be replaced by the name of the two people being married. {spouse/her/him} Principal/Family Will be replaced by the name of the individual's spouse or 'her' or 'him', depending on the context. {couple} Principal/Family Will be replaced by the names of the two participants in a family fact (e.g. marriage), or by 'they', depending on the context. {date} Either/any Will insert the date in a text format, with an appropriate prefix. For example, if the date is an exact day, the prefix will be 'on' (e.g. on "30th January, 2001"). If the date is a month or year, the prefix will be 'in' (e.g. in 1998). If the date is a range or a period, again appropriate prefixes will be used. The date code can be qualified to specify a particular date format. See Advanced Features of Sentence Template Codes below. {age} Either/Individual Inserts details of the person's age at the time of the event, if recorded. {age range} Either/Individual Inserts details of the person's age at the time of the event, if recorded. If no age information has been recorded, the person's possible age range will be calculated from their date of birth, and the fact date, if these have been supplied. {their ages} Principal/Family Inserts details of the ages of the parents/spouses in a family record at the time of the event, if recorded. {their age ranges} Principal/Family Inserts details of the ages of the parents in a family record, at the time of the event, if recorded. If no age has been recorded for either parent, that person's possible age range will be calculated from their date of birth, and the fact date, if these have been supplied. {place} Either/any Inserts the place name (usually in the 'Tidy' format where repeated commas are reduced to a single comma), with the prefix 'in'. Tip: In narrative reports you can opt to only use the first part of a place name when replacing template codes for places, if that particular place has already been mentioned in full earlier in the same section. This avoids unnecessary repetition of information and is enabled by default. See the Use Short Form for Repeated Place Names option in the Main tab of the Options dialog for the narrative report in question. {_place} Either/any Inserts the place name (usually in the 'Tidy' format where repeated commas are reduced to a single comma), with no prefix. If you want a prefix, but just don't want 'in', see How to Add a Prefix or Suffix to Any Sentence Template Code below. {_place2} Either/any Secondary place. Used with immigration and emigration events only as each of these, unlike all other fact types, are associated with 2 places: the place the person immigrated to and the place they emigrated from. This code causes the secondary place to be inserted. {cause} Either/any Inserts the cause, if any, associated with the relevant fact. Usually only used with Death events. {address} Either/any Inserts the address, if any, associated with the relevant fact. Tip: see How to Add a Prefix or Suffix to Any Sentence Template Code below, for suggestions about how to add a prefix to an address. {address/place} Either/any Inserts the combined text of the address and place associated with the relevant fact, if either or both are known. Will insert the address text if the address only is known, or the place text if only the place is known. In all cases, the text is output in comma-separated, 'tidy' format, with repeated commas reduced to a single comma and repeated spaces reduced to a single space. Duplicated parts (that is, comma-separated text parts which are common to both address and place) are removed. {note} Either/any Inserts the note, if any, associated with the relevant fact. Is most suitable for long notes, such as notes which contain one or more whole sentences. The {note} code is normally the last code in the sentence template. If you want the note to appear within its own separate paragraph, you can use formatting codes before and after it, within angle brackets - like this: <{note}> (see How to Add a Prefix or Suffix to any Sentence Template Code below). {inline-note} Either/any Inserts the note, if any, associated with the relevant fact. Is most suitable for notes which are short, and typically less than a full sentence. The {inline-note} code is typically used for notes which are intended to be inserted as a clause within a sentence. {label} Either/any Inserts the fact label (e.g. 'Occupation'). {value} Either/attributes only Inserts the attribute value (e.g. for the 'Occupation' attribute, the value might be 'Accountant'). {a/an value} Either/attributes only Inserts the fact value prefixed by 'a' if the value begins with a consonant (e.g. 'a sailor') or by 'an' if the value begins with a vowel (e.g. 'an airman'). {abbr} Either/any Will be replaced by the fact abbreviation if there is one, or the fact label if there isn't {'children'} Child Count attribute only. Is replaced by the word 'child' if the person had 1 child only. Otherwise it is replaced by the word 'children'. {'spouses'} Marriage Count attribute only. Is replaced by the word 'spouse' if the person had 1 spouse only. Otherwise it is replaced by the word 'spouses'. {temple} Either/LDS ordinances only Is replaced by the value of the Temple field for the LDS ordinance in question. {lds status} Either/LDS ordinances only Is replaced by the value of the Status field for the LDS ordinance in question. {blank} Either/any Use this code on its own if you don't want a sentence to appear. * The possible sentence types are 'Principal' (the sentence used for principals, and the one displayed at the bottom of the Facts tab of the Property Box), or 'Witness' (the sentence used for witnesses, and the one displayed at the bottom of the Witnesses Window). Facts can be Individual facts with one principal (like 'Death' or 'Occupation') or Family facts with up to 2 principals (like 'Marriage' or 'Divorce'). Facts can also be events (like 'Death') or attributes (like 'Occupation'). Attributes are identical to events in all respects except that they have a value, which events do not. For example, the value of the 'Occupation' attribute might be 'Accountant'. Role Codes Role codes can only be used in Witness sentences. Code Description {role name} Will be replaced by the current witness's role in the current fact (e.g. the word 'bridesmaid' if that was their role). {role=____} The blank must be filled by one or more role names or the words 'principal' or 'principals'. Multiple values are allowed and must be separated by a comma. For example, {role=bridesmaid} will be replaced by a comma-separated list of all witnesses that have the role 'bridesmaid'. The expression {role=bridesmaid,best man,principal} will return a list of everyone who is either a witness with the role 'bridesmaid', a witness with the role 'best man', or a principal, for the fact in question. If a person qualifies to be in the list more than once, they will only be listed once. This code may be used in both principal and witness sentences. In practice, it will almost always be 'wrapped' within angle brackets like this: "" (see How to Add a Prefix or Suffix to any Sentence Template Code below). The 'role' code can be qualified to specify a particular name format. See Advanced Features of Sentence Template Codes below. {role(single)=____} This code behaves exactly like the code {role=____} above, except that if more than one person qualifies to be in the list, it will return nothing. This means that an expression such as "" will be blank in its entirety, if there is more than one bridesmaid (or none). The 'role(single)' code can be qualified to specify a particular name format. See Advanced Features of Sentence Template Codes below. {role(plural)=____} Again, this code behaves exactly like the code {role=____} above, except that it will return nothing unless more than one person qualifies to be in the list. This means that an expression such as "" will be blank in its entirety if there was just one bridesmaid (or none). The 'role(plural)' code can be qualified to specify a particular name format. See Advanced Features of Sentence Template Codes below. {other=____} This code behaves exactly like the code {role=____} above, except that the current witness is excluded from the list of people. This makes it possible to construct witness sentences like this "{individual} was a bridesmaid.< The other bridesmaids were {other=bridesmaid}.>." {other(single)=____} This code behaves exactly like the code {role(single)=____} above, except that the current witness is excluded from the list of people. The 'other(single)' code can be qualified to specify a particular name format. See Advanced Features of Sentence Template Codes below. {other(plural)=____} This code behaves exactly like the code {role(plural)=____} above, except that the current witness is excluded from the list of people. The 'other(plural)' code can be qualified to specify a particular name format. See Advanced Features of Sentence Template Codes below. {others} Will be replaced by a list of all witnesses for the current fact, irrespective of role, excluding the current witness. Formatting Codes Formatting codes are used to control the presentation of information. Code Description
Forces a new line to be started. Forces a new paragraph to be started. Sex-Version Codes It is possible to have two versions of your template: one for males and one for females. To achieve this, two special codes are required: Code: .... ... The second code is optional. The first code must be the first item in the template. The male version template starts immediately after the male version code and is deemed to be terminated by the code, if supplied, or by the end of the template if not. The female version template starts immediately after the female version code, if supplied, and is terminated by the end of the template. This is an example of the use of these codes: {individual} injured himself {date} {place}{individual} injured herself {date} {place} The male version template is "{individual} injured himself {date} {place}". The female version template is "{individual} injured herself {date} {place}". If there is no female version code, the male version template will be used for everyone (but the male version code is redundant in that case). If both version codes are supplied, the female version template will be used for everyone whose sex is female, and the male version code will be used for everyone whose sex is either male or unknown. Advanced Features of Sentence Template Codes How to Use a Specific Date Format The {date} template code can be qualified to specify a particular required format. To qualify the date code, add a colon followed by the qualifier. For example, the code {date:YEAR} will return the year part (only) of the date. The code {date:ABBREV3} will return the date in ABBREV3 format. The code {date:DAY_OF_WEEK} will return the day of the week of the date. See Date Formats for a complete list of qualifiers and the date formats they produce. Please note that the simple {date} code automatically adds various prefixes (different ones depending on the date type) and other language elements, to make the date information fit correctly into a narrative sentence. If you use the qualifiers LONG, COMPACT, ABBREV, ABBREV2, ABBREV3 or ABBREV4, the appropriate language elements are also added in these cases, as needed. When you qualify a date with any other qualifier, no additional language elements are added. If you want prefixes in these cases, you will have to add them yourself (see How to Add a Prefix or Suffix to any Sentence Template Code below). How to Use a Specific Name Format For Role Codes The following role codes can all use name qualifiers: 'role', 'role(single)', 'role(plural)','other', 'other(single)', and 'other(plural)'. To qualify the role code, add a colon followed by the qualifier after the code label, and before the equal sign. For example, the code {role:GIVEN=bridesmaid} will return the given name only of the person who has role 'bridesmaid' for the given fact. If more than one person has that role, the expression will return a list of all the given names of the relevant people. The code {other(plural):SURNAME=beneficiary} will return a list of the surnames of the people who have the role 'beneficiary' (e.g. of a will), who match the 'other(plural)' code (see above). See Name Formats for a complete list of qualifiers and the name formats they produce. How to Add a Prefix or Suffix to Any Sentence Template Code If a given field has no value, the template code will be simply removed from the sentence that is output, without being replaced by anything. For example, if you had a template: {individual} was born at {address} {date} and you had no address information for John Smith, the sentence generated for his birth event might be, say, John Smith was born at on 19 January, 1903. Notice the unwanted occurrence of the word 'at'. To avoid this happening you need to attach the 'at' to the address as a prefix, so that it only appears when there is an address. You do this by putting angle brackets <> around the code. Any text within the angle brackets will only be output if the code is not empty. So for example, if you changed the code to {individual} was born {date} the sentence generated would be John Smith was born on 19 January, 1903. and the unwanted 'at' would no longer appear. You can use this technique to add a prefix and/or suffix to any code. Formatting codes may be included within the angle brackets if required. So, for example, <{note}> is valid and ensures that if a note is added, a new paragraph will be inserted before and after it. Note: Unlike all other codes, the {place} and {date} codes automatically insert an appropriate prefix (e.g. 'in', 'on', etc.) as required; so there is no need to write (say) and indeed you should not do that. Smart Spacing In the example of John Smith's birth above, it might seem that you would get two spaces after the word 'born', if there were no address. In fact, you only get one. This is because Family Historian intelligently handles spacing for you. If it didn't do so, you couldn't use expressions like "{date} {place} {age}". Instead you would need to use (don't do this!) "< {date}>< {place}>< {age}>". By managing spacing intelligently, Family Historian makes it possible for expressions to be simpler and more readable; and there are other advantages. A common mistake is to try to manage spacing yourself when using angle bracket expressions, by leaving a space after the first angle bracket, and no space before it. Doing so, will disrupt Family Historian's ability to manage spacing for you. Instead, to ensure normal spacing with an angle bracket expression, you should leave a single space before the first angle bracket, and no space after it - as in the example above ("... ..."). How to Add Data References or Functions to Sentence Templates This section describes advanced features. It is primarily intended for advanced and technically-minded users (especially the part about functions). In other words - please do not be discouraged if it makes no sense to you. These features are only needed if you have complex and advanced requirements that cannot be met using standard sentence template codes. Data references and functions are both advanced features. The former are described in Understanding Data References and the latter are described in Understanding Functions. You can add data references or functions to sentence templates. Doing so allows you to reference any field associated directly or indirectly with the current context. When inserted into narrative sentences, data references must be wrapped within curly brackets {}. This is in addition to the percentage signs that ordinarily wrap data references. Although data references can be typed 'by hand', you are strongly recommended to use the Data Reference Assistant dialog to insert them wherever possible, as it will make it much easier to get the results you want. For example, to open the Data Reference Assistant dialog when editing a sentence template in the Fact Definition dialog, click on the << Insert Code button to the right of the Sentence Template field and then choose Data Reference from the dropdown menu that appears. To open the Fact Definition dialog, incidentally, click on Fact Types on the Tools menu, select the fact type you wish to edit and press the Edit button. The Data Reference Assistant dialog is not available if you choose to edit the Sentence field by hand (that is, override the template) in the Fact tab of the Property Box. In that case, you would have to type data references by hand if you wish to use them. Functions must always be typed by hand. Data references that reference the current event or attribute itself, or a sub-field of it, begin with the 'FACT' tag. Some examples are shown in the table below. Please note that in the first two examples, there is a standard sentence template code which is the equivalent to the data reference. Where you can use a standard sentence template code instead of a data reference, you are recommended to do so as the former are simpler and therefore easier to understand. Data Reference* Meaning {%FACT.DATE%} Date of the current fact (i.e. equivalent to {date}). Example: "{individual} was born {%FACT.DATE%}" {%FACT.NOTE2%} Note about the current fact (i.e. equivalent to {note}). Example: "{individual} was born {date} {%FACT.NOTE2%}" {%FACT.NOTE2.SOUR>%} First source for the note about the current fact. Example: "{individual} was born {date} {note} <(source: {%FACT.NOTE2.SOUR>%})>". Note: as this example iillustrates, you can use angle brackets with data references and functions, to add prefixes or suffixes. See How to Add a Prefix or Suffix to Any Sentence Template Code above. In the example, the prefix is "(source:" and the suffix is the closing bracket, ")". {%FACT.PHON%} A phone number associated with the current fact. Example: "{individual} was resident {date} {place} <(tel: {%FACT.PHON%})>" {%FACT.PLAC>LATLONG%} {%FACT.PLAC>LATLONG%} Latitude and longitude of the place at which the fact occurred. Example: "{individual} was born {date} {place} <(lat/long: {%FACT.PLAC>LATLONG%} )>" * As always if you try these out, please remember that data references only return data if the data has been recorded. If there is no telephone number recorded for a given fact, for example, any data reference for it will return nothing. What if you want to reference more detailed information about the principal in an event (or attribute) than you get using a standard sentence template code? In that case, you must use a contextual data reference – specifically one that begins CUR_PRIN - as in {%CUR_PRIN%}. That expression is similar to the standard code {individual} but there are some important differences. First, {individual} will often in practice be replaced by 'he' or 'she' when a sentence is generated . That will not happen with {%CUR_PRIN%}. Second, in a witness sentence, {individual} refers to the current witness, whereas {%CUR_PRIN%} still refers to the principal (or the first principal, if there are two) in the current fact. Some facts (such as a marriage or divorce event) have more than one principal. To refer to the second principal, there is another contextual data reference: CUR_PRIN2. The expression {%CUR_PRIN2%} is similar to the standard sentence template code {spouse/her/him} but the latter will often be replaced by 'her' or 'him' when a sentence is generated and that will not happen with {%CUR_PRIN2%}. Also, {spouse/her/him} cannot be used in a witness sentence, whereas {%CUR_PRIN2%} can - it refers to the second principal (or nothing, if there isn't one). As we have seen, both CUR_PRIN and CUR_PRIN2 can be used in both principal and witness sentences. There is also a third type of contextual data reference, beginning CUR~WITN, which can only be used in the context of a witness sentence – to refer to the witness. The table below gives some examples of all three: Data Reference* Meaning {%CUR_PRIN%} Current or first principal. Example: "{%CUR_PRIN%} was born {date}". {%CUR_PRIN2%} Other or second principal (i.e. equivalent to {spouse}. Example: "{%CUR_PRIN%} married {%CUR_PRIN2%} {date}". {%CUR_PRIN.FAMC>HUSB>%} Current or first principal's father {%CUR_PRIN.FAMC>WIFE>%} Current or first principal's mother {%CUR_PRIN.FAMC>HUSB>FAMC>HUSB>%} Current or first principal's paternal grandfather {%CUR_PRIN.FAMC>HUSB>FAMC>HUSB>NAME:SURNAME%} Current or first principal's paternal grandfather's surname {%CUR_PRIN2.BIRT.DATE:YEAR%} Other or second principal's year of birth {%CUR~WITN>%} Current witness (witness sentences only) {%CUR~WITN.ROLE%} Current witness's role in the current current event (witness sentences only) {%CUR~WITN.NOTE2%} Note about current witnesses role in the current event (witness sentences only) {%CUR~WITN>NAME:SURNAME%} Current witnesses' surname (witness sentences only) {%CUR~WITN>FAMC>HUSB>NAME:SURNAME%} Current witnesses' father's surname (witness sentences only) The concept of a function will be familiar to everyone who has ever done any programming or written scripts using scripting tools. When you use a function in the context of a sentence template, the function call must be wrapped within curly brackets, just as data references are. The start of a function call is always marked by an equals sign; so this must come immediately after the opening curly bracket. A typical function call will take a number of parameters. The arguments to these parameters will often be data references, or other function calls. You can't use a standard sentence template code as an argument to a function. Family Historian has over 100 functions (sometimes called 'built-in' functions to distinguish them from the Family Historian API functions), providing a wide variety of services. The table below gives just a handful of examples of what you can do. To learn more, see Understanding Functions. Function call Meaning {=TextPart(%FACT.PLAC%, 2)} The 2nd comma-separated part (if there is one) of the place where the current event or attribute occurred. For example, if the relevant place was "Glen Park, San Francisco, California, United States", this call would return 'San Francisco' and would work in any narrative sentence template. See the TextPart help for more details on using this function. {=TextPart(%CUR~WITN>BIRT.PLAC%, -2)} The second-last comma-separated part of the birth place of the current witness. For example, if the witness was born in "Glen Park, San Francisco, California, United States", this call would return 'California'. This example uses a contextual data reference that will only work in the context of a witness sentence. See the TextPart help for more details on using this function. {=GetLabelledText(%CUR~WITN.NOTE2%, "Occupation:")} The 'GetLabelledText' function returns the section of a note (up to the end of the paragraph) that follows the specified label – in this case 'Occupation:'. So, for example, if you used the Census event to record each person mentioned in the census as a witness, you could add a note for each witness and record their occupation in the note on a line beginning 'Occupation:'. Then you could use the expression on the left to insert the recorded occupation for each witness into the relevant witness sentence. You could record other details such as age in the same note, and reference them using the same technique, but with a different label (e.g. 'Age:'). The example also uses a contextual data reference that will only work in the context of a witness sentence. See the GetLabelledText help for more details on using this function. {=TextIf(%CUR~WITN>SEX% = "Male", "his", "her")} The 'TextIf' function returns a different result depending on a condition. In this example, the function will return the word 'his' if the current witness is male, and 'her' if the current witness is female. This example also uses a contextual data reference that will only work in the context of a witness sentence. See the TextIf help for more details on using this function. {=RecordId(%CUR_PRIN%)} Inserts the record id of the current or first principal for the current event or attribute. Will work in any narrative sentence template. See the RecordId help for more details on using this function. {=RecordId(%CUR~WITN>%)} Inserts the record id of the current witness. Uses a contextual data reference that will only work in the context of a witness sentence. See the RecordId help for more details on using this function. The Escape Character Occasionally you may wish to prevent a character from having a special meaning. To do this, place '\' in front of the character. For example, if you want the word "{date}" to appear exactly like that and not be treated as a code, write it like this "\{date}". The word "{date}" (without the escape character) will be output. Even the escape character itself can be 'escaped' in this way.

title: Create and Edit Folder Sets in Design Mode
breadcrumb: Smart Folders in the Query Window
Create and Edit Folder Sets in Design Mode
text:
Smart Folders in the
Query Window

Create and Edit Folder Sets in Design Mode

Smart Folder Pane in the Query Window in Design Mode

All editing of folder sets is done in the Query Window in design
mode. To enter (or leave) design mode, click on the Design
Mode button
on the Smart Folder toolbar.
The folder set button has a light-orange background when displayed in
design mode, and the folder icons are different (see image above).

Standard folder sets are not editable, but you can save a copy of any
standard folder set as a custom folder set and then edit the custom
folder set.

To create a new folder set, you can either copy an existing folder set
and modify that, or create a new one from scratch. To do the
latter, choose the "New Custom Folder Set" command on the cog menu
of the Smart
Folder toolbar. Or click New on the Manage
Folder Sets Dialog. Folder sets can also be cloned in the Manage
Folder Sets Dialog.

In design mode, the items in the smart folder pane are either smart
folders or column set variants. Column set variants are
not smart folders themselves. They are always displayed as
children of smart folders and have no children of their own. They
specify a variant set of columns that can be used by a smart folder, in
particular circumstances.

All smart folder can optionally have child smart folders, nested to any
level.

To edit a custom folder set, right-click on the background of the
folder set pane and select from the available commands in the dropdown
menu that appears; or right-click on any item in the pane, and select
from the available commands in the dropdown menu.

The following dropdown menu appears when you right-click on the
background of the folder pane:

Paste Branch at Top Level
If you previously copied a branch using the "Copy Branch"
command (see below), you can paste it at the top level within the
current folder set.

Add New Top-level Folder
This command will create a new top-level smart folder in the
current folder set.

The following dropdown menu appears when you right-click on a smart
folder or column set variant in the folder pane:

Copy Branch
Copies the selected item and any subfolders or column set
variants attached to it, to the clipboard.

Paste Branch as Sibling
If you previously copied a branch using the "Copy Branch"
command, you can paste it as a 'sibling' of the selected folder.

Paste Branch as Child
If you previously copied a folder using the "Copy Branch"
command, you can paste it as a 'child' subfolder of the selected
folder. You cannot paste a branch as a child of a column set
variant.

Add New Sibling Folder
Creates a new smart folder as a 'sibling' of the selected
folder.

Add New Child Folder
Creates a new smart folder as a 'child' of the selected folder.

Add Column Set Variant
Creates a new column set variant as a 'child' of the selected
folder.

Edit
Opens the Edit Smart Folder
dialog to edit a selected smart folder. This command
will be greyed if a column set variant is selected.

Move Up
Moves the selected items up.

Move Down
Moves the selected items down.

Delete
Deletes the select item.

VIewing Output

If at any point you want to see what a folder set will look like in
normal mode, simply untick the Design Mode button , and select whichever
smart folders you want in the smart folder pane on the left-hand side of
the Query Window. The results (with the correct columns) will be
displayed on the right-hand side of the Query Window. To re-enter
design mode, just click the Design Mode button once again.

Design Mode
Icons

There are 4 smart folder types: simple, query, plugin
and auto. These are discussed in detail
below. There is also another item called a column set
variant which is also discussed below. The icons used in
the smart folder pane in design mode are different from the icons used
when not in design mode. The meaning of the design mode icons are
as follows:

Icon
Meaning

Simple smart folder (no filtering and it does not
specify display columns). No associated query.

Query smart folder that does not specify display
columns. It has an associated query which is used for filtering
and grouping (see below), but the query does
not specify display columns.

Query smart folder that does specify display
columns. It has an associated query which is used for
filtering and grouping (see below), and also
for specifying display columns

Plugin smart folder that does not specify display
columns. It has no associated query.

Plugin smart folder that does specify display
columns. It has an associated query that is used to specify
display columns in its 'Columns' tab.

Auto smart folder (only available for 'Source' and
'Source Citation' folder sets). No associated query.

Column set variant. Has an associated query that is used
to specify display columns in its 'Columns' tab and conditions for
use in its 'Filters' tab.

Smart Folder Types

You specify the type of each folder in the Edit
Smart Folder Dialog.

Some folder types can have associated queries, which can be used for
various different purposes. If a smart folder has an associated
query, it will be displayed on the right side of the Query Window (to
the right of the smart folder pane), when that smart folder is
selected. The query name field, at the top of the Query
Window, is blank when a smart folder is selected that has an associated
query. The Run Query button
on the query toolbar is enabled (not greyed) at this point. You
can click this button to run the query and see the results in the
'Result Set' tab if you want to. Doing this is not the
equivalent of running the query in the context of a smart folder.
Its purpose is mainly to see what the current column selection looks
like (if you are specifying display columns) without having to leave
design mode.

When a smart folder has an associated query, the tabs displayed for the
associated query will differ somewhat from the tabs that would be
displayed for an ordinary query.

If you select a smart folder that has no associated query, in design
mode, the area of the Query Window to the right of the smart folder
pane, will be blank.

In general, a single smart folder in design mode can result in an
entire branching folder structure of any number of levels, when viewed
in normal mode. Smart folders in design mode can (and frequently
do) expand dramatically in this way, when viewed in normal mode.
The exception is simple folders (see below). Unlike all other
smart folder types, there will only ever be one displayed folder in
normal mode, corresponding to each simple folder in design mode.

The following table shows the various smart folder types.

Type
Description

Simple

A simple smart folder does
no filtering. It can be the child of another smart folder,
and it can have smart folders as children. It also does not
specify any special columns. If it is a top-level folder, it
uses the default columns and displays all items of the relevant
type. If it is a child of another folder, it inherits both
the set of items that the parent displays and whatever set of
columns its parent folder uses. Simple folders are often
useful as a convenient way of grouping other subfolders (child
folders) together.

As mentioned above, there is a one-to-one correspondence with each
simple smart folder in a design mode, and a single display folder
in normal mode. This is not true of other smart folder
types.

As also mentioned earlier, simple folders have no associated
query. When you select a simple folder in the smart folder
pane of the Query Window in design mode, the main part of the
Query Window to the right will therefore be blank.

Query

A query-type smart folder can do everything that a
simple smart folder does, but it has additional
functionality. If it has a parent folder, it will
effectively take as input whatever set of items the parent folder
contains. If it has no parent folder, it takes as input the
entire set of items of the folder set type (e.g. all Individual
records, if it is an "Individual" folder set). It can then
optionally apply filtering to this set of items. It can also
do more than that. Whereas there is only ever one display
folder corresponding to a simple smart folder, a single query-type
smart folder can generate an entire branching tree of display
folders. This is called grouping. A query-type
smart folder can effectively then do 3 things:

filtering (potentially reducing the input set of items to
some subset)

grouping (expand into a branching folder structure in
display mode)

specifying columns

All 3 are optional.

When you select a query-type smart folder in the smart folder pane
of the Query Window in design mode, regardless of whether it
specifies display folders or not, the main part of the Query
Window to the right will have 3 tabs: "Columns", "Filters", and
"Result Set".

Filtering
is done on the
Filters tab. This is no different from the filtering
that is done in an ordinary query. You can use whatever
filtering criteria you like, or none.

Grouping is
done on the
Columns tab. To create a group of child display
folders (as will appear in normal mode), add a column to the
Columns list, and set the 'Type' field of the column to "Group
By". The effect of this, in normal mode, will be that the
result set will effectively be sorted by the 'Group By' column,
and then it will be divided into display folders, one for each
different value. So, for example, if the 'Group By' column
has a total of 3 different values across all rows - say 'Apples',
'Bananas' and 'Pears' - you will get one display folder called
'Apples' which contains all the items which have the 'Apples'
value, another display folder called 'Bananas' for all the items
where the value is 'Bananas'' and a third display folder called
'Pears', for all the items where the value is 'Pears'. You
can have as many 'Group By' columns as you wish. If you have
a second 'Group By' column, this will create a second level of
display folders, nested within the first. So, for example,
if the values of the second 'Group By' column are all either
'Red', 'Green' or 'Blue', and if it just so happens that of the
items which have the 'Apples' value, several of them have 'Red'
and 'Green' for the second value, but none of them have 'Blue',
then in normal mode the user will see two display folders,
labelled 'Red' and 'Green', nested within the 'Apples' display
folder, showing these items. And so on for further levels of
'Group By' columns.

'Group By' columns are always processed in order. By
convention, the 'Group By' columns normally appear at the top of
the 'Columns' tab, before all other columns. However, this
is just a convention. The order of 'Group By' columns with
respect to one another is important, but their ordering with
respect to any other columns is not.

The "Attributes" smart folder, within the 'Facts' folder set, is
an example of a smart folder that has 2 levels of 'Group By'
columns. Suppose in your project you had an attribute called
'Hobby', and 2 common values were 'Sailing' and 'Tennis'.
The two 'Group By' column would bring it about that, within the
"Attributes" folder in normal mode, the user would see one folder
called 'Hobby' (which would list everyone who has a hobby), and
within that they would see another folder called 'Sailing' (which
would list everyone who sails), and another folder called 'Tennis'
(which would list everyone who plays tennis).

Specifying display columns is
also done on the
Columns tab. If you want a query-type smart folder to
specify its own display columns, you must tick the option "Query
specifies display columns" in the Edit
Smart Folder Dialog, for the folder in question. If
this option is not ticked, any column specified in the "Columns"
tab will be ignored, unless their type is 'Group By'. Notice
that 'Group By' columns are always hidden, so the 'Group By'
columns are not included in the list of display columns, if
specified. So if you want the value of a 'Group By' column
to appear as a displayed column in normal mode you must add it
twice: once as a 'Group By' column and once as a 'Normal'
column. For more on how to specify the columns in a query,
see the
Columns Tab.

Plugin

A plugin-type smart folder
is similar in many ways to a query-type folder in what it
does. But it is also more powerful. A query-type smart
folder will divide a set of items into different subfolders,
possibly spread over multiple levels of folders within
folders. But it will not put the same item into more than
one sibling folder. A plugin-type smart folder could do that
if required.

Plugin-type smart folders contain the entire script for a plugin,
written in Lua - an embedded scripting language. Writing
plugins is not for everyone. But Family Historian provides
all the tools you need (including a built-in editor and debugger)
for those who want to give it a try. Full instructions and
documentation are available in the Plugin Help.

Like query-type smart folders, plugin-type smart folders can
effectively do 3 things:

filtering (potentially reducing the input set of items to
some subset)

grouping (into a folder structure)

specifying display columns

Filtering and grouping are both done within the plugin script (the
Lua code). As with query-type smart folders, if you want a
plugin-type smart folder to specify the display columns associated
with the folder in normal mode, you must tick the option "Query
specifies display columns" in the Edit
Smart Folder Dialog, for the smart folder in question.
If that option is ticked, the smart folder will have an associated
query which will displayed in the main part of the Query Window to
the right, when that smart folder is selected in design
mode. In this case there will be two tabs displayed for the
query: "Columns" and "Result Set". You specify the display
columns in the
Columns tab. If "Query specifies display columns" is not
ticked, for a plugin-type smart folder, there will be no
associated query for the smart folder; so when you select the
smart folder in this case, in design mode, the main part of the
Query Window to the right will be blank.

If you specify the columns for a plugin folder, you should not set
their type to 'Group By' as any such columns will be
ignored. The 'Group By' column type is for use with
query-type smart folders only.

To learn about plugins and how to write them, please see the help
for the Plugins Dialog and the
Family Historian Plugin Help. Within the latter, look for
the "Special Plugin Types" section, and within that the "Smart
Folder Plugins" section.

Auto

Only smart folders within "Source" or "Source Citation" folder
sets can have the auto folder type. Auto folders
have no child folders (or column set variants). This is
because when you open an auto smart folder, Family Historian will
automatically use an internal wizard tool to generate appropriate
display folders with the appropriate columns.

To learn more about auto smart folders, see the discussion of the
Source & Citation Wizard in the Manage
Folder Sets Dialog.

Column

Set Variants

Column set variants are not smart folders. They are modifiers
of query-type or plugin-type smart folders. If used, they appear
as children of query-type or plugin-type smart folders in design mode
only, to modify the behaviour of the smart folder they are associated
with. They have this icon: .
They specify a variant set of columns, and the conditions under which
this variant set of columns is to be used.

Simple and auto smart folders cannot have column set
variants.

For the query associated with a query-type smart folder, the main part
of the Query Window to the right will have 3 tabs: "Columns", "Filters",
and "Result Set". For the query associated with a plugin-type
smart folder that specifies display folders, the main part of the Query
Window to the right will have 2 tabs: "Columns" and "Result Set".
With column set variants, the main part of the Query Window to the right
will again have 3 tabs: "Columns", "Filters", and "Result
Set". However, the Filters tab looks a little different from
usual when used with column set variants. Ordinarily, the form at
the bottom of the window has a tab for each type of filter that is
relevant to the current folder set type. The possible tabs in that
case are some combination of General, List, Relationship,
and Subgroup. When used with column set
variants, however, none of these tabs appear. Instead there is one
filter type called 'Group By' Column Test with a single field
labelled 'Value'. The purpose of this field is to specify which
'Group By' folders, this query is applicable to.

a Column Set Variant in the Facts Folder Set

The Facts folder set is an example of a standard folder set that uses
column set variants.

Figure 1 - the Facts folder set displaying the 'Marriage' folder

In figure 1, we are looking at the Facts folder set.
The 'Events' folder, on the left-hand side, has been expanded, and it
contains 14 subfolders - one for each event type in the project
('Baptism', 'Birth' etc.). The 'Marriage' folder has been
selected, and a list of all marriage events in the project is displayed
on the right-hand side. Notice that the columns on the right-hand
side are ones that are relevant to marriage. They include "Spouse
1", "Spouse 2", "Best man", "Bridesmaid 1", etc. If you look
at this folder set in the Query Window, you will find that don't see
those marriage-related columns in the area on the right, when you select
a folder for any event type other than 'Marriage'. As we will see
shortly, this association of marriage-related columns to the 'Marriage'
folder, was achieved using a column set variant.

Figure 2. The Columns tab for the "Events" folder

In figure 2, we are looking at the 'Facts' folder set in design
mode. Or rather, to be strictly accurate, we are looking at a
custom copy of the 'Facts' folder set. For the purposes of this
page, a copy was made of the 'Facts' folder set, as a custom folder
set. This was done so that the various fields and buttons would
not all be greyed out in the various screenshots (remember that standard
folder sets are not editable, but you can copy them and modify the
copy).

To switch to design mode, we pressed the Design Mode button on the folder set toolbar.

Notice that the 'Events' folder ()
is selected, and that we are viewing the 'Columns' tab for that folder (). We can see from the folder
icon ()
that this folder uses a query both for grouping and also to
specify display columns. Both of these goals are achieved
on the Columns tab. Grouping is achieved by (in this
case) a single column labelled 'Event' which is Group By type
(). It is thanks to
this 'Group By' column that, within the 'Events' folder in figure 1,
there are subfolders for all the various event types.

The remaining columns in the list - that is, Date, Event
(again), Fact Owner 1 and Fact Owner 2 - are
the display columns for this folder. Or rather, they are the
columns that will display unless they are overridden by a column set
variant. We can see that the 'Events' folder has 6 column set
variants: Adoption, Baptism, Census, Marriage,
Will, and Christening. We will look at the Marriage
column set variant shortly, but before we do, we will look
briefly at the filter tab for the 'Events' folder.

Figure 3. The Filters tab for the "Events" folder

In figure 3, we are still looking at the 'Events' folder (). But we have switched to viewing the
Filters tab (). This is
where any filtering for the folder is specified. In this case, the only
filter () is there to ensure
that the rows consist of events only (that is, attributes are
excluded). The important point to notice, for present purposes, is
that filtering at this level has no relevance to column set variants.

Figure 4 - the "Columns" tab for the "Marriage" Column Set
Variant

Now in figure 4, we have changed selection to the Marriage column
set variant ().
There are still 3 tabs on the right-hand side ("Columns", "Filters" and
"Result Set"), but instead of providing information about the 'Events'
folder (as they did in figures 2 and 3), they now provide information
about the Marriage column set variant. In figure 4, the
"Columns" tab () is
selected. The list of columns ()
are, as you would expect, all columns that are relevant specifically to
marriage ('Best man', 'Bridesmaid 1', etc). These are the columns
that are visible on the right-hand side in figure 1. These columns
were specified here, in the 'Marriage' column set variant.

But how did Family Historian know that it should use this column set
variant, with the Marriage folder? For that, we need to look at
the Filters tab for the Marriage column set variant.

Figure 5 - the "Filters" tab for the "Marriage" Column Set Variant

In figure 5, we are still looking at the settings for the "Marriage"
column set variant (), but
we have now switched to the Filters tab ().
In this example, there is only one filter in the list (). It says "Event = 'Marriage'". This
filter is editable in the "'Group By' Column Test" filter type
pane below (). It has that
name because filters in a column set variant relate to 'Group By'
columns specified in the "Columns" tab of the parent folder. In
this particular example, the effect of the filter is to associate this
column set variant with any folder in which the value of the 'Events'
Group By column (see
in figure 2 above) is 'Marriage'.

In this example, only one Group By column was used; so there
is only one nested layer of subfolders, generated for the 'Events'
folder. But you can have as many Group By columns as
you want, to generate as many layers of subfolders as you want. If
you have 3 Group By columns, you could also have 3 filters
for each column set variant for that folder. But you don't
necessarily have to. Each column set variant can specify the
display columns to use for any subfolder at any level. A
high-level column set variant might just use one filter. A
lower-level column set variant might use two or more (but never more
than the number of 'Group By' columns at the folder-level, of
course). If one column set variant specifies the display columns
to use at a lower-level than another, the lower-level one will take
precedence over the higher-level one, if they are both applicable.

You can see examples of 3-level filtering in column set variants if you
generate a folder set by clicking the Source &
Citation Wizard button in the Manage
Folder Sets dialog - or at least, you will if you do so in the
Family Historian sample project, or any other project that uses source
templates.

Design Tips

Avoid Prompts

When designed well, smart folders should feel completely intuitive and
easy for users to use. When designing smart folders, the goal
should be simplicity and clarity for users. However, as we have
seen, smart folders can use both queries and plugins, and there is
nothing to stop you from prompting the user for input, in either queries
or plugins used in smart folders. Our recommendation is that you
do not do this. Family Historian will automatically run any query
or plugin used within a smart folder, when it needs to do so, to display
information. The user will have no easy way of telling when a
query or plugin is about to be run, so if a prompt appears, it is likely
to feel unexpected and inappropriate. Also, with some folder sets
Family Historian may need to run several queries or plugins in
succession. If some of them displayed prompts, the user would have
no easy way of knowing which prompt relates to what. It would
probably feel confusing and uncomfortable for the user. For this
reason, we recommend that you do not put up any kind of prompt to the
user in any queries or plugins that you use as part of the design of
smart folders. If you have a requirement which requires input from
the user, smart folders are probably not the right way to solve the
problem. Consider using an ordinary query or plugin instead - or
perhaps a custom report or diagram.

Special Considerations with Record-type Smart Folders

When specifying display columns using a query, in record-type smart
folders, you are recommended to always make the first displayable column
(that is, the first column which is enabled and not either hidden or a
'group-by' column) to be the default column for that record type.
The default column for any record type has an expression consisting of a
simple data reference that references the record. For example,
the default column for an Individual query has "%INDI%" as its
expression. The default column for a Family record query has
"%FAM%" as its expression. And so on. The easy way to add a
column of this type is to select the first item (that is, the record
item) in the top-left corner of the "Fields etc." list on the left-hand
side, and then click "Add Column" (using the button to the right of the
list) to add this column to the list of columns. Then move the new
column up to the first position in the list (or, if you prefer, above
all columns except 'group-by' columns). The reason that this is
recommended is that when displayed in the record window, or in any
record selector, the first displayed column always has to directly
reference the record itself. It isn't essential that you provide a
column which does this. If you don't, Family Historian will
automatically generate one for you. However, this can look odd if
you have a similar column later in the column list. Also, it means
that the output of this smart folder will be a little different,
depending on whether you are viewing the smart folder in the Records
window (or record selector) on the one hand, or in the Query Window, on
the other. This is because no additional column is generated when
you view a smart folder in the Query Window. So, for these
reasons, you are usually recommended to keep things simple by always
making the first column a default column for that record type.

No similar consideration applies to non-record-type smart folders (i.e.
for facts, citations, and witnesses) which can only ever be displayed in
the Query Window in any case.

title: Edit Smart Folder Dialog
breadcrumb: Smart Folders in the Query Window
text:
Smart Folders in the
Query Window

Edit Smart Folder Dialog

Edit Smart Folder Dialog

To open the Edit Smart Folder Dialog right-click on a smart folder in the
Smart Folder Pane of the Query Window when in design mode (see
Create and Edit Folder Sets in Design Mode).
The dialog will also be displayed if you take an option to create a new
smart folder (again, see Create and
Edit Folder Sets in Design Mode).

Fields

Folder Name
Name of the current smart folder

Folder Type
The possible types are:

Simple

Query

Plugin

Auto

See Smart Folder Types.

Edit Plugin...
Always hidden unless the folder type is 'Plugin'. Click
this button to view or edit the actual plugin code (written in
Lua).

Query specifies display columns
Always hidden and not available unless the folder type is either
'Query' or 'Plugin'.

If this option is ticked, the columns displayed for this smart
folder are the columns defined in the 'Columns' tab of the
associated query. If this option is not ticked, the columns
displayed for this smart folder will be inherited from its parent
folder, if there is one, or will be the default columns for the
record or query type.

title: Manage Folder Sets
text:
Smart Folders

Manage Folder Sets

The Manage Folder Sets Dialog

Folder sets are collections of smart
folders. The Manage Folder Sets dialog allows the full list of
folder sets to be viewed and managed. It can be accessed by clicking
on the Query button
on the main application toolbar and choosing "Manage Folder Sets" from the
dropdown menu that appears. When the folder set pane is displayed in
the Records Window
or in the Query Window,
you can also access the Manage Folder Sets dialog from the cog menu
on the Query Window smart
folder toolbar when the Smart Folder Pane is open.

The description field at the bottom of the window contains information
about all standard folder sets. You are recommended to also provide
a description for any custom folder sets you create. To do this,
right-click on the folder set in the list and select 'Description' from
the dropdown menu that appears. When you do this, the description is
displayed in a popup window. The descriptions for standard folder
sets are read-only.

Fields and Buttons

Type
There are 15 types of folder set, exactly corresponding to the
15 types of query. There is one for each of the 12 data
record types (that is all record types, except the Header
record). In addition to these 12 record types, there are
also 3 non-record folder set types (and query types). These
are: Fact (event or attribute), Source Citation, and Witness
(shared events). Select the type your require, or choose
"<All>".

New
Opens the New
Folder Set Dialog to create a new custom folder set.
You are recommended to provide a description for all custom
folder sets. To do this, right-click on the folder set in
the list and select 'Description' from the dropdown menu that
appears.

Open
When you open a folder set, it is displayed in the smart folder
pane of the Query
Window (not in design mode though - see next).

Edit
Folder sets are maintained in the in the smart folder pane of
the Query Window, in design mode. If you select a
folder and click this option, the folder set will be displayed in
the Query Window in design mode.

Rename
Only custom folder sets can be
renamed.

Clone
Any folder set, standard or custom,
can be cloned - that is, copied as a custom folder set. You
will be prompted to specify a name for the copy.

Source & Citation Wizard
There is rarely any need to use the Source
& Citation Wizard button and it is not usually
recommended to use it. However, in rare circumstances, it
may be useful.

There are 4 types of smart folder: Standard, Query, Plugin or Auto
(see Smart Folder Types).
The Source & Citation Wizard is used internally by Family
Historian whenever an "Auto" smart folder is
opened. For this reason, there is rarely any need to
use the Source & Citation Wizard directly via the Source
& Citation Wizard button. It is usually a
better option to let Family Historian use it for you via 'Auto'
smart folders (the two standard folder sets, "Sources" and "Source
Citations", both contain 'Auto' smart folders, for example).
'Auto' smart folders will always match whatever source templates
you may have in your project. If you switch to another
project, with different source templates, or if you change the
source templates used within a project, there is no need to update
'Auto' smart folders. If, however, you generate a folder set
using the Source & Citation Wizard, the resulting folder set
will match the source template data in the current project at the
time that you run the wizard. If you subsequently switch to
another project, or change your source template data, the smart
folders in the folder set may not perfectly reflect the new source
template data. This is why we recommend that you do not use
the wizard unless you really have to, and use 'Auto' smart folders
instead.

Despite the above recommendation, you might want to use the Source & Citation Wizard button to
generate a custom folder set if you want to customize source
and/or source citation folder sets, in a way that cannot be
achieved using 'Auto' smart folders. If you do this, you
will need to rebuild the folder set every time you change your
source template data, if you wish to ensure that it accurately
reflects the updated source template data.

Another possible reason for using this button is simply to improve
your understanding of what 'Auto' smart folders do, and to see
examples of the use of Column
Set Variants.

Delete
Deletes the currently selected folder set(s). Only custom
folder sets can be deleted.

Import
Import a folder set from a folder set file. Folder set
files have a ".fhsf" suffix.

Export
Export a folder set as a folder set file.

title: Smart Folders
text:
Smart Folders

A Section of the Smart Folder Pane in the
Records Window

Smart folders are a powerful technology, unique to Family Historian,
introduced in version 8. They allow data to be displayed in folder
structures. They make it easy to browse, view and explore complex,
large data sets, and to reveal many new perspectives. Users can
create their own custom sets of smart folders, to create even more new
additional ways of breaking down and understanding their own data.

Smart folders can be viewed wherever the smart folder icon is
displayed:
. This icon is displayed in 3 contexts:

The Records Window

Any record selector dialog

The Query Window

Expandable Folders, Tip Folders, and Folder Sets

When you click on the smart folder icon, a pane appears on the
left-hand side, showing records (but not just records, as we will see)
organised into convenient, meaningful folders and subfolders.
Folders can be expanded to show subfolders. Folders which admit of
further expansion (expandable folders) have a yellow folder
icon: .
Folders which contain results only, and which cannot be expanded further
are called tip folders - as in, 'tip of the branch' - and they
have this icon: .

The example screenshot at the top of this page, shows a section of the
"Individuals" folder set (a folder set is a collection of
smart folders). This particular folder set is designed to display
information about Individual records. It is the only standard
folder set designed to display information about Individual
records. However, you can create your own custom folder sets and
select the one to display from the dropdown list at the top of the
pane. In the context of the Records Window, or a record selector
dialog, the list of folder sets available will depend on the record type
being displayed. If you are viewing Individual records, you will
see folder sets for Individual records. The smart folders
belonging to whichever folder set you select will be displayed in the
smart folder pane.

There are folder sets for all record types, and these can be accessed
from the appropriate tab of the Records
Window, or in record selector dialog boxes. You can create
custom folder sets for all (but not only) record types.

The Smart Folder Pane and the List Pane

In the Records Window, the normal
pane that shows lists of records, is called the List Pane. The
smart folder pane, when opened, appears on the left, alongside the list
pane. Normally the list pane will not change when you first open
the smart folder pane. But as you select folders in the smart
folder pane, the list pane will display the matching records.

Subfolders effectively act as refinements on their 'parent'
folder. They may display all the same records as their parent
folder or a smaller subset. By default, each folder name is
followed by a number which indicates the number of results at that
level. We can read off from the example above, that in this
particular project there are 104 Individual records ("All Individuals
(104)") and that all of them have names ("Names (104)"), all of them
have surnames ("Surnames (all) (104)"), and given names ("Given Names
Used (104)"), but only 2 of them have nicknames ("Nicknames (2)").
What's more, we also see that 23 of them have occupations ("Occupations
(23)"), and within that, 2 of them have the occupation "fisherman"
("fisherman (2)").

If you click on "Occupations (23)" you will see a list of 23 Individual
records in the list pane. These will be the 23 Individual records
who have an Occupation field. Notice that 23 is not the
number of occupations. There could be more than 23 occupations
(some people may have more than one occupation) or fewer than 23
(several Individuals could all share the same occupation).

In the screenshot example at the top of this page, "Nicknames (2)"
means that 2 Individual records have nicknames - and because this folder
is selected, we can see the 2 people in the List Pane. But this is
not the total number of nicknames. There are 3 nicknames in fact:
Caro, Jay and Judy. In fact, "Jay" and Judy" are both nicknames
for the same person: Judith Anderson.

Columns In the List Pane

One of the most useful features of smart folders, is that they can have
their own set of columns - ones that are appropriate to whatever list
they are displaying. For example, in the screenshot above, the
"Nicknames (2)" folder is selected in the Smart Folder Pane on the
left. The list pane columns in the List Pane on the right include
"Nickname", "Nickname 2", and "Nickname 3". These are not standard
columns that normally appear in the Columns Window. When
non-standard columns are displayed, the background of the list pane is a
light green
shade as a hint to pay attention to the column names. See the
example image at the top of this page which uses non-standard columns.

Although each different smart folder can have its own set of columns,
they don't have to. Every record type in the Records Window has a
configurable set of columns. These are the default columns, and
any smart folder can be designed to use those. The columns
displayed in a smart folder are effectively configurable too. To
configure the default columns for any particular record type,
right-click on any row in the appropriate tab of the Records Window and
choose "Configure Columns" from the dropdown menu that appears (you may
want to close the smart folder pane first to ensure that default columns
are being displayed). To configure the columns associated with a
smart folder, you have to edit the smart folder itself. Standard
folder sets cannot be edited directly - but you can make a copy of the
folder set and edit that.

Query Window and Records Window Differences With Respect to Smart
Folders

When Smart Folders are viewed in the Records
Window, or in a record selector dialog, they only display
records. In the Query Window,
however, they can also be used to display information about facts (events
& attributes), witness information (for shared events), and
source citations. Also, all editing of smart folders, and
all customization, is done in the Query Window. To learn more about
features of smart folders which are specific to the Query Window, see Smart
Folders in the Query Window. See also Smart
Folders in the Records Window.

Creating and Maintaining Custom Folder Sets

As well as being able to view folder sets in the Query Window, the
Query Window is also where folder sets (collections of smart folders)
are created and maintained. See Smart Folders in the Query
Window. Some aspects of maintaining folder sets can also be
done on the Manage
Folder Sets Dialog.

Smart folders Bridge The Lumper/Splitter divide with Sources

Smart folders provide a vital searchlight for examining records of all
types; but they are perhaps especially vital for Source records.
With templated Source records, for example, they allow sources to be
viewed in ways that precisely mirror the structure of whatever Source
Templates are used in a project - including any custom Source Templates
that a user may have created themselves. Genealogists who like to
use a small number of Source records for large datasets are called lumpers.
A lumper might have one Source record for an entire census
say. The opposite of a lumper is a splitter. A
splitter might have one Source record for every household entry within a
census, perhaps. Most genealogists are a mixture of the two.
A person might be a lumper with respect to one source type, and a
splitter with respect to another. But everyone, whether lumper or
splitter, wants to be able to interrogate their source data and to be
able to distinguish all the shared and distinct aspects of the
data. For example, whether you are a lumper or a splitter, you are
likely to have some way of recording information found in
newspapers. And you may want to find all information that relates
to a particular newspaper, or even perhaps a particular issue of a
newspaper on a given date. And this will be true even if you
record all newspapers with a single Source record (ultra-lumper), or
have one Source record for each different issue of each newspaper for
given dates (ultra-splitter).

To try to resolve the conflicting needs of lumpers and splitters, some
genealogy programs sometimes resort to creating extra intermediary
levels of data structures, when dealing with source information.
For example, they may have not just source templates, source records,
and citations (3 levels), but even throw in an intermediate citation
record - not usually called that, but that is in effect what it is - and
have 4 levels. This has the practical effect of making recording
source citations slower and more bureaucratic. But it is done in
order to allow both splitters and lumpers to subdivide and group their
source citation data in all the different ways that genealogists want,
and to be able to explore their data in ways that replicate their own
systems of organisation.

Smart folders make these extra data structures unnecessary. Now
both lumpers and splitters can record their data in the most logical way
(and in the fastest and easiest way), while still being able to get all
the benefits of having a much more complicated structure, when they
explore and interrogate their data. You don't actually need to
have the added bureaucracy of citation records, for example, to be able
to see your citations grouped as if they did all belong to citation
records - if that's what you want.

Smart folders effectively bridge the lumper/splitter divide. They
allow source data to be presented in as complex and varied a way as any
genealogist could want, without the need for any additional complexity
in the way that the data is actually recorded and structured.

title: Smart Folders in the Query Window
breadcrumb: Smart Folders in the Query Window
text:
Smart Folders

Smart Folders in the Query Window

Smart Folder Pane marked in red, in the Query Window (not design
mode).

To display a folder set in the Query Window, click the Query button on
the main application toolbar and choose "Smart Folders" from the
dropdown menu that appears. This will display the Query Window
with the Smart Folder Pane open on the left-hand side.
Alternatively, any time you have the Query Window open, click on
the Smart Folders button
on the Query Window's window
toolbar to open or close the smart folder pane. Then choose
the folder set you wish to view from the "Folder Set" dropdown list at
the top of the folder set pane.

When the Smart Folder Pane is open, it has its own toolbar which is
displayed at the top of the pane. The various toolbar commands,
and the dropdown menu that appears when you click on the menu button
on the toolbar, are described in the Query
Window Toolbars page.

Why the Query
Window?

As discussed
elsewhere, smart folders can be viewed in the Records
Window, and in any record selector dialog. They can also
be viewed in the Query Window.
There are a number of reasons for why you might want to display them
in the Query Window, in preference to the Records Window. Some
folder set types can only be viewed in the Query
Window. Specifically any folder set where the set type is not
a record type (that is, fact, witness or source
citation) can only be viewed in the Query Window. Also,
when you view the contents of a smart folder in the Query Window,
the output is displayed in the result set pane. The result set
pane lays out tabular information in a grid. There are several
advantages to this:

You can select
cells, or the entire result set, and copy-and-paste them into a
spreadsheet or other similar program.

You can save
the entire grid in CSV format, for easy transfer to a
spreadsheet.

You can, if
the cell is 'data-linked', simply double-click on a cell to view
the original field that the data comes from. Or, again with
data-linked cells, you can right-click on cell and choose
'Properties' to view the data in the Property Box.

Cells that
represent records will use the appropriate record icon, which
makes them easier to identify.

You can print
the entire pane as a report, with configurable headings, etc.

You can
easily copy selected cell records in the result set to a named
list.

One further reason for displaying smart folders in the Query Window, is
if you wish to modify a custom folder set in any way, or create a new
custom folder set. All editing of folder sets is done in the Query
Window when the smart folder pane is in Design Mode -
see Create and Edit Folder Sets in
Design Mode.

title: Smart Folders in the Records Window
breadcrumb: Smart Folders in the Records Window
text:
Smart Folders

Smart Folders in the Records Window

Smart Folder Pane marked in red, in the Records Window

To open or close the Folder Set Pane in the Records
Window, click on the Smart Folders button in the top-left corner of the
window. When the Smart Folder Pane is open, this toolbar is
displayed at the top of the pane:

The various toolbar commands, and the dropdown menu that appears when
you click on the menu button , are described in the Records
Window Toolbars page.

To learn more about smart folders, see Smart
Folders.

title: Simple Date Fields
text:
Date Entry Assistant Dialog

Simple Date Fields

The following date fields occur at least once, on each of the tabs of
the Date Entry Assistant Dialog:

Calendar
4 calendars are supported. The current calendar of the Western
world is Gregorian. You are recommended to use this wherever
possible.

Day
Leave blank if not known

Month
Different calendars have different months (except that Gregorian
and Julian share the same months). Leave this blank if the month
is not known.

Year
If entering a simple date, you must specify a year. If you do
not know the year, you should enter the date information you have
as a Date
Phrase. Years must always be entered as 4 digit values. The
year 98, for example, will be interpreted as 0098.

With the Gregorian calendar only you can optionally specify a year
modifier - a 2-digit value in the second year field, following the
‘/’ character. Where a date is shown in this format (e.g. 1639/40), the
year after the slash indicates the year as we think of it now (1640 in
this case), and the year before the slash is the year as it would have
been recorded at the time (1639 in this case). This way of writing dates
is called double dating.

The year modifier, if supplied, should always be 2 digits, and one
greater than the 2 digits before the slash character, or 00 if the last
2 digits before the slash character are 99 (e.g. 15 April 1699/00). For
English and American dates, year modifiers are only applicable to years
prior to 1752, and even then are only used for dates between 1 January
and 24 March. The date 23rd November 1712 in England, for example, is
not ambiguous, and therefore should not have a year modifier, whereas
23rd January 1712 is ambiguous. Is it 23 Jan 1711/12 or 23 Jan 1712/13?

With Gregorian calendars only, you can also specify B.C. dates by
ticking the B.C. box.

See The Gregorian
Calendar for a brief description of the Gregorian calendar, and
the complexities involved in its introduction.

See How to Enter
Dates for tips on entering dates.
