Item Pointers: Confusions and Pitfalls to Avoid

Items Pointers are Lua Objects

Item pointers are of central importance in the Family Historian API, so
it is important to learn how to use them to access records and
fields. If you previously have encountered pointers in other
programming languages, you may be tempted to think of item pointers as
being similar to these. But actually item pointers are not much
like pointers in other programming languages. They are Lua objects
and behave like Lua objects. If you want to understand how
to use an item pointer, you need to look at the API reference for its
methods, to see what they do and how to use them.

Variable Assignment With Tables and Objects

When you assign an ordinary value to a variable (in Lua and in most
programming languages), the variable acts like a container and stores a
copy of that value. For example, look at the code below:

var1 = 3
var2 = var1 -- this assigns the value of var1 to var2
var1 = 7
fhMessageBox(var2) -- what is the value of var2 at this point?
There are 2 variables in that snippet of code (var1 and
var2). In the first line, the number 3 is assigned to the
variable var1. In the second line, the value of var1 is assigned
to a second variable, var2. At this point, both var1 and var2
store the same value - that is, 3. In the 3rd line, the number 7
is assigned to var1. At this point, var1 contains 7. In the
4th line, the value of var2 is displayed in a message box. What
value would you expect to see? What does var2 contain? If
your answer is 3 - well done, you are correct! When storing
ordinary values like numbers or strings, each variable gets its own copy
of the value. If you change the value in one variable, that
doesn't affect the values stored in any other variable. That may
seem obvious. But something very different happens if you store an
object or a table in a variable. Here is an example with a table:

var1 = {} -- this creates a table
var1.a = 3 -- this assigns 3 to a field called 'a' within the table
var2 = var1 -- this assigns the value of var1 to var2
var1.a = 7
fhMessageBox(var2.a) -- what is the value of var2.a at this point?
Tables in Lua are very powerful programming structures that can be used
for many things, including storing data in a structured way (like the
'data structures' used in some other programming languages). In
the example above, a table is created in the first line, and in the
second line, a value of 3 is assigned to a named field (called 'a'),
within the table. In line 3, the value of var1 is assigned to
var2. In line 4, the 'a' field, within var1, is assigned the value
7. In the last line, the value of the 'a' field within the table
stored in var2 is displayed. What will this value be? If
your answer is 3, you are wrong. This time the answer is 7.
What is going on?

When you assign a table or an object to a variable in Lua, the variable
does not get its own copy of the table or object. That could be
inefficient if the table or object were large. Instead what
happens is that, internally, the variable is in effect given a reference
to the table or object. If you like you could say that the
variable is told where the table or object is (i.e. where it is located
in memory within your computer). And if you assign that variable
to another variable, what happens is that now both variables share a
reference to the same table or object. So if you change the table
(using either of the 2 variables to reference it), the change will
become manifest if you then try to access the same field via the other
variable.

Parameters are Variables

A parameter (to a function or object method) is effectively another
kind of variable. So when you pass a table or object as a
parameter to a function, you are still not creating a copy of
that table or object. You are still passing a reference to that
table or object. Here is another example to illustrate this.

-- first let's define a function 'MyFunction'
function MyFunction(varX)
varX.a = 7
end

-- code execution proper starts here...
var1 = {} -- this creates a table
var1.a = 3 -- this assigns 3 to a field called 'a' within the table
var2 = var1 -- this assigns the value of var1 to var2
MyFunction(var1) -- this calls MyFunction passing in var1
fhMessageBox(var2.a) -- what is the value of var2.a at this point?
So what is the value displayed in the message box when the program
executes? Hopefully you will have guessed at this point that the
answer is 7. The 'MyFunction' function is created (defined) in the
first 3 lines, but isn't actually called (executed) until the second
last line. It is called then with var1 as parameter. Within
the function, the value of 7 is assigned to a field called 'a' within
the referenced table. But there is only one table. So when
we look at the value of 'var2.a' in the last line, we are looking at
this value. Which is why the value displayed is 7.

Assignment 'By Value' and 'By Reference'

When each instance of a variable gets its own copy of the data (as
happens with strings and numbers), this is called assignment by
value. When each instance of a variable gets a reference to
a shared instance of the data, this is called assignment by
reference. So, in Lua, strings and numbers are assigned by
value. But objects and tables are assigned by reference.
Just to be clear: the issues discussed above apply to all objects (and
tables). They don't just apply to item pointers. But a
potential additional source of confusion with item pointers, is that,
unlike most ordinary objects, each item pointer itself also stores
a reference - specifically a reference to the data item that it is
'pointing' to. So, for example, if you have 3 variables that
reference the same item pointer, and the item pointer references John
Smith, you could say that the 3 variables are referencing John Smith,
albeit via the same item pointer.

Garbage Collection

How do you delete a table or object? The answer is: Lua does this
automatically when there are no variables that reference it. This
is called 'Garbage Collection'. If a variable stores a table or
object (that is, in our terms, a reference to a table or
object) you can remove that reference and thereby make that table or
object available for garbage collection (assuming there are no other
variables still referencing it) by assigning anything else to the
variable, such as a number, a string, another object or (most commonly)
'nil'.

Cloning Item Pointers

We have seen that you can't just create a separate copy of an item
pointer by assigning it to more than one variable. That way you
just get 2 variables that reference the same item pointer. So how
can you create a separate copy when you need to (which you sometimes
will)? This is what the item pointer Clone
method is for. It creates and returns a new instance - a separate
copy - of an item pointer. See the documentation for this method for an
example of how it can be used.

Item pointers are used everywhere within Family Historian
plugins. It is important to have a clear understanding of when you
are, or are not, creating a new instance of an item pointer. In
general, any function or object method which returns an item pointer (as
fhNewItemPtr and the
item pointer Clone
method both do, for example), creates a new instance.

Note: as well as the Item
Pointer object, the Date,
and Date Point objects
also each have a Clone method of their own, which can be used to create
a new instance of those objects. In addition, the Age
and Rich Text
objects have Copy methods which are similar, in that they can be used to
copy the values of an object of the same type.

title: Rich Text Syntax
text:
The Family Historian API

Rich Text Syntax

In Family Historian, some fields such as notes can store rich text -
that is, text which uses word-processing features, such as tables,
fonts, styles, record links, and much more. These fields are
stored in FTF syntax.

eFTF syntax is a superset of FTF
syntax, used primarily with reports and books.

Finally, tFTF syntax is a variant of
eFTF syntax, provided for the convenience of plugin authors.

title: Special Issues with Place and Address Fields
breadcrumb: Special Issues with Place and Address Fields
text:
The Family Historian API

Special Issues with Place and Address Fields

How To Keep Life Simple

This page describes special rules which apply to place and address
fields. And at first sight they may appear dauntingly complicated.
However, these rules are only relevant to you if you are working
directly with Place or Address records, or if you wish to use fhSetValueAsLink
or fhSetValue_Copy to
set the value of place and address fields in other records. If
instead of using those functions, you use fhSetValueAsText
to set the value of place and address fields in other records (such as
when you set the place and/or address for an event in an Individual
record, say), you can avoid the complexity described below.

Ordinary Place and Address Fields

There are some special issues that apply to place fields and address
fields, which plugin authors should be aware of. Place and address
fields are common throughout the program. All facts (events and
attributes) have associated place and address fields, for example.
For most purposes, place and address fields look and behave like simple
text fields, but internally they are in fact implemented as links.
When a user enters a value (e.g. "London, UK") in a place field, Family
Historian looks to see if there is already a Place record with this
name. If there is, internally, it stores a link to that Place
record in the place field. If there isn't, it creates a new Place
record with the name required, and stores a link to that Place record
instead. It also takes care of updates to place names, and
deletion of place names in a similar way. If at any point, a Place
record is left with no links to it, as a result of an update, Family
Historian will automatically delete that place record - but only if
there is no information stored in the Place record. Address fields
work in a similar way.

Most of the time, there is no need for ordinary users to be aware of
the special nature of place and address fields, and the extra work
regarding Place and Address records that Family Historian does with
respect to them. However, if users wish to store extra information
about places or addresses (e.g. notes, pictures, longitude and latitude,
etc), they will find that this information is stored in Place or Address
records. Moreover, this data can be accessed using data
references. For data reference purposes, all place fields can be
treated as a link to a Place record, and all address fields can be
treated as a link to an Address record. So, for example, this
expression is valid and will return the latitude and longitude of a
person's date-of-birth, if known:

%INDI.BIRT.PLAC>LATLONG%

All of the above applies also to plugins. Although, as we have seen,
internally place and address fields are really links, they can be treated
as text fields by plugin authors. So, for example, if you want to
set the value for a place field for a given event, you can use fhSetValueAsText.
In fact, until 6.0.2 this was the only option. From 6.0.3 onwards,
you can alternatively use fhSetValueAsLink
to link a place field to a Place record (although, as we will see below,
this can fail if used incorrectly); and from 8.0 onwards, you can use fhSetValueAsLink to link an
address field to an Address record (again, as we will see below, this can
fail if used incorrectly). If you want to get the value of a place or
address field you will ordinarily use fhGetValueAsText.
But you can also use the function fhGetValueAsLink
to get the associated Place or Address record. Plugin authors can,
of course, also use data references which treat place fields as links, to
access Place record data, and can use address fields as links, to access
Address record data.

The Text Field in Place Records

So far when talking about "place fields" we have been talking about
ordinary place fields. But there is one special kind of place
field which behaves differently. This is the place field in a
Place record which stores the actual text of the Place record.
This latter field has the tag "TEXT" unlike all ordinary place fields
which have the tag "PLAC". The TEXT place field is a level one
field within a Place record. It differs from ordinary place fields
in the following respects:

Internally it is not implemented as a link to anything. So
using fhGetValueAsLink or fhSetValueAsLink will fail for this field.

Although you can update the value of this field (using
fhSetValueAsText) be aware that the update will fail if you try to set
the field to an empty value, or if you try to set the value to a place
name that is already in use in another Place record. No two
Place records can share exactly the same place name.

Also, if you do update the value of this field (by providing it with
a valid value), you will in doing so effectively update the value of
all ordinary place fields that link to this Place record.

Unlike ordinary place fields, the TEXT place field cannot be
separately deleted. You can delete a Place record as a whole,
but you cannot separately delete the TEXT place field within it.

Creating Place Records

When you first create a place record, a TEXT field will be
automatically be created for it, with no text in it. You should
set a text value (subject to the above constraints about uniqueness)
straight away. If the user saves and reloads a project that
contains a place record with an empty TEXT field in it, Family Historian
will automatically generate a unique place name value for it. This
will be "(Unidentified place)" followed by a suffix to make it unique,
if necessary.

Addresses, Address Records and the Address-Place Consistency Rule

Addresses in Family Historian can be linked to places, and usually are,
and are unique within their associated place. If they not linked
to a place, they are unique amongst all address that also are not linked
to a place. Every Address record can have an optional link to a
single Place record. An Address record can be linked to at most
one Place record. If an Individual or Family fact is
associated with an address, the following rule applies:

The
Address-Place Consistency Rule

If a fact is linked to an Address record, it must also be linked to the
same Place record that the Address record is linked to, if any. If
the Address record is not linked to a Place record, the fact must not be
linked to a Place record.

To enforce this rule, the following policies are used:

If you set the value of a fact's address field (new or existing)
using fhSetValueAsText,
a new Address record will be automatically created for that address,
if necessary, linked to whatever Place record the fact is linked to,
or to no Place record if the fact had no link to a Place record.
If there is already a suitable Address record, the address field will
be set to link to that Address record.

If you set the value of a fact's place field (new or existing) using
fhSetValueAsText, a new
Place record will be automatically created for that place, if
necessary. If there is already a suitable Place record (the text
matches exactly), the place field will be set to link to that Place
record. If the fact in question also has an address field, the
address field value will be changed to become an address for that
Place record. This will cause the internal link for the
address field to be changed, and may result in a new Address record
being created.

If you try to set the value of a fact's address field (new or
existing) using fhSetValueAsLink
or fhSetValue_Copy, to
specify a link to an Address record, the call will fail if the link
would break the Address-Place Consistency Rule - that is,
if the Address record's Place record link is different from and
inconsistent with the Place record linked to by the fact's place
field.

If you try to set the value of a fact's place field (new or
existing) using fhSetValueAsLink
or fhSetValue_Copy, the
call will again fail if setting the link would break the
Address-Place Consistency Rule. Note that a call to set
the link value of a place field will always succeed if the fact has no
address field. But setting the link value of an address field to
an Address record, will not necessarily succeed if the fact has no
place field. In fact it will only succeed in that case, if the
Address record being linked to also has no associated Place record.

If you delete the place linked to a fact using fhDeleteItem,
if the fact has an address field, the address field value will be
removed - that is, the address field item will be left with a NULL
value. The address field item will not actually be deleted
however.

Within an Address record, the link to a Place record is stored in
the _PLAC field. This is an ordinary link, except in this
respect: you cannot set it using fhSetValueAsLink
or fhSetValue_Copy, or
delete it using fhDeleteItem,
if the Address record has any inbound links (e.g. from an event in an
Individual record). You can however delete the entire Address
record, even if it has inbound links. These will be handled
automatically in that case.

The Text Field in Address Records

So far when talking about "address fields" we have been talking about
ordinary address fields. But there is one special kind of address
field which behaves differently. This is the address field in an
Address record which stores the actual text of the Address record.
This latter field has the tag "TEXT" unlike all ordinary address fields
which have the tag "ADDR". The TEXT place field is a level one
field within an Address record. It differs from ordinary address
fields in the following respects:

Internally it is not implemented as a link to anything. So
using fhGetValueAsLink or fhSetValueAsLink will fail for this field.

Although you can update the value of this field (using
fhSetValueAsText) be aware that the update will fail if you try to set
the field to an empty value, or if you try to set the value to an
address name that is already in use in another Address record linked
to the same Place record. No two Address records linked to the
same Place record can share exactly the same address text. And
no two Address records which at not linked to a Place record can share
exactly the same address text either.

Also, if you do update the value of this field (by providing it with
a valid value), you will in doing so effectively update the value of
all ordinary address fields that link to this Address record.

Unlike ordinary address fields, the TEXT address field cannot be
separately deleted. You can delete an Address record as a whole,
but you cannot separately delete the TEXT address field within it.

Creating Address Records

When you first create an address record, a TEXT field will be
automatically be created for it, with no text in it. You should
first link the Address record to a Place record (if it is to be linked
to a Place record), and then set a text value straight away (subject to
the above constraints about uniqueness). If the user saves and
reloads a project that contains an Address record with an empty TEXT
field in it, Family Historian will automatically generate a suitably
unique address name value for it. This will be "(Unidentified
address)" followed by a suffix to make it unique, if necessary.

title: String Encoding and Unicode
text:
The Family Historian API

String Encoding and Unicode

Introduction

Prior to version 6, Family Historian stored all text (that is, text
'strings') internally using a method of storing text called 'ANSI'.
Since version 6, it now uses 'Unicode'. The significant difference
between the two concerns accent characters and non-English
characters. Using ANSI, it is only possible for an application to
handle a small set of accent characters and a few non-English characters
- mainly, those that are used in a few of the best-known European
languages such as French and German. And even where you can use accent
characters with ANSI, there can be big problems if you try to share your
ANSI data files with people from other countries. Using Unicode,
however, an application can handle all accent characters and all
characters from all the world's languages, and Unicode files can be
shared unproblematically with people from all over the world. So Unicode
is a good thing and a big improvement over ANSI. But there are practical
implications for this change, which plugin authors should be aware of.
Plugins can support Unicode if they wish to, but they don't have to.

Supporting Unicode in Plugins

The Family Historian API specifies the type of parameters that can be
passed to its functions and objects methods, and the type of values
returned by its functions and methods. For example, the parameters and
return values can be pointer objects, date objects, date point objects,
numbers, booleans or tables. They can also be text strings (usually
called either just 'text' or 'strings' for short). The function fhGetDisplayText,
for example, takes up to three parameters, two of which are strings
(both optional as it happens, in this case). It also returns a string.
Hitherto, these parameter strings and string return values have always
been in ANSI (we say that they are 'encoded' as ANSI). From version 6
onwards, depending on the plugin, they may be ANSI or they may be
'UTF-8' - that is, Unicode (UTF-8 is a Unicode encoding).

Plugin scripts are of course themselves written in text. They are saved
in text files. Prior to version 6, plugin scripts have always been saved
in ANSI. From 6 onwards, you have a choice. You can save your script in
either ANSI or UTF-8. This is called the file encoding.
There is also something called the current string encoding.
The rule for the current string encoding is this:

The encoding of all text strings passed as parameters to the
Family Historian API must match the current string encoding. Also, all
strings returned by the Family Historian API will also use the current
string encoding. The only exception to this are the two conversion
functions provided by the Family Historian API (fhConvertANSItoUTF8
and fhConvertUTF8toANSI) which specify what encoding they require and
return.

By default, the current string encoding is the same as the file
encoding. But you can change it if you wish, using the fhSetStringEncoding
function.

A plugin's file encoding is set on the 'Encoding' submenu of the File
menu, within the Plugin Editor.

Pros and Cons of ANSI Plugins

All plugins that were written before version 6, and not updated since,
will be ANSI (that is, both the file encoding and the string encoding
will be ANSI). They will continue to work because Family Historian,
knowing that the plugin is an ANSI plugin, will automatically convert
all strings to (or from) ANSI as required. So, for example, if your
plugin uses the fhGetValueAsText
function to get an Individual's name, Family Historian will return a
string copy of the name converted to ANSI (remember that internally, the
name is now stored in Unicode). What happens if the name contains some
characters that cannot be represented in ANSI? Suppose, for example,
that the person's name is 'Ǥéd'. 'Ǥ' cannot be represented in ANSI, so
in this case Family Historian will return its nearest ANSI equivalent
which is 'G'. The 'é' character can be represented in ANSI - remember
that ANSI can handle some accent characters, just not all of them - so
it will be unchanged (actually, as indicated earlier, there are
complexities relating to ANSI's handling of accent characters, but we
will ignore these for present purposes). And of course 'd', as a simple
alphabetic character, is not a problem. So, if an ANSI plugin called the
function, the value returned would be the string 'Géd' - which is close
to the original, but not 100% correct.

Internally, whenever Family Historian is unable to do a perfect
conversion from Unicode to ANSI, it sets a special 'flag' called the
'Conversion Loss' flag. When it starts running any plugin, Family
Historian will initially set this flag 'off'. But it will be set 'on'
whenever Family Historian has to do an imperfect conversion. Family
Historian itself never sets the flag back off while the plugin is
running. The plugin can find out at any time whether the flag is set or
not by calling the function fhIsConversionLossFlagSet.
The plugin can also manually set this flag on or off at any time by
calling another function fhSetConversionLossFlag.
If when the plugin finishes, the Conversion Loss flag is set, Family
Historian will report to the user that the plugin has completed, and
will mention that "Some accent characters may not have been handled
correctly".

Pros and Cons of UTF-8 Plugins

From version 6 onwards, all new plugins will be encoded in UTF-8 by
default (that is, the file encoding defaults to UTF-8, which means that
the string encoding also defaults to UTF-8). The big advantage of a
UTF-8 plugin is that there is no conversion loss, and all accent
characters and non-English characters can be handled. However, there are
also some disadvantages. UTF-8 strings can be harder to work with and
supporting them may require more work by plugin authors (and a good
understanding of how UTF-8 works). Also, Lua libraries, and even Lua's
own String Manipulation functionality, often provide only limited
support for UTF-8, and, for some purposes, may not support it properly
at all.

Tips on Choosing Between ANSI or UTF-8

If your plugin doesn't work with strings at all, it doesn't matter
which you use.

Unless you have good reason to use ANSI for a plugin, we recommend
that you use UTF-8. This is because it provides better functionality
than ANSI.

Writing plugins in UTF-8 can be harder than ANSI - but isn't
necessarily harder. It depends on what the plugin does. If your plugin
does complex string manipulation (for example, searches for
sub-strings within a string, or replaces or updates portions of a
string), then UTF-8 will be potentially more complicated, and we would
recommend that unless you know what you're doing or relish a
challenge, you should consider using ANSI after all. But if your
plugin doesn't actually alter the contents of strings at all, or
perhaps does only very simple string manipulation (such as appending
one string to another), then working with UTF-8 strings may well be no
harder than working with ANSI - in which case there is no reason not
to use it.

Don't forget that Family Historian provides two conversion
functions, fhConvertANSItoUTF8
and fhConvertUTF8toANSI.
If your plugin is UTF-8, and you want to use a Lua library which
expects ANSI strings, you can use the conversion functions to convert
between the two.

Be aware that there is considerable overlap between ANSI and UTF-8,
and this makes life much easier than it would otherwise be. ANSI
supports 255 characters. The first 127 of these characters are called
'ASCII' characters, and they are the overlap characters - that is,
they are identical in ANSI and UTF-8. These 127 ASCII characters
include all the most common characters that you are likely to come
across - including all ordinary (unaccented) alphabetic characters,
the digits 0 to 9, and all ordinary English punctuation characters,
such as full-stop, comma, question mark, exclamation mark, hyphen,
underscore, brackets, and so on.

All 'constant strings' in the Family Historian API are always ASCII
and are consequently identical in ANSI and UTF-8. For example, suppose
you want to call fhGetContextInfo
to get the name of the current plugin. To do this, you need to pass it
the text string 'CI_PLUGIN_NAME' - a constant string. This string
consists of alphabetic characters and underscores, all of which are
ASCII characters, so it is both a valid ANSI string and a valid UTF-8
string. So there is no need to write
fhGetContextInfo(fhConvertANSItoUTF8('CI_PLUGIN_NAME')), even in a
module (see next section). It will work, but it's unnecessary.
You instead write fhGetContextInfo('CI_PLUGIN_NAME'), and this will
work, regardless of the current string encoding.

All data references and tags in the Family Historian API are also
guaranteed to only use ASCII characters. So, again, you don't need to
worry about whether these are ANSI or UTF-8 as they will always be
valid strings in either encoding.

Special Handling for Modules

The rule that string encoding (by default) matches the file
encoding does not apply to modules (scripts that provide functions
designed to be called by other scripts). If a module calls the Family
Historian API, it must be aware that the string encoding that Family
Historian expects and returns, will be determined by the encoding of the
main plugin script (or by the most recent call to fhSetStringEncoding if
there has been one), and is not affected by the file encoding of the
module script. A module can check what kind of string encoding is in use
by calling either fhGetStringEncoding() or
fhGetContextInfo('CI_STRING_ENCODING').

title: tFTF Syntax
text:
The Family Historian API

tFTF Syntax

tFTF syntax is a text-only alternative to eFTF
syntax that is provided for the convenience of plugin
authors. It is currently only supported as an option in the
context of the SetText
method of RichText objects. It allows rich-text to be
constructed entirely as a text string (unlike FTF
syntax and eFTF syntax which
require the use of rich text object methods to add record links and
citations). The only limitation of tFTF syntax is that you
cannot add citations using this syntax. You can however
add record links. The tFTF syntax for record links is given
below. Apart from record links and citations, tFTF syntax is in
all other respects identical to eFTF syntax.

Record Link Syntax

Record links in tFTF have a very similar syntax to their syntax in FTF
syntax. A tFTF record link is still marked by the <rec=(params)>
command. Like FTF syntax, this has three parameters. The
only difference is with respect to the first parameter. In FTF
syntax, this is an index into the record table. In tFTF
syntax it is the qualified record id (see fhGetQualifiedRecordId)
Parameters 2 and 3 are the same in both syntaxes: these are display
text, and a flag. The latter indicates whether
the link is automatic or not. The display text is used
if the qualified record id is invalid or if the record is not found or
if the link is not automatic. The flag (the 3rd parameter) is set
to 'auto' if the link is automatic and 'text' if it isn't. If a
link is automatic, this means that the link is displayed as the record's
display name, and it is updated automatically if that changes. If
the flag is 'text', the display text is always shown as the display for
the link. This is an example of what a record link might look like
in tFTF syntax: <rec=I67,"my
father",text>; and this is another example: <rec=I67,"John Smith",auto>. The
qualified record id consists of a letter indicating the record type (in
the example, this is the letter 'I' for 'Individual') followed by the
record id (67 in the example).

title: The fhFileUtils Module
text:
The Family Historian API

The fhFileUtils Module

The fhFileUtils module is a library of functions to handle files with
Unicode file names that are not supported by the standard Lua LFS and IO
methods To make use of the fhFileUtils module, you must include a link
like this near the start of your plugin:

fhfu = require("fhFileUtils");

Thereafter you can call fhFileUtils functions like this:

local bResult = fhfu.copyFile('fromfile.txt','tofile.txt');

You don't have to use 'fhfu' as the module name. That is just a
convention.

The documentation for the fhFileUtils module is located at http://pluginstore.family-historian.co.uk/fhutils/files/fhFileUtils.html.

title: The fhSQL Module
text:
The Family Historian API

The fhSQL Module

The fhSQL module is a library of functions to access SQL based databases. You
must include a link like this near the start of your plugin:

require("fhSQL");

Thereafter you can call fhSQL functions like this:

local db = fhSQL.connect("Provider=Microsoft.Jet.OLEDB.4.0;Data Source="..dbfile)

The documentation for the fhSQL module is located at http://pluginstore.family-historian.co.uk/fhutils/files/fhSQL.html.

Additional examples can be found here.

title: The fhUtils Module
text:
The Family Historian API

The fhUtils Module

The fhUtils module is a library of functions (and one object: PCite) that
was created to make it easier to write Source-driven
Data Entry Plugins. However, it can be used for other purposes
too. To make use of the fhutils module, you must include a link like
this near the start of your plugin:

fh = require("fhUtils");

Thereafter you can call fhUtils functions like this:

local PCite = fh.LoadPreparedCitation();

You don't have to use 'fh' as the module name. That is just a
convention.

The module implements an object called PCite, which represents a prepared
citation. In the example above, a PCite object has been created and
returned by the LoadPreparedCitation function.

The documentation for the fhUtils module is located at http://pluginstore.family-historian.co.uk/fhutils/files/fhUtils.html.

title: Introduction to Family Historian Plugins
text:
Introduction to Family Historian Plugins

Plugins are a way of extending the capabilities of an application -
in this case, Family Historian. Some applications support a kind
of plugin that can only be written by software developers using
special tools. Family Historian plugins are not like that.
They are user-level plugins - which means that they can be
written by anyone. Family Historian provides all the tools you need,
and all the documentation - either in this Help file, or in linked
websites.

Plugins can be used to access, analyze and manipulate Family
Historian data in any way. Family Historian plugins are stored
in files, and can be shared between users in the same way that queries
can. You can download plugins written by others from the Family
Historian Plugin Store, or from other sources. Family Historian
plugins are written using a language called Lua,
which is simple to use, but also very powerful. In order to
access and update Family Historian data, a selection of functions
and objects are provided by the Family
Historian API (Application Programming Interface).

What can you do with plugins?

The short answer is that using plugins, you can do just about
anything with the data in your projects. You can access all of
your data, and make any changes you want to your data records. Plugins
can be very small and simple, or very large and ambitious. Here
are just some examples of possible applications:

Create a new search-and-replace tool for doing a special kind of
search and replace on data throughout your file, perhaps using
complex conditions

Create a new tool for importing data directly from a spreadsheet
or from some other genealogy program

Make changes to data throughout an entire project to restructure
the way data is organised within it

Design new kinds of charts, queries or reports

Create a new kind of website generator or family tree CD/DVD
generator

Build new data-entry forms, to make it easier to enter particular
kinds of data

Create a new tool for analysing data and/or presenting it
graphically

'Clean up' data and resolve inconsistencies throughout a project

and much more...

Writing Plugins

Getting started with plugins is not difficult, even if you have never
done any kind of programming before. A good place to start is How
To Write Plugins. If you have previously written scripts,
macros, plugins or computer programs, you can if you wish jump straight
in by checking out the Lua Quick Guide
and the Family Historian API.

title: Additional Lua Libraries
text:
Lua

Additional Lua Libraries

Introduction

We have already seen that the toolkit library, IUP, can be used to
create user interfaces. IUP is an example of a Lua module - a
library of functions and objects, that extend the powers of Lua.
This section describes various other Lua modules which are available to
be used, as part of the Family Historian implementation of Lua.

LFS - the Lua File System

Version 1.7

To use LFS you must add the following line to your plugin (usually near
the top of it):

require('lfs')
LFS offers the following functions:

lfs.attributes (filepath [,
aname])
Returns a table with the file attributes corresponding to filepath
(or nil followed by an error message in case of error).
If the second optional argument is given, then only the value of the
named attribute is returned (this use is equivalent to lfs.attributes(filepath).aname,
but the table is not created and only one attribute is retrieved from
the O.S.). The attributes are described as follows; attribute mode
is a string, all the others are numbers, and the time related
attributes use the same time reference of os.time:

dev
On Windows systems, represents the drive number of the disk
containing the file
mode
string representing the associated protection mode (the values
could be file, directory, link,
socket, named pipe, char device,
block device or other)
nlink
number of hard links to the file
rdev
On Windows systems represents the same as dev
access
time of last access
modification
time of last data modification
change
time of last file status change
size
file size, in bytes
blocks
block allocated for file; (Unix only)
blksize
optimal file system I/O blocksize; (Unix only)

This function uses stat internally thus if the given filepath
is a symbolic link, it is followed (if it points to another link the
chain is followed recursively) and the information is about the file
it refers to. To obtain information about the link itself, see
function lfs.symlinkattributes.
lfs.chdir (path)
Changes the current working directory to the given path.

Returns true in case of success or nil
plus an error string.
lfs.lock_dir(path,
[seconds_stale])
Creates a lockfile (called lockfile.lfs) in path if it
does not exist and returns the lock. If the lock already exists checks
it it's stale, using the second parameter (default for the second
parameter is INT_MAX, which in practice means the lock
will never be stale. To free the the lock call lock:free().

In case of any errors it returns nil and the error message. In
particular, if the lock exists and is not stale it returns the "File
exists" message.
lfs.currentdir ()
Returns a string with the current working directory or nil
plus an error string.
iter, dir_obj = lfs.dir (path)
Lua iterator over the entries of a given directory. Each time the
iterator is called with dir_obj it returns a directory
entry's name as a string, or nil if there are no more
entries. You can also iterate by calling dir_obj:next(),
and explicitly close the directory before the iteration finished with
dir_obj:close(). Raises an error if path is
not a directory.
lfs.lock (filehandle, mode[,
start[, length]])
Locks a file or a part of it. This function works on open files;
the file handle should be specified as the first argument. The string
mode could be either r (for a read/shared
lock) or w (for a write/exclusive lock). The optional
arguments start and length can be used to
specify a starting point and its length; both should be numbers.

Returns true if the operation was successful; in case of
error, it returns nil plus an error string.
lfs.mkdir (dirname)
Creates a new directory. The argument is the name of the new
directory.

Returns true if the operation was successful; in case of
error, it returns nil plus an error string.
lfs.rmdir (dirname)
Removes an existing directory. The argument is the name of the
directory.

Returns true if the operation was successful; in case of
error, it returns nil plus an error string.
lfs.setmode (file, mode)
Sets the writing mode for a file. The mode string can be either binary
or text. Returns the previous mode string for the file.
This function is only available in Windows, so you may want to make
sure that lfs.setmode exists before using it.
lfs.symlinkattributes
(filepath [, aname])
Identical to lfs.attributes except that
it obtains information about the link itself (not the file it refers
to). This function is not available in Windows so you may want to make
sure that lfs.symlinkattributes exists before using it.

lfs.touch (filepath [, atime [,
mtime]])
Set access and modification times of a file. This function is a bind
to utime function. The first argument is the filename,
the second argument (atime) is the access time, and the
third argument (mtime) is the modification time. Both
times are provided in seconds (which should be generated with Lua
standard function os.time). If the modification time is
omitted, the access time provided is used; if both times are omitted,
the current time is used.

Returns true if the operation was successful; in case of
error, it returns nil plus an error string.
lfs.unlock (filehandle[, start[,
length]])
Unlocks a file or a part of it. This function works on open
files; the file handle should be specified as the first
argument. The optional arguments start and length
can be used to specify a starting point and its length; both should be
numbers.

Returns true if the operation was successful; in case of
error, it returns nil plus an error string.
More information on LFS can be found at keplerproject.github.io/luafilesystem/

N.B Extended UTF-8 file names are not well supported by LFS. See fhFileUtils
for an alternate option.

LuaCom

Version 1.3

Also available is LuaCOM, which allows Lua programs to use and
implement objects that follow Microsoft's Component Object Model (COM)
specification and use the Automation technology for property access
and method calls. This means it can be used to write directly to
Microsoft Office documents or to make web requests. It is very
much an advanced module, but there are examples on the User group
Knowledge base for using it.

Currently, the LuaCOM library supports the following features:

dynamic instantiation of COM objects registered in the system
registry, via the CreateObject method;

dynamic access to running COM objects via GetObject;

COM method calls as normal Lua function calls and property accesses
as normal table field accesses;

ability to read type libraries and to generate HTML documentation
on-the-fly for COM objects;

use of COM objects without type information;

type conversion between OLE Automation types and Lua types;

object disposal using Lua garbage collection mechanism;

implementation of COM interfaces and objects using Lua tables;

implementation of OLE controls using Lua tables

use of COM connection point mechanism for bidirectional
communication and event handling

To use luacom simply include:

require "luacom"
For more information on using LuaCom can be found at LuaCom Documentation

Penlight

Version 1.8

Penlight brings together a
set of generally useful pure Lua modules, focusing on input data
handling (such as reading configuration files), functional
programming (such as map, reduce, placeholder expressions, etc), and
OS path management. Much of the functionality is inspired by the
Python standard libraries.

There are several ways to require Penlight, the simplest is to use:

require "pl.init"
Please see the Penlight Documentation for more information.

LuaSocket

Version 2.0.2

LuaSocket is a Lua extension library
that is composed by two parts: a C core that provides support for the
TCP and UDP transport layers, and a set of Lua modules that add support
for functionality commonly needed by applications that deal with the
Internet.

The core support has been implemented so that it is both efficient and
simple to use. It is available to any Lua application once it has been
properly initialized by the interpreter in use. The code has been tested
and runs well on several Windows and Unix platforms.

Among the support modules, the most commonly used implement the SMTP
(sending e-mails), HTTP (WWW access) and FTP (uploading and downloading
files) client protocols. These provide a very natural and generic
interface to the functionality defined by each protocol. In addition,
you will find that the MIME (common encodings), URL (anything you could
possible want to do with one) and LTN12 (filters, sinks, sources and
pumps) modules can be very handy.

The base use of Socket can be started by using

local socket = require("socket")
See the LuaSocket Documentation for more information

MD5

Version 1.2

MD5 offers checksum facilities for Lua 5.X: a hash (digest) function,
a pair crypt/decrypt based on MD5 and CFB, and a pair crypt/decrypt
based on DES with 56-bit keys.

Note that although MD5 was designed to be used as a cryptographic hash
function, it was found that key collisions could be calculated in a few
seconds, thus it should not be used where a cryptographic hash is
required.

Its most common use in plugins is checking the MD5 value of files or
strings, for example

md5 = require "md5"
sTest = 'This is my string'
print(md5.sumhexa(sTest))

See the MD5 documentation for more information.

UTF 8

Version 13 Jul 2021

This library provides simple way to add UTF-8 support into your
application.

See User Group documentation for usage.
IUP and related Modules

IUP Version 3.28

CD Version 5.12 required for IUP see CD Documentation

IM Version 3.13 required for IUP see IM Documentation

See the User Group knowledge base for more information. Lua References and Library Modules

Additional Family Historian Modules

See also

fhUtils

fhFileUtils

fhSQL

title: Converting Lua 5.1 Plugins to Lua 5.3
text:
IUP

Converting Lua 5.1 Plugins to Lua 5.3

Description

From Version 7, Family Historian uses Lua 5.3. This means some plugins
written for Version 5 or 6 of Family Historian will need to be changed
to work on Version 7. Care is needed if you wish to make these
changes in a way that is backwardly compatible with Lua 5.1 (that is, if
you want your plugin to be able to run under Family Historian 7, but
also be able to run under version 5 or 6 of Family Historian).

The guidance given here is not exhaustive. For more information,
please see the sections on ‘Incompatiblities with the Previous
Version’ of the Lua 5.2 Reference Manual and the Lua 5.3 Reference
Manual (at https://www.lua.org/manual/5.2/manual.html#8
and https://www.lua.org/manual/5.3/manual.html#8
respectively).

Checking Your Version

Within a plugin, you can check which version of Lua is running by using
the _VERSION value.

if _VERSION == 'Lua 5.1' then
fhMessageBox('Lua 5.1 in use')
end

Modules

User-written modules need to be created using tables. See Modules
in the Lua Quick Guide for more information.

Lua Patterns

Previously, both % and the slash character were permitted as escape
characters. Lua
patterns can now only use % as the escape character; so all plugins
using patterns will need to be checked to ensure that the correct
escape character is used.

IUP

Plugins that use IUP must now explicitly 'require' it (this was
optional in V6 and earlier) and the IUP CUSTOMQUIT flag must be
set. See Using IUP for details.

TABLE.GETN and unpack

The getn option to count the number of items in a table has
been removed. This can be worked around by defining getn in your
plugin. In 5.1 you could use unpack to unpack a table.
This has been replaced with table.unpack. You can get
around this by defining it or by replacing unpack with
table.unpack. The former option is backwardly compatible with 5.1.

if not(table.getn) then
function table.getn(t)
local count = 0
for _, __ in pairs(t) do
count = count + 1
end
return count
end
end
if _VERSION == "Lua 5.3" then
unpack = table.unpack
end

arg

The arg table which was automatically created in 5.1, is no
longer created in 5.3. You can workaround this, and retain
backwards compatibility with 5.1, by inserting the following code into
functions which use the ... argument:

arg = {...}
arg['n'] = #arg
The following example illustrates this:

function test(...)
arg = {...}
arg['n'] = #arg
for i,v in ipairs(arg) do
print(i,v)
end
end

print(_VERSION)
test(1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8)
os.tmpname

The os.temp variable now returns the full file name with the
path. The following will make the call backwardly compatible with
5.1:

local filename = os.tmpname()..'.html'
if _VERSION ~= 'Lua 5.1' then
filename = os.getenv('TEMP')..filename
end
string.gfind

string.gfind has been renamed string.gmatch.

-- Either
string.gfind = string.gmatch

-- or replace string.gfind with string.gmatch then use

if _VERSION == 'Lua 5.1' then
string.gmatch = string.gfind
end

title: iup.Alarm
text:
IUP

iup.Alarm

Description

Shows message box, with a number of buttons. It returns the number of the button pressed. Up to 3 buttons can be used.

Syntax

iButton = iup.Alarm(strTitle,strMessage,strbutton1[,strbutton2[,strbutton3]])

Parameters

strTitle
string: title for the message box
strMessage

string: text to appear in message box. \n can be used to split the lines of the message.

strButton

string: title of the button. Any number of buttons can be defined.

Returns

iButton
integer: number of the button pressed.

Example

b = iup.Alarm("iupAlarm Example", "File not saved! Save it now?" ,"Yes" ,"No" ,"Cancel")

-- Shows a message for each selected button
if b == 1 then
iup.Message("Save file", "File saved successfully - leaving script")
elseif b == 2 then
iup.Message("Save file", "File not saved - leaving script anyway")
elseif b == 3 then
iup.Message("Save file", "Operation cancelled")
end

title: iup.GetParam
text:
IUP

iup.GetParam

Description

Allows a complex input box to be built easily within a single action.

Syntax

iRet,mixedvalues, ... = iup.GetParam(strTitle,fnparm_action,strLayout,[initial
values,...])

Parameters

strTitle
string: title for the text box
fnparm_action
function: function to handle cancel and close processing, can be
nil for default actions

strLayout
string: string containing the layout for the dialog.
initial values
One or more values to be displayed on the dialog, depending on the
layout string.
Returns

iRet
integer: a status code 1 if the OK button is pressed, 0 if the
user canceled or if an error occurred.
mixedvalues
One or more values returned from the dialog, depending on the
layout string.

Layout String Instructions

The format string must have the following format, notice the "\n" at
the end of eacb parameter line.

"text%x[extra]{tip}\n",
where:

text is a descriptive text, to be placed to
the left of the entry field in a label.

x is the type of the parameter. The valid
options are:

b = boolean (shows a True/False toggle, returns 1
or 0 not true false)

i = integer (shows a integer number filtered text
box)

r = real (shows a real number filtered text box)

a = angle in degrees (shows a real number
filtered text box and a dial)

s = string (shows a text box)

m = multiline string (shows a multiline text box)

l = list (shows a dropdown list box)

t = separator (shows a horizontal line separator
label, in this case text can be an empty string, not included in
parameter count)

f = string (same as s, but also
show a button to open a file selection dialog box)

c = string (same as s, but also
show a color button to open a color selection dialog box)

u = buttons names (allow to redefine the OK and
Cancel button names, and to add a Help button, use [ok,cancel,help]
as extra data, can omit one of them, it will use the default name,
not included in parameter count)

o = list (shows a list of toggles inside a radio)
(since IUP 3.3)

n = string (same as s, but also
show a font button to open a font selection dialog (since
IUP 3.3)

extra is one or more additional options
for the given type

[min,max,step] are
optional limits for integer and real types. The max
and step values can be omitted. When min
and max are specified a valuator will also be added
to change the value. To specify step, max
must be also specified. step is the size of the
increment.

[false,true] are optional strings for boolean
types to be displayed after the toggle. The strings can not have
commas ',', nor brackets '[' or ']'.

mask is an optional mask for the string and multiline
types. The dialog uses the MASK attribute internally. In this case we
do no use the brackets '[' and ']'
to avoid confusion with the specified mask.

|item0|item1|item2,...| are the items of the list.
At least one item must exist. Again the brackets are not used to
increase the possibilities for the strings, instead you must use '|'.
Items index are zero based start.

[dialogtype|filter|directory|nochangedir|nooverwriteprompt]
are the respective attribute values passed to the
GetFile control when activated. All commas must exist, but you
can let empty values to use the default values. No mask can be set.

tip is a string that is displayed in a TIP for the
main control of the parameter. (since 3.0)

There is no extra parameters for the color string. The mask is
automatically set to capture 3 or 4 unsigned integers from 0 to 255 (R
G B) or (R G B A) (alpha is optional).

The number of lines in the format string ("\n"s) will determine the
number of required parameters. But separators will not count as
parameters.

Example

premoveblanks = 1
pconvertnotes = 1

-- Prompt User to Confirm Options
ret, premoveblanks, pconvertnotes =
iup.GetParam("Family Historian Note Tidy", param_action,
"Remove Blank Start Lines: %b\n"..
"Convert single use Notes to Local: %b\n",
premoveblanks, pconvertnotes)

if (ret == 0) then
return
end

title: iup.GetText
text:
IUP

iup.GetText

Description

Shows a multiline text box. It returns the contents of the text box,
when OK is pressed.

Syntax

strEndingText = iup.GetText(strTitle,strStartingText)

Parameters

strTitle
string: title for the text box
strStartingText
string: text to appear in text box. \n can be used to
split the lines of the message.

strButton
string: title of the button. Any number of buttons can be defined.
Returns

strEndingText
string: Text from text box, nil if window closed or cancel
button pressed.

Example

strStory = [[Example Story
This is a long story
with many lines of text
to present
]]
strNewStory = iup.GetText('Tell me a Story',strStory)

title: iup.Message
text:
IUP

iup.Message

Description

Shows a simple message box similar to that for fhMessageBox,
but allows the title of the message box to be controlled.

Syntax

iup.Message(strTitle,strMessage)

Parameters

strTitle
string: title for the message box
strMessage
string: text to appear in message box. \n can be used
to split the lines of the message.

Returns

none

Example

iup.Message('A Simple Lua Script', 'Hello World!')

title: iup.GetFile
text:
IUP

iup.GetFile

Description

Shows a file prompt. It returns the file selected, when OK is pressed.

Syntax

strEndingText = iup.GetFile(strFileName,strReturn)

Parameters

strFilename
string: This parameter is used as an input value to define the
default filter and directory. Example: "../docs/*.txt". As an
output value, it is used to contain the filename entered by the
user.
strStartingText

Returns

strFileName
string: The selected Filename.
strReturn
integer: return status number.

0
Existing File Selected
1
New file selected
-1
Operation Cancelled
-2
Allocation Error
-3
Invalid Parameter

Example

f, err = iup.GetFile("*.txt")
if err == 1 then
iup.Message("New file", f)
elseif err == 0 then
iup.Message("File already exists", f)
elseif err == -1 then
iup.Message("IupFileDlg", "Operation canceled")
elseif err == -2 then
iup.Message("IupFileDlg", "Allocation error")
elseif err == -3 then
iup.Message("IupFileDlg", "Invalid parameter")
end

title: Create User Interfaces with IUP
text:
IUP

Create User Interfaces with IUP

The Family Historian API only contains three functions which display a
user interface. These are:

fhPromptUserForDate
prompt for a date.

fhPromptUserForRecordSel
a prompt for record selection (any record type)

fhMessageBox
a simple message box

If you have more complex user interface requirements, you need to use
IUP. IUP is a toolkit for building graphical user interfaces. It is
designed to be used from within Lua. Here is an example of a very simple
Lua script, written using IUP:

require("iuplua")

iup.SetGlobal("CUSTOMQUITMESSAGE","YES")

iup.Message('A Simple Lua Script', 'Hello World!')

All that this script does is to display a simple message with the
caption "A Simple Lua Script", and the message "Hello World!".

Whenever you wish to use IUP in a Lua script, you must add these two
lines:

require("iuplua")
iup.SetGlobal("CUSTOMQUITMESSAGE","YES")

Do not omit the second line! If you do, Family Historian is
likely to close when the plugin exits. This is due to the way IUP
is designed.

To learn more about using IUP see http://www.tecgraf.puc-rio.br/iup/.
Bear in mind when reading the documentation that IUP was designed to be
used from within one or two other languages, as well as Lua.

A few of the more commonly-used IUP functions have been included in
this help file.

iup.Message
Simple Message Box

iup.Alarm
Prompt User for response with multiple buttons

iup.GetText
Prompt for a long string of text, for example a note

iup.GetFile
Prompt for a file or directory name

iup.GetParam
Prompt for a list of parameters

Some IUP options such as graph plotting require additional libraries to
be loaded. In order to use them you simply require the additional
libraries, after you have loaded IUP. In the example below a graph is
created and then displayed using the iup_plot library.

require("iuplua")

iup.SetGlobal("CUSTOMQUITMESSAGE","YES")
require("iuplua_plot")

plot = iup.plot{
TITLE = "Simple Line",
MARGINBOTTOM="65",
MARGINLEFT="65",
AXS_XLABEL="Year",
AXS_YLABEL="Number",
LEGENDSHOW="YES",
LEGENDPOS="TOPLEFT",
}

iup.PlotBegin(plot, 0)
iup.PlotAdd(plot, 1800, 6)
iup.PlotAdd(plot, 1900, 21)
iup.PlotEnd(plot)

d = iup.dialog{plot, size="600x200", title="IUP Plot"}
d:show()

iup.MainLoop()

Calling fhUpdateDisplay
before calling IUP functions

You must always be careful to call the function fhUpdateDisplay
just before calling any IUP function or method that displays a window or
dialog box, if there is any chance that you have previously changed any
Family Historian data since the start of the script, or since you last
called fhUpdateDisplay.
The purpose of the function fhUpdateDisplay
is to give Family Historian a chance to update any part of its display
that may be affected by any changes you have made. Suppose, for example,
that you have deleted a record. If this record was showing on a diagram,
or in the Records Window, calling fhUpdateDisplay
will give Family Historian a chance to remove it. If you don't call that
function, when you call an IUP function to display a window or dialog
box, the consequences can be unpredictable (the Family Historian display
is likely to look odd and wrong, at the very least).

Here is an example (DON'T RUN THIS SCRIPT - read the note below
first!):

ptrDelete = fhNewItemPtr()
ptrDelete:MoveToFirstRecord('INDI')
fhDeleteItem(ptrDelete) -- deletes the first Individual record in the project
fhUpdateDisplay() -- Only needed because fhDeleteItem will have changed data
iup.Message('Another Lua Script', 'One Individual record has been deleted!')
-- can now be called safely thanks to fhUpdateDisplay

Don't run this script - or not unless you know
what you are doing and are running it on a test project. The reason you
shouldn't run it is it simply deletes the first Individual record in the
current project! The point of the script is simply to illustrate the use
of fhUpdateDisplay.
The script incidentally is not a very good one as it has no error
checking. If it you run it in an empty project, it will still display a
message box saying that an individual record has been deleted, even
though in fact it hasn't.

If at any given point in a script, you're not sure whether you have
made any data changes or not, you should call fhUpdateDisplay
anyway to be on the safe side. It will do nothing if no changes have
been made, so it never does any harm to call it. There is no need to
call this function before calling a Family Historian API function, like
fhMessageBox or fhPromptUserForRecordSel
as 'fh' functions will automatically take care of updating the
application display themselves.

Ensuring your Window stays on top

-- Get Family Historian Parent Window
hWnd = fhGetContextInfo("CI_PARENT_HWND");

btn = iup.flatbutton { name="ok", title="OK",
flat_action = function()
return iup.CLOSE
end
}
dlg = iup.dialog{btn; title="Test dialog"}
-- Set Parent Window for Dialog
iup.SetAttribute(dlg, "NATIVEPARENT", hWnd);

title: Introduction to Lua
text:
Introduction to Lua

Lua is a powerful, fast, lightweight,
embeddable scripting language. It is used in many commercial
applications, such as Adobe Lightroom and the major online game "World Of
Warcraft". Its emphasis is on ease-of-use for non-programmers. Many
of the things which programmers of other languages need worry about are
handled automatically by Lua. As implemented in Family Historian, it
provides the ability to access and amend all of the data in your project -
that is, all fields and all records. Family Historian uses Lua
version 5.3.
Getting Started With Lua

Getting started with plugins is not difficult, even if you have
never written any scripts before. A good starting-point is How
To Write Plugins. If you have previously written scripts, macros
or plugins, you can jump straight in by checking out the Lua
Quick Guide and the Family Historian
API Introduction.

More Information On Lua

There are links to Lua websites on the Help menu of the Plugin
Editor. More information can also be found by clicking on the
links below:

lua.org

lua.org
Reference Manual On-line - Version 5.3

FHUG : Lua Knowledge Base

Lua
Users Wiki

Programing
In Lua

A
short Lua FAQ

title: Lua Quick Guide
text:
Lua

Lua Quick Guide

This quick guide is aimed primarily at people who have developed
plugins, programs or macros previously using other macro, script or
programming languages. Newcomers to plugins should first see How
to Write Plugins.

Some Basics...

Lua is a case-sensitive language

Lua is dynamically typed. Variables in Lua do not have fixed
types, and there are no type definitions for them.

Keywords

and break do else elseif end false for
function if in local nil not or repeat
return then true until while

Note: keywords are case sensitive so you can define a variable called
For and it will not be treated as a keyword.

Comments

Comments starts with a double hyphen (--) anywhere outside a
string. If the text immediately after a double hyphen (--)
is not two opening square brackets ([[), the comment is
a short comment, which runs until the end of the line. Otherwise, it
is a long comment, which runs until the corresponding closing pair of
square brackets (]]). Long comments are
frequently used to disable code temporarily.

Example:

fhMessageBox("Hello Family Historian !") -- this is a line with a comment at the end

Variables

Variables have to start with a character or an underscore

Numeric Lua variables are 32 bit signed floating point or
integers

Variables used in the script header must be lowercase
latin characters from a to z

Before the first assignment to a variable, its value is nil
.

There are three kinds of variables in Lua: global variables,
local variables, and table fields.

Any variable is assumed to be global unless explicitly
declared as a local.

Global variables are visible from anywhere

Local variables are only visible from inside their scope:
the scope of this variables begins at the first statement after
their declaration and lasts until the end of the innermost block
that includes the declaration. They can be declared anywhere inside
a block and start with the initial assignment local

Strings

Strings are delimited by single quotation marks ' ' ,
double quotation marks " " or square brackets [[ ]]
. Only the bracket form may cover multiple lines.

Strings can be concatenated by two dots ..

They can contain most of the C-like escape sequences like '\f'
(form feed), '\r' (carriage return) or '\t'
(horizontal tab).

If a backslash character is required in a string (e.g. in a folder
path) the \ must be doubled (e.g c:\\).

Strings in Lua can contain any 8-bit value, including embedded
zeros, which can be specified as '\0'

Control Structures

Lua supports a range of control structures including

if then else

if bCondition then
-- condition true
else
-- condition
end
if bCondition then
-- condition true
elseif bCondition2
-- condition false and condition 2 true
end

for

for i=1,10 do
-- loops 10 times
end

while

i = 1
while i < 10 do
-- loops 10 times
i = i + 1
end

repeat

i = 10
repeat
print(i)
i = i-1
until i==0

Tables

tables are declared using curly brackets (e.g. tblSurnames = {})

they can contain values of all types, including other tables

To iterate over the elements contained in a table, the operators
ipairs() or pairs() can be used:

ipairs() iterates only over the indices in a
table (only outputs the numerically indexed content)
pairs() iterates over the keys in a table
for i,strdata in ipairs(tbldata) do
print(i,strdata)
end

Tables as arrays

Tables can be used to hold arrays of information. Table
constructors can contain a comma separated list of objects to
create an array. The array elements can be accessed using square
brackets, table[index].

t = { 1,1,2,3,5,8,13 }
print( t[1] ) -- returns: 1
print( t[0] ) -- returns: nil
print( t[4] ) -- returns: 3

Notice that the indexing into the array starts at 1, not
at zero. t[0] has the value nil , i.e.
there is no element at position 0.

Tables as dictionaries

Tables can also be used to store information which is not
indexed numerically, or sequentially, as arrays are.
In this dictionary usage, each element pair has a key
and a value. The key is used to identify
the element (either for setting the value or for retrieving it).
A key need not be a number. It can be a string -
or a value of any other Lua variable type (but not nil).

t = { apple="green", orange="orange", banana="yellow" }
for k,v in pairs(t) do print(k,v) end
returns: apple green
orange orange
banana yellow

Note: that there's no guarantee as to the order in which keys will
be stored in a table when using dictionaries so the order of
retrieval of keys using pairs() is not defined.

A single table can be used as both an array and as a
dictionary. You are not restricted to using table constructors
as just sequentially indexed lists, or as dictionaries. You
can mix the two together.

More information and table examples can be found here: lua-users.org/wiki/Tablestutorial

functions

Functions are named bits of processing code that perform some
tasks, such as calculating values or displaying information.
Lua itself provides many functions you can call from within your own
plugins. The Family Historian API also provides many more
functions that you can also call (How
to Write Plugins shows you how to call the fhMessageBox
function for example). But you can also define and call your
own functions. Functions can take one or more parameters
which act as data input to the function.

Functions are defined using the following syntax:

function functionname(parameters)
-- function action
return variable
end

objects

Objects, in Lua programming terms, are in some ways like a new data
type for variables (remember that variables have a data type, like string
or number). Like other data types, objects
too can be assigned to variables. So you could see an object
as a new and different kind of value for a variable.
But they are also somewhat similar to functions in that
they can contain named processing code. Where a named bit of
processing is part of an object, it is called a Method.
The Family Historian API includes seven types of object, each of
which has numerous methods. Like functions, methods can also
take parameters.

To call a function in a plugin, you simply write the name of the
function followed by round brackets. Any parameters are added
between these round brackets. Calling an object method is the
same, except that the method name must be preceded by the name of
the variable that stores the object, with a colon (:) separating the
variable name from the method name. A common mistake is to
write a full-stop instead of a colon, so be careful not to do that -
it can be a hard mistake to spot!

In the example below, ptrBase is a variable which stores
the item pointer object return by the function function call
'fhNewItemPtr'. The second line calls the 'MoveToFirstRecord'
method for the item pointer object, passing in the string 'INDI' as
parameter.

ptrBase = fhNewItemPtr()
ptrBase:MoveToFirstRecord('INDI') -- Get First Individual in File

Recommended Script header

It is recommended, although not essential, to include a comment
header in your scripts in the format illustrated by this example:

--[[
@title: test script
@author: Fred Blogs
@lastupdated: June 2010
@description:
This is a Test Script which provides an example header layout.
It displays a message box saying "Hello World"
]]

fhMessageBox("Hello Family Historian !") -- this is a line with a comment at the end
If you add a header such as the one above, the Plugin List window
will display the information in it, when you select the script -
making it much easier to identify the required script. To quickly add
a script header, select Insert Script Header from the Edit menu.

Modules

Lua makes it easy to create and use modules of
functions. Modules are libraries of functions which are stored
in their own plugin script file. They can be included within any
script, using the require statement.

require "module"
Modules are saved and stored in the plugin area, like any other
plugin. Although not essential, it is recommended that all
modules should start with the following code:

if ... == nil then error('This is a Module') end
module(..., package.seeall)
--------------------------------
This code will throw an error, stating that the plugin is a module,
if the module is run directly (instead of being called from another
plugin). The use of modules makes it easy to re-use code.
However, it is a requirement of the Family Historian plugin store that
each plugin can be run independently, and has no dependencies - i.e.
makes no use of modules. So if you have a plugin and you wish to
submit it for inclusion in the plugin store, all module functions
called by the plugin must be moved "inline", prior to submission.

For More Information

Lua links are provided on the Help menu of the Plugin Editor.
See also: Lua
Reference Manual 5.3.

title: Lua: Reading and Writing Files
text:
Lua

Reading and Writing Files

Reading A Single Line From a File:

Suppose that you have a file that has
multiple lines of text, and you want to read a line of text from
that file, and display it. We can use the io.open() command to
open the file. This command has the syntax of io.open(filename,
mode). The mode we will use for this will be r, for read mode.
For reference here is a list of all modes available.

r - read mode

w - write mode (overwrites existing)

a - append mode (appends to existing)

b - binary mode

r+ - update mode (existing data preserved)

w+ - update mode (existing data erased)

a+ - append update mode (existing data preserved, append
at end of file only)

The first thing we will do is to open the file and store opened
file (so to speak) in a variable.
file = io.open("testRead.txt", "r")
Now that the file testRead.txt has been opened, it is ready to be
read. We will use the read() command to read a single line from
the file into another variable.
ourline = file:read()
This reads the first line of our text file. The next time we use
the read() command it will read the second line. The next time,
it would read the third line - and so on. Notice that we use the
name of our file variable along with this command, separated by
a colon. There are also some arguments you can use with
file:read(). You can put any of the following arguments inside
the parentheses with quotation marks.

*n - reads a number and returns it. e.g.
file:read("*n")

*a - reads the entire file from the current position.
e.g. file:read("*a")

*l - (default) - reads the next line. It returns
nil on End-of-File (EOF). e.g. file:read("*l")

number - returns a string with up to that many characters
in it, or nil on EOF. e.g. file:read(5)

Now that we've read our line, we need to close the file we
opened, which we do like this:
file:close()

Reading All Lines:

To read all the lines in a file you could
use the same technique with a for statement.
Look at the code below.
file = io.open("testRead.txt","r")
for line in file:lines() do
print(line)
end
file:close()

This code simply outputs the content of the file a line at a
time, to the Output Pane (remember though that the Output Pane
is only visible if you run a plugin the Plugin Editor).

Writing To Files (Overwrite):

Writing to files is done in much the same
way.
The first method shown here will overwrite anything previously
written in that file:
file = io.open("testRead.txt","w")
file:write("hello")
file:close()

This time notice we used the w mode
instead of r since we're writing, and not
reading. We use file:write() with the text we want written to
the file in parentheses and quotes. You could also use a
variable instead. If you use a variable do not use quotation
marks. Here's an example.

file = io.open("testRead.txt","w")
myText = "Hello"
file:write(myText)
file:close()

Writing To Files (Append):

You can use append mode so that when you write text to a file
it gets added after all the text that is already in that file,
instead of replacing it all. This is done in exactly the same
way as the above, except that we use a mode, for append.

file = io.open("testRead.txt","a")
myText = "\nHello"
file:write(myText)
file:close()

You may have noticed that this time, in the myText variable,
we added \n inside the text string.
This command is a line break, and will cause the text to go to
the next line when written to our file. Some text file viewers
may not display the line break correctly (it may be display on
the same line as the surrounding text, as a little square),
but technically it is a new line. The same method is used in
C/C++.

title: FH_GetAgeRangeText (entry-point)
text:
Language Plugins

FH_GetAgeRangeText (entry-point)

Description

This entry-point is called to render age range information into text,
in a specified format, in the output language.

Syntax

strRenderedAgeRangeText = FH_GetAgeRangeText(strFormat,
iYear1, iYear2, bMale, strName)

Parameters

strFormat
String. The date format required. Possible values are
"SENTENCE", "ADVERB" or "ADJECTIVE" - see table below:

SENTENCE
Use the name supplied, if there is one, to create a
sentence in the output language, giving the age range for
the person. If no name is supplied, use an appropriate
pronoun instead. e.g. "John was 45-49 years old" or
"he was 45-49 years old".

ADVERB

Create an adverbial phrase like
"aged 45-49"

ADJECTIVE

Create an adjectival phrase like "age 45-49"

iYear1
Integer. The starting year for the range.

iYear2
Integer. The ending year for the range.

bMale
Boolean. True if the person is male.

strName
String. May be an empty string. If supplied it is the
person's name. Only used when constructing sentences.

Returns

strRenderedAgeText
String. The rendered age text. Return nil if unable to render a
particular age value.

Example

function FH_GetAgeRangeText(sFormat, iYear1, iYear2, bMale, sName)
local sText;
if sFormat == "SENTENCE" then
sText = GetSentenceStart(bMale, sName, true);
sText = sText .. iYear1 .. "-" .. iYear2 .. " ans";
elseif sFormat == "ADVERB" then
if bMale then
sText = "âgé de ";
else
sText = "âgée de ";
end
sText = sText .. iYear1 .. "-" .. iYear2 .. " ans";
elseif sFormat == "ADJECTIVE" then
sText = iYear1 .. "-" .. iYear2 .. " ans";
end
return sText;
end

title: FH_GetAgeText (entry-point)
text:
Language Plugins

FH_GetAgeText (entry-point)

Description

This entry-point is called to render age information into text, in a
specified format, in the output language.

Syntax

strRenderedAgeText = FH_GetAgeText(strFormat,
age, bMale, strName)

Parameters

strFormat
String. The date format required. Possible values are
"SENTENCE", "ADVERB" or "ADJECTIVE" - see table below:

SENTENCE
Use the name supplied, if there is one, to create a
sentence in the output language, giving the person's
age. If no name is supplied, use an appropriate
pronoun instead. e.g "John was 45 years old" or "he
was 45 years old", or"he was a child" or "she was an
infant".

ADVERB

Create an adverbial phrase like
"aged 7" or "as a child" or "stillborn".

ADJECTIVE

Create an adjectival phrase like "age 7" or "as a child"
or "stillborn".

age
A Family Historian Age
object.

bMale
Boolean. True if the person is male.

strName
String. May be an empty string. If supplied it is the
person's name. Only used when constructing sentences.

Returns

strRenderedAgeText
String. The rendered age text. Return nil if unable to render a
particular age value.

Example

function FH_GetAgeText(sFormat, age, bMale, sName)
local sAgeType = age:GetType();
if sAgeType == "=" or sAgeType == "<" or sAgeType == ">" then
return GetAgeText(sFormat, sAgeType, age:GetYears(), age:GetMonths(), age:GetDays(), bMale, sName);
else
return GetAgeTypeText(sFormat, sAgeType, bMale, sName);
end
end

title: FH_GetAttributeValueText (entry-point)
text:
Language Plugins

FH_GetAttributeValueText (entry-point)

Description

This entry-point is called primarily to translate attribute values -
such as the values entered in the Fact tab of the Property Box, for a
person's Occupation, Religion or Education
(all attributes, in Family Historian terms) It is also used to
translate other similar data values stored in the project, such as Cause
of Death (entered in the Cause field, for a Death
event). The default implementation of the plugin does a lookup
in a table called g_trans_attr, which is stored in a separate file
("lang_trans_attr.fh_lua") in the language pack folder. The user
can add and edit items in this table using tools in the Language Pack
window, without needing to access the plugin and without needing to
understand Lua. By default, Family Historian will mark report
text with a distinctive colour, if this function returns nil (i.e.
fails to find a translation for the text). This way, the user
can easily correct the problem if there are missing entries in the
'Attribute Value' lookup table.

Syntax

strTranslation = FH_GetAttributeValueText(strText,
tContext)

Parameters

strText
String. Text to translate.

tContext
Table or nil if not supplied (so test that it is not nil before
using it). If supplied, holds some or all of the following
contextual information:

bFemale
boolean. True if the context
is female. For example, in some languages you will need a
different word for various occupations, if the person who had
that occupation was female.

bArticle
boolean. True if in English an
indefinite article ('a' or 'an') would be expected before the
noun. May or may not be relevant to your language.

If the relevant value is not applicable, the value will not have
been set - i.e. will be nil. See the example below for an
illustration of how to test these values.

Returns

strTranslation
String. The translated text. Return nil if none.

Example

function FH_GetAttributeValueText(sText, tContext)
local sTrans;
if tContext and tContext["bFemale"] then
sTrans = g_trans_attr['~FEMALE:' .. sAttributeValueText];
end
if sTrans == nil then
sTrans = g_trans_attr[sAttributeValueText];
end
return sTrans; -- may be nil
end

title: FH_GetDateText (entry-point)
text:
Language Plugins

FH_GetDateText (entry-point)

Description
